What makes an Atlantic City home sale different?

Selling here means dealing with a barrier-island city of about 11 square miles of land where casino tourism, flood maps and a renter-heavy housing stock all affect the price a buyer offers and the pace of closing. Your three realistic paths are a traditional listing, a sale handled by yourself, or an as-is cash purchase.

Whichever you pick, the same local paperwork applies: a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate, any city occupancy or landlord filings tied to the property, and a deed recorded with Atlantic County. The sections below walk through each piece and point to the city or county office that handles it.

How big is Atlantic City and what do local housing numbers look like?

Atlantic City had an estimated 38,787 residents in mid-2025, up slightly from the 38,497 people counted in April 2020, and it covers 10.76 square miles of land. Owners live in only 30.3% of the city's homes, which means rentals make up most of the housing stock.

Atlantic City housing and population figures; 2020-2024 estimates unless a date is shown
MeasureAtlantic City
Population estimate, July 202538,787
Owner-resident share of housing30.3%
Middle price tier for houses their owners live in$207,400
Mortgage-holder housing cost per month$1,830
Typical gross monthly rent$1,136
Households16,567
Median household income$41,028

Those figures describe the whole city, from Ducktown to the Marina District, so a house near the Boardwalk and one in an inland block can sit far apart on price. Ask for recent sold prices on your own street instead of relying on a citywide median.

How does the casino economy shape home sales on Absecon Island?

Casinos set the rhythm of the local economy, and that carries into housing demand. New Jersey voters approved casino gambling in Atlantic City in 1976, and the first casino opened in 1978. The census shows accommodation and food service sales of about $3.79 billion for 2022, the largest line in the city's business totals.

Gross gaming revenue for the nine operating casinos reached $2.79 billion in 2022, as reported on Wikipedia. Four casinos closed in 2014, and Wikipedia also notes that the Atlantic City area had the highest foreclosure rate in the nation in 2019. Expect buyers to ask detailed questions about condition, flood status and rent rolls.

  • Tourism district areas named in state planning include the Marina District, Ducktown, Chelsea, South Inlet, Bader Field and Gardner's Basin.
  • The Boardwalk runs about 4 miles inside city limits, with casino hotels along it.
  • AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center, founded in 1898, runs its Atlantic City campus in town.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Atlantic City house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Do flood maps change how an Atlantic City house sells?

Yes, because the whole city sits on a barrier island and buyers and lenders look at flood zone status early. Superstorm Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, caused flooding and power outages, and destroyed the northern boardwalk section fronting Absecon Inlet in the South Inlet neighborhood.

The city's website carries a Property Flood Information page, a Flood Insurance Rate Map, links to the FEMA flood map viewer and a floodplain development form. Before you list, look up your lot's flood zone and pull any elevation certificate you have, since a buyer's insurance quote can change their offer.

What inspections and certificates does Atlantic City require?

Atlantic City's Licensing and Inspection division runs occupancy inspections, and its Fire Prevention forms include a Smoke Detector Application and a Smoke Certificate Affidavit. Call the division before you list so you know which certificate your sale needs.

The city publishes a checklist for the certificate of occupancy on a residential rental unit. Inspectors look at both outside and inside conditions, and the list is a useful pre-sale walkthrough even for an owner-occupied house.

  • Outside: trip hazards in curbs and sidewalks, house number, siding, gutters, windows, railings, roof, fence, steps, foundation and high grass.
  • Inside: working deadbolt, smoke detectors on each level within 10 feet of sleeping areas, a 2A10BC fire extinguisher, carbon monoxide detection, GFCI outlets in bathrooms, two outlets per bedroom, working appliances and no leaks.
  • Seasonal items: window screens from May 1 to October 1 and heat at 68 degrees from October 1 to May 1.
  • Utilities must be on and the unit clean at the time of inspection.

What if the house is a rental or short-term rental?

You will need to deal with the city's landlord and rental rules, because Atlantic City has a Landlord Registration form, a Short Term Rental Public Form and a short-term rental complaint hotline. If tenants live in the house, confirm your registration is current ahead of any contract.

The city also lists a Lead Certification form under Licensing and Inspection, with a list of certified lead evaluation contractors. Landlords should ask the department whether a lead certificate is on file for your unit. Give any buyer copies of the leases so they know what they are taking over.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Atlantic City houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How are the deed and sale fees handled at closing?

Atlantic County Clerk's Office staff review and record every Atlantic City deed, and the main office is at 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, with a satellite office at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City. The clerk's recording page says checks for recording and realty transfer fees go to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, while Gross Income Tax checks go to the State of NJ Division of Taxation.

New Jersey puts the realty transfer fee on the seller. For a sale of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. With homes in the city valued around $207,400, many local deals fall into that lower schedule.

Sellers who live outside New Jersey file a GIT/REP form, and the state sets a minimum prepayment of 2% of the consideration shown in the deed. Your closing agent usually handles those filings.

Which sale route fits an Atlantic City house best?

Your best route turns on the house's condition, your timeline and how much prep you want to take on. Listing with an agent can reach more buyers but usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal and inspection timeline.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can skip the repair list, though the city certificate, deed recording and fee steps above still apply. If foreclosure, back taxes or a tenant problem is driving the sale, compare the written terms of every option, including who pays the transfer fee and whether any certificate work falls on you. The city's website also lists a First Time Homebuyer Program, which can matter if your likely buyer is a local household.

Frequently asked questions

Does Atlantic City require an inspection before I sell?

Ask Licensing and Inspection before listing, since the city issues occupancy permits and runs the smoke certificate process through Fire Prevention. Its published checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, outlets, heat and exterior condition, so fixing those items in advance avoids delays.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on an Atlantic City sale?

The seller pays it. The state sets the rate per $500 of consideration, and the clerk takes payment at the counter once the deed is filed.

Where do I record the deed for an Atlantic City house?

Deeds go to the Atlantic County Clerk, whose main recording office is on Main Street in Mays Landing. A satellite office operates on Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

Can I sell an Atlantic City house that has tenants or short-term guests?

Yes. Keep landlord registration and any short-term rental paperwork current, and hand the buyer the lease terms. The city has registration forms and a complaint hotline, so open violations are worth clearing first.

Does flood risk change how an Atlantic City house sells?

It can, because the city sits on a barrier island and buyers check flood zones and insurance costs. The city website links to its flood map, FEMA tools and a property flood information page you can review before you list.

What should I know before selling a house in Bayonne?

Bayonne is a dense Hudson County city, with 74,744 residents on a peninsula that has 5.82 square miles of land. A sale there involves a resale certificate through the city, a deed recorded by the Hudson County Register, and for many sellers a look at short-term rental and rent control rules.

This page covers the local numbers, the city steps and the county and state filings, so you can decide whether to list, sell on your own or accept an as-is cash purchase.

What does Bayonne look like on paper?

Bayonne sits on Bergen Neck, a peninsula bounded by Newark Bay, the Kill Van Kull and Upper New York Bay, and it borders Jersey City to the north. The 2020 census counted 71,686 people, up 13.7% from 63,024 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 74,744 for mid-2025.

Bayonne housing and household figures, Census Bureau QuickFacts (2020-2024 survey period unless noted)
MeasureBayonne
People per square mile, 202012,315.1
Homes occupied by their owners36.2%
Median home value, owner-occupied$460,100

With about 36% of homes owner-occupied, two- and three-family houses and condos are a large part of the market, and landlords are common sellers. The median home value of $460,100 also sets the price range most buyers will compare against.

How does Bayonne's history and economy affect sellers?

Bayonne was set off as a township in 1861 and reincorporated as a city in 1869, uniting Bergen Point, Constable Hook, Centreville, Pamrapo and Saltersville. Manufacturing, distribution and maritime work still anchor the economy, and part of the Port of New York and New Jersey lies in the city at Port Jersey.

The Cape Liberty Cruise Port sits at the end of the peninsula on the former Military Ocean Terminal, where The Peninsula at Bayonne Harbor now has housing and businesses. Bayonne Medical Center anchors the Broadway shopping district and is the city's largest employer, with more than 1,200 employees. Census retail sales for 2022 reached about $849 million, and transportation and warehousing receipts topped $520 million.

Which roads, rail and schools shape Bayonne home values?

Commuters rely on the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail, which has four Bayonne stops at 45th Street, 34th Street, 22nd Street and 8th Street, and on the Newark Bay Extension of the New Jersey Turnpike (Interstate 78). The Bayonne Bridge, which opened in 1931 and was raised between 2013 and 2019, links the city to Staten Island.

The Bayonne School District serves pre-kindergarten through twelfth grade with 13 schools and 10,059 students in 2020-21. Parks matter to buyers too, including the Hackensack RiverWalk at Collins Park and the Stephen R. Gregg Hudson County Park.

  • The light rail connects Bayonne with Jersey City and its neighbors, and with PATH stations and ferry terminals.
  • The Route 440 retail corridor includes Bayonne Crossing.
  • Average travel time to work is 33.7 minutes, so listings near transit tend to note it.

What resale certificate does Bayonne require?

Bayonne requires a resale certificate whenever a building is sold, and a May 2026 city notice moved that process to the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall. Applicants pick up the application from the Fire Prevention office, complete the inspection, and the Fire Department issues the certificate for the sale.

This replaced an earlier arrangement. On October 1, 2025, the Building Department stopped issuing Continuing Certificates of Occupancy and began issuing Resale Certificates for one-family, two-family and multi-family dwellings and commercial buildings. The city said at the time that only the name changed and that the application was shorter. Because the office handling it moved again in 2026, call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you schedule closing. The September 2025 notice listed Building Department lines at 201-858-6334 and 201-858-6073 for certificate questions, which may also help with permit history on the property.

Can I sell a Bayonne house that has been a short-term rental?

Yes, but the city's short-term rental ordinance sets rules that a buyer will want proof of. Under Chapter 33, a short-term rental is occupancy of 60 consecutive days or fewer, and only a property owner can hold the license.

  • Applications go through the city's Spatial Data Logic online portal.
  • Fire safety, building and zoning inspections come first, and the city says a license follows within 30 calendar days of satisfactory inspections.
  • Applicants show no outstanding taxes or water and sewer charges, prior code violations abated and open construction permits closed.
  • A zoning determination letter costs $50 and is requested from the zoning officer at City Hall.
  • A tenant cannot hold the license.

The city website also lists a Rent Control board and a Small Landlord Emergency Grant Program page. If your building has tenants, ask the Planning, Zoning and Development office whether rent control covers it.

Who handles the deed and the state filings in Bayonne?

Bayonne is in Hudson County, so the deed is recorded by the Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which lists a phone number of 201-395-4760 on the county directory. Sellers pay the state realty transfer fee. For sales over $350,000, the schedule starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 and rises to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000.

If you own a Bayonne house but live outside New Jersey, the state requires a GIT/REP form with the deed. Nonresident sellers prepay the larger of 10.75% of their gain or 2% of the deed consideration, so a landlord with a rental in Bayonne should ask the closing agent to calculate the payment before the day of settlement.

Bayonne sale paperwork and where it comes from
ItemOffice
Resale certificateBayonne Fire Prevention Bureau, City Hall
Short-term rental licensePlanning, Zoning and Development, through the SDL portal
Deed recordingHudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages
Nonresident seller tax prepaymentGIT/REP form with the deed, State Division of Taxation

Should I list, sell myself, or take a cash offer in Bayonne?

Compare the three on time, cost and risk, using written numbers from each buyer or agent. A cash purchase as-is can avoid repair work and showings, while a listing may reach more buyers on a $460,100 median market.

Whichever way you go, schedule the resale inspection early, since the certificate gates the closing. Mortgage payoff, tax bills and any water and sewer balance come off the proceeds at settlement, and the city lists online payment pages for taxes and water and sewer so you can pull current balances. The same site links an Emergency Rescue Mortgage Assistance page, which is worth reading if missed payments are pushing you to sell.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Bayonne resale certificate?

It is the certificate the city requires whenever a building is sold. As of the city's May 2026 notice, the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall issues it after an inspection.

Did Bayonne get rid of the continuing certificate of occupancy?

Yes. The Building Department replaced the CCO with a Resale Certificate on October 1, 2025, and the city described the change as a rename with a shorter application.

Where is a Bayonne deed recorded?

The Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records it. The county directory lists that office at 201-395-4760.

Can I sell a Bayonne property that I rent short term?

Yes. The city's Chapter 33 ordinance limits short-term rentals to 60 days or fewer and requires an owner license with inspections, so confirm your license status before you sign a contract.

Do out-of-state owners owe tax when selling in Bayonne?

They owe a prepayment with the GIT/REP form. The minimum is 2% of the consideration shown on the deed, and the state formula can produce a higher amount based on the gain.

Sell Your Bergenfield House for Cash

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Bergenfield?
We buy Bergenfield houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How can a Bergenfield owner get a house sold quickly?

An owner has three paths: engage an agent, run the sale personally, or accept a purchase offer from a buyer who pays cash. All three finish at the same municipal checkpoints covering permits, alarms and taxes.

The choice follows the shape the house is in and the date you must close. A listing reaches the biggest audience, yet it means open houses, repair demands after the inspection and a bank's calendar. A cash buyer offers less money in return for dropping most of that, which helps when relatives left you the house, tenants are staying in a two-family, repairs have piled up, or a moving date is fixed.

  • Agent: widest audience, a fee paid from proceeds, and a schedule driven by the buyer's bank.
  • On your own: no fee to an agent, but pricing, showings and borough inspections are yours to manage.
  • Cash buyer: the house is taken as it stands, and a fast closing is possible.

What does the housing stock in Bergenfield look like?

Bergenfield is a dense inner suburb. In 2020 the Census Bureau measured 9,752.4 residents on each of the borough's 2.90 land square miles, and its July 2025 estimate is 28,754 people. Owners live in 70.6 percent of the housing units, and the Census Bureau's five-year survey puts the median owner-occupied house at $491,500.

Households are large, at 3.04 people on average. Median household income is $130,045 and median gross rent is $1,752. Foreign-born residents account for 39.1 percent of the population. Roughly a third identify as Hispanic or Latino, and 18.4 percent listed Filipino ancestry in 2016, which is why Bergen County's "Little Manila" label stuck to the borough.

The borough was formed by referendum on June 25, 1894, from parts of Englewood Township and Palisades Township. Railroad officials in 1873 printed "Bergen Fields" on tickets when residents could not agree on a station name, and the borough shortened it. Population then climbed from 8,816 in 1930 to 17,647 in 1950, so many of the houses you will sell are decades old. Buyers and inspectors tend to ask about finished basements, additions and garage conversions in that kind of stock.

What must be in order before a Bergenfield closing?

Start with the borough's own advice to sellers: ask your attorney to order a municipal tax search from the Tax Collector, then confirm with the Construction Office that every permit has its final inspection. Both offices work out of the municipal building at 198 North Washington Avenue.

Open permits cause most of the trouble. When no certificate of occupancy is on file, or an added or omitted assessment is pending, the borough says the buyer's and seller's attorneys should settle the fines or assessments in the closing documents. Closing old permits before you list costs less than haggling over them at the table.

A state-mandated certificate confirms that the home's carbon monoxide and smoke alarms and its portable extinguisher meet code. Owners of one- and two-unit houses can get it only from the municipality, and it lapses after six months. In Bergenfield the Fire Prevention Bureau enforces the State Uniform Fire Code from the same municipal building.

ItemDetail
Municipal tax search$10, processed in 2 to 4 days; flags unpaid taxes, open permits and pending added or omitted assessments
Permit and occupancy reviewConstruction Office, second floor, Room 223, to close permits before the sale

What costs come out of a Bergenfield seller's proceeds?

The state's realty transfer fee is the one charge fixed by law. It lands on the seller, and the county recording officer collects it when the deed is lodged. In the Division of Taxation's own example, a $325,000 deed without an exemption owes $1,910.

A few transfers escape it. Parent to child is exempt, and so is an executor handing a house to an heir named in the will. A stepchild is not covered unless legally adopted. A separate 1 percent buyer fee applies when the price passes $1,000,000, which touches only the largest Bergenfield deals.

  • The transfer fee, figured from the price stated in the deed.
  • An agent's commission, negotiated case by case and not set by statute.
  • Payoff of the mortgage, an equity line or any lien.
  • Your portion of the current quarter's tax, prorated to the closing day.
  • Money to clear open permits or settle related fines.
  • A New Jersey attorney to handle contract and closing.

Can an assessment change complicate a Bergenfield closing?

The Tax Department values every property under state guidelines and checks building permits to update those values. Improvements such as additions, finished basements, garage conversions, in-ground pools, fireplaces, decks and kitchen or bathroom remodels can trigger an added assessment. Paint, fences, replacement windows, skylights, air conditioning and above-ground pools do not.

An added assessment bill goes out in October and is payable on November 1, then February 1 and May 1, before merging into the regular bill the next June. Appeals of a regular assessment are due by April 1, with applications available from the Bergen County Board of Taxation after February 1. Appeals of an added assessment are due by December 1. A late bill can follow the house to the buyer, which is why the tax search should be ordered early.

What do bus routes and schools mean for Bergenfield buyers?

Washington Avenue, which is County Route 39, is the borough's spine, joined by Main Street, Prospect Avenue, River Edge Road and New Bridge Road. Bergenfield has about 60.5 miles of roadway, and the municipality maintains roughly 54.75 miles of it. NJ Transit routes 166 and 167 go to Midtown's Port Authority Bus Terminal, and route 186 goes to the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. Passenger rail on the West Shore line ended in 1959, so commuters rely on those buses.

Bergenfield Public Schools operate seven buildings: five elementary schools, Roy W. Brown Middle School and Bergenfield High School. The district counted 3,710 students for 2023 to 2024. Students may also apply to Bergen County Technical Schools programs. A special improvement district runs a mile along Washington Avenue, and the borough counts more than 50 restaurants and food stores within a mile of it.

Does a cash buyer suit a Bergenfield homeowner?

It does when speed or condition matters more than a slightly higher price. Think of a house with permits nobody wants to chase, an estate whose heirs live in other states, a two-family with tenants, or an owner leaving town on a deadline.

The borough steps remain, though. Someone has to order the tax search, review permits and get the alarm certificate, so settle in writing who does it and whether the cost is deducted from what you receive. Put any cash figure next to what a listing would clear once commission, repairs and holding costs are paid, and let a New Jersey attorney read the agreement first.

Frequently asked questions

Which alarm certificate does Bergenfield require?

Yes, an alarm certificate. State rules require proof of compliant smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a one or two family house is sold, and the municipality issues it for six months. Contact the Bergenfield Fire Prevention Bureau at the municipal building and time the application near closing.

Which side owes the state transfer fee in Bergenfield?

The seller. The county recording officer takes it at recording, and the Division of Taxation shows $1,910 on a $325,000 deed without exemptions. A buyer owes a further 1 percent only above $1,000,000.

What is the Bergenfield assessment appeal deadline?

By April 1 for a regular assessment. The Bergen County Board of Taxation supplies the form after February 1, following your assessment notice. Added assessments follow a separate December 1 deadline.

What does a Bergenfield municipal tax search cover?

Unpaid taxes, open building and plumbing permits and pending added or omitted assessments. The Tax Collector's Office charges $10 and needs 2 to 4 days, and your attorney normally orders it for the closing.

Can I sell in Bergenfield with permits still open?

Yes, but fix them first if you can. The borough tells owners to have the Construction Office confirm permits and final inspections before closing. A missing certificate of occupancy is dealt with in the closing documents, and any fines or assessments can reduce your proceeds.

Bridgeton is a renter-heavy city with modest values. The 2020-2024 survey period shows owner-occupied homes at a median $145,500, rent at $1,340, and only 36.4% of the 7,481 households owning. Median household income is $55,781, and the average household has 3.21 people, larger than in most New Jersey cities. Those numbers explain why many sellers here are landlords or heirs rather than long-term single-family owners.

The city sits on the tidal Cohansey River near the center of the Delaware Bay lowlands and is the Cumberland County seat. It divides into three sections: Northside, Southside and Hillside. Philadelphia is about an hour away, Wilmington about 50 minutes, and Atlantic City and Cape May roughly an hour. That mix of a low entry price and a reachable job market draws investors, which is one reason cash offers are common.

  • Victorian and Federal-era houses near the downtown core often need roof, porch and plumbing work.
  • Many blocks of "doubles" were built as working-class housing and are now often rentals.
  • Occupied rentals can be sold with tenants in place, but the buyer will ask for the rental registration and inspection record.

Does Bridgeton's historic district affect a sale?

For a large share of the city it can. The Bridgeton Historic District covers about a quarter of Bridgeton and includes more than 2,000 properties ranging from early Federal buildings to 1920s construction. Listed on the federal register of historic sites in 1982, it is described as the biggest district of its kind inside any New Jersey municipality.

If your house is inside the district, ask the city's Historic District Administrative Officer, who works alongside Code Enforcement, what review applies to exterior work before you replace windows, siding or porches ahead of a sale. Buyers who plan renovations will ask the same question. Notable landmarks nearby include Potter's Tavern (built about 1750), the 1795 Old Broad Street Presbyterian Church, and the 1816 Cumberland National Bank building that is now part of the library.

What work and schools shape buyer interest in Bridgeton?

Bridgeton's economy has moved from glass, textiles and iron to agriculture, food processing, health care and public employers. Ardagh Group runs one of the state's larger glass plants in the city, South Woods State Prison (opened 1997) is the largest state prison and a large employer, and the Rutgers Food Innovation Center helps startup food makers. The city lost its remaining glass and textile factory jobs in the 1980s, and farm work continues to draw workers from Mexico and Guatemala; Census data show 54.8% of residents speak a language other than English at home.

Bridgeton Public Schools runs eight schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and had 6,313 students in 2020-21. Schools include Broad Street, Buckshutem Road, Cherry Street, Indian Avenue, Quarter Mile Lane and West Avenue, plus Bridgeton High School. The district is one of the former Abbott districts the state now funds for school construction. Students can also apply to the Cumberland County Technical Education Center in Millville. For getting around, Routes 49 and 77 and County Route 552 are the main roads, and NJ Transit's 410 bus runs between Bridgeton and Philadelphia.

What does Bridgeton require when a house is sold or rented out?

Bridgeton's Code Enforcement Office enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code and also handles home sales. Its page states that on the sale of any property in the city, a resale Certificate of Property Compliance (CPC) form must be filled out and filed with the office. Ask the office about inspection timing early, because a failed inspection means a notice, repairs and a re-inspection before a certificate issues. The Housing and Code department is at 181 E. Commerce Street.

Landlords carry extra steps. Every rental unit must be registered each year by March 1, whether vacant or occupied, and must pass inspection before tenants move in or whenever occupancy changes. The city also adopted a rent leveling ordinance, Ordinance 25-28, which matters to anyone buying or selling an occupied building. Tree removal above set trunk sizes needs an application too.

How do Bridgeton property taxes work for a seller?

Bridgeton's tax load is heavy relative to its home values, which is a common reason owners want out. The assessor's page shows a 2023 total of $5.075 for each $100 of assessed value, built from county ($1.222), county health ($0.068), open space ($0.013), school district ($0.751), municipal ($2.979) and library ($0.042) pieces. Ask the tax collector for the current rate before you quote a monthly carrying cost to a buyer.

The tax collector bills property tax in four installments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The same office collects water, sewer and the solid waste charge, listed at $150 for residents and $90 for seniors. Unpaid balances can attach to the sale, so ask for a payoff or statement before closing.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation, 2475 S. Delsea Drive, Vineland, (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days after notices are mailed, whichever is later, or May 1 after a municipal-wide revaluation.
  • Assessments above $1,000,000 may be filed directly with the State Tax Court.
  • Senior, disabled and veteran deductions are $250 each and require an application to the assessor.

What costs and exemptions does New Jersey apply to an inherited or family sale?

Many Bridgeton sales involve an estate or a relative, and New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee has exemptions that fit those cases. According to the Division of Taxation, the fee does not apply to a deed between a parent and child, between spouses, from an executor or administrator to an heir under a will or intestacy, or recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. A seller claiming an exemption files Form RTF-1 with the deed.

An ordinary sale is different: the seller owes the fee at recording, calculated per $500 of consideration. On a sale of $150,000 or less, the schedule for deals not over $350,000 is $2.00 per $500, so the fee on a typical Bridgeton price is modest compared with the repair cost of an older house. The Division of Taxation publishes the full schedule.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Bridgeton?

The city requires a resale Certificate of Property Compliance form to be filed with Code Enforcement on the sale of any property. Call the Housing and Code department at 856-455-3230 to schedule and ask what the inspector checks.

Can I sell a Bridgeton house with tenants in it?

Yes. Keep the unit registered (due each March 1) and have the current Certificate of Property Compliance and rent records ready, because the buyer takes the property subject to the city's rent leveling ordinance.

How much is the annual rental registration in Bridgeton?

It costs $45 per unit if filed by March 1 and $75 per unit after that date. The registration renewal also covers the rental certificate fees.

Where do I appeal my Bridgeton tax assessment?

Appeal to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation in Vineland at (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days from the mailing of notices, whichever is later. Properties assessed over $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

Is the realty transfer fee owed if I inherited the house and sell it?

The fee applies to the sale deed. A deed from an executor to an heir is exempt, but the later sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance, so plan for the seller's fee at recording.

A listing can work for houses in good shape in neighborhoods with active demand, but the city's resale rules add steps whichever way you go. Selling yourself without an agent is allowed, with the same paperwork.

Camden is the Camden County seat on the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia. The Census Bureau estimates 71,430 residents on July 1, 2025, a 0.5% dip from the 2020 base, down from 77,344 at the 2010 Census. It covers 8.92 square miles of land and 1.42 square miles of water, with a 2020 density of about 8,047 people per square mile.

What are Camden homes worth, and who owns them?

Camden values sit far below the rest of the Philadelphia area. Census figures for 2020 to 2024 give a median owner-occupied value of $112,000, median gross rent of $1,226, and just 34.4% of the city's 24,443 households as owners. Median household income is $40,546 and 30.2% of residents are in poverty, so many sellers are carrying a house they cannot afford to repair, or an heir inheriting one.

The most common housing type is the rowhouse, much like Philadelphia's. Yorkship Village, now called Fairview, was the nation's first federally funded planned community for working-class residents. The city recognizes more than 20 neighborhoods, including Cooper Grant, Cramer Hill, East Camden, Parkside, Waterfront South, Rosedale, Pyne Point and Gateway.

  • Rowhouses share walls and roofs, so a buyer's inspection will look closely at party walls and roof drainage.
  • Vacant or fire-damaged houses can still sell, but the buyer may sign an agreement not to occupy until permits are closed.
  • Homes near the waterfront, the Rutgers campus and the hospital district are close to the city's largest employers.

What drives Camden's economy and buyer demand?

About 45% of local employment is in education and medicine, often called "eds and meds." Major employers include Cooper University Hospital, Rutgers University-Camden, Our Lady of Lourdes Medical Center, Campbell's, the Delaware River Port Authority, L3Harris, the State of New Jersey and Subaru of America, which moved its headquarters here from Pennsauken in 2018. The Port of Camden handles wood products, cocoa and other cargo, and the Philadelphia 76ers training complex sits on the waterfront near the Adventure Aquarium, the Battleship New Jersey and the Freedom Mortgage Pavilion.

In October 2025, the state's Economic Development Authority invited proposals for 16 acres on the North Camden waterfront at the former prison site. Projects like that move buyer attention to nearby streets, but they do not change what your own house is worth, so get a fresh comparison before you decide.

How do schools and transit shape Camden home sales?

Camden City School District runs 19 schools and had 7,553 students in 2020-21, with Camden High, Eastside High, Brimm Medical Arts High, Creative Arts Academy and others serving high school grades. It is one of the former Abbott districts for which the state pays school construction costs. Charter and renaissance schools operate alongside the district, which buyers with children will ask about.

Transit is a real selling point. The PATCO Speedline runs 24 hours to Philadelphia and to Collingswood, Haddonfield, Cherry Hill and Lindenwold, and NJ Transit's River Line light rail runs from Camden to Trenton with four stops in the city. The Walter Rand Transportation Center at Martin Luther King Boulevard and Broadway joins PATCO, River Line and NJ Transit buses. By road, Interstate 676 and U.S. 30 lead to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge, Interstate 76 crosses briefly, and Route 168 touches the south. Mean travel time to work is 23.8 minutes.

What certificate does Camden require before a house is sold?

Camden requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (the city's building bureau also calls it a Camden Resale Occupancy Certificate) to be applied for and issued before any property in the city is sold or conveyed. The seller is responsible for applying, though the buyer may apply with the seller's written permission. The certificate is issued to the buyer, not the seller. If a buyer closes without one, the buyer stays liable for penalties of up to $2,000 until it issues.

The process starts with a zoning permit at City Hall, then an application to the Construction and Building Bureau, followed by four inspections: building, plumbing, electric and fire. All open building permits must be closed first. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and commit to pulling permits and doing the work. Plan submissions are digital only. A change of tenant in a rental is a different step and goes through the Housing Department.

What rules apply to Camden rental properties?

Camden's Bureau of Housing enforces the city's property maintenance code. Rental properties must be inspected at a change of ownership or occupancy and hold a Rental Approval Certificate before anyone moves in, and buildings with three or more units need a license. To schedule an inspection, all taxes must be current, utilities must be on, the fee is paid when scheduling, and the property must be registered with both the Rent Control office and the Municipal Clerk.

The city has had a rent control ordinance since March 12, 1981. At lease expiration a landlord may raise rent by no more than the lower of the 12-month average consumer price index for the Philadelphia area or 6% of the latest rent, and rent cannot rise during a lease. A buyer of a rental building takes on those limits, so a landlord selling should have the registration file ready.

How do taxes and state fees work when selling in Camden?

Camden's Office of Assessments maintains the tax map, processes senior and veteran deductions and exemptions, receives abatement requests, and handles assessment appeals filed with the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The office is in City Hall, Room 329, at 520 Market Street. Check that taxes are current before listing, since the city requires current taxes to schedule a rental inspection and a lien can hold up a closing.

New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller. At Camden-level prices below $350,000, the schedule is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that. Senior citizens, blind or disabled sellers and certain low and moderate income housing sales qualify for lower rates, starting at $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000. The Division of Taxation lists the rates and exemptions.

Frequently asked questions

Who applies for the Certificate of Continued Occupancy in Camden?

The seller. The buyer may file as the seller's agent with written permission, but the certificate is issued to the buyer. The application costs $200 plus a separate $64 fire safety fee.

How long is a Camden occupancy certificate application good for?

Six months. After that a new application must be filed and paid for, unless there are open permits on the property.

Can I sell a vacant or damaged house in Camden?

Yes. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and then obtain permits, do the work and apply for the certificate. Open permits have to be closed before a certificate issues.

Is there rent control in Camden?

Yes. Camden has had a rent control ordinance since 1981, with a cap at the lower of the Philadelphia-area consumer price index or 6% at lease expiration, and landlords register each rental unit annually for $25.

Where do I appeal a Camden property assessment?

Appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The city's Office of Assessments, at 520 Market Street, Room 329, can explain the process and handles deductions.

How should a Carteret owner start planning a sale?

Begin with the borough's occupancy inspection and a current tax bill, because a Carteret sale can go through an agent, a for-sale-by-owner listing or an investor and all three paths pass the same two checkpoints. After those, the deed gets filed in New Brunswick at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry.

About 55 percent of Carteret homes are lived in by their owners, which leaves a large share of the housing stock as rentals. Sellers therefore include landlords, heirs and people with older houses and repairs put off. For those owners the paperwork below weighs as much as the listing photos, and it is worth reading before you set a closing date.

Where is Carteret and what is the housing like?

Carteret sits in northeastern Middlesex County, on the Arthur Kill across from Staten Island, with the Rahway River forming its northern edge against Linden. Woodbridge Township touches it on every land side. The borough began in 1906 as Roosevelt, carved out of Woodbridge after a referendum, and took the Carteret name in 1922 after an early proprietor of the province. Local place names still in use include Chrome, Lamar, Canda, Silvan Beach and West Carteret, the part west of the Turnpike.

Census Bureau estimates show who owns and who rents. Figures come from the latest five-year survey unless the row says otherwise.

  • Residents, mid-2025 estimate: 25,781
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 54.7%
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $405,800
  • Typical gross rent: $2,032
  • Households: 8,224
  • People per household: 3.10
  • Household income, midpoint: $96,862

Households average more than three people, against 2.53 nationally, and roughly nine in ten residents stayed in the same home over the previous year. The borough's occupancy form has separate lines for one-family and two-family houses, and a house with a clean certificate and working mechanicals gives a buyer fewer reasons to renegotiate.

How do roads, the waterfront and the local economy affect a Carteret sale?

Access is the strength here, though some buyers will want to talk about truck traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike is the only major highway through the borough, with Interchange 12 inside its limits. NJ Transit local buses run the 116 route toward Midtown Manhattan and Perth Amboy and the 48 route toward Elizabeth. The Census Bureau's average commute is 31.4 minutes.

The economy leans toward moving goods. Census data show about $592 million in 2022 transportation and warehousing receipts for Carteret, against roughly $901 million in retail sales. With an economy built around freight and warehousing, buyers may ask about noise, truck routes and flood exposure along the Arthur Kill and Rahway River edges. Walk the block at rush hour before you price the house so you can answer honestly.

  • Know how far the house sits from the Turnpike ramps and from CR 602.
  • Pull together any flood or sump-pump history, since tidal water borders the east side.
  • Keep the block and lot number handy, because every borough form asks for it.

What does the borough require before a Carteret house can close?

Carteret requires a residential certificate of continued occupancy, issued by the Department of Code Enforcement at 61 Cooke Avenue, before a house changes hands. The application asks for the owner, the purchaser, the realtor if there is one, the block and lot, one family or two, the listed price and the names and ages of everyone living there. Code enforcement answers at (732) 541-3925, and inspections are booked through (732) 541-3810.

An addendum to the application works as a plain checklist, and the inspector holds you to it. The seller certifies each item, and the form warns that false statements can be prosecuted with a fine of $2,000 per occurrence.

  • Smoke detectors on each level, plus a smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, within ten feet.
  • Battery-powered units that carry sealed 10-year batteries.
  • A 2A:10BC fire extinguisher mounted near the kitchen, also within ten feet.
  • Working heat, hot water, electric, water and sewer.
  • No unpermitted work and no open permits.
  • Exterior, grounds, concrete, asphalt and masonry free of disrepair and trip hazards.

The fees are printed on the application itself.

The base fee pays for the first visit and one follow-up. Since the application lapses after 90 days, file it close to your expected closing rather than months ahead. The form lists cash, certified check, or an attorney or broker check as payment, and the borough reserves the right to inspect again later.

What happens with Carteret's tax bills at closing?

The borough mails one tax bill a year, in July, with stubs for the installments due on the first day of February, May, August and November. Finance allows ten days of grace after each date. After that, late installments accrue 8 percent a year on up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any larger amount, counted from the original due date. A delinquency above $10,000 also draws a 6 percent year-end penalty, and balances left open for a year or more are swept into the annual tax sale.

The borough's own advice is to have the latest bill at the closing table, because the buyer's side needs the next installment amount. The tax collector works from the finance department at 100 Cooke Avenue on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Call (732) 541-3820 extension 3818 for a payoff figure.

If you believe the assessment is off, take it up with the borough assessor first, at extension 3110. Next comes an appeal package from the Middlesex County Tax Board in New Brunswick. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 in a revalued town, and the owner must show the assessed value is unreasonable next to market value. People who hold a senior or veteran deduction also send in an annual statement by March 1 to keep it.

How does Middlesex County record the deed, and which tax forms apply?

Carteret deeds are filed at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick. The office serves the public on weekdays and asks visitors to arrive by 4 p.m. Your attorney or title company usually handles the filing. The county's online search reaches back to 1929 for deeds and 1950 for mortgages, so you can pull your own chain of title before listing, although staff do not run title searches.

Per the county's schedule, a deed costs $45 for page one and $10 for each added page, with a $6 name fee after the fifth name. State charges sit on top of those: the seller owes the realty transfer fee, and every seller hands over a gross income tax form. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification and settles income tax on the regular return. An out-of-state seller, including a former Carteret resident who has relocated, prepays either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate applied to net gain, unless an exemption listed on the form fits.

Federal rules let an owner keep $250,000 of profit free of tax, or $500,000 for a married couple, after living in the home two of the previous five years, and the state follows that approach.

Which routes get a Carteret house sold fastest?

The quickest routes are a cash purchase from an investor or a short listing of a well-prepared house, and the borough certificate gates both. A cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the inspection, the tax payoff and the deed filing still apply.

  • Choose an agent if the house is in good shape and you can sit through showings and a lender's calendar.
  • Choose an as-is investor sale if the house needs work, has tenants, carries back taxes or belongs to an estate.
  • Choose a sale by owner only with an attorney lined up for the contract, the certificate and the closing forms.

Whichever way you go, order the inspection early, replace alarms and the extinguisher yourself, and ask the buyer's attorney who will book the final walk-through. If a repair cannot be finished before the closing date, ask the borough code office whether a temporary certificate is available.

Frequently asked questions

Is an occupancy inspection mandatory for Carteret sellers?

Yes. The Department of Code Enforcement issues a residential certificate of continued occupancy after an inspection, and the application lapses 90 days after issuance, so time it close to closing.

How much does the Carteret inspection run?

The borough form lists $100 for a one-family house and $150 for a two-family house. A temporary certificate is $75, and every extra inspection after a failure or no-show is $50.

What are Carteret's quarterly tax dates?

Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with ten days of grace. Late balances accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 and 18 percent on anything above that.

Which Middlesex County office files a Carteret deed?

The County Clerk's Registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick. A closing attorney or title agent usually delivers it with the state transfer and income tax forms.

Can a Carteret house with tenants or open repairs still sell?

Yes, but the occupancy inspection still applies and the application lists everyone living in the home. Ask the code office about open permits first, since the form requires that none be open.

Cliffside Park ranks fifth in population density among New Jersey's 565 municipalities, so a sale here may involve a condominium, a co-op unit or a house on a very small lot. The borough still requires a certificate of continued occupancy for a sale, issued through its building department, and the deed is filed in Hackensack through the Bergen County Clerk.

The borough covers less than one square mile, so distance to the bus lines on Anderson and Palisade Avenues and the view from the unit are easy points to describe in a listing. This page covers the local paperwork, the tax calendar and the Bergen County steps that apply when you sell.

Where is Cliffside Park and how did the borough form?

Cliffside Park sits on top of the Hudson Palisades in Bergen County, about 0.96 square miles in all, and it borders Edgewater, Fairview, Fort Lee and Ridgefield, with North Bergen in Hudson County to the south. The borough was created on January 15, 1895 from part of Ridgefield Township during the wave of borough formation that swept Bergen County in the 1890s, and its name describes the setting: a park by the cliffs.

Palisades Amusement Park, which straddled Cliffside Park and Fort Lee, ran from 1898 to 1971 on a 38-acre site, and high-rise apartment buildings now stand where the rides were. Gorge Road runs down the cliff face to the Edgewater waterfront, and the old place names Grantwood and Shadyside are still used for parts of the borough.

The middle owner-occupied value of $588,200 sits far above the national $332,700, and close to half the homes are not owner-occupied. A seller with a condo, a rented unit or an inherited multifamily building is dealing with a different market than a suburban house seller.

How do transit, roads and schools shape the Cliffside Park market?

Commute time is the headline number: the average trip to work runs 35.5 minutes, well above the 26.4 minutes for the country as a whole. Anderson Avenue and Palisade Avenue carry most north-south traffic, and Palisade Avenue has views toward the Hudson River and the Manhattan skyline. NJ Transit bus lines 156, 159 and 181 go to Manhattan, the 22 serves Jersey City, and the 751 and 755 run locally.

The Cliffside Park School District runs five schools, topped by Cliffside Park High School, which also takes students from Fairview under a sending and receiving arrangement. Students can apply to the Bergen County Technical Schools, including the academies in Hackensack. Because a large share of households speak a language other than English at home, about 65 percent by Census estimate, listing materials in more than one language can widen your buyer pool.

  • Photograph the view if you have one, and note which floor you are on.
  • For a condo or co-op, collect the association's budget and rules before the first showing.

What does the borough require before a Cliffside Park sale?

Cliffside Park's building department lists a Certificate of Occupancy as required for the sale of property. The department is at the Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, reachable at 201-313-2042, with counter hours of 8:30 to 4:30 The applications page carries a form titled Certificate of Continued Occupancy for Sale, with a separate form for rentals.

After the inspections are done and the requirements are met, the Construction Code Official issues either a Certificate of Occupancy or a Certificate of Approval. Work done on the property matters here: the department also issues permits for alterations, demolitions and interior renovations, so work done without a permit can surface during the sale. Cash is no longer taken in any borough department, so plan to pay by check, debit or credit card.

The Planning Board sits on the first Monday of each month and the Board of Adjustment on the fourth. Those dates matter if you need a variance before selling. The current charge for the sale certificate is on the borough's own form, so ask the department before you file.

How and when are Cliffside Park property taxes paid?

Cliffside Park collects real estate tax in four installments, on the first of February, May, August and November. The tax collector sits on the second floor of 525 Palisade Avenue, and the phone is 201-313-2050. You can pay through the borough's online lookup page, mail a check to the Tax Collector at that address, or use the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

The borough has published figures showing a modest bill by Bergen County standards. A borough release reported an average residence assessed at $373,110 with an annual bill of $9,982, the ninth lowest among the county's 70 municipalities, based on state Department of Community Affairs data. That release reflects an earlier tax year, so use your own current bill for closing math.

For state relief programs, the finance page points to the Division of Taxation's relief page. If you receive a homestead benefit and sell, the state's selling guide says to mark the move on the application or take the benefit as a credit at closing, otherwise it is applied to the new owner's taxes.

Can you appeal a Cliffside Park assessment before selling?

You can, through the Bergen County Board of Taxation in Hackensack, but timing is strict. The state filing date is April 1, moved to May 1 after a revaluation, and the Bergen board's own page says the 2026 deadline has gone by. The board encourages online filing and can be reached at 201-336-6300. Start with the borough assessor at 201-313-2009, whose office also defends appeals.

The board's guidance is blunt: your current assessment is assumed correct, and you must show it is unreasonable compared with market value. Evidence means recent comparable sales, not a complaint about the tax bill. An appeal mainly benefits whoever owns the property after the ruling, so ask your attorney whether filing makes sense before a sale.

  • Compare your assessment with recent sales of similar units in your building or block.
  • Check that the assessor shows the correct square footage and unit count.
  • Ask whether a pending appeal could affect the closing adjustments.

What happens to the deed and the state fees on a higher-priced Cliffside Park sale?

The Bergen County Clerk handles the filing and keeps the county's deeds, mortgages and liens. The seller owes the state realty transfer fee, and above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee applies on residential and cooperative-unit deeds: 1 percent of the total price between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000, rising to 3.5 percent above $3,500,000. With a middle value of $588,200, most Cliffside Park sales land under that line, but a penthouse or a multifamily building can cross it. In addition, the buyer pays a separate 1 percent fee on certain purchases above $1 million.

Every seller also gives a gross income tax form at closing. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification. An owner who has left New Jersey prepays estimated income tax, calculated at either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate on the gain. Separately, the federal rule for a principal residence can shelter $250,000 of profit, or $500,000 for a married couple.

Which routes sell a Cliffside Park home fastest?

Two routes move fastest: an investor purchase, or a well-priced listing with the certificate already in hand. A unit with a clean inspection history and complete association paperwork leaves a buyer fewer open questions.

If you inherited a unit, have tenants or owe back taxes, get permit status and a tax payoff in writing before you accept an offer. An as-is buyer will still need the occupancy certificate and a clear deed, so those items belong on your checklist whichever route you choose.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate required to sell in Cliffside Park?

Yes. The borough building department lists a Certificate of Occupancy as required for the sale of property, and its applications page carries a separate sale form.

Where is the Cliffside Park sale certificate filed?

At the building department, Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, or by phone at 201-313-2042. The borough accepts check, debit or credit card, not cash.

What are the Cliffside Park tax installment dates?

The first of February, May, August and November. You can pay online, by mail, or in the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

Can I still appeal my Cliffside Park assessment for 2026?

No. The Bergen County Board of Taxation says the 2026 filing deadline has gone by. Later appeals are due April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation.

Which office records a Cliffside Park deed?

The Bergen County Clerk in Hackensack files deeds and mortgages for the borough, usually through your attorney or title agent along with the state fee and income tax forms.

What should you know before selling a house in Clifton, NJ?

In Clifton, no closing can take place without a valid dwelling certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau, and the city has also been revaluing property, which affects assessed values. Those two facts shape how long a sale takes more than the listing itself does.

Clifton is the second-largest city in Passaic County and a bedroom community for New York, with more than a dozen named neighborhoods ranging from Botany Village to Montclair Heights. A seller here usually owns a one- or two-family house or a condo, and the same city paperwork follows the property whether you list it, sell it yourself or accept an offer from an investor. Below is the process in order.

Where is Clifton and how did it grow?

Clifton covers about 11.3 square miles in Passaic County, with the Passaic River along its northeastern edge and Route 3 across the southern part. European settlement dates to 1679, when a Lenape leader deeded about 11,000 acres along the river to Hans Frederick. The city took its name from the cliffs of Garret Mountain, was incorporated on April 26, 1917 to replace Acquackanonk Township, and for decades was farmland. A federal animal quarantine station operated here from 1903 until the late 1970s, and three small working farms remain.

The neighborhoods are distinct, and buyers ask for them by name.

  • Main Mall is the downtown, and Allwood is the other business district, along Route 3.
  • Athenia and Delawanna each have a train station, and Dutch Hill sits near downtown.
  • Botany Village is the northernmost neighborhood, and Lakeview runs along the western edge.
  • Montclair Heights and Rosemawr are among the wealthier residential areas, with Albion Place beside Garret Mountain Reservation.

A city of 91,127 people in mid-2025, up from 90,296 in the 2020 count. The owner-occupied rate is 59.6 percent, the median owner-occupied home is valued at $461,900, and median gross rent is $1,711. Median household income is $98,237, and about 35 percent of residents were born abroad. Those numbers describe a city where about four in ten homes are not owner-occupied, so many sellers are landlords as well as owner-occupants.

How do Clifton's highways, trains and schools affect a sale?

Clifton is crossed by Route 3, Route 21, Route 19 and U.S. Route 46, and the Garden State Parkway runs through the city with interchanges 153 through 156. NJ Transit trains stop at Clifton station and Delawanna station on the Main Line toward Hoboken and Suffern. Buses on the 190, 191, 192 and 195 routes go to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 13, 27 and 72 go to Newark. The Census Bureau's mean commute is 28.3 minutes.

Clifton Public Schools runs 18 schools and about 10,500 students, as of the 2020 to 2021 data, with numbered elementary schools, Christopher Columbus and Woodrow Wilson Middle Schools, and Clifton High School. A listing that names the elementary school number and the nearest station answers two of the first questions buyers ask.

How do you get the Clifton dwelling certificate for a sale?

You file a dwelling application with the Fire Prevention Bureau, at 900 Clifton Avenue, after checking with the Building Department that the property has no open permits. The city's instructions give the steps in order, and the application must be signed by both the seller and the buyer.

  • Call the Building Department at 973-470-5809 to confirm there are no open permits and to learn where to get the application stamped.
  • Bring the stamped application, payment and, if you use unverified digital signatures, a copy of the sales contract to Clifton Fire Headquarters. An after-hours drop box is available.
  • Inspections are scheduled on Wednesdays from 9 a.m. to noon, and an adult over 18 has to be present with every area of the structure accessible.
  • Call about seven business days after the inspection, since certificates must be picked up in person.

The certificate depends on passing the building, tax and zoning departments, and it expires six months after the fire department inspection, so schedule it after you have a signed contract and a target closing. The fee schedule on the packet is below.

Clifton dwelling certificate fees, per unit, City of Clifton Fire Prevention Bureau
ServiceFee
Sale certificate, standard$125
Rental certificate, standard$75
Expedited, available within 4 to 20 days$200
Expedited, available within 4 business days$300

Fees are charged per dwelling unit, so a two-family house costs double. Payment can be by personal check, money order, cashier's check, exact-change cash or credit card with a transaction fee, and everything is payable to the City of Clifton. The city will not accept an application without payment or payment without an application.

What alarm and safety items does a Clifton inspector check?

The inspector checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide alarms and a label for homes with backup power, so fix these before the appointment. Failing and rescheduling costs time on a closing calendar that already depends on a Wednesday slot.

  • Smoke detectors on every level, except crawl spaces and unfinished attics reached by pull-down stairs.
  • A detector within 10 feet of the outside of each bedroom door on any floor that has bedrooms.
  • All detectors under 10 years old, with 10-year sealed batteries when battery operated, and hardwired systems kept in service.
  • Carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas, with more on each additional floor that has sleeping areas.
  • A central station fire alarm tested beforehand, with the test record from a certified company handed over, because inspectors do not test those systems and a missing report fails the inspection.

One- and two-family homes also need a label within 18 inches of the main electrical panel and meter warning about secondary power sources such as generators, solar panels or battery storage. The Fire Prevention Bureau supplies and installs that label on the day of your inspection, so owners with solar should know it is coming.

How does Clifton's revaluation change what a seller should expect?

Clifton has been carrying out a city-wide revaluation, described on the assessor's page and in a city presentation from January 2026. The presentation lists the criteria for a revaluation, including a last revaluation in 1991 and an average ratio of 31.87. A ratio that low indicates assessments sit well below market value, so new values are expected to be higher while the tax rate is meant to fall.

The city's explanation is that a revaluation does not raise the total amount collected. The levy is set by the school, county and municipal budgets, and revaluation spreads it according to value. The presentation's illustration, labeled as an example only, shows a house assessed at $180,000 rising to $540,000 while the rate drops by a factor of three, leaving the bill about the same. Your own result depends on whether your house moved more or less than the city average.

For a seller, that means the assessed value printed on old paperwork may not match the new notice. The state sets the appeal deadline at April 1, or May 1 in a newly revalued municipality, and the presentation adds that an appeal has to prove value with comparable sales. Call the assessing department at 973-470-5838 for your property record.

When are Clifton taxes due and what relief exists?

Clifton taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. The tax collector is at 900 Clifton Avenue, first floor, phone 973-470-5830. The city accepts online payment by e-check only, and there is a lockbox at City Hall for mailed or dropped-off payments, with no cash accepted there. A $35 fee applies to a returned check from wrong account numbers.

The assessor's page lists a $250 deduction for qualifying veterans or surviving spouses and a $250 deduction for seniors or disabled persons. The senior deduction requires age 65 or older, ownership and residence in the house, and annual income of $10,000 or less after permitted exclusions. The tax collector's page also links to the state's ANCHOR program for homeowners and renters. If you receive any of these, tell your closing attorney so the adjustments are right.

Where is a Clifton deed recorded and what does the clerk require?

A Clifton deed is recorded with the Passaic County Clerk's Registry Division, 401 Grand Street, Room 113, in Paterson, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. The office does not do title searches, and it does not record surveys. The county lists specific requirements:

  • Deeds must carry the words Prepared by, the tax block, lot and consideration.
  • Every document needs a record and return address, and original signatures with names printed beneath.
  • Use the official county cover sheet, or pay an extra $20 per document.
  • Pay the realty transfer fee with an attorney trust check, title agency trust check, certified check or cash.

The county also posts the seller forms you need: the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, the Seller Residency Certification, the Nonresident Seller Tax Declaration and the waiver form. A Clifton owner who has moved out of New Jersey is treated as a nonresident for the sale, which can mean an estimated payment at closing, while a federal principal residence exclusion may shelter up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a qualifying couple.

Frequently asked questions

Can I close on a Clifton house without a dwelling certificate?

No. The city's instructions state that no closing shall take place without a valid Certificate of Inspection, and the certificate expires six months after the fire department inspection.

How much does a Clifton sale certificate cost?

The standard fee is $125 per unit for a sale. Expedited service costs $200 per unit for a 4 to 20 day turnaround or $300 per unit for four business days.

When does the Clifton fire department inspect?

Inspections run on Wednesdays between 9 a.m. and noon, and an adult over 18 must be home. Call about seven business days afterward, because certificates are picked up in person.

When are Clifton property taxes due?

February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. Online payment is by e-check only.

What is the deadline to appeal a Clifton assessment?

The state deadline is April 1, or May 1 in a municipality that has just been revalued. Clifton's revaluation presentation says an appeal must prove value with comparable sales.

What are the quickest ways to sell in East Orange?

East Orange owners generally pick among a listing, a private sale, and a direct cash purchase. Listing brings the most buyers, but here the paperwork often decides the closing date. East Orange requires a Certificate of Conformity before a property is sold, and the fire department issues a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide certificate for one and two family homes. Both take scheduling.

East Orange is a dense city. The city had an estimated 72,159 residents in July 2025 on 3.93 square miles, and the 2020 count came to about 17,700 per square mile. Owners live in just 31.0 percent of homes, which makes rentals a big slice of the stock.

  • Agent listing: fits a house that can clear the city's certificate inspections with little work.
  • Cash purchase: fits an inherited or tenant-occupied house, or one carrying open code violations.
  • Private sale: still needs the Certificate of Conformity, a deed, and the state's seller forms.

What is East Orange's housing stock like?

East Orange sits in Essex County and shares borders with Newark on the east and south, South Orange to the southwest, Orange to the west, and Glen Ridge and Bloomfield to the north. The area traces to a 1666 settlement that was part of Newark at first. It took the name Orange in 1780, broke from Newark in 1806, was organized as East Orange on March 4, 1863, and was reincorporated as a city on December 9, 1899. Long streets of shade trees are still a feature of the northern neighborhoods.

The city has five official wards and several informal neighborhoods. Ampere, built on land once owned by the Orange Water Works after a nearby factory spurred growth, sits at the northeast. Greenwood, called the Teen Streets for its numbered cross streets, was cut up by the building of Interstate 280 and the Garden State Parkway. Presidential Estates in the north has larger homes on streets named for early presidents, and Elmwood in the southeast centers on Elmwood Park and a Carnegie library branch that opened in 1912.

How do transit and highways help an East Orange sale?

East Orange has two commuter rail stops, East Orange and Brick Church, both on NJ Transit's Morris and Essex Lines with daily trains to New York Penn Station and weekday trains to Hoboken. The East Orange station sits beside Interstate 280, directly across a parking lot from City Hall. More than a dozen NJ Transit bus routes, including the 5, 21, 24, 34, 41, 44, 71, 73, 79, 90, 92, 94 and 97, cover the city.

By road, the Garden State Parkway is reached at Interchange 145 for I-280 and Interchange 147 for Springdale Avenue. County Route 508 follows Central Avenue, County Route 510 follows South Orange Avenue, and County Route 509 follows Grove Street. Newark Liberty International Airport lies 7.8 miles off. Of the city's 83 miles of road, about 73 are municipal and 6 are county-owned. The average commute is 35.4 minutes.

What do schools, hospitals and business zones add to East Orange?

The East Orange School District serves grades pre-K through 12 and enrolled 9,337 students across 20 schools in 2023-24. East Orange Campus High School occupies the former Upsala College campus and had 1,751 students, and East Orange STEM Academy and the Cicely Tyson School of Performing and Fine Arts both run grades 6 to 12. East Orange Community Charter School operates independently of the district.

Two large medical sites sit inside the city: CareWell Health Medical Center, a 211-bed hospital on Central Avenue that was formerly East Orange General, and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical center on Tremont Avenue. Part of the city lies in an Urban Enterprise Zone, where shoppers pay a reduced 3.3125 percent sales tax at eligible merchants. The zone's status runs through June 2027, and Central Avenue and Main Street are the main commercial strips.

How does East Orange stack up against the state on housing?

Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024 value the middle owned home in East Orange at $365,900 against $454,400 across New Jersey. Rent runs $1,441 here and $1,720 statewide, and households average 2.44 people against the state's 2.62.

What is a Certificate of Conformity in East Orange?

It is the city's pre-sale compliance certificate. Under Section 159-50, the Housing and Inspections page explains, the certificate must be in hand before a property is sold. It shows the property conforms to the city code, and the code holds seller and buyer both accountable for getting it. Applications are made in person at the Department of Property Maintenance, East Orange City Hall, 44 City Hall Plaza, third floor, paid by certified check or money order with no cash taken. The phone is 973-266-5320.

Following an inspection, the city mails a Notice of Code Violations with everything found and a correction deadline. Items left uncorrected can bring a summons and fines between $100 and $2,000 per offense. Ask Code Enforcement whether any open notices sit on your house before you list it.

Does East Orange issue a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate for my house?

For a one or two family home, yes. The Fire Department issues a Certificate of Smoke Alarm and Carbon Monoxide Compliance, and the city's FAQ says owners or managers of those dwellings need it to show compliance. Ask the buyer's attorney whether it is expected at your closing. Call the Fire Prevention Bureau at 973-266-5520 to book, at least a day ahead. Appointments are available Monday to Thursday between 9 and 3. Pricing follows lead time: $100 for ten or more business days, $125 for four to nine, and $175 for one to three, and $50 applies to a failed inspection, a re-inspection or a no-show. One and two family homes can also get free smoke detector installation from the city.

The fee ladder rewards planning: a one-to-three day booking costs $75 more than one made ten business days out.

What else surfaces in an East Orange closing?

  • Water, sewer and refuse: owners are responsible for charges run up by tenants, and the Water Department's FAQ says a property that owes money at the end of the prior calendar year is included in that year's tax lien sale. Call the Water Department at 973-266-8869 for a final reading and balance.
  • Service line: the piece beyond the curb box belongs to the owner, so a leak there is the owner's repair.
  • Superintendent license: a building with four or more dwelling units needs a designated superintendent who is licensed and registered, renewing yearly.
  • Lead paint: the state inspection law applies to rentals built before 1978 and not to home sales, but federal rules still require a seller to disclose known lead hazards in a pre-1978 home.

What does an East Orange seller owe, and who files the deed?

The state's realty transfer fee is the seller's cost. A $365,900 sale, the Census middle value for owned homes in the city, comes to about $2,888 on the state schedule. Senior, blind or disabled sellers and certain affordable housing sales use a lower schedule.

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages files East Orange deeds. It occupies Room 130 of the Hall of Records, 465 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard in Newark, takes its last transaction at 4:15 on weekdays, and answers at 973-621-4960. A certified deed copy costs $8 for page one and $2 for each page after, and the staff will not conduct title searches.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is a Certificate of Conformity mandatory for an East Orange sale?

Yes. The city requires it before a property is sold, and the code makes both seller and buyer responsible for obtaining it. Apply in person at the Department of Property Maintenance, third floor of City Hall.

What does the East Orange fire department charge for the detector certificate?

It is $100 with ten or more business days of notice, $125 with four to nine, and $175 with one to three. A failed inspection or a missed appointment costs $50.

Can a house with open code violations be sold in East Orange?

Yes. The violations stay with the property, and the owner receives a Notice of Code Violations with a deadline. A cash buyer can accept the house as it stands and adjust the offer for the open items.

Does the state lead paint inspection law reach home sales?

No, it covers rentals built before 1978. Federal law still requires a seller to disclose known lead hazards in a house older than 1978.

What makes selling a house in Elizabeth, NJ different from other Union County towns?

Elizabeth is a dense port city: 141,675 residents on 12.32 square miles of land, about 11,145 people per square mile by the 2020 count. Only 25.6 percent of homes are owner occupied, so many houses for sale are two, three and four family buildings that investors and live-in owners both compete for. Where is Elizabeth, and how is it laid out?

The city sits in Union County between Newark to the north and Linden to the southwest, with Roselle, Roselle Park, Union and Hillside to the west. Newark Bay and the Arthur Kill form its eastern edge, and the Goethals Bridge lands here on the way to Staten Island. The Elizabeth River runs 4.2 miles through the city, mostly in a channel.

The street plan is unusual for New Jersey. Instead of a grid, it is largely circular, with streets radiating from the central railroad station. A buyer driving the neighborhoods will notice that a house a block from Elizabeth station and one near Warinanco Park are very different propositions.

Elizabethport, the oldest neighborhood, grew around businesses serving ships, and Bayway grew up around the refinery on the Linden line. Whatever the age of your building, gather permit records and any boiler, roof or electrical paperwork before you list.

Deeds are recorded with the Union County Clerk, whose land records site is clerk.ucnj.org. Quarles Early Childhood Center to Dwight Morrow High School, which also takes students from Englewood Cliffs.
