What is the first step in selling a house quickly in Fair Lawn?

The first step is the Certificate of Continued Occupancy, which the borough requires before the title of a one or two family home can transfer. Everything else about a fast Fair Lawn sale, from price to closing date, depends on how soon the Building Department inspects the house and signs off.

Fair Lawn is a Bergen County borough about 12 miles northwest of New York City, and the Census counted 34,927 people there in 2020. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 37,128, a gain of 6.3 percent over the 2020 base. The borough covers only 5.14 square miles of land, so density is around 6,800 people per square mile and houses sit close together.

What is Fair Lawn's history, and how does it show in the housing?

Fair Lawn was farmland before it was a suburb, and the oldest houses on Berdan Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue still reflect that. Dutch and Irish settlers divided the land into large farm lots in colonial times, and Victorian homes went up along Berdan Avenue beside five Berdan family farms. The borough takes its name from Fairlawn, the estate David Acker built in 1865, which later became the Fair Lawn Municipal Building.

Residents petitioned to leave Saddle River Township because they felt the schools were poor value for the taxes they paid, and Fair Lawn became its own borough in 1924. Suburban growth came in three pockets: Memorial Park around River Road and Fair Lawn Avenue, Columbus Heights at Lincoln Avenue and Wagaraw Road, and Warren Point east of the railroad and south of Broadway.

Radburn, founded in 1929 as a town for the motor age, is one of the first planned communities in the United States and lies inside the borough. Eight sites in Fair Lawn are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Radburn station and the Naugle House on Dunkerhook Road. If your home is near one, ask the building office whether any review applies before you change the exterior.

How do Fair Lawn's numbers compare with the rest of the country?

Fair Lawn homes are worth considerably more than the national figure, and the borough has an unusually stable population. The table shows Census QuickFacts estimates for 2020 to 2024.

What does Fair Lawn's Certificate of Continued Occupancy involve?

Fair Lawn requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title in a one or two family dwelling, and the borough's published fee is $175. The Building Department is in Room 112 of the municipal building, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and its number is (201) 794-5307. Fire Prevention handles the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

  • An application and the $175 fee go in first, then the department inspects the property and may photograph conditions.
  • A smoke certificate from Fire Prevention, or a written waiver, is part of the file.
  • A failed public sidewalk must be repaired or replaced before the certificate is issued.
  • A buyer who flips the house must apply again as the seller at the next sale.

If a buyer will do the repairs, the borough offers a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only, with no occupancy. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming the buyer understands that, and after closing the buyer reapplies for the full certificate, paying another $175. On an as-is sale, the buyer must acknowledge that anything the inspection finds becomes the buyer's responsibility to correct.

How does the grid address system affect a Fair Lawn listing?

Most Fair Lawn addresses use a hyphenated number, such as the library's 10-01 Fair Lawn Avenue, and buyers who search online sometimes get no match unless they leave the dash out. Nearly 10,000 Fair Lawn addresses use this system, which accounts for almost half of the hyphenated addresses in New Jersey.

The first number tells you the block distance from Broadway on north-south streets, or the numbered street on east-west ones. Addresses south of Broadway or Route 4 begin with a zero. The system dates to at least the 1930s and was designed so emergency crews could find a house fast. Exceptions exist on the Glen Rock, Hawthorne and Saddle Brook sides and inside Radburn.

When you advertise the house, write the address both with and without the dash, and confirm it on the tax record so title and survey work match what appears on the deed.

Which roads, trains and neighborhoods define Fair Lawn?

Fair Lawn works as a commuter town because of two stations and two highways. Route 4 reaches the George Washington Bridge in under 10 miles from the Broadway district, and Route 208 runs northwest to Interstate 287. The Radburn and Broadway stations on NJ Transit's Bergen County Line serve Hoboken, with connections at Secaucus Junction to New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 144, 145, 148, 160, 164 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Local roads form a rough three-by-three grid: Saddle River Road, Plaza Road and River Road run north to south, and Broadway, Morlot Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue run east to west. The borough had about 99.6 miles of roadway in 2010, 84 of them municipal.

  • Berdan Grove: single-family streets around Berdan Grove Park, with the borough's highest concentration of Asian American residents.
  • Broadway District: the main shopping strip and a train stop at Warren Point and Lyncrest.
  • Radburn: the planned community with its own station and pathways.
  • Parks: Memorial Park, Berdan Grove Park, Gregory Park and Cresthill Park.

Which schools serve Fair Lawn, and who employs its residents?

Fair Lawn Public Schools run from prekindergarten through twelfth grade, with nine schools and 5,529 students in 2022 to 2023. Elementary schools are Forrest, Lyncrest, Milnes, Radburn, Warren Point and Westmoreland for kindergarten through fourth grade, and Memorial and Thomas Jefferson middle schools cover grades 5 to 8. Fair Lawn High School had 1,624 students and has been recognized as a Blue Ribbon School.

Employers include Columbia Bank, headquartered in the borough, Kuiken Brothers building materials, Zerega's pasta, and U.S. Technologies. The large Nabisco and Mondelez bakery on Route 208 operated from 1958 and was announced for closure in 2021, with demolition beginning in January 2023. The Fair Lawn Promenade, a mixed-use complex, opened on April 1, 2014. The Broadway shopping district continues to supply local retail jobs.

What are the closing steps and costs in Fair Lawn?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the Bergen County Clerk records the deed, and for a sale over $350,000 the fee runs from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $4.80 on the band from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 between $550,000 and $850,000. Over $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

Sellers who are New Jersey residents, including estates and trusts, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. For an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so a rejection should be resolved with the clerk's office first, then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Property tax appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, and its page says the filing deadline for 2026 assessment appeals has passed. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

Frequently asked questions

Does Fair Lawn require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The borough requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title in a one or two family dwelling. The fee is $175, and applications are made in Room 112 of the municipal building. Fire Prevention supplies the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

Can a buyer take a Fair Lawn house that fails the inspection?

Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney must send a letter confirming that the buyer understands there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk must still be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?

The estate completes the form, signed by the executors who sign the deed or by the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?

The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering system, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms only accept the number without the dash.

Which county office records a Fair Lawn deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Bergen County Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Ask your closing attorney or title company to confirm the filing method for your closing date.

Who is selling a house or unit in Fort Lee, and what do they face?

Fort Lee is a high-rise borough, so a quick sale usually involves the borough's Certificate of Compliance for sales, any association paperwork and, for rented units, rent leveling records. The Census Bureau lists 55.4 percent of homes as owner-occupied, which leaves close to half occupied by renters.

Fort Lee sits on the Hudson Palisades at the eastern edge of Bergen County, at the western end of the George Washington Bridge. The borough covers 2.87 square miles, 12.33 percent of it water, and counted 40,191 people in 2020. The Census estimate for July 2025 is 40,345. The 2020 density was about 15,960 people per square mile of land.

How did Fort Lee get here, and does the history matter to a sale?

Fort Lee began as a Revolutionary War outpost, then became the first center of American filmmaking, and later a skyline of residential towers. Fort Constitution was renamed Fort Lee after General Charles Lee, and in November 1776 Thomas Paine wrote The American Crisis while retreating along what is now Main Street. The New Jersey Legislature formed the borough on March 29, 1904 from remaining parts of Ridgefield Township.

Kalem began filming in Fort Lee in 1907, the Champion Film Company built the first studio in 1909, and many more studios followed during the 1910s and 1920s. The Barrymore Film Center, a theater and film museum that cost $16 million, opened in October 2022.

High-rise apartment construction along Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East began in the 1960s and raised the borough's density sharply. As of 2019 ten structures here, including the bridge, stood over 300 feet. Two 47-story towers called The Modern, finished in 2014 and 2018, are among Bergen County's tallest buildings. For a seller, this means most inventory is built after 1960 and sits under an association or a building management company.

What do Census figures say about Fort Lee residents and housing?

Fort Lee has high rents, an older population and one of the most international resident bases in the state. The table gives QuickFacts estimates for 2020 to 2024.

There are 18,287 households averaging 2.19 people, and 60.5 percent of residents age five and over speak a language other than English at home. About 43.6 percent of residents are Asian alone, and the borough is one of the largest and fastest-growing ethnic Korean enclaves outside Korea.

What local paperwork does Fort Lee ask of sellers?

Fort Lee has its own Certificate of Compliance for sales, issued through the Fire Prevention Bureau, and the borough's forms page offers a separate version for rentals. Ask the bureau for the current packet, the inspection fee and the earliest appointment before you fix a closing date.

Other borough forms a seller or landlord may need include:

  • A subcode application for a certificate through the Building Department.
  • A sidewalk permit application, if the frontage needs repair.
  • Rent leveling registration for newly rented apartments, and a separate form for a newly rented condo, co-op or one-family home.
  • A landlord identity registration form for rent leveling.
  • A tax assessor property record search and deduction forms for senior, disabled and veteran owners.

Fort Lee also has a Parking Authority that issues residential parking permits, so tell a buyer who will not have a garage how permit parking works.

How do condos, co-ops and associations affect a Fort Lee sale?

Selling a unit in a Fort Lee tower can add association steps before the deed passes. Ask the board or management office what it requires from a seller, whether it issues a resale package, and whether a buyer of a co-op unit needs board approval.

Make that request at the start of the process, before a contract is signed, so the closing date reflects the association's timetable.

For co-op units, the state classifies them as Class 4C property, and the Division of Taxation applies the graduated percent fee to them on deeds above $1 million. The fee starts at 1 percent of the total price for sales between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 and rises in steps to 3.5 percent above $3.5 million, and the seller is responsible for it.

How do Fort Lee's roads and transit affect buyers?

Fort Lee's position at the George Washington Bridge shapes how buyers judge a property. The bridge, signed as I-95, U.S. 1-9 and U.S. 46, is the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge and carries traffic to Washington Heights in Upper Manhattan.

Roads through the borough include Route 4, Route 5, Route 67, U.S. 9W, U.S. 1/9, U.S. 46, County Route 505, the Palisades Interstate Parkway and Interstate 95. The borough had about 51 miles of roadway in 2010, and the municipality maintained roughly 35 of them.

  • NJ Transit buses 154, 156, 158 and 159 go to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown.
  • NJ Transit routes 171, 175, 178, 181, 182, 186 and 188 go to the George Washington Bridge Bus Terminal.
  • Rockland Coaches runs along Route 9W to Port Authority and the bridge terminal.
  • China Airlines and EVA Air have run private buses from Fort Lee to JFK Airport.

Mean commute time in Fort Lee is 35 minutes, nearly nine minutes above the national mean of 26.4, so buyers will ask how close a building is to a bus stop.

Which schools and neighborhoods define Fort Lee?

The Fort Lee School District serves prekindergarten through twelfth grade with six schools and had 4,074 students in 2021 to 2022. It operates four elementary schools numbered 1 to 4, Lewis F. Cole Middle School for grades 5 to 8, and Fort Lee High School. School 3 won a National Blue Ribbon award in 2010 to 2011. Students can also apply to Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack.

The borough's named communities include Coytesville, Linwood, Palisade and Taylorville, along with the Palisade Avenue and Boulevard East tower corridor and downtown Main Street. Fort Lee Koreatown, a dining district since the mid-1980s, is a draw for visitors, and Monument Park hosts summer outdoor Shakespeare shows.

Cliffside Park, Edgewater, Englewood, Englewood Cliffs, Leonia, Palisades Park and Ridgefield border the borough. A buyer comparing prices will look at those towns too, so keep your asking price consistent with nearby recent sales.

What are the closing costs and filings for a Fort Lee sale?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, which is based on the price recited in the deed. For a sale over $350,000, the rate is $4.80 per $500 for the band from $200,000 to $550,000, which is where a price near Fort Lee's $448,000 median value lands. The deed, the fee and the Gross Income Tax form are filed with the Bergen County Clerk.

Corporations, partnerships and multi-member LLCs file a GIT/REP-3 and check Box 5, and so do single-member LLCs. Individual sellers who live outside New Jersey owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price, or the gain times 10.75 percent if that is higher, unless the form's assurances apply. The state GIT/REP Unit answers questions at 609-322-9275.

For assessment disputes, the Bergen County Board of Taxation, 201-336-6300, handles appeals, and its page says the 2026 filing deadline has passed.

Frequently asked questions

Does Fort Lee require a certificate to sell a home?

Yes, the borough issues a Certificate of Compliance for sales through its Fire Prevention Bureau. The packet is on the borough's forms page. Ask the bureau for the fee and inspection schedule before setting a closing date.

Are Fort Lee rentals subject to rent leveling?

Fort Lee has a rent leveling office with registration forms for newly rented apartments and for newly rented condo, co-op or one-family units. Landlords should confirm their registrations are current and give the buyer copies. Contact the rent leveling office for the current rules.

What is the mansion tax on a Fort Lee condo sale?

It is the graduated percent fee on deeds above $1 million, and the seller pays it. It starts at 1 percent for sales up to $2 million and reaches 3.5 percent above $3.5 million. It applies to Class 2 residential and Class 4C cooperative units.

How does an LLC sign the seller form in Fort Lee?

An LLC files the GIT/REP-3 and checks Box 5, which covers sellers that are not individuals, estates or trusts. Single-member LLCs follow the same instruction.

Which county office records a Fort Lee deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records Fort Lee deeds. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the Gross Income Tax form are filed with the deed. Your closing attorney or title company will handle the submission and confirm the fee.

Why does Garfield, NJ work differently from a typical suburban sale?

Garfield is a compact Bergen County city where renters outnumber owners, and its sale paperwork is priced by unit count. The Census Bureau estimates 33,353 residents for July 2025, packed onto 2.11 square miles of land (15,469 per square mile at the 2020 count).

Just 44.7% of households own their home (2020-2024), compared with 69.3% in Franklin Township, Somerset County. Median home value sits at $475,500 and median gross rent at $1,688. With that split, a Garfield seller tends to see two buyer types: an occupant, and an investor who plans to rent the units out.

Both buyer types face the same city paperwork before title passes. The sections below take it in order, beginning with the resale certificate Garfield asks for on every sale.

How did Garfield take shape as a city?

Garfield began as a handful of houses and became a city within 44 years. Gilbert D. Bogart put up the first seven homes in 1873 in what was then called East Passaic. The community took the name Garfield in 1881, became a borough in 1898 and turned into a city on April 19, 1917, after a referendum.

The city shares land borders with Elmwood Park, Lodi, Saddle Brook and South Hackensack, and the Saddle River separates it from Wallington. Old neighborhood names such as Belmont, Bogart Heights, Dundee Dam and Plauderville still appear on deeds and listings.

One piece of local history matters for diligence. The EPA identified groundwater contamination from a 1983 chromic acid spill at a former electroplating company in Garfield and announced a $37 million cleanup in 2016. Buyers and lenders sometimes ask about nearby cleanup sites, so look up your street in the EPA's records early.

What does Garfield require before a house can be resold?

Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale plus a separate smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. The city's own instruction sheet says to submit the request through the Building Department citizen portal or by email, then wait for the email that tells you when fees are due.

The sheet also gives a timeline and a warning. Processing is listed as 10 business days from the day the application is received, and sellers are told not to schedule a closing until the certificate is in hand. Ignoring the ordinance can bring a fine of $2,000.

  • Send the property address and the full names, current home addresses, phone numbers and emails of buyer and seller. Do not list a business, attorney or real estate office address.
  • If an LLC or corporation is selling, give the contact person's details as well.
  • For an estate sale, attach the Surrogate letter to the application.
  • Pay the certificate fee to the City of Garfield and the smoke certification fee to the Bureau of Fire Prevention, each with its own check or money order.

The fees are charged by building type, and the city asks sellers to wait for its fee email before paying.

How do tenants, repairs or an open estate change a Garfield sale?

Each of these situations adds one step to the process without blocking it. An as-is house can still receive its paperwork once the smoke and fire items pass.

The detector rules are specific. Under the city's dwelling certificate sheet, ten-year sealed-battery smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms must sit within ten feet of every bedroom, and a common stairwell needs smoke alarms at the top and bottom. Inspectors also ask for access to the attic and basement.

  • A tenant-occupied house may also need a dwelling certificate. Ordinance 2213 requires one on any change of occupancy, with a $60 fee per unit that includes the smoke certification, unless an inspection happened within the previous eleven months.
  • A second visit costs another $60 per unit if the unit fails or the paperwork is not on site.
  • For a house with a deceased owner, the application asks for the Surrogate letter, so have it ready before you apply.

If repairs are the problem, fix the detector items first. They are the cheapest part of the checklist, and the city's sheet cites the state rule at N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3 for them.

What state paperwork gets recorded with a Garfield deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records a Garfield deed, and the state attaches two filings to it: the Realty Transfer Fee and a gross income tax residency form. Under the Division of Taxation's description, the seller owes the fee and it is computed from the consideration recited in the deed.

For prices of $350,000 or less, the schedule starts at $2.00 per $500 of the first $150,000 and tops out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A higher schedule applies above $350,000, opening at $2.90 per $500 and reaching $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000.

The state lists exemptions for deeds between husband and wife or parent and child, and for an executor's deed distributing an estate to an heir. An arm's-length purchase does not fit any of them.

The residency paperwork is the GIT/REP. A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax, never less than 2% of the deed consideration, unless a listed assurance on the form applies. According to the Division's FAQ, no deed gets recorded without a signed GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

What do Garfield schools, roads and transit offer a buyer?

Garfield sells on access: two NJ Transit rail stops and Route 46 both sit inside the city. The Garfield and Plauderville stations on the Bergen County Line run to Hoboken Terminal, with a transfer at Secaucus Junction for Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 160 and 161 run to Midtown Manhattan's Port Authority terminal.

By road, U.S. Route 46 and County Route 507 pass through, and Midland Avenue, Outwater Lane, River Drive and Passaic Street are the other main streets. Mean commute time for workers is 28.0 minutes (2020-2024).

The public schools are the Garfield Public Schools, a pre-K to grade 12 district with 12 schools and 4,713 students in 2020-21, one of the state's former Abbott districts. Garfield High School enrolled 1,159 students that year. Residents can also apply to the Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack. A buyer with children will ask about these, so have the district name ready.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Garfield houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which sale route fits a Garfield owner best?

Your deadline and the condition of the building decide it. Listing reaches the most buyers but puts showings and repair requests on you. A private sale or cash buyer trims the repair list, yet the city certificate and fire certification apply to all three.

  • List with an agent if the building is in good order and you can wait on a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Sell privately if a buyer is already lined up, such as a tenant, relative or neighbor.
  • Consider a cash offer for a building that needs work, carries tenants or belongs to an estate, and settle in the contract who orders the certificate and pays the $50 or $100 city fee.

Fix the closing date first, then count back 10 business days to learn the last day to file with the city.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection mandatory when I sell in Garfield?

Yes. Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale and a smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. The city lists 10 business days for processing and tells sellers not to schedule a closing before the certificate is issued.

How much is the Garfield resale certificate?

One-family houses pay $50 and two-family houses pay $100 on the city's sheet. Bigger buildings pay $100 for two units plus $25 for each one after that. The Bureau of Fire Prevention charges its smoke and CO certification on the same scale.

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in a Garfield sale?

The seller pays it. The county recording officer collects the state fee at recording, and the amount scales with the price in the deed. Spouse-to-spouse and parent-to-child deeds carry an exemption.

Can I sell a Garfield house that I inherited and have not cleared up yet?

Yes, once you have the right papers. Garfield wants the Surrogate letter with the certificate application on an estate sale. Selling to an outside buyer is a taxable transfer, though an executor's deed to an heir is exempt.

Do I need a dwelling certificate if tenants live in the house?

Possibly. City Ordinance 2213 calls for a dwelling certificate on a change of occupancy, at $60 per unit, unless the unit was inspected in the previous eleven months. Ask the Fire Prevention Bureau whether your tenant situation triggers it.

What is the quickest way to move a house in Hackensack?

The quickest sale is the one with the fewest open items at the start: a passed fire inspection, a clear tax balance and a price grounded in recent Hackensack sales. Hackensack is the Bergen County seat and the county's largest municipality, home to 46,030 people in 2020 and an estimated 46,380 by July 1, 2025.

Only 36.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, which tells you that renting dominates the housing stock. An owner of a two-family house or a small building should plan on tenants, leases and rent questions arising during the sale. Agents, private sales and cash buyers all follow the same city inspection, tax payoff and recording steps. A cash buyer simply removes the lender's appraisal and approval from the timeline.

What kind of housing does Hackensack offer?

The city sits about 12 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan on 4.35 square miles, and each block can differ from the next. Wikipedia's description lists a residential high-rise strip about a mile long on Prospect Avenue, single-family streets covering roughly a third of the city (mostly west), older two-family neighborhoods, big garden apartment complexes and a small-city downtown.

Hackensack University Medical Center, the Bergen County Court House, Fairleigh Dickinson University's Metropolitan Campus and a Bergen Community College site fill out the map. Bordering towns are Bogota, Hasbrouck Heights, Little Ferry, Lodi, Maywood, Paramus, Ridgefield Park, River Edge, South Hackensack, Teaneck and Teterboro.

  • West side: single-family homes, some on lots of an acre or more.
  • Older central blocks: two-family houses.
  • Prospect Avenue and the garden complexes: apartment living at scale.
  • Downtown and small neighborhood business districts: mixed-use buildings.

Which Hackensack figures should shape my asking price?

Hackensack pairs a renter-heavy population with a large tax bill: the average home was billed $10,307 in 2025. The table lines up the numbers that matter when you set a price.

Hackensack at a glance, from Census Bureau and state tax division data

Which inspection does Hackensack require before a house sale?

The Fire Prevention Bureau issues a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and a seller needs it before closing. The city's form lists a $70 fee, a six-month validity period and issuance on the day of the inspection.

If the house fails or nobody is home for the appointment, the city charges a new fee on a new application. The form wants the buyer's name, the seller's name and the real estate company, and the city warns that wrong details void the report.

The requirement traces to the state Uniform Fire Code, which calls for a smoke alarm certificate whenever a one-family or two-family dwelling is sold, leased or changes occupants. Only the municipality can issue it. Prepare the house first:

  • Smoke alarms on every level including the basement, in shared stairwells and hallways, and within 10 feet of each sleeping area.
  • Sealed ten-year battery alarms in place of old ones, since the Division of Fire Safety advises swapping alarms every decade.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm and a portable fire extinguisher, both listed on the city form.

Also ask the Building, Housing and Land Use department whether other resale paperwork applies to your type of property.

What does the Hackensack tax collector expect from a seller?

Taxes fall due on the first day of February, May, August and November, and each date carries a 10-day grace period. Late balances up to $1,500 accrue 8 percent annually, and anything above that accrues 18 percent. The collector says everything must be paid by November 10 to avoid the accelerated tax sale starting November 11.

The city's page gives a 2026 final rate of $3.530 per $100 and reports that final bills went out on September 16, 2026. New owners are warned that the county can take three to six months to record a deed and tell the city, so a buyer should send the collector a mailing address after closing. Request a written balance from the collector before you review the closing statement.

Owners who think the assessment overshoots market value can appeal to the Bergen County Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack. The annual filing date is April 1, and the 2026 window is over. Property assessed above $750,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by April 1.

What will a Hackensack seller pay at the closing table?

The state charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. Using the state's rate table for sales above $350,000, a $400,000 sale produces a fee near $3,215. A graduated percent fee applies above $1,000,000, and the state's page lists that schedule.

  • The state transfer fee, collected at recording.
  • The $70 fire certificate.
  • Mortgage payoff and any recorded liens.
  • The seller's portion of the quarter's property tax.

Resident sellers sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification so the clerk will take the deed. Out-of-state sellers prepay Gross Income Tax, with a floor of 2 percent of the sale price unless a listed assurance covers them. An executor's deed to an heir named in the will falls under the state's list of exempt transfers.

How should a landlord handle a Hackensack rental sale?

Roughly 63 percent of occupied homes here are rented, and typical rent is $1,911. The Department of Building, Housing and Land Use also staffs the Rent Stabilization Board, so check with that office on whether your building is covered before you price from market rents.

The state fire certificate applies to leases as well as sales, so a tenant turnover and a sale may each need an inspection. Book the inspection late enough that the six-month certificate still covers your closing date.

How do Hackensack's roads and rail lines influence demand?

Interstate 80, Route 17, Route 4 and County Route 503 cross the city, and bridges at Court Street, Midtown and Anderson Street span the Hackensack River. The city counted 79.69 miles of roadway in 2010, with 62.10 city-maintained, 15.10 county-maintained and 2.49 state-maintained.

The Pascack Valley Line stops at Anderson Street and Essex Street on its way to Hoboken and connections to Penn Station New York. Buses leave the Hackensack Bus Terminal for the Port Authority and the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. A listing close to a station or the terminal puts that commute in front of buyers.

Is a fire inspection certificate mandatory for a Hackensack sale?

Yes. State rules require a smoke alarm certificate for one-family and two-family sales, and the city fire bureau issues it for $70 on a form that also covers carbon monoxide alarms and a portable fire extinguisher. It stays valid for six months.

What would the state transfer fee be on a $400,000 Hackensack sale?

About $3,215 by the state's schedule for prices above $350,000. The seller pays it at recording, and exemptions are limited to the transfers the state lists, such as a deed between parent and child.

Does a Hackensack house with unpaid taxes still sell?

It can, once the balance is cleared at or before closing. The city wants current-year taxes paid by November 10 to avoid the tax sale that begins November 11, and late balances accrue interest at 8 percent up to $1,500 and 18 percent above.

May I sell while tenants live in the house?

Yes, a tenant-occupied house can sell. Ask the Building, Housing and Land Use department about rent stabilization and have an attorney read every lease, because the buyer steps into the occupancy.

What changes when the house came through an estate?

The estate signs a GIT/REP form for its residency status, and an executor's deed to an heir named in the will is exempt from the transfer fee. A sale to an outside buyer is taxed, and the fire certificate is still required.

What are the quickest ways to sell a house in Hoboken, New Jersey?

Hoboken sellers can list on the open market, sell on their own or take a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. The right one depends on what you own: a condo unit, a rowhouse or a small building with tenants each hit different city offices.

The city's housing stock is dense and mostly renter-occupied, so many sales involve a lease, a registration or a rent ordinance. Sorting those out first shortens the path to a closing date more than any price cut would.

  • Traditional listing: strongest for a renovated unit in good condition, with showings, inspections and a buyer's financing to schedule.
  • Private sale: saves the commission, but you handle disclosures, contracts and the city's resale certificate yourself.
  • Cash purchase: suits a unit with deferred repairs, tenants in place or a deadline, since there is no mortgage approval to wait for.

What is Hoboken's layout and how did the city develop?

Hoboken sits on the west bank of the Hudson River in Hudson County, directly across from Manhattan's West Village and Chelsea. It is called the Mile Square City, though it holds about 1.25 square miles of land and 0.75 square miles of water, for a total of 2 square miles. The ZIP code is 07030.

The street plan is a grid. North-south streets carry names such as Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe and Jackson, while the numbered east-west streets begin near Observer Highway and end around 16th Street by Weehawken Cove. The Northwest section, once industrial, has been rezoned and rebuilt as housing.

Dutch colonists settled the area in the 17th century, and Hoboken became a township in 1849 and a city in 1855. A steam ferry began running to Manhattan in 1811, and later the rail terminal and shipping lines tied the city to the Port of New York and New Jersey. Maxwell House, Lipton and Hostess once operated here, and the old factory blocks are now condominiums and shops.

What do Census numbers say about Hoboken housing?

Hoboken's 2020 to 2024 estimates show a city of renters with high incomes and high home values. Only about one in three housing units is owner-occupied, so a seller is often competing with a landlord market as well as other owners.

How did Hurricane Sandy change flood questions for Hoboken sellers?

Buyers will ask about flooding, and the history gives them reason. In October 2012 Hurricane Sandy flooded about 1,700 Hoboken homes and caused roughly $100 million in damage, according to the city's encyclopedia entry, and it shut down the PATH station at Hoboken Terminal.

The response was large. The federal housing department set aside $230 million through the Rebuild by Design competition for Hoboken, Weehawken and Jersey City. The city describes a four-part plan: resist surge with barriers, delay runoff with green infrastructure, store rainwater in basins and parks, and discharge it through upgraded sewers and pump stations. Sewer separation work finished in 2022, and the second construction phase began in 2023.

The city's home page also advertises ResilienCity Park, which it calls New Jersey's largest resiliency park, able to hold up to 2 million gallons of rain. When a September 2023 storm dropped 3.5 inches of rain, the entry reports standing water of only a few inches at three of 277 intersections by evening.

If your building took water in 2012, keep repair records, flood insurance history and any elevation paperwork ready. Buyers' attorneys ask for them.

What drives Hoboken's economy and commuting?

Hoboken has the highest share of public transit commuters of any American city, with 56 percent of working residents riding each day. Hoboken Terminal in the southeast corner is a national historic landmark, built in 1907.

  • Rail and subway: NJ Transit's Main, Bergen County, Pascack Valley, Montclair-Boonton, Morris and Essex and Meadowlands lines end at the terminal, and PATH runs to 33rd Street, the World Trade Center and Journal Square.
  • Light rail, bus and ferry: the Hudson-Bergen line has three Hoboken stops, nine NJ Transit bus routes terminate at Hudson Place, and NY Waterway ferries cross to Battery Park City, Pier 11 and West Midtown.
  • Roads: the 14th Street Viaduct leads up to Jersey City Heights, and the Lincoln and Holland tunnels are nearby. The city has no airport.

Major employers include one of the John Wiley and Sons headquarters and, since 2025, a North American headquarters for Unilever at Waterfront Corporate Center. Stevens Institute of Technology supports about 1,285 full-time jobs.

Hoboken Public Schools run five schools with 3,531 students in 2023-24, and three charter schools operate separately.

Which Hoboken city rules apply when you sell or rent out a property?

Three city offices matter most: Construction Code, the Fire Department and Rent Leveling and Stabilization. City Hall is at 94 Washington Street.

Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new buildings, additions and altered space, and a certificate of approval for other work. The city's site also carries an application titled Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, which is the form to ask about for a resale. Ask the fire inspection office whether your unit needs it.

Rent Leveling and Stabilization administers Chapter 155, the municipal rent control ordinance. Its staff answer which apartments are covered, what the legal base rent is, and how annual adjustments, vacancy decontrol and surcharges apply. Owners of single-family homes, condominiums, multiple dwellings and mixed-use buildings must register each year through the SDL portal. If you are selling a building with tenants, ask the office for the file on your property and give the buyer's attorney a copy.

How are Hoboken property taxes billed, and what do buyers and sellers owe?

Hoboken sends one tax bill with four quarterly stubs. It combines municipal, school, county and library taxes, plus a Special Improvement District assessment for properties inside that district. The office does not accept postmarks, so a payment counts only when the tax office receives it or it is paid online by the end of the grace period.

Added and omitted assessment bills for improvements go out in October and fall due November 1, with a grace period to November 10. For a lien payoff, call the Tax Collector for a redemption statement, because balances shown on the website may be wrong, and expect to pay by certified check or money order.

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, normally by April 1. A successful judgment is credited first to fourth-quarter taxes, then to any third-quarter balance, and any leftover is refunded to the petitioner or their attorney.

State fees matter at Hoboken prices. With a median owned-home value of $895,100, many sales approach the $1,000,000 line, above which the seller owes a graduated fee of 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000 and the buyer owes an extra 1 percent. Residents who keep their New Jersey residency sign GIT/REP-3 at closing instead of making an estimated payment.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a rent control law I should know about before selling a Hoboken rental?

Yes. Hoboken enforces Chapter 155, a municipal rent control ordinance, through its Rent Leveling and Stabilization office. The office can tell you which apartments are covered, the legal base rent and the allowed increases. Owners register their properties every year through the SDL portal, and the office keeps a public file on each residential property.

Does Hoboken require a certificate to sell a home?

The city publishes an application for a Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new or altered space. Ask the fire inspection office and your closing attorney which one your sale needs, since it can differ for a condo, a rowhouse and a multi-unit building.

Does Hoboken flood, and what should a seller have ready?

Parts of the city flooded badly in Hurricane Sandy in 2012, and the city has since built sewer, park and barrier projects with $230 million in federal funds. Buyers and their attorneys ask about past water damage, so gather repair records and insurance history for your address and review them with your attorney before listing.

When are Hoboken property taxes due?

In four quarterly installments listed on the single annual bill. The Tax Collector charges interest back to the due date once the grace period ends, and does not honor postmarks. Pay online or deliver the check to City Hall at 94 Washington Street, and call the office for a redemption figure if a lien exists.

How long do I have to appeal my Hoboken assessment?

Generally until April 1, filed with the Hudson County Board of Taxation on Form A-1. Owners of properties assessed above $1,000,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by the same date. If you disagree with the board's judgment, the Tax Court appeal must be filed within 45 days.

Hudson County's seat and New Jersey's second-largest city, Jersey City had an estimated 302,013 residents on July 1, 2025, 3.2% more than the 2020 base of 292,742. Owners live in only 27.9% of the housing units, which means many sellers hold a condo or rental property instead of a home they live in.

How is Jersey City laid out for buyers?

Land area is only 14.74 square miles, a 2020 density near 19,835 people per square mile, and water adds another 6.39 square miles. Water bounds the city on both sides: the Hudson River and Upper New York Bay to the east, the Hackensack River and Newark Bay to the west, with Manhattan across the harbor. Jersey City also includes most of Ellis Island, the parts New Jersey won in the 1998 Supreme Court case, and waters around Liberty Island.

Six wards divide the city, and the neighborhoods differ sharply. Historic Downtown has brownstones around Van Vorst Park and Hamilton Park, with Paulus Hook, the Village and Harsimus Cove close by. Newport and Exchange Place are waterfront office and residential towers. The Heights occupies the Palisades ridge and was once the separate city of Hudson City. Bergen-Lafayette, to the south, holds the 17.5-acre Berry Lane Park and The Beacon, a former medical center turned into residences, and it borders Liberty State Park along with Downtown. Library Hall, built in 1866 as a town hall for Bergen, is now a residential building.

  • The city's charter dates to February 22, 1838, and Hudson County was carved out two years later.
  • The 1630 Dutch land grant to Michael Pauw, covering what is now Hoboken and Jersey City, is the earliest known conveyance of the land.

  • Its 2024 tax base, valued above $57 billion, is the biggest of any New Jersey municipality.

  • Driveways and front-yard parking: the Division of Zoning has refused new front-yard parking since 2000. A space built earlier counts as legal if it was at least 18 feet deep, and residential zones cap a curb cut at 10 feet. A buyer who values a parking space can ask zoning for a Zoning Determination Letter.
  • Lead paint: single-family, two-family and multiple rental dwellings built before 1978 need a lead inspection at tenant turnover or every three years, whichever is sooner. Skipping it can cost up to $1,000 a week.

With tenants in place, give the buyer the lead-safe certificates or exemption papers alongside the leases.

Does storm flooding still affect Jersey City sales?

Yes, near the waterfront. Two storms shape the conversation. Irene, in August 2011, flooded parts of Downtown and the waterfront, and Sandy, in October 2012, pushed storm surge into Downtown, the Country Village neighborhood, the West Side and Liberty State Park. The flooding damaged city utilities and shut down PATH and the Holland Tunnel for days.

For a waterfront property, gather flood insurance papers, elevation certificates and repair invoices before listing. Buyers and insurers will ask about the flood zone, and a paper trail of dry basements and replaced systems settles it before it turns into a price cut.

How do transit and schools shape Jersey City values?

Transit explains much of the pricing. Four PATH stations serve the city (Exchange Place, Newport, Grove Street and Journal Square), with trains to Hoboken, 33rd Street in Midtown, Lower Manhattan's World Trade Center and Newark Penn Station. Thirteen of the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail's 24 stations are inside Jersey City. NJ Transit buses reach Newark and, through the Lincoln Tunnel, Midtown, and Hoboken Terminal runs commuter rail. The Census Bureau's mean commute is 36.8 minutes.

Jersey City Public Schools enrolled 27,134 students in 39 schools in 2021-22, and as a former Abbott district it has its school construction paid for by the state. High schools include Dickinson, Ferris, Lincoln, McNair Academic and Snyder. The waterfront known as Wall Street West holds more than 13 million square feet of Class A office space, which keeps demand strong around Exchange Place and Newport. The city is a regional job center with more than 100,000 public and private positions, and about one-third of private-sector jobs are in financial services. The National Stock Exchange is headquartered there, and companies such as ADP, Fidelity Investments and Computershare run operations in the city.

The city's tax assessor page sends you to taxrecords-nj.com, where Records Search lets you pick Hudson County and Jersey City and search by address, owner or block and lot. Not a new one, according to the city. The state does want a smoke alarm compliance certificate on a one- or two-family house before it sells, so reach the fire prevention office early.

The seller owes it, in price bands per $500 that run from $2.90 to $6.05 for a standard sale above $350,000. Going over $1 million also brings the graduated percent fee. Your closing agent does the arithmetic.

Yes, for pre-1978 rentals. They need inspections every three years or at tenant turnover unless exempt, so have the certificate or exemption papers ready for the buyer.

A cash sale moves fastest here because it avoids the buyer's mortgage commitment and appraisal, while a listing is slower and usually priced higher. Kearny, in Hudson County, had an estimated 40,862 residents on July 1, 2025, down 2.7% from a 2020 base of 42,004. Only 42.9% of housing units are owner-occupied, so a good share of Kearny sellers are landlords as well as homeowners, and a few own buildings with tenants.

How is Kearny laid out, and where did its housing come from?

Kearny sits on a peninsula between two rivers: the Passaic separates it from Newark and Belleville, and the Hackensack separates it from Secaucus and Jersey City. The town has 8.84 square miles of land and about 4,749 people per square mile, and it splits into three areas: the Kearny Uplands, the Kearny Meadows and South Kearny, where the two rivers meet.

Kearny Township was created in 1867, and the housing grew out of mills. Clark Thread opened its Kearny plants in 1875, and Nairn Linoleum followed in 1887, drawing Scottish workers who also gave the town its soccer reputation. Cargo ships were built at the Kearny yards in World War I and warships in World War II, and Western Electric's Kearny Works, opened in 1928, employed as many as 24,000 people. Population rose from 777 in 1880 to 40,716 in 1930, so much of the older housing dates from that surge.

  • Main streets include Kearny Avenue, Bergen Avenue, Midland Avenue, Schuyler Avenue and Passaic Avenue.
  • Riverbank Park, Bunnyland Hill and West Hudson Park (shared with Harrison) are the largest green spaces.
  • The Kearny Public Library, a Carnegie library, houses a local museum on its third floor.
  • The Highland Hose No. 4 firehouse, built in 1895, is on the National Register of Historic Places, and the present Town Hall, built of Indiana limestone, dates from 1909.

Who lives in Kearny, according to the Census?

Kearny is a mostly renting town where 45.0% of residents were born abroad and 65.2% speak another language at home. Median household income is $79,154, and the median home value is $459,400.

How do roads, buses and schools affect a Kearny sale?

Buyers who commute to Manhattan or Newark will look at the road network first. NJ Transit buses reach the Port Authority Bus Terminal and Newark on the 1, 30, 40 and 76 routes. Passenger service on the old Newark Branch ended in October 1966, and the Arlington station is abandoned.

The Kearny School District had 5,142 students in seven schools in 2021-22: Franklin, Garfield, Roosevelt, Schuyler and Washington elementary schools, Lincoln Middle School and Kearny High School. Hudson Arts and Science Charter School operates two campuses in town, an elementary school on Midland Avenue and a middle school on Chestnut Street, with 815 students combined, and Kearny Christian Academy has taught kindergarten through grade 12 since 1981.

Which Kearny office handles certificates and permits?

The Construction Code Enforcement Department posts a residential certificate of occupancy package: a checklist, an application, and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide detector compliance form for one- and two-family houses. Phone (201) 955-7880; the counter opens weekdays from 8 to 4. The department says certificate inspections run only on select days and that inspections requested just before closing cannot be fitted in, so book well ahead.

  • A building subcode construction permit costs $20 per $1,000 of listed work, with a $50 minimum.
  • Processing usually takes 5 to 7 business days, and the office has up to 20 working days to issue a permit.

These numbers matter if the house has unfinished work. A garage conversion or an addition done without permits is the kind of gap a buyer's attorney will ask about.

Can buyers or investors rent a Kearny house short term?

Not in a single-family house. Section 15-4 of the Town Code, which grew out of Ordinance 2017-61, restricts short-term rentals of single-family homes, and at its February 10, 2026 meeting the Town Council took up an amendment that would apply the ban to any single- or multi-family dwelling, define a short-term rental as less than 30 consecutive days, and bar advertising or facilitating one. The draft sets fines of $750 per day for a first violation. Ask the town clerk whether it has been adopted before you promise a buyer short-term income.

For taxes, call the tax collector at (201) 955-7888, in the lower level of Town Hall and open 9 to 4 on weekdays, for the current balance and the next installment.

Do I need a detector certificate to sell in Kearny?

Yes, for a one- or two-family house. The state requires a compliance certificate before a sale, and the town's residential certificate package includes the application. Once issued, it lasts six months.

Can I rent my Kearny house on a short-term basis?

Section 15-4 restricts short-term rentals of single-family homes, and an amendment taken up on February 10, 2026 would extend the ban to every dwelling and start fines at $750 a day. Ask the town clerk which version is in force.

Who covers the state transfer fee in a Kearny sale?

The seller does, when the deed is filed in Hudson County. Rates step up with price, and sales above $1 million add a graduated percent fee. The closing agent computes the total.

What happens to Kearny taxes at closing?

Ask the tax collector for the current balance and, if any lien exists, a redemption statement, which costs $20. Confirm there are no older balances before you set a closing date.

How did Linden develop, and where are its neighborhoods?

Linden was formed as a township on March 4, 1861, from pieces of Elizabeth, Rahway and Union Township. Cranford, Linden Borough and Roselle were later carved out of it. A state act of January 1, 1925 replaced the township and borough with a single city, and linden trees brought from Germany gave it a name.

The population shows how late the growth came: 8,368 people in 1920, 21,206 in 1930, and 39,931 by 1960. Named areas inside the city include Bayway, Grasselli, Tremley, Wheatsheaf, Morses Mill, Vreeland Mills and Warners. The residential section west of St. Georges Avenue is called Sunnyside, named for a former golf club. Linden borders Clark, Cranford, Elizabeth, Rahway, Roselle and Winfield Township in Union County, plus Carteret and Woodbridge across the county line.

Linden is also a regional center of Polish settlement. About 13.1% of residents report Polish origin, and the city holds an annual Polish Heritage Day Festival.

General Motors ran Linden Assembly from 1937 to 2005, and most of the plant was later torn down for a redevelopment on a 100-acre site. Merck, one of the larger pharmaceutical companies in the country, is based across Linden and Rahway.

School No. 5 was named a National Blue Ribbon School in 2020. Families will ask which numbered school covers your block, so find out before you list.

Ask about open permits on the property too, and request the answers in writing for the buyer's attorney.

Recordings for Linden go to the Union County Clerk at 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth (908-527-4787). The recording office keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30, takes over-the-counter filings until 3:30, and needs no appointment. Online land records cover June 1, 1977 onward, and a free property fraud alert program emails or calls subscribers when their name shows up on a recorded document.

At a median value of $419,700, a typical Linden sale falls in the state's schedule for prices above $350,000, where the rate rises in steps with the price. Residential deeds above $1 million also carry a percentage fee. The seller bears both charges.

When does a cash purchase suit a Linden house?

When the house needs work, has tenants, or must close by a fixed date. Paying cash as-is takes repair requests and mortgage approval out of the schedule. A listing can still bring a higher price for a house in good condition, since it reaches owner-occupants and investors.

The seller. It is calculated on the deed price and paid when the Union County Clerk records the deed. Sales over $1 million add a graduated percent fee, also on the seller.

Speed depends on who buys and on city paperwork. Without mortgage underwriting a cash deal can move sooner, but deed recording and any required city certificate still take their own time.

How quickly can a Lodi house change hands?

Three routes exist: a retail listing, a for-sale-by-owner deal, or a purchase by an investor who pays cash and takes the house in its present state. The third route is usually the shortest in Lodi, because the borough's older housing needs work that a conventional buyer's lender may question.

A handful of items under your control set the real pace. Having them ready before you sign a contract trims days off the schedule.

  • A clean title and the recorded deed, plus finished estate paperwork if the owner has died.
  • The borough's resale certificate application, begun early because inspections need appointments.
  • Tax bills paid up and old building permits closed.
  • A decision on tenants: empty house at closing, or leases transferred to the buyer.

What is Lodi like for someone selling a home?

Lodi packs into 2.27 square miles of land in Bergen County, around 11,500 residents per square mile by the 2020 count. Voters created the borough on December 22, 1894, in the burst of borough-making that swept Bergen County, and mills along the Saddle River drew immigrant workers. Dye and chemical plants replaced the old textile works after the 1940s.

Many buyers commute. Route 17, U.S. Route 46 and Interstate 80 cross the borough, and NJ Transit routes 144, 161 and 164 carry riders to midtown Manhattan. Felician University has its campus in Lodi, and Lodi Public Schools run seven schools from pre-K to grade 12, among them Thomas Jefferson Middle School and Lodi High School. Bergen Arts and Science Charter School also enrolls Lodi students, and every Bergen County district can send students to the selective Bergen County Technical Schools programs. Immaculate Conception High School, an all-girls Catholic school founded in 1915, closed after the 2022-23 year.

Inspectors raise one local issue early: parts of the borough flood in heavy rain. Expect buyers to ask about wet basements and drainage, and keep any repair invoices where you can find them.

What does the Census Bureau record about housing in Lodi?

The Bureau's QuickFacts profile shows a borough where tenants outnumber owner-occupants, which shapes who sells and who buys.

  • The 2025 estimate is 26,187 people, nearly level with the 26,206 counted in 2020.
  • Only 42.4 percent of housing units are lived in by their owners (five-year survey ending 2024).
  • The middle value of a home that its owner occupies is $475,000, and the middle gross rent is $1,714.
  • Household income sits at a midpoint of $89,305.
  • About 39.5 percent of residents were born abroad, and 55.0 percent of those aged five and over speak another language at home.

In practice, many Lodi properties are one- and two-family houses with a rental unit, so buyers include small investors and families who plan to live in one apartment and rent out the other.

The borough's Zoning Department issues permits for use and occupancy, and its forms list includes a Resale/New Tenant Certificate application. Call that office before listing to learn whether your sale needs the certificate and what the inspection covers, so a failed item does not push the closing date.

Rental owners face a second layer. The Fire Prevention Bureau inspects one- and two-family homes that the owner rents out rather than occupies, and it bills fees under the state fire code. If you are selling a landlord property, ask whether that inspection record is current.

New Jersey bills the seller for a realty transfer fee at the moment the deed goes on record. The Division of Taxation posts the rate table on its Realty Transfer Fee page, and a surcharge applies to sales above $1,000,000, beginning at one percent of the price.

Each seller also gives the settlement agent a GIT/REP form. A New Jersey resident signs the residency certification, known as GIT/REP-3. An owner who lives out of state, as many Lodi landlords do, files a different form and prepays income tax equal to no less than two percent of the sale price unless a listed exemption fits.

The Bergen County Clerk records the deed. Ask that office for its present recording charges, and have your attorney or title agent produce a written payoff and settlement statement ahead of the closing day.

How do Lodi property taxes and appeals work?

The assessor values each property as of October 1 of the preceding year. An owner who thinks the figure is too high can appeal annually before April 1; the borough says to phone the Bergen County Board of Taxation at (201) 336-6300 once the February postcard arrives and ask for a Petition to Appeal.

Improvements get assessed even without a permit. When an added assessment bill arrives, the borough says you must pay it in full whatever your view, and the window to appeal that bill closes December 1.

Before closing, ask the tax collector for the current-quarter payoff. Quarterly bills come due at the start of February, May, August and November, and the attorney splits the open quarter between you and the buyer.

Begin with the basement and the lot, since drainage is the first thing an inspector probes in a borough where heavy rain floods low spots. Collect receipts for sump pumps, waterproofing, boiler service and roof work, and find the paperwork for past permits.

The assessor's office compares building permits with its records, and unpermitted work can still be assessed. Closing out old permits before you list prevents a surprise during the buyer's attorney review and gives a cash buyer less reason to cut an offer.

When is a cash buyer the right choice for a Lodi house?

Cash suits a property that needs more repair than a retail buyer will finance, an inherited house, or a building with tenants, liens or a damp basement that would stall a listing. A well-kept home with time on your side usually earns more through a listing, since cash offers price in the buyer's repair costs and risk.

Get at least one cash offer and compare it with an agent's estimate of list price minus commission and repairs. Ask each buyer who covers recording costs, whether the offer is as-is, and how tenants and open permits would be handled.

Lodi's Zoning Department issues a Resale/New Tenant Certificate and posts the application among its forms. Phone the department before listing to find out whether your property needs one.

Appeals go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation before April 1 each year. A separate bill for an added assessment can be appealed until December 1.

The seller covers it. Your closing attorney can quote the exact amount, since the state's table depends on the price.

Can I sell a Lodi house with tenants inside?

Yes, either with the tenants in place or empty. For a one- or two-family rental owned by someone who lives elsewhere, make sure the Fire Prevention Bureau inspection is current before closing.

Will flooding history hurt a Lodi sale?

It can lower offers, so disclose what you know. Parts of the borough take on water in heavy rain, and cash buyers typically accept the condition without demanding repairs.

What is the shortest path to a sale in Long Branch?

The shortest path skips the lender's appraisal and the repair list: a buyer who pays cash and accepts the property as it stands. An agent listing also works in this shore city, though the city's own inspection step, described below, adds days to any sale that transfers title.

Line up these pieces before you accept an offer, since they are what most often slows a Long Branch closing.

  • Property tax paid through the current quarter, with a printout from the tax office.
  • Sewer charges paid to the current quarter at the Long Branch Sewerage Authority.
  • A sign-off from the Building Department that no construction permits are open.
  • Smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a fire extinguisher that meet the city's rules.

What is Long Branch like as a place to sell?

Long Branch sits on the Monmouth County shoreline with 5.12 square miles of land and 1.16 of water. It was formed as the Long Branch Commission on April 11, 1867 and incorporated as a city on April 8, 1903. It grew as a seaside resort in the late 1700s and drew seven U.S. presidents during the Gilded Age; Seven Presidents Oceanfront Park carries that history.

Neighborhood names buyers use include Pier Village and the oceanfront, Downtown, Uptown, the North End, West End, Elberon, Branchport, Hollywood, Kensington Park and Pleasure Bay. Elberon has its own train stop, and the main Long Branch station sits three blocks from the beach on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line.

Route 36 and Route 71 are the main highways. Local NJ Transit buses 831 and 837 run in the city, and Academy Bus serves New York City on its Route 36 and Shore Points lines. The city's public schools run pre-kindergarten through grade 12 across eight schools and are one of the state's former Abbott districts.

How does the shore climate affect a Long Branch house?

Summers are humid with an afternoon sea breeze, and winters bring nor'easters. Precipitation averages about 52.5 inches a year, August runs wettest, and a typical snow season delivers 18 to 24 inches. A buyer's inspector will look hard at roofs, siding, windows and basements for the wear that salt air and storm water cause.

Hurricane Sandy struck on October 29, 2012. Long Branch avoided the worst of the surge compared with barrier-island towns, but flooding still occurred, many residents lost power for up to two weeks, and the boardwalk was destroyed before it reopened in April 2016. If your house took water then, keep repair records and any elevation or flood insurance paperwork, because buyers ask for them.

Who lives in Long Branch homes, according to the Census Bureau?

The QuickFacts profile for Long Branch describes a growing city where renters are the majority.

  • The 2025 estimate of 33,321 residents is 5.3 percent above the April 2020 base.
  • Owners occupy 42.5 percent of homes.
  • A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $574,000.
  • A typical rent runs $1,876 a month.
  • The city counts 13,140 households of about 2.45 people each.
  • Workers spend 29.6 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

Those figures explain why small investors and landlords are common sellers here. The 2020 census counted 14,944 housing units with 17.1 percent vacant, so a fair number of houses and apartments sit empty at any given time.

What does Long Branch require before a sale closes?

The Fire Marshal's office issues the Residential Certificate of Compliance under city ordinance 262-25. For a one- or two-family home, a Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Portable Fire Extinguisher certificate is required on a change of occupancy or transfer of title, and the compliance certificate itself is required before a change of occupancy. The application packet says both forms apply to one- and two-family homes.

The packet also says an inspector will not inspect a unit while it is occupied. Plan the inspection for the vacant window between tenants or after you move out.

Can a buyer purchase a Long Branch house as-is?

Yes. The Fire Marshal publishes a Letter of Intent for Purchase of a Building in As-Is Condition. The buyer circles 30, 60 or 90 days to make repairs, accepts responsibility for permits, and agrees that nobody occupies the building until the Fire Prevention Bureau inspects it and issues a Certificate of Compliance.

That form is useful if your house has deferred maintenance. It lets a cash buyer close first and complete the repairs afterward, while still satisfying the city.

Rentals changed in 2026. Ordinance 16-26, adopted July 22, 2026, amends section 262-25 to require that rentals of one- to four-family dwellings run a minimum of 60 days. Investors planning short stays should read it before buying.

What if tenants live in the Long Branch house you want to sell?

Tell the buyer early. The compliance application asks for the type of occupancy (rental, sale or owner re-occupy), requires every lease to be attached, and lists the prospective occupants. Names of occupants can be changed only within two weeks of the inspection date, after which a new application must be filed.

Because the inspector will not enter an occupied unit, a seller with a tenant in place usually has to wait until the lease ends or negotiate a move-out date. A buyer who plans to keep the tenant may prefer to complete the as-is letter and handle the certificate after closing. Either way, agree on the sequence in the contract so no one is surprised by a $95 fee or a missed appointment.

How do Long Branch taxes and appeals work for sellers?

Installments come due at the start of February, May, August and November. The collector allows ten days before interest runs, records the day a payment arrives instead of its postmark, and wants the block and lot written on every payment. Checks go in a secure box at 344 Broadway, or you can pay online.

Monmouth County follows an alternate assessment calendar, so the appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. The Division of Taxation lists the Monmouth County Board of Taxation at 732-431-7404. The city lists the state's property tax reimbursement (senior freeze) and homestead rebate programs, which are aimed at owners who live in the home.

The seller also pays the state's transfer fee when the closing agent records the deed, and the agent collects a GIT/REP form. Yes for the compliance application. The packet requires a Building Department form stating there are no open construction permits on the property.

Can I rent my Long Branch house for a weekend?

Not under the 2026 change. Ordinance 16-26, adopted July 22, 2026, requires rentals of one- to four-family dwellings to run at least 60 days.

By what date must a Long Branch tax appeal be filed?

By January 15, because Monmouth County runs an alternate assessment calendar. Confirm the date with the county board of taxation for your filing year.

Yes. Use the city's as-is letter of intent so the buyer takes 30, 60 or 90 days to complete repairs, and the Certificate of Compliance is issued before anyone occupies the house.

What should I know before selling a house in Millville, NJ?

Millville is a Cumberland County city where the main local rule for a seller concerns tenants. Roughly 36 percent of occupied homes are rented, so many sales involve a registered rental unit, and the city's registration and inspection code shapes what a buyer inherits.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate puts Millville at 28,098 residents, and its 2020 to 2024 survey counts 11,845 households averaging 2.30 people. Owner occupancy is 64.1 percent, the median owner value is $219,000, and median gross rent is $1,261. Median household income is $70,275, and 20.2 percent of residents are 65 or older. With a median value that low, comparable Cumberland County sales matter more to your price than any statewide average.

How did Millville grow into the city it is today?

Millville was incorporated as a township on February 24, 1801, from part of Fairfield Township, and became a city on March 1, 1866 after a referendum. The name comes from a proposal for a mill town on the Maurice River. Sawmills came first, then in 1806 an Irish immigrant opened the first glass factory, drawing on local silica sand and wood. Millville roses, a style of paperweight, take their name from the city.

The city covers 44.50 square miles, 42.00 of them land, and borders Commercial, Deerfield, Downe, Fairfield, Lawrence and Maurice River townships plus Vineland. Clarks Mill, Farmingdale, Manatico, North Newark and Union Lake are named places inside the city lines. In 1936 the city opened Roosevelt Park, the country's first retirement colony for older residents, on land it had repossessed for back taxes. Millville Army Air Field opened in January 1943 as a gunnery school and later returned to the city as Millville Airport.

What happens when a Millville house has tenants?

Chapter 11, Article VII of the Millville code requires every residential rental unit, single family homes included, to be registered and inspected each year and again with each change in occupancy. No one may live in an unregistered unit. After a satisfactory inspection the city issues a certificate of continued occupancy, and none is issued while violations remain open.

An owner who lives outside Cumberland County must name an agent who lives or works in the county. The lease must say it is subject to city ordinances, and at a change of occupancy the owner hands over the state Truth in Renting guide. If you are selling a tenant-occupied house, ask the Bureau of Permits and Inspections for the registration status before you list.

How do roads, jobs and local attractions compare in Millville?

Workers in Millville average 25.2 minutes getting to their jobs, by the Census count. The city sits between the southern ends of the New Jersey Turnpike, the Garden State Parkway, Route 55 and the Atlantic City Expressway.

  • Roads: Routes 47, 49 and 55 cross the city, and 172.73 miles of roadway are split among the city, Cumberland County and the state.
  • Transit: NJ Transit bus routes 313 from Cape May to Philadelphia, 408 between Millville and Philadelphia, and 553 toward Atlantic City.
  • Air: Millville Airport, run by the Delaware River and Bay Authority, serves general aviation.
  • Culture and recreation: the Glasstown Arts District, Wheaton Arts, the Levoy Theatre (reopened September 2012), New Jersey Motorsports Park and Laurel Lake.

Rowan College of South Jersey, Cumberland Campus, sits partly inside the city limits.

How do Millville schools and weather affect a listing?

Millville Public Schools run nine schools with 5,107 students in 2021-22, among them Lakeside Middle School and Millville Senior High School with 1,638 students. The district is one of the state's former Abbott districts, which means the Schools Development Authority covers its building projects. A $137 million expansion that began in 2019 adds 82,000 square feet at the high school so every high schooler can attend in one building. Commercial, Lawrence and Maurice River townships send their high school students here, and the Cumberland County Technical Education Center in Millville is tuition free for county residents.

The climate is humid subtropical, with 43.37 inches of precipitation in an average year. January lows average near 24 degrees, the record high is 103 and the record low is minus 10. Roofs, gutters and crawlspace drainage get the closest look in an inspection after a wet stretch.

How do Millville taxes, appeals and the transfer fee work?

The Millville Tax Collector bills on a calendar year, mails bills in mid to late July, and each bill has four stubs for August, November, February and May. The city allows a 10-day grace period, and the collector cannot honor postmarks, so a payment must arrive by the 10th. Interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent above that, with a 6 percent year-end penalty on balances over $10,000 left on June 30. Charges unpaid on the 11th day of the 11th month are delinquent and subject to the annual tax sale.

Cumberland County's Board of Taxation takes regular appeals from the first business day of January through April 1 at 4:00 PM, with no exceptions for lateness. In a town revalued for the current year the window runs to May 1, and added or omitted assessments can be appealed from October 1 through December 1.

The seller also owes the state's Realty Transfer Fee at recording. At the Census median of $219,000, the state's rates for sales up to $350,000 work out to $1,083.20: $600 on the first $150,000, $335 on the next $50,000 and $148.20 on the remaining $19,000.

Where does a Millville deed get recorded?

A Millville deed is recorded with the Cumberland County Clerk, which keeps an office in Bridgeton and another at the Cumberland Mall. Ask the clerk's office for the current recording fee and cover sheet requirements before closing day, and ask your closing agent who files the deed and settles the transfer fee.

What does Millville charge to register a rental house?

Millville charges $100 per unit each year, rising to $125 when paid late. A single family house that is rented counts as a unit, and added inspections or short-notice cancellations cost $50 each.

When is the Cumberland County appeal deadline for a Millville assessment?

The regular deadline is April 1 at 4:00 PM, and the county says there are no exceptions for lateness. When April 1 falls on a weekend the deadline moves to the next business day, and a municipality revalued that year gets until May 1.

When do Millville property taxes become delinquent?

Bills are due on August, November, February and May stubs with a 10-day grace period. Charges still owed on the 11th day of the 11th month are treated as delinquent and can go to the city's annual tax sale.

Do tenants have to move out before a Millville sale?

Nothing in the city's rental registration rules requires it. The city requires the unit to stay registered and inspected at each change in occupancy, so the new owner must keep that registration current for anyone who stays.

How large is the state transfer fee on a typical Millville sale?

At the Census median value of $219,000 the fee comes to $1,083.20 under the state's schedule for sales up to $350,000. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded, and exemptions exist for deeds between spouses or from parent to child.
