Which routes get a New Brunswick house sold fast?

Three paths are open to a New Brunswick owner. An agent listing reaches the most buyers, a private sale saves the fee, and a direct as-is purchase trades some price for speed. Whichever you pick, the deed is recorded at the Middlesex County Clerk's office on Bayard Street, inside the city.

This is a renter city. An owner-occupied rate of just 21.4% for 2020 to 2024, spread over 15,676 households of about 3.13 people each. A sale here often involves a house with tenants or a landlord seller, so the rental rules covered below matter as much as the repair list.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, though showings, repairs and a lender's timetable come with it.
  • Private sale: no commission, but you still need an attorney, a deed and the municipal paperwork.
  • As-is purchase: often no lender and a closing date you set, with the house taken in its current state.

What is New Brunswick like as a place to sell?

New Brunswick holds 5.23 square miles of land along the Raritan River in Middlesex County. Across the water sit Piscataway, Highland Park and Edison, while North Brunswick, East Brunswick and Somerset County's Franklin Township share its other borders. A July 2025 estimate of 57,133 people.

The first European settlement dates to 1681, and the name New Brunswick arrived in 1714. A town charter in 1736 became a city charter in 1784. Rutgers began as Queen's College in 1766 and settled here in 1771, and Old Queens, finished in 1811, remains the oldest building on campus.

Residents refer to the Fifth Ward, Feaster Park, Lincoln Park, Raritan Gardens and Edgebrook-Westons Mills. When you describe your house to a buyer, naming the section it sits in gives a clearer picture than the street address alone. Winters bring about 29 inches of snow a season with roughly 50 inches of total precipitation a year, so clear gutters and check the roof before the first showing.

Who looks for homes in New Brunswick?

Hospital staff, students and commuters make up much of the demand. City Hall promotes the Health Care City nickname, and Johnson & Johnson keeps its global headquarters here beside several medical teaching and research institutions. Rutgers has three campuses inside city limits, and Robert Wood Johnson Medical School spans New Brunswick and Piscataway.

Commuting also shapes who looks at a house. Residents spend 23.3 minutes getting to work on average, and the city sits on the Northeast Corridor rail line between New York and Trenton. Route 18, U.S. 1 and Route 27 cross the city, and a short piece of the New Jersey Turnpike touches it.

Schools matter to families. The New Brunswick Public Schools run 12 schools with about 9,690 students, are one of the former Abbott districts, and include a health sciences high school tied to a teaching hospital. The Greater Brunswick Charter School serves grades K to 8, and eighth graders countywide can apply to the Middlesex County magnet schools.

  • Hospital and university staff looking for a short commute.
  • Landlords weighing a rental house against the city's rent control rules.
  • Households who want rail access to Penn Station.

What local steps come before a New Brunswick closing?

Begin with the alarm check. New Brunswick's Division of Fire Safety inspects smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms in one and two family houses being sold or leased, and it offers an online form for booking the visit. Schedule it early so a dead battery does not push the closing back.

The Construction Department, at 25 Kirkpatrick Street, also issues a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy for situations where the city calls for one. Phone 732-745-5075 and ask whether your sale needs it, since the answer depends on the property and its permit history.

If tenants live in the house, read the Rent Control Ordinance before you list. Most rental units in the city are regulated, and each regulated unit must register by April 1 every year. Owners of unregistered units face summonses and fines, so confirm your registration status with the Rent Control office first.

How does rent control affect the price of a New Brunswick rental?

It sets a ceiling on income. Rents may rise only by the yearly allowance unless the unit has an approved vacancy decontrol or is exempt, so the rent roll you show is the figure a buyer will underwrite.

What does the state take from a New Brunswick seller?

The seller pays the state's realty transfer fee when the deed is filed. It climbs in bands as the price rises, and above $350,000 a second schedule begins that reaches $4.80 for each $500 of price in the $200,000 to $550,000 band.

The middle owner-occupied value in the city at $353,800, just over that $350,000 line, so many local sales fall into the higher schedule. The settlement statement from your closing attorney will show the exact fee.

An owner who lives out of state faces one more step. At closing the seller prepays at least two percent of the deed price toward New Jersey income tax, unless an assurance on form GIT/REP-3 applies. Who records a New Brunswick deed, and what must it show?

Filings go to the Middlesex County Clerk's registry on the fourth floor of the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 until 4:10, though the last arrivals are taken at 4 pm. The main line is 732-745-3002, and walk-ins are welcome, with appointments served first.

  • Everything must be legible English, properly acknowledged, with original signatures and printed names.
  • A deed carries the drafter's name after the words Prepared by, plus tax block, lot and the price.
  • A return address is required.
  • Paper filings need a cover sheet or the county adds a $20 indexing charge.

Attorneys and title companies can also submit electronically at any hour through the county's e-recording portal. Owners worried about fraud on an empty house can sign up for the clerk's email alerts, which announce any document recorded against their block and lot.

Can a New Brunswick house be sold while tenants are still in it?

Yes. A sale does not end a tenancy. Keep your rent control registration current and have each lease and the rent history on hand, because regulated units register by April 1 every year and unregistered ones risk fines.

Is an inspection required before selling a small home in New Brunswick?

At minimum a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm check through the Division of Fire Safety for one and two family houses. Call the Construction Department at 732-745-5075 to learn whether a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy is also needed.

Which office files the deed after a New Brunswick sale?

The Middlesex County Clerk's registry, in the County Administration Building on Bayard Street. Your closing attorney or title company usually submits it, either on paper or electronically.

I own the house but live in another state. What changes?

You complete a GIT/REP form at the closing table. A nonresident seller prepays at least two percent of the deed price toward state income tax unless the GIT/REP-3 assurances apply, and can request a refund later if less is owed.

What would the transfer fee be on a $350,000 New Brunswick sale?

The lower schedule applies at exactly $350,000: $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 up to $200,000, then $3.90 per $500 on the rest. One dollar over that figure moves the whole sale to the higher schedule.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Newark?

Pick the route that removes the most waiting. For one owner that means a buyer paying cash with no lender in the way, and for another it means a listing priced to move. How does Newark's geography shape a sale?

Newark covers 24.14 square miles of land plus 1.74 of water, and it leads the Gateway Region in size. The ground drops from about 230 feet above sea level in the west to the tidal flats in the east, and the whole city behaves like a basin draining to the Passaic River. In earlier generations the ridges, such as Forest Hill, High Street and Weequahic, drew the wealthier households.

Across its borders lie Belleville, Bloomfield, East Orange, Irvington, Maplewood and South Orange in Essex County, Bayonne, East Newark, Harrison, Jersey City and Kearny in Hudson County, and Elizabeth and Hillside in Union County. Major streets spoke outward from downtown, and a few are named for their destinations, among them Springfield Avenue and Bloomfield Avenue. The city itself maintains 318.77 of its roughly 368 miles of roadway, which means a pothole or sidewalk complaint on your block usually goes to city hall, while the highways belong to the state, the county or the Turnpike Authority.

A Connecticut Puritan colony settled the site in 1666. The royal charter came in 1713 and city status in 1836. Rapid industrial growth after that left a great many older blocks, so expect a buyer's inspector to study roofs, wiring and heating systems closely.

Which Newark neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Buyers think in wards first and neighborhood names second, and Newark has five wards.

  • Central: University Heights, beside NJIT, Rutgers-Newark, Essex County College and the medical school.
  • North: Branch Brook Park is the anchor, with Mount Pleasant, Upper Roseville and the Forest Hill Historic District, known for its older mansions.
  • West: Vailsburg, Ivy Hill, West Side and Fairmount.
  • South: Weequahic, Clinton Hill, Dayton and South Broad Valley.
  • East: Downtown plus the Ironbound, dense with apartment buildings, rowhouses and restaurants.

The airport, seaport and heavy industry cluster in the East and South wards. Most homes sit in the North, Central and West wards. When you advertise, say which ward the house is in and what surrounds it.

Work and rail. Over 100,000 workers travel into the city on a typical weekday, giving Newark the biggest job base in New Jersey across insurance, finance, healthcare, law and government. Port Newark handles more cargo than any other terminal in the Port of New York and New Jersey, and part of Newark Liberty International Airport lies within city lines. At Newark Penn Station riders can change between PATH, three NJ Transit rail lines and Amtrak, and the Newark Light Rail runs from there to the northern neighborhoods, Belleville and Bloomfield.

Workers who live here average 32.6 minutes to their jobs, and about 40% of households own no car, so say how far the house is from a station. Newark Public Schools is the state's largest district, with 65 schools and 40,423 students in 2020-21, and it counts among the former Abbott districts.

Every rented unit in the city has to be registered with the Department of Economic and Housing Development. A unit that passes earns a Certificate of Habitability, the document that allows it to be rented. One that fails must stay unleased until the problems are corrected, and the certificate can be suspended or revoked for overcrowding or danger. Lead service lines have been a problem in Newark's water system, and the city hired a contractor to replace them at many properties. Ask the water department what material the service line is at your address, since a buyer's inspector may bring it up.

Can a Newark house with open code violations still be sold?

How can a Paramus owner get a house sold fast?

Three routes lead to a closing here: an agent listing, a private sale, or an investor who takes a house left as is. All three finish at the same borough inspection and the same deed filings, so what changes is the amount of preparation you do first.

Paramus is a borough in central Bergen County, roughly 15 to 20 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan. The borough is best known for its two retail corridors along Routes 4 and 17, yet it is also a suburban bedroom community of New York City. To compare the routes, start with this short list:

  • Check whether any permit for past work on the house is still open at the Building Department.
  • Decide whether you can wait for a conventional buyer's financing and inspection period.
  • Locate the deed, a payoff letter from your lender and, if you inherited, the estate papers.
  • Have a closing attorney confirm which deed forms the sale needs.

Skipping the marketing stage saves weeks. The borough's Certificate of Compliance stays in the path, and Paramus describes it as mandatory for closings.

What sets Paramus apart as a place to sell a house?

Paramus covers 10.5 square miles and was incorporated in April 1922 after it split off from Midland Township, which is now Rochelle Park. It was farm country until the 1950s, when the George Washington Bridge and wider Routes 4 and 17 pulled in shopping centers. Garden State Plaza sits where those two routes cross, and the Census Bureau reports 2022 retail sales in the borough of about $5.45 billion.

The borough names five residential areas: Arcola, Bergen Place, Dunkerhook, Fairway Oaks and Spring Valley. Van Saun County Park (146 acres, with the county zoo) lies on the east side, and Saddle River County Park runs along the west side with a six-mile bike path. Paramus Public Schools run eight schools from pre-kindergarten through grade 12, and Bergen Community College has its main campus in the borough.

Most trips here are by car. The borough counts 121.92 miles of road, including Route 17, Route 4 and Garden State Parkway Interchange 165, and NJ Transit buses reach the Port Authority Bus Terminal and the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. Sellers who live near the highways should expect buyers to ask about traffic noise and commute time, since the Census puts the mean trip to work at 30.8 minutes.

How do Paramus homes and households measure up in Census data?

Paramus skews toward owners and high values: more than four in five homes are occupied by their owners. Treat these Census Bureau numbers as a borough-wide picture rather than a price for any single street.

What does Paramus require before my house can close?

Paramus requires a Certificate of Compliance for any resale or rental, and the borough states that this certificate is mandatory for closings. The Building Department asks sellers to confirm first that every earlier permit has been closed out, then file an application with a $100 fee for a sale.

After the application is accepted, an inspector visits. Resale inspections run weekday mornings from 9:00 to 12:00, and someone needs to be at the house to let the inspector in. The borough's guidelines list what gets checked:

  • Smoke alarms on every level and near bedrooms, plus carbon monoxide detectors near sleeping areas, following the borough's NFPA-based guidelines.
  • A permanent label within 18 inches of the electrical panel and meter if the house has solar panels, a generator or battery storage.
  • The street number visible from the street on the mailbox, front door or garage.
  • Borough-issued garbage and recycling containers on the property with their serial numbers.
  • A fence around any pool.

Open permits cause the most delays. Unpermitted renovations must be permitted and inspected before the certificate is released, and permitted jobs lacking a final inspection hold up the Certificate of Occupancy. The guidelines also ask that open permits be closed a full week ahead of the resale inspection. Call the Building Department at 201-265-2100, extension 2230, for the current process.

Which state charges follow a Paramus sale?

The seller carries the Realty Transfer Fee, which the county collects at recording. The Division of Taxation steps the charge from $2.90 to $6.05 for each $500 of price on sales above $350,000, and a Graduated Percent Fee is layered on once a sale passes $1,000,000. Your closing attorney or title agent can turn the schedule into a dollar figure for your deed.

Estate sales are one common exemption: an executor's deed to an heir following a will is excused, as is a deed between parent and child. Form RTF-1 goes on record with the deed for any seller claiming relief.

Recording also requires a GIT/REP form under N.J.S.A. 54A:8-9, so the State can tell whether a seller living outside New Jersey owes prepaid income tax. Whoever signs the deed completes it, and only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trustee sales are left out.

Does a Paramus seller have to disclose flooding?

Yes. Beginning March 20, 2024, the property condition disclosure statement has to carry flood answers before a buyer is committed to the contract: whether the lot falls inside a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and whatever flood history you personally know.

The Department of Environmental Protection runs a Flood Risk Notification Tool that helps sellers look up the answers. Check your own parcel on that tool instead of assuming the answer. Cash buyers and conventional buyers receive the same disclosure.

How are Paramus property taxes set, and how do I contest them?

Every New Jersey county assesses at 100 percent of market value as of October 1, and the local rate applied to that figure produces your bill. Because Paramus lies in Bergen County, contested assessments go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation.

  • Filing: Form A-1, in the board's hands by April 1.
  • After a revaluation: the cutoff moves to May 1.
  • Large assessments: above $1,000,000 can skip to the State Tax Court.
  • Next level: 45 days to take a board ruling to the Tax Court.

The burden is yours: prove the figure is out of line with market value or with the district's common level range. Ask the Paramus tax collector for your payoff and quarterly status before closing, so any open installment is cleared at the closing table and the buyer inherits no surprise.

Frequently asked questions

Is a borough certificate really required to close a sale in Paramus?

Yes. The borough treats the resale Certificate of Compliance as mandatory at closing. The seller applies to the Building Department, pays $100 and passes the inspection.

What happens if I made changes to the house without permits?

The resale certificate is withheld until the missing permits are applied for and the work is inspected. Permitted work that never received a final inspection holds up the Certificate of Occupancy.

Is the New Jersey transfer fee my bill in Paramus?

The seller. It is a state charge on the seller at recording, sized by the price brackets on the Division of Taxation schedule.

At what point must a buyer receive flood information?

Before the buyer is committed to the purchase contract. The statement covers FEMA flood zone status and any flood problems the seller knows about.

How late can I file a Paramus assessment appeal?

April 1, or May 1 following a revaluation or reassessment, and the petition must reach the county board by then. Ask the Bergen County Board of Taxation for the form and current filing steps.

Selling for cash as the house stands is usually the shortest path, since it drops repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval. A listing or private sale takes longer, yet every route has to clear the city's occupancy certificate and fire certification before closing.

Passaic is dense, and many buildings hold more than one unit. Census Bureau data shows owners living in just 23.8 percent of homes, so sellers here are often landlords, heirs, or owners of condos and co-ops. Whichever you are, sort out these items first:

  • The deed and the block and lot numbers, which every city application asks for.
  • Tenant leases and rent rolls, if any unit is occupied.
  • Mortgage payoff figures and any open municipal charges.
  • The name the buyer will take title in, because Passaic issues the occupancy certificate under the buyer's name.

What should I know about Passaic as a place to sell?

Passaic sits on the west bank of the Passaic River, 10 miles from New York City and 12 miles from Newark Airport. It covers 3.13 square miles of land, with 71,337 residents counted in the 2025 estimate, about 22,500 for every square mile. Clifton wraps around it on the north, south and west, and six bridges carry traffic across the river toward Wallington, Garfield and Rutherford.

Dutch traders settled the area in 1679 under the name Acquackanonk, and the city and river take their name from a Lenape word often read as valley or place where the land splits. It became an independent village in 1871 and was chartered as a city in April 1873, growing into a textile and metalworking center. Main Avenue follows the river from Passaic Park to downtown, and Broadway crosses the city east to west. Passaic Park is known for its large park and larger homes in Queen Anne and Tudor styles, along with condominium towers and garden co-ops.

Industry shaped the street grid. The Okonite company ran its wire plant here from 1878 to 1993, supplying insulated cable for early telegraph lines and for Thomas Edison's first generating station in Lower Manhattan, and 36,000 mill workers walked out in the 1926 textile strike. Experimental television broadcasts began from the city in 1931. Condominium and co-op owners in Passaic Park, in complexes such as the 21-floor Carlton Tower and the post-war Barry Gardens garden apartments, should ask their association what documents a buyer needs. Passaic Park today holds an Orthodox Jewish community of more than 1,300 families, with over 20 yeshivas and other institutions and many kosher food shops, and Main Avenue reflects a growing Latino population. The city's inspection steps below apply to every sale, whoever the buyer is.

The Passaic City School District runs 17 schools and enrolled about 14,500 students in 2018-19, and Passaic County Community College opened a campus in the city in 2008. Route 21 is the main road, and the Passaic rail station on NJ Transit's Main Line serves Hoboken and Secaucus Junction. Local and Port Authority buses stop at the Passaic Bus Terminal, and jitneys run along Main Avenue.

What does the City of Passaic require before a sale?

A sale in Passaic needs two approvals: an occupancy certificate, and a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. The one-family application, filed with the Division of Housing under Inspections and Code, asks for the seller's details and the buyer's name, because the certificate is issued to the buyer. Companies buying through an LLC or corporation must supply the registered agent and the certificate of formation.

  • Certificate fee: $65 on the one-family application, with an expedite option at $300.
  • Inspection and violation reports are emailed to both seller and buyer, and extra copies require an OPRA request.
  • Fire Prevention charges $45 for the first smoke and carbon monoxide inspection and $25 for a reinspection.
  • The fire certification stays valid for three months and covers only the buyer named on it.

The fire inspector looks for a smoke detector on each level, detectors and a carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, working units, and a fire extinguisher within ten feet of the kitchen. A 90-day temporary certification is available when items fail. The city notes that the occupancy certificate says the property meets Passaic's zoning and property maintenance laws and does not replace construction permits or health approvals. Condo, one, two and three family homes all use the fire form.

What state fees and forms apply to a Passaic sale?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee lands on the seller at recording. A home valued at the Census median of $429,900 lands above the $350,000 line, where the rate starts at $2.90 per $500 of price. Sales at or below $350,000 pay $2.00, $3.35 or $3.90 per $500 in steps. Passaic sellers who inherit a house from a parent, or who deed to a child, usually qualify for an exemption, which is claimed on a notarized Form RTF-1 recorded with the deed.

The GIT/REP form rides along with the deed as well, telling the State whether a seller living out of state must prepay income tax. Whoever signs the deed completes it.

Flood disclosure has been mandatory since March 20, 2024. Passaic is hemmed in by the river on one side, so look up the FEMA zone for your lot with the DEP Flood Risk Notification Tool and answer the disclosure statement questions before the buyer is bound.

How are Passaic property taxes appealed?

An owner who thinks the city's figure is too high files Form A-1 with the Passaic County Board of Taxation. The board must have it by April 1, or by May 1 where Passaic has carried out a revaluation or reassessment.

Proof is on the owner: the assessment must be shown unreasonable against market value or the district's common level range. Anything assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court, and a county board decision can be carried to that court within 45 days. The city tax collector can supply your balance and open charges, and the county board can tell you where to deliver the petition and how its hearings are scheduled.

The buyer's. The city's one-family application says it issues the certificate under the buyer's name, and an LLC buyer must supply its registered agent and certificate of formation.

What does the Passaic occupancy certificate cost?

The one-family application lists a $65 certificate fee, plus a $300 expedite charge if you need faster handling.

How long does the fire certification last?

Three months from approval, and only for the person named on it. When the inspection finds problems, a 90-day temporary certification can be issued.

Does the seller cover the state transfer fee in Passaic?

Yes. The State bills the seller at recording, and the fee steps up with the sale price.

Where does a Passaic owner take an assessment appeal?

To the Passaic County Board of Taxation, by April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation. Owners above $1,000,000 in assessed value may skip ahead to Tax Court.

Can a Paterson house be sold without waiting on a listing?

A cash offer on a house left in its current state skips repairs and showings, while a listing or direct sale takes more time. Paterson adds its own layers for vacant buildings, rent leveling and certificates of occupancy, so learn which apply before you choose a route.

Paterson serves as Passaic County's seat and its largest municipality, home to 161,793 people in the 2025 Census estimate and spread over 8.41 square miles of land. Owners live in just 26.9 percent of its homes, so sellers often hold small rental buildings or inherited the property. Start with this checklist:

  • Confirm whether the property counts as vacant, which triggers a city registration.
  • Find out if tenants live there and whether the building is covered by the rent leveling ordinance.
  • Collect the deed, the payoff figure and any code violation notices.
  • Ask the Division of Community Improvements what inspection a change of occupancy needs.

What is Paterson like for people selling a home?

Paterson was founded in 1791 by the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, which wanted to run mills off the Great Falls of the Passaic River. The first plans came from Pierre L'Enfant. The city grew into Silk City in the 19th century, and after a fire in 1902 downtown was rebuilt with four to seven story Beaux-Arts buildings, including City Hall from 1894. Today the Great Falls are part of the national park system, and the Paterson Museum sits in the Great Falls Historic District.

Paterson City Hall dates to 1894 and was designed by the New York firm Carrere and Hastings after the Hotel de Ville in Lyon, the silk capital of Europe. The Passaic County Courthouse Annex stands in the same downtown. Paterson's Farmers Market operates in the Lakeview section, and many North Jersey shoppers drive in for produce. The Passaic River winds northeast past Totowa into Paterson, then turns south toward the city of Passaic and Newark, which is why riverside lots deserve a close look at the flood map.

Parks include Eastside, Westside and Pennington Parks, and Lambert Castle, built in 1892 for a silk mill owner, is a local landmark. Neighborhood character changes quickly from ward to ward. The Eastside and the Manor Section are in the 3rd Ward, Hillcrest is a largely residential area west of downtown, Lakeview sits in the south near the farmers market, and People's Park centers on Twenty-First Avenue. South Paterson is home to large Turkish and Arab communities.

Interstate 80 runs through the city, and State Routes 4, 19 and 20 serve it, with the Garden State Parkway crossing the south end. NJ Transit's Main Line train at Paterson station goes to Hoboken Terminal with a connection at Secaucus Junction, and the Broadway Bus Terminal in downtown is the end of many bus lines. Paterson Public Schools operate 43 schools with 24,692 students in 2023-24.

In August 2011 Hurricane Irene sent the Passaic River up to levels unseen in about a century, displacing thousands of people and closing river bridges. Anyone selling a riverside house should prepare an honest flood answer for the buyer.

Which Paterson city rules should a seller know?

Building, electrical, plumbing and fire inspectors enforce the state construction code in Paterson. They issue permits and final approvals, including Certificates of Occupancy and Continued Certificates of Occupancy. Inspections, licenses, permits and certificates of occupancy run through the Division of Community Improvements, and its construction code page posts weekday hours, mornings through late afternoon. The city's posted number for that division is 973-321-1232, so call for what a sale requires.

  • Vacant buildings: an owner must register a vacant building within 30 days of it becoming vacant or of taking ownership, and the annual registration fee is $2,000. The owner names a local agent aged 21 or older who can be reached at all hours.
  • Foreclosed property: a creditor must register within seven days of starting foreclosure, at $500 a year.
  • Sold or transferred property: once a vacant property is sold or transferred, the owner gives the city proof within 30 days.
  • Rent leveling: owners of covered rentals submit an annual property registration form under Chapter 381 of the municipal code, at no fee, within 30 days of receiving it.

A property can be deemed abandoned in Paterson once it has gone six months without legal occupancy and meets another test: no rehabilitation, stalled construction, an unpaid and delinquent tax installment, or a nuisance finding by the public officer. Inspectors look for signs such as boarded windows, disconnected utilities, piled-up mail and overgrown yards when they decide a building is vacant. Check with the Division of Community Improvements whether your house has been flagged, ahead of any contract.

What state fees and forms apply when a Paterson house sells?

Trenton, not City Hall, sets the Realty Transfer Fee, and the seller pays it. The rates climb in bands from $2.90 up to $6.05 per $500 for prices above $350,000, and from $2.00 up to $3.90 for prices at or below it. The Census median home value of $360,100 sits right above that $350,000 line, so ask your closing attorney for the exact dollar amount.

Sellers who are seniors, blind or disabled pay reduced bands, and the claim is made on a form recorded with the deed. An estate deed to an heir is exempt. A GIT/REP form is recorded too, signed by whoever signs the deed, so the State can tell if a seller from another state must prepay income tax.

Flood answers are required as well. Since March 20, 2024, the disclosure statement has to state the FEMA flood zone and any known flooding before the buyer signs, and the DEP offers a Flood Risk Notification Tool to help.

How can I appeal Paterson property taxes?

Appeals go to the Passaic County Board of Taxation, and the petition must be in its hands by April 1. After a citywide revaluation or reassessment the date is May 1.

The owner must show the assessment misses market value or falls outside the district's common level range, which is 15 percent either side of the average ratio. Property assessed above $1,000,000 can skip to the State Tax Court, and a county board ruling can be taken to that court within 45 days. Your balance comes from the Paterson tax collector.

Yes, when it fits the city's definition of a vacant building. Registration is due within 30 days, with a $2,000 yearly fee.

The creditor that files the foreclosure complaint registers the property within seven days, at $500 for the first year and each renewal.

The Division of Community Improvements, which enforces the Uniform Construction Code. The city's construction code page posts weekday office hours.

Raritan Bay and the Arthur Kill border this northeastern Middlesex County city, whose boundaries take in 4.66 square miles of land and 1.27 of water. About 56,739 people lived in the city by the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate, and the 2020 count worked out to 11,891 residents for every square mile of land. The code's fee schedule covers everything from one-family homes to four-family buildings.

Settlement dates to 1683, when Scottish colonists arrived, and the city served as capital of East Jersey from 1686. Its royal charter dates to August 4, 1718, and City Hall, first built as a county courthouse in 1714, is described as the oldest city hall in continuous use in the country. Victorian houses climb the hills above the waterfront, and a clay layer hundreds of feet thick under the city fed a terra cotta industry in the late 1800s.

What does the Perth Amboy Certificate of Code Compliance require?

Chapter 181 of the city code bars any transfer, conveyance or sale of a residential, commercial or industrial building until the Department of Code Enforcement issues the certificate. The inspection checks zoning, the fire safety code and substantial conformity with the property maintenance code.

The code gives sellers several ways to keep a closing on schedule:

  • A conditional certificate can run 45 days, and the Director may grant a second 45 days on request.
  • A buyer who says in writing that the purchase is as-is can receive a temporary, nonrenewable certificate good for up to six months from transfer, unless a life-safety hazard exists.
  • A certificate may issue even if the building does not match every code, provided it is in substantial compliance and safe, sound and sturdy.
  • A denial can be appealed in writing within 10 days to a three-member Certificate of Code Compliance Appeals Board.

Some transfers are exempt, including those between immediate family members, transfers through probate, sales of a building inspected or certified within the previous six months, and purchases made to demolish the building. Violations carry a fine up to $1,000, jail up to 90 days, or both, with each day counted separately. The code also lists a $25 per unit residential reinspection fee and exempts holders of a senior citizen property tax exemption from the fees. Ask Code Enforcement for current inspection charges, because the fee table printed in the code is a multi-year schedule that began in 2012.

How many Perth Amboy homes are rentals, and why does that matter?

Most of them. Only 35.4 percent of homes are occupied by their owners in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures, so renters hold the majority. Median gross rent is $1,688 and median household income is $61,977.

A buyer of a tenant-occupied building steps into the city's rent control ordinance, Chapter 353, which a Rent Leveling Board enforces. Since November 1, 2022, increases are capped at 3 percent where water is included in rent and 2.5 percent where it is not. Periodic tenants on terms shorter than a year cannot be charged an increase until the tenancy passes twelve months. Anyone pricing a sale on rent growth should work from those caps.

Half of residents (50.7 percent) were born abroad, and 79.5 percent of those aged five and up speak another language at home. With 83.6 percent of residents Hispanic or Latino, many sellers and tenants read Spanish first. The city posts its rent control information in English and Spanish, and a seller who does the same with notices will answer questions sooner.

They can, if the building stands in or beside a historic district. The Historic Preservation Commission, formed in 1993, reviews proposed changes to designated sites and structures and new construction within or next to districts, under Chapter 258 of the city code.

The historic waterfront neighborhood holds much of the old building stock, including the Proprietary House built in 1764 as a royal governor's residence, and Market Square across from City Hall. A buyer planning exterior changes in that area should expect commission review, so mention it up front when you market the house.

How do the roads and transit around Perth Amboy affect buyers?

Perth Amboy puts buyers within reach of New York and central Jersey by road and rail.

  • The Outerbridge Crossing, opened June 29, 1928, links the city to Staten Island.
  • The Victory Bridge carries Route 35 across the Raritan River to Sayreville.
  • Route 440, Route 184, County Route 501 and County Route 616 also serve the city.

Rail riders use Perth Amboy station on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line, which reaches Newark, Hoboken, Secaucus and New York Penn. Bus 116 runs to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. The Census Bureau lists a mean commute of 23.5 minutes for workers who live here.

The public school district, a former Abbott district, listed 12 schools and about 10,800 students for 2020 to 2021. The Middlesex County Magnet Schools also operate a campus in the city, and Catholic schools in the Diocese of Metuchen serve grades pre-K to 8.

How are the deed and the taxes handled for a Perth Amboy sale?

The assessor's office maintains files on over 9,500 parcels and reviews each transfer. Request a tax search and payoff from the Tax Collection office ahead of closing, and confirm the city has your current mailing address.

Deeds for Perth Amboy parcels go to the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick, where walk-in filers must arrive by 4 p.m. on weekdays. A paper deed without its cover sheet draws a $20 indexing charge, and title agents can skip the counter by filing electronically.

If the house sits in an estate, the executor signs the seller's Gross Income Tax form on the estate's behalf, and the city's code exempts probate transfers from the compliance certificate. Heirs who sell after taking title sign for themselves, using the form that matches their own residency.

When does a cash offer help a Perth Amboy seller?

A cash offer helps when the building would fail the code inspection, carries tenants a seller no longer wants to manage, or must close before a conditional certificate runs out. In each case the as-is certificate route can let the buyer take the repairs after closing.

Ask any buyer whether the offer assumes the temporary certificate, who pays for inspections, and how existing leases and security deposits will be handled. Compare offers by net proceeds, not by the top-line price.

Yes, with limits. If the buyer states in writing that the purchase is as-is, the city can issue a temporary, nonrenewable certificate for up to six months, unless a life-safety condition exists.

Are probate and family transfers exempt in Perth Amboy?

Yes. The code exempts transfers between immediate family members and transfers made through probate proceedings from the certificate requirement.

How much can rent rise in a Perth Amboy rental I am selling?

Up to 3 percent a year where water is included and 2.5 percent where it is not, under the rent control cap in force since November 1, 2022.

Where is a Perth Amboy deed recorded?

At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick. Title agents and attorneys can also submit electronically.

What should I know before selling a house in Plainfield?

Plainfield requires a Certificate of Compliance inspection before a sale closes, and that single step controls your timeline more than any other local rule. A separate fire certificate is also expected, so plan for two inspections that run on different tracks.

The city sits on the southwestern edge of Union County in the Raritan Valley, and it covers 5.96 square miles of land. Owners here choose between a broker listing, a private sale and an as-is cash purchase. Each route still ends with the same paperwork: the compliance certificate, a recorded deed in Elizabeth, and the state transfer filings.

How large is Plainfield and what do its housing numbers show?

The 2020 count for Plainfield was 54,586 people, and the Census Bureau's estimate for mid-2025 is 57,141. Fewer than half of its households own the home they live in, so rentals make up the larger part of the housing stock.

With 3.41 people per household, many Plainfield homes serve larger families or hold more than one unit. Buyers and appraisers look closely at legal unit counts, which is one reason the city checks occupancy during a sale inspection.

How did Plainfield develop and which areas draw buyers?

Quakers settled the area in 1684. Plainfield Township was created on April 5, 1847, Union County was formed in 1857, and the legislature incorporated the city on April 21, 1869. The nickname "Queen City" grew out of a 19th century promotion of the local climate as healthful.

That age shows in the housing stock. Plainfield has six residential historic districts, and a few carry real weight with buyers who want large older houses:

  • Van Wyck Brooks Historic District, with more than 150 properties, locally designated since 1982 and placed on the federal historic register in 1985.
  • Netherwood Heights, named for a vanished hotel and located near the Netherwood rail station.
  • Crescent Area and Hillside Avenue districts.
  • Sleepy Hollow, a section of larger homes on winding streets in the northeast.

If your house sits in one of these districts, ask the city's planning office whether any exterior repair you plan before listing needs historic review.

How do roads, trains and jobs shape demand for Plainfield homes?

Plainfield has no federal highway inside its borders. Route 28 is the main through road, and US 22 and Interstates 287 and 78 are reached by driving into neighboring towns. Park Avenue runs north to south and Front Street runs east to west, and both carry most local traffic.

Rail is the stronger selling point. The Plainfield station downtown and the smaller Netherwood station are both on NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line, and buses 113 and 114 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan. Newark Liberty airport is about 30 minutes away, and workers in the city report a mean commute of 29.5 minutes.

Downtown has two commercial areas on the federal register, the North Avenue Commercial District and the Plainfield Civic District. Census data for 2022 shows about $291 million in retail sales and roughly $155 million in medical and social service receipts, which gives the local economy some footing beyond commuting.

Which school district serves Plainfield homes?

The Plainfield Public School District serves every grade from kindergarten through 12. It is one of the former Abbott districts created after the New Jersey Supreme Court's Abbott v. Burke decision, which means the state pays school construction costs through the Schools Development Authority.

The district enrolled 10,097 students in 2022-23, and Plainfield High School alone had 1,925. Families comparing neighborhoods often ask which elementary school feeds their street, so keep your address ready and ask the district office for the attendance zone before you promise anything in a listing.

What does Plainfield's Certificate of Compliance for sale cover?

You file the Certificate of Compliance for Sale application with the city's Property Maintenance Unit and book an inspection before closing. The form asks about the property's legal occupancy, the buyer, the closing date, permits and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. An LLC seller must add its Certificate of Formation.

The June 2026 forms list a $50 fee for the first residential unit and $25 for each added unit. A missed appointment costs $25, and the exemption application costs $75. An adult must be present to let the inspector in.

Inspectors look at both the structure and the way the property is used:

  • Exterior walls, roofs, porches, stairs, railings and accessory buildings.
  • Yards, driveways, trash, tall vegetation and abandoned vehicles.
  • Kitchens, bathrooms, basements, crawlspaces and bedrooms.
  • Plumbing, hot water, heating equipment, outlets and fixtures.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, windows, doors and floors.
  • Signs of leaks, moisture or vermin, and the legal number of units.
  • Open permits or work that appears to have been done without one.

Other paperwork may be due as well. Sellers can be asked for a heating system certification on a professional's letterhead, a Fire Division certificate for smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable extinguisher, and permit approvals for completed work. A building with three or more units needs a current certificate from the state Bureau of Housing Inspection.

What happens if a Plainfield house fails the inspection?

The owner receives a notice of violation, fixes the items, pulls any missing permits and requests a reinspection. A clear certificate is issued only after that. Most notices allow up to 30 days. Exterior items such as trash and overgrown vegetation can carry a deadline as short as five business days, and an immediate safety threat can require action within three days.

The city may approve a temporary certificate when the property is in substantial compliance. That route requires a $500 per unit escrow, and the buyer signs a notarized affidavit accepting responsibility for the remaining violations. Approval is discretionary, so do not count on it before you sign a contract.

Some transactions qualify for an exemption, and the city makes the final call after reviewing documents:

  • The construction official issued a certificate of occupancy or continued occupancy within 90 days before the sale.
  • The house is owned by the City of Plainfield.
  • A refinance with no change in ownership.
  • A building officially found unfit for habitation and headed for rehabilitation or demolition.
  • Certain documented foreclosure or short sale closings where the property cannot be reached for inspection.

How are the transfer fee and deed recording handled in Plainfield?

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee. On a sale above $350,000 the schedule runs $2.90 per $500 up to $150,000, $4.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 from $200,000 to $550,000, per the Division of Taxation. A typical Plainfield sale near the $410,800 median value lands in that bracket.

Your deed goes to the Union County Clerk's recording office at 2 Broad Street in Elizabeth. Weekday hours are 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, counter recording ends at 3:30 pm, and nobody needs an appointment. The clerk's land records site notes that deeds over $1,000,000 recorded after July 10, 2025 may carry a revised fee.

Your closing agent normally prepares the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the Gross Income Tax residency form, and you sign them at the closing table.

Which way of selling suits a Plainfield owner best?

It depends on repairs, timing and who is living in the house. A listing may reach more buyers, but it brings repair requests, showings and a lender's appraisal, all of which interact with the compliance inspection.

An as-is cash purchase lets you skip the repair list, though the inspection, fire certificate and recording steps still apply. Compare written terms before signing: who orders the compliance application, who carries the $500 escrow if a temporary certificate is used, and who pays the transfer fee. If tenants are in place, remember that a new Certificate of Compliance for rental is generally needed whenever the tenant named on the old one leaves.

Is a Certificate of Compliance required when I sell in Plainfield?

Yes. The Property Maintenance Unit asks sellers to file the Certificate of Compliance for Sale application and schedule an inspection before closing. A recent certificate of occupancy issued by the construction official within 90 days can support an exemption request.

How much does the Plainfield sale inspection cost?

The first residential unit costs $50 and each added unit costs $25, according to the June 2026 application. A missed appointment adds $25 and an exemption application costs $75. A separate fire certificate fee may apply, so ask the Fire Division for its current charge.

Can I close in Plainfield with violations still open?

Sometimes. The city can issue a temporary Certificate of Compliance when a property is in substantial compliance, but it requires a $500 per unit escrow and a notarized buyer affidavit. The decision is discretionary and does not apply to every violation.

Where is a Plainfield deed recorded?

At the Union County Clerk's recording office, 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth. Over the counter recording runs until 3:30 pm on weekdays and needs no appointment. The clerk requires a cover sheet with each land document.

What extra steps apply if my Plainfield house has tenants?

A rental unit needs its own Certificate of Compliance whenever a new tenant moves in, and a building with three or more units needs a current state Bureau of Housing Inspection certificate. Give the buyer copies of the leases and ask the Property Maintenance Unit whether your rental certificate is current.

The seller pays the realty transfer fee. On sales above $350,000 the Division of Taxation schedule reaches $5.80 per $500 between $850,000 and $1,000,000 and $6.05 per $500 above $1,000,000.

A second charge, the Graduated Percent Fee, applies to residential deeds with consideration above $1,000,000. It is 1% of total consideration up to $2,000,000, 2% above that to $2,500,000, 2.5% to $3,000,000, 3% to $3,500,000 and 3.5% beyond. For illustration only, a $1,050,600 sale would carry about $10,506 in that fee. Form RTF-1EE is attached to every deed over $1,000,000.

Rahway is a compact Union County city of about 3.9 square miles of land, so the city's inspection checklist reaches nearly every sale. The sections below cover the numbers, the local rules and the state filings that follow.

How big is Rahway and what do its housing numbers show?

Rahway counted 29,556 residents in 2020, and the Census Bureau estimates 31,010 for July 1, 2025. About half of its households own, and the city packs roughly 7,586 people into each square mile of land.

How did Rahway grow and where does the river run?

The Lenape lived here first. In January 1777 colonial forces defeated British troops at the Battle of Spanktown, named after the city's original settler name, Spanktown. Rahway grew along the stagecoach and railroad routes between New York and Philadelphia, and the navigable Rahway River helped its factories. The legislature made it a city on April 19, 1858, and the first council met on May 3 of that year.

The river enters from Clark, takes in Robinsons Branch near Elizabeth Avenue and the South Branch near East Hazlewood Avenue, then leaves toward Linden and Woodbridge and drains into the Arthur Kill. Inman Heights and North Rahway are named sections of the city. How have downtown and Merck changed the Rahway economy?

After postwar factory closures hollowed out the center, the city began a downtown revitalization plan in the late 1990s that added market-rate housing, a hotel, galleries and shops. The old Rahway Theatre reopened as the Union County Performing Arts Center after a $6.2 million renovation, and the American Planning Association named downtown a Great Downtown in 2020.

Merck is the largest private employer in the city. It returned its global headquarters to its Rahway research campus, completing the move in 2024. The Watt Hotel opened across from the train station in 2019 with 100 rooms inside a 17-story building.

  • Census data for 2022 shows about $283 million in retail sales in Rahway.

How do trains and highways serve Rahway?

Rahway station is on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line and Northeast Corridor Line, and a typical ride to New York Penn Station takes 38 minutes. A 524-space parking deck opened across from the station in January 2005. NJ Transit route 115 reaches the Port Authority Bus Terminal and route 48 reaches Elizabeth and Perth Amboy.

US 1/9, Route 27 and Route 35 serve the city, and the Garden State Parkway and the New Jersey Turnpike each lie about two miles outside its limits. Newark Liberty International Airport is 10.2 miles northeast, roughly a 20-minute drive.

The city has more than ten parks. Rahway River Park, which Union County maintains and which extends into Clark, has the Walter E. Ulrich pool, renovated and retiled in 2021. City government follows the Faulkner Act mayor-council plan adopted in 1955, with a nine-member council.

What does the Rahway CACO inspection cover and cost?

The Property Maintenance Division in the Department of Code Enforcement accepts the Application for Certificates of Approval for Continued Occupancy. You check the change of ownership box, list the closing date and give seller and buyer contact details. The 2025 form lists $100 per residential unit for a CACO and $100 per unit for a temporary CACO. Commercial or industrial units cost $200, and a rental built before 1978 costs $125 and is subject to dust wipes.

Properties with two or more units, and commercial or mixed-use buildings, must first obtain a zoning permit and a Fire Department approval. A temporary CACO is possible once all fire prevention measures are met and the buyer signs an affidavit agreeing to handle the rest.

The city's list of common concerns tells you what to fix in advance:

  • Foundations, roofs, porches and stairs must be sound, with no open cracks or leaks.
  • Stairs with more than four risers need a handrail 30 to 42 inches high.
  • Windows need working glazing and screens on openings used for ventilation.
  • Habitable rooms need two outlets, kitchens need three, and any outlet within six feet of water needs ground fault protection.
  • Cellars and crawl spaces must be free of dampness, and drains must run clear.
  • Peeling paint, loose plaster and decayed wood on interior surfaces must be corrected.

What does the Rahway fire inspection look for?

The Fire Prevention Bureau inspects single-family houses when a smoke detector compliance certificate is requested for a sale. A fire safety inspection also accompanies a change in ownership. The city's guidance sets these standards:

  • One smoke alarm on every level, basements included, and none farther than 10 feet from a bedroom door.
  • Battery units must carry sealed 10-year batteries, hard-wired alarms cannot be swapped for battery types, and no alarm may be more than 10 years old.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • One extinguisher rated at least 2A:10BC, no heavier than 10 pounds, mounted within 10 feet of the kitchen and no more than 12 years old.

Replace expired alarms before you book the inspection so a failed visit does not push back closing.

What state forms and fees follow a Rahway sale?

The deed is recorded with the Union County Clerk, whose record room holds land transactions from 1857 forward and whose Elizabeth recording office takes documents over the counter on weekdays.

Gross Income Tax forms depend on who is selling. A New Jersey resident individual, estate or trust signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller files the GIT/REP-1 at closing, with an estimated payment calculated as the gain times 10.75%, and never less than 2% of the consideration in the deed. The county clerk forwards that payment to the state. An out-of-state heir selling an inherited Rahway house should plan for this withholding.

Yes. A CACO is needed when ownership changes, and the Fire Prevention Bureau inspects single-family houses when a smoke detector compliance certificate is requested for a sale. Apply early so both inspections fit before closing.

How much is a Rahway CACO for a residential sale?

The 2025 application lists $100 per residential unit for a CACO and $100 per unit for a temporary CACO. A rental built before 1978 costs $125 per unit and receives dust wipes during inspection.

Can I close in Rahway with repairs still unfinished?

Possibly. A temporary CACO is available when all fire prevention measures are completed and the buyer endorses an affidavit agreeing to address the remaining inspection items. Properties with two or more units need zoning and Fire Department approval first.

What must a nonresident Rahway seller pay at closing?

A nonresident files the GIT/REP-1 and makes an estimated Gross Income Tax payment equal to the gain times 10.75%, subject to a 2% of consideration minimum. The payment goes through the county clerk with the deed.

Where can I look up Rahway property records?

The Union County Clerk's online land records search lets you search by name, book and page, instrument number or date range, and the record room in Elizabeth holds land transactions from 1857 to the present.

What is Ridgewood's history, and which houses have protected status?

Johannes Van Emburgh built the first house in 1700 on 250 acres he had bought two years earlier. The Village of Ridgewood was created on November 20, 1894, with the same boundaries as Ridgewood Township, and the village took over municipal government while the township stayed on as a school district. The village later gained land from Franklin Township in 1925, Washington Township in 1971 and Ho-Ho-Kus in 1974.

Several Dutch-era homes are on the National Register of Historic Places, among them the Ackerman houses on Doremus Avenue and Lincoln Avenue, the Archibald-Vroom House at 160 East Ridgewood Avenue and the Westervelt-Cameron House on East Glen Avenue, built around 1767. Ridgewood Station at Garber Square was added in 1984.

The village building page lists the Historic Preservation Commission among the bodies that may review exterior changes, so an owner of an older house should ask the Building Department whether any approval applies before listing a project as a selling point.

Which permits and village rules can slow a Ridgewood closing?

Ridgewood's building FAQ says replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater requires a permit, as does creating habitable space in a basement or attic, adding a bathroom or laundry room, and building a deck, generator pad or accessory structure. Pools, patios, driveways, sheds and fences need a zoning certificate first.

Painting, flooring, trim, and replacing a window or door in the same opening do not need permits. Permits expire if work does not start within 12 months, or if work is abandoned for 6 months.

Ridgewood Public Schools run from prekindergarten to grade 12 with 10 schools and 5,613 students in 2020 to 2021. The state places the district in District Factor Group J, the highest of its eight categories.

Graydon Park has a pool, Veterans Field has four ball fields and a bandshell, Citizens Park sits across from George Washington Middle School, and the Wild Duck Pond is part of Saddle River County Park with a 6-mile path to Glen Rock, Fair Lawn, Paramus, Rochelle Park and Saddle Brook.

What do Bergen County appeals and closing costs look like for Ridgewood?

Bergen County takes assessment appeals through its Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack, 201-336-6300, and its page says the deadline for 2026 appeals has passed. Hearings come after the annual April 1 filing date. If an assessment tops $750,000, a Ridgewood owner may file directly with the Tax Court by April 1.

On a sale at the village's $891,200 median value, the state Realty Transfer Fee works out to about $8,313 when each band's rate is applied to the slice of price inside it. Above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller: 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000, which is $15,000 on a $1.5 million sale.

No. The village Building Department does not issue one for the resale of a one or two family house. A smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification from the Fire Prevention Bureau is required before closing.

What happens if the Ridgewood inspection is done after closing?

The owner pays a $500 penalty on top of the $200 certification fee. The schedule is $120 more than 10 days out, $150 inside 10 days and $200 inside 3 days.

Do I need a permit to remove a tree before selling in Ridgewood?

Yes for a qualifying tree, meaning one eight inches or wider at breast height on private land. Trees in the public right-of-way need consent from the village arborist.

Some will. Ridgewood Water entered a consent order with the state in May 2023 to treat PFAS in its groundwater supply, with a stated goal of finishing treatment by the end of 2026. The utility publishes current test data.

About $8,313 at the village's $891,200 median home value. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded, and sales over $1,000,000 add a percentage fee.

The borough runs resale applications online. You create an account, fill in the application, submit it, and the office emails the fee, usually within one business day. After you pay online you request an appointment, and resale inspections are held on Mondays and Wednesdays, while rental inspections use Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Questions go to the Code Enforcement contact at 732-390-7077. The borough asks owners and agents to call as soon as the house is listed so the office can check the file for open permits. The inspector looks for recently installed water heaters, furnaces and finished basements, and a permit that was never closed out can hold a certificate.

What does the Sayreville resale checklist cover?

The borough's checklist has 20 items, and violations bring a correction notice and a reinspection before the certificate is released. Inspectors may also cite other violations of the International Property Maintenance Code and borough ordinances.

  • Exit doors must open from inside without a key, and double-keyed deadbolts are prohibited.
  • Stairs with three or more steps need a handrail, and house numbers must be at least 4 inches tall and visible from the street.
  • Kitchen stoves need anti-tip devices, and a single-family house may have only one working kitchen.
  • A basement, attic or garage used as a bedroom must meet habitable-space rules, including an approved egress window that needs a construction permit, or the house fails.
  • Pools deeper than 18 inches need a fence at least 48 inches high with a self-closing, self-latching gate.
  • The water curb stop must work, and the Water Department at 732-390-7060 should be called before closing.

The checklist states that houses sold as-is are not exempt from permit requirements, and that a New Jersey licensed contractor must apply for and finalize any missing permits.

Alarms go on every finished level, within 10 feet of each sleeping area, at the bottom of basement stairs, and in finished attics with 7 feet or more of ceiling height. The area was called Roundabout, then Wood's Landing, and was renamed in the 1860s for James R. Sayre Jr., co-founder of the Sayre and Fisher Brick Company. DuPont began making gunpowder here in 1898, and in 1918 explosions at the Gillespie Shell Loading Plant killed dozens and damaged hundreds of buildings. Low-lying ground near the river floods in storm surges. After Hurricane Sandy in 2012, residents accepted a federally funded offer in 2013 to buy out 250 floodplain houses. It is the borough's clearance after an inspection against a 20-item checklist covering life safety, interior conditions, building systems, exterior conditions and permits. It is separate from the fire marshal's alarm certificate.

Mondays and Wednesdays. Rental inspections are on Tuesdays and Thursdays. You request a date after paying the emailed fee online.

No. Since February 3, 2025, state law no longer requires one for resale inspections. Solar, battery or generator systems need a printed power-source warning label instead.

Is Sayreville flood-prone?

Parts are. Low ground along the Raritan River floods in storm surges, and after Hurricane Sandy 250 houses in the floodplain were bought out under a federally funded offer in 2013.

The fastest route in Trenton is a cash sale to a buyer who accepts the house as it stands and handles the city's transfer paperwork. A listing with an agent can work for a well kept house, and a sale without an agent is legal, but every route passes through the same city inspection before the deed changes hands.

Trenton is the state capital and the Mercer County seat. The Census Bureau estimates 91,506 residents for mid-2025, up 0.8% from the 2020 base, on 7.58 square miles of land. By land area it is the second-smallest state capital in the country, which is why the housing stock sits so tightly packed.

What is Trenton like, and which neighborhoods matter to a seller?

Trenton sits on the Delaware River across from Morrisville, Pennsylvania, and borders Ewing, Hamilton and Lawrence townships in Mercer County. Quakers settled the river falls in 1679, the city was formed in 1792, and Washington's crossing and the Battle of Trenton in December 1776 are the events most visitors know. The city later became a factory town for pottery, rubber and wire rope, and the city adopted the slogan "Trenton Makes, The World Takes" in 1917, now displayed on the Lower Free Bridge.

Locals sort the city into four wards, and the neighborhoods inside them have very different buyer pools.

  • Downtown, including Mill Hill and Hanover/Academy, is close to the State House and the state office buildings.
  • South Trenton includes Chambersburg, Franklin Park and the Lamberton waterfront, an older rowhouse area with a long Italian and now Latino history.
  • North Trenton covers Battle Monument (Five Points), North 25 and Top Road, with some of the city's oldest architecture and a large Polish-American community near the Lawrence line.
  • Western Trenton neighborhoods such as Hiltonia, Glen Afton, Cadwalader Heights and Berkeley Square have the most suburban feel.
  • East Trenton, with Villa Park, Wilbur and Coalport, is home to the Trenton Transit Center.

What do Trenton homes cost, and who owns them?

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show a median owner-occupied value of $160,700 in Trenton, against a median gross rent of $1,294. Only 37.9% of the city's 32,052 households own the home they live in, and median household income is $52,537. Those numbers mean many sellers are landlords, heirs or owners of older houses that need work.

Median owner costs run $1,717 a month with a mortgage and $752 without one, so a paid-off house is cheap to hold. That is one reason inherited houses can sit for a long time before anyone decides to sell. Persons in poverty are 21.6% of the population, and 30.9% of residents are foreign-born.

What must a Trenton seller obtain before closing?

Trenton requires a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance before the change of ownership of any residential property. The Division of Housing Inspections issues it after confirming zoning and fire-safety compliance, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and substantial conformity with the city's habitability standards.

The seller or the seller's agent files the application, because the buyer has no legal right to enter the property before the sale. A buyer who has agreed to obtain the certificate may file instead. After the inspection the city hands over a list of violations, and the certificate is issued once they are corrected. A Certificate of Approval or a Certificate of Continued Occupancy can stand in for it. Commercial transfers need no inspection unless the structure contains a residential unit.

If the house cannot pass, the owner can instead file an affidavit with the Department of Inspections stating the property will stay unoccupied until a certificate is obtained. That is the usual path for a cash buyer who plans a full renovation.

How do Trenton's landlord and vacant-property rules affect a sale?

Trenton runs an Absentee Owner Program that requires every owner of rented residential or commercial property to hold a license, renewed each January. A single-family rental carries a $115 minimum fee. An owner who sells a tenant-occupied building should confirm the license is current, because a lapse can complicate the transfer.

Rental units also need their own inspection before a tenant moves in, and the city no longer issues stickers, so a tenant or buyer calls to confirm a current rental certificate. Vacant structures face the steepest charge. The registration fee is a flat $500, then $1,300 on the first renewal, $2,000 on the second and $3,000 after that.

  • A house that sits empty for a year or more costs its owner real money in registration fees.
  • Owners of vacant land and vacant buildings answer to the same Division of Housing Inspections.
  • Sidewalk damage from tree roots is handled by the division's sidewalk inspection section, which is worth checking before a buyer's walkthrough.

How are Trenton property taxes billed and appealed?

Trenton bills quarterly, with payments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1 and a 10-day grace period. Interest runs at 8% a year on delinquencies up to $1,500 and 18% above that, and a 6% penalty can apply to a delinquency over $10,000 left unpaid at year end. Tax bills go out twice a year, in late June or early July for the August and November quarters and in late December or early January for February and May.

Appeals of a regular assessment must be filed by April 1 each year, and appeals of added or omitted assessments by December 1. Forms come from the Tax Assessor or the County Tax Administrator. Any municipal charge unpaid on May 11 of the fiscal year can go to tax sale before June 30. Trenton Water Works has also announced that eligible unpaid water and sewer balances can be certified to the tax sale. When a house sells, the tax bill goes to the new owner, and the seller's closing statement should show the quarter that was paid.

What makes Trenton buyers move quickly, and how do roads and rail help?

The state is the city's largest employer, and roughly 20,000 state workers commute in each weekday. Trenton is the only New Jersey city served by Amtrak, NJ Transit and SEPTA, and the Trenton Transit Center is the end of the Northeast Corridor line to New York Penn Station and of SEPTA's line to Philadelphia. The River Line light rail runs to Camden with stops inside the city.

Drivers use U.S. Route 1, Route 29, Route 129 and U.S. 206, with Interstate 295 close by. Bridges to Morrisville, Pennsylvania, are run by the Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission. Trenton Public Schools, a former Abbott district, enrolled 14,852 students across 25 schools in 2022-23, and Thomas Edison State University and a Mercer County Community College campus are in the city.

The weather is the usual mid-Atlantic mix: about 22 days a year at 90 degrees or above, 17 winter days that never rise above freezing, and roughly 45 inches of precipitation. Heating systems, roofs and basements are the items inspectors and buyers tend to check first. The city's news page also reports that the former St. Francis Medical Center closed its remaining operations in June 2025 and demolition began in 2025, with the city studying new uses for the site.

Does a Trenton house have to pass inspection to sell?

Yes, a residential transfer needs a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance, or an affidavit that nobody will occupy the house until one is obtained. The base fee is $200, and the certificate lasts six months.

Can a buyer apply for the Trenton certificate instead of the seller?

A buyer can apply only when the buyer is the one responsible for obtaining it, because the buyer has no legal right to the property before the sale. Otherwise the seller or the seller's agent files, authorizes access and pays the fee.

What happens if my Trenton house fails the inspection?

The city gives the seller a list of violations, and the certificate is issued after they are fixed. Re-inspections cost $50 each after the first for one or two units, and $25 per unit for larger buildings.

What are the Trenton tax due dates?

Taxes are due on the first of February, May, August and November, with a 10-day grace period before interest starts. Interest is 8% on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18% above it.

Do I need a landlord license to sell a rental in Trenton?

Owners who rent out property need a yearly license under the Absentee Owner Program, renewed in January. Call the Division of Housing Inspections to confirm the license is current before listing or accepting an offer.

German immigrants built the lace and embroidery trade that earned the city the nickname "Embroidery Capital of the United States," and Cuban arrivals from the late 1940s onward gave it the other nickname, "Havana on the Hudson."

The city touches Hoboken, Jersey City, North Bergen, Weehawken and West New York, and it is the only Hudson County municipality completely surrounded by other municipalities in the county. What drives Union City's economy and buyer interest?

Bergenline Avenue is the center of local commerce. It began as a narrow cowpath, became the trolley route in the 19th century, and grew into one of the longest commercial avenues in the state, with its main retail stretch beginning at 32nd Street and running north into North Bergen. At the southern end, shopping gathers around Summit Avenue and the old Transfer Station, where the city rebuilt sidewalks and lighting from 7th to 13th Street in 2009.

Embroidery faded as a trade by the late 1990s, and the city dedicated Embroidery Square on New York Avenue in 2014 to mark it. Union City is also one of the Hudson County cities with a state-established Urban Enterprise Zone. Retail sales in 2022 were $434,135,000, or $6,706 per resident, per the Census Bureau, and health care and social assistance receipts were $209,773,000.

How do roads, schools and transit shape demand in Union City?

Union City has about 41.67 miles of roads, most of them maintained by the city. Route 495 leads to the Lincoln Tunnel, and the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail stops at 49th Street near the West New York and North Bergen lines. New Jersey Transit buses serve the city with routes to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown Manhattan, the George Washington Bridge Bus Terminal and Jersey City.

The Union City School District, a former Abbott district, enrolled 12,848 students in 14 schools in 2022-23. The main green space is Washington Park, a 22-acre county park on the Jersey City line, and the 14.4-acre Reservoir Park. Median travel to work is 33.1 minutes, and 28.3% of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

What letter does Union City require to sell a house?

A Sale of Property letter from the Building Department, which costs $100 to process and requires a mandatory lead inspection first. The letter is good for 60 days after issuance.

Taxes are due on the first of February, May, August and November. Interest is 8% up to $1,500 of delinquency and 18% on the amount above that.

The rent control program applies to covered rental units, so the buyer takes the building with its registration and legal rents. Gather the annual registration statement and legal rent records before you list.

It can sell, usually to a cash buyer, but the Building Department publishes a procedure for legalizing non-conforming basement units and open issues can delay the sale letter. Ask the department what applies to your building before you go to market.

Landis bought 30,000 acres in 1861 and laid out a temperance, farming community, with Landis Avenue built 100 feet wide through the center.

How did West New York grow into one of the densest towns in the country?

After a referendum held on July 5, the legislature incorporated West New York as a town on July 8, 1898, replacing Union Township. Textile mills fueled early growth and earned North Hudson the label Embroidery Capital of the United States, and the early population was largely Italian and German. Cuban families began arriving in the 1960s, giving the town the nickname Havana on the Hudson.

Apartment towers along Boulevard East later pushed density to among the highest in the country, and since the 1980s the old industrial waterfront has turned into housing and the Hudson River Waterfront Walkway. Older buildings remain among the towers, including the Excelsior Engine Co. No. 2 firehouse on Polk Street, which was added to the federal historic register in 2022.
