How do transit, roads and schools help a West New York listing?

Bergenline Avenue, home to over 300 shops and restaurants, is the commercial spine, while 60th Street is the main crosstown road and the site of Town Hall. County Route 501 follows Kennedy Boulevard along the west edge and County Route 505 follows Boulevard East, so no state highway enters the town. The Turnpike, Route 1/9 and Route 495 sit in adjacent municipalities.

  • NJ Transit buses 128, 154, 156, 158, 159, 165, 166 and 168 reach Midtown's Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 181 and 188 go to the George Washington Bridge Bus Terminal.
  • The Hudson-Bergen Light Rail stops at Bergenline Avenue on the Union City line, and the Port Imperial ferry terminal is in Weehawken.
  • Jitneys along Bergenline Avenue can arrive as often as once a minute.

The West New York School District runs nine schools from pre-K to Memorial High School and counted 8,545 students in 2019-20. As one of the former Abbott districts, it has school construction costs covered by the state. Catholic families can look at the Academy of St. Joseph of the Palisades, a K-8 school. North Hudson Regional Fire and Rescue protects the town in place of a local fire department. Newark Liberty International Airport is 13.6 miles away, and LaGuardia is 13.5 miles away through the Lincoln Tunnel.

What does West New York require before a property is transferred?

Chapter 148 of the town code bars anyone from selling a residential building, or taking title to one, until the town issues an ownership certificate following an inspection. The rule reaches one-, two- and three-family homes, buildings of four or more units, commercial and mixed-use buildings, and vacant land through a separate certificate. A missed certificate brings a $1,000 fine.

  • Seller or buyer may file the application, and both carry liability if none is obtained.
  • When the contract calls for an as-is sale, a copy goes in with the application, signed by both parties.
  • Inspectors look at housing, building, fire, electrical and property maintenance codes.
  • If repairs will not be finished by closing, the town can grant a temporary certificate lasting up to six months with no renewal, and the buyer takes on the duty to correct the violations.

State fire rules separately ask for an alarm certificate covering smoke and carbon monoxide detectors when a house of one or two units is sold, so ask the town which office issues it and book both visits once you have a signed contract.

How does the West New York Tax Collector handle payments and tax sales?

The Tax Collector bills and collects municipal property taxes from the office at 428 60th Street, and the phone line is 201-295-5110. A ten-day grace period applies. Interest is counted from the original due date starting on day eleven, and a postmark does not count as payment.

The town schedules its tax sale in December and announces the date by the end of November. For example, an online auction of delinquent 2025 and earlier taxes ran on December 17, 2025. Owners with a balance should request a payoff figure before listing so a lien can be cleared out of the proceeds.

Where is a West New York deed recorded, and what does the seller owe the state?

The Hudson County Register records the deed, not Town Hall. Paper filings need the county cover sheet, checks go to Hudson County Register, and a personal or LLC check cannot exceed $200. Questions can go to 201-395-4760.

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee on the price. A slice of a sale between $200,000 and $550,000 costs $4.80 per $500, which is where a typical West New York price falls, and anything above $1 million adds the Graduated Percent Fee. The closing statement shows the total.

How can I sell a West New York property?

Owners here usually weigh a listing, a private deal and a direct purchase for cash, and the town certificate applies to every one of them.

  • A listing fits a house or unit in good order that a lender can appraise, with the inspection and loan timeline that follows.
  • A private deal works when a tenant, relative or neighbor is already the buyer and a lawyer drafts the contract.
  • A cash purchase can fit a building with open violations, a tenancy you no longer want to run, or an estate that needs to close.

Write down who pays for certificate inspection and corrections before you sign anything.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection required before a West New York sale?

Yes. Under Chapter 148 an ownership certificate must be issued after inspection before a residential building transfers. Skipping it costs $1,000, and the seller and the buyer are both responsible.

Can I sell a West New York building with open violations?

Often, yes. The town may grant a temporary certificate for up to six months when violations remain at closing, and the buyer agrees to fix them. The Department of Public Affairs decides which items qualify.

How long is the West New York property tax grace period?

Ten days. Interest is charged back to the due date beginning on the eleventh day, and postmarks do not count. The Tax Collector at 201-295-5110 can give you a current balance.

Which office records a West New York deed?

The Hudson County Register. File with the county's cover sheet and a check made out to Hudson County Register, which your closing attorney or title agent normally arranges.

Do most West New York residents own their homes?

No. Only 23.0 percent of occupied homes are owned by the people living in them in the 2020-2024 Census figures, and median gross rent is $1,716, so many buyers are investors who weigh rental income.

What does a Westfield seller face between signing and closing?

Three things: a fire department alarm check, a deed filed in Elizabeth and a quarterly tax bill. Westfield asks for no resale certificate of occupancy, and its high price level is the more unusual feature, because the town's typical home value sits just under the million-dollar mark where a surcharge begins.

What follows lays out local figures, the alarm inspection, recording and tax steps, then compares an agent listing, a sale handled alone and an as-is cash purchase.

How big is Westfield and what do homes cost there?

The Census Bureau puts Westfield at 32,595 people for mid-2025, against 31,032 counted in 2020. The land area is 6.72 square miles, giving about 4,615 residents for each square mile, and roughly four of every five homes are occupied by the people who own them.

A suburb like this draws buyers who compare it with Cranford, Scotch Plains and Mountainside. For pricing, the most useful evidence is a handful of recent closings close to your own address.

How do Westfield's old village, downtown and schools shape demand?

Settlers arrived in the area in 1720, the place became a separate township in January 1794, and it took its present form as a town in 1903. The shopping district north of the station is run through a special improvement district by the Downtown Westfield Corporation and, holds over 200 retail businesses.

The railroad also divides the town into a North Side and a South Side, and the school system follows that line. Westfield Public Schools enrolled 5,979 students across ten buildings in 2023-24:

  • Lincoln Early Childhood Center for pre-kindergarten and kindergarten;
  • six elementary schools, three on each side of the tracks;
  • Roosevelt Intermediate in the north and Edison Intermediate in the south;
  • Westfield High School, with 1,784 students.

Green space helps too. Mindowaskin Park and Tamaques Park lie inside town limits, and Lenape Park, at 450 acres, belongs to the Union County Rahway River Parkway.

Why does commuting access matter so much for Westfield prices?

NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line serves Westfield station, with direct trains into New York Penn Station outside weekday rush hours and some non-stop rush-hour service toward Newark Penn. A bus numbered 113 reaches the Port Authority terminal.

By road, Route 28 follows the tracks for about two miles. Garden State Parkway Exits 135 and 137 and the Route 22 ramps at Lawrence, Mountain and Springfield Avenues lie a short distance away. The town has 108.63 miles of roadway, and the municipality maintains 96.69 of them.

Offer the walk time to the platform and the drive to the nearest ramp when you describe the house. Commuters weigh those two numbers heavily.

Does a Westfield sale need a certificate of occupancy?

It does not. The Westfield building department states the town requires no certificate of occupancy or continued certificate of occupancy for a home sale. What it does require is a Certificate of Smoke Detector and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Compliance.

State fire safety law makes the owner of a one- or two-family house obtain that paper from the Bureau of Fire Prevention before the buyer takes over, and a failure to do so brings a $200 fine. Points sellers raise most often:

  • Crews inspect on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, without a phone call about the arrival time.
  • The price depends on lead time: $100 for a slot more than ten business days out, $125 for four to ten, $150 for under four.
  • Someone aged 18 or over has to let the crew in, because they will not enter an empty house alone.
  • Sealed ten-year battery alarms pass, and so do hardwired detectors.
  • Any open construction permit has to be closed first.
  • Since March 14, 2025 the fire extinguisher is no longer part of the check.

The certificate arrives by email at the single address given on the application, so use the one belonging to your closing attorney or agent. A house headed for demolition still needs one.

Where does a Westfield deed get recorded, and what does the state charge?

Union County records the deed at the County Clerk's courthouse office, 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth. Over-the-counter filing runs until 3:30 in the afternoon, and no appointment is needed. A second clerk's office in Westfield, on North Avenue East, covers passports, notary commissions and trade names, so deeds still go to Elizabeth.

The seller owes the state's realty transfer fee. Above a $350,000 price the schedule starts at $2.90 for each $500 of the first $150,000, climbs to $4.25 through $200,000, and then charges $4.80 until $550,000, with $5.30 and $5.80 tiers above that. Westfield's typical value of $953,400 falls in the $5.30 tier.

Residential sales over $1,000,000 also draw the Graduated Percent Fee, 1 percent of the whole price up to $2,000,000. On a $1,050,000 sale, that is about $10,500, so have the closing attorney run the arithmetic before you accept an offer near the threshold.

How are Westfield property taxes billed around a sale?

The Tax Collector at 425 E Broad Street bills four times a year, on the first of February, May, August and November, and extends each deadline by ten calendar days. If the tenth lands on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.

Interest on late payments is 8 percent of the first $1,500 and 18 percent of anything beyond, reaching back to the original due date, and a bounced check adds $20. Sewer fees come on a different cycle, due April 1. The office tells new owners to request a bill because an unreceived bill does not excuse payment, so ask for a written payoff of tax and sewer before closing and let the closing agent split the current quarter.

Senior and veteran relief applications also pass through this office, so confirm any deduction on the account is settled.

Which Westfield path suits you: agent, solo sale or cash buyer?

An agent listing generally reaches the most buyers, a cash purchase closes fastest, and a solo sale saves the commission at the cost of doing all the work. Condition and timing usually decide it.

  • Choose an agent when the house shows well and you can sit through open houses, buyer inspections and mortgage underwriting.
  • Handle it alone when you know your block's recent sales and will pay an attorney to prepare the contract.
  • Choose an as-is cash buyer for an inherited house, a tenant in place, or repairs you would rather not make before moving.

Whichever you pick, request a fire department date once a closing date is penciled in, since only two mornings a week are available. Compare written offers by the amount left after the transfer fee, any surcharge above $1,000,000, taxes and the loan payoff.

Frequently asked questions

What costs come with selling a Westfield house?

The seller pays the state realty transfer fee, which follows the price, plus a fire department inspection of $100 to $150. Sales above $1,000,000 add a 1 percent surcharge. A listing agent's commission, if you use one, is separate.

Is an inspection needed before closing in Westfield?

Yes, an alarm and carbon monoxide inspection by the Bureau of Fire Prevention. The building department says no certificate of occupancy is needed. Crews come on Tuesday and Thursday mornings.

What are the Westfield tax installments?

Four bills fall due on the first of February, May, August and November, each with a ten-day cushion. Sewer is separate and due April 1. Late interest is 8 percent up to $1,500 and 18 percent beyond.

Can a Westfield house with problems still sell?

Yes. The alarm check covers only alarms and detectors, though open permits must be closed. A buyer can take on cosmetic or structural work, which is how as-is purchases function.

Which office files a Westfield deed?

The Union County Clerk in Elizabeth, at 2 Broad Street. Walk-in filing needs no appointment, and your closing attorney or title company normally files it for you.

What should I know about selling a house in Egg Harbor Township, NJ?

Egg Harbor Township is a large Atlantic County municipality, 75.47 square miles of which 67.05 is land, and it is separate from Egg Harbor City, which has its own entry in the state's municipality lists. The Census Bureau estimates 48,435 residents for 2025. Owner-occupancy is high at 84.4 percent, the median owner-occupied home value is $312,700, and median household income is $97,190.

Both the home value and the owner share lead to one practical point for sellers: most houses here are owned, not rented, and the main pre-closing task is the state fire-safety certificate.

Does Egg Harbor Township require a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate?

New Jersey's Division of Fire Safety runs an online smoke certification application with "Change of Ownership" as a stated reason, and it asks for the closing date, block, lot and whether you are the seller or the buyer's representative. Sheriff's sales, foreclosures, forfeitures and purchases from a federal agency work differently: the new owner must obtain the certificate before moving in. A building that is uninhabitable and will be rehabilitated or demolished can be exempt from the certificate, but it cannot be occupied until a new certificate of occupancy comes from the local construction official.

For the township's own form, fee and timing, ask the Bureau of Fire Inspections before you set a closing date.

How settled is the Egg Harbor Township housing market?

Census data show a population up 1.2 percent from the April 2020 base of 47,849 to 48,435 in 2025. The township has 17,261 households averaging 2.78 people, and 93.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

  • Median owner costs are $2,371 a month with a mortgage and $954 without one.
  • Median gross rent is $1,456.
  • 17.7 percent of residents were born abroad, and 29.8 percent speak another language at home.

The township's density is 713.6 people per square mile, a fraction of the Elizabeth or Englewood figure.

How did the township get its shape?

Lenape families summered near Bargaintown Lake and along Patcong Creek. A 1694 act placed the Egg Harbour settlers under Gloucester County, and Atlantic County was separated in 1837. Since then, ten municipalities have split from the original township, among them Atlantic City in 1854, Somers Point in 1886 and Ventnor City in 1903.

What remains is spread out. The seat of government is in Bargaintown, and the township includes Cardiff, English Creek, Farmington, Scullville, Steelmanville and West Atlantic City, plus part of McKee City. West Atlantic City and Anchorage Poynte are not contiguous with the main body. A listing should name the section, because buyers search by those names.

How do the Pinelands rules affect a house here?

The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of it lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The Pinelands Commission classed Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton and Galloway as Regional Growth Areas, which pushed residential building here so that trees in the preserved Pine Barrens stay standing.

  • In 2007 the planning board approved 667 homes in the Farmington section: townhouses, homes for buyers 55 and older, and single-family houses.
  • If your lot sits near wetlands or protected land, ask the township's construction office about limits before planning a deck, shed or addition.
  • Wildlife management areas including Malibu Beach, Pork Island and Lester G. MacNamara are public land in the south and east.

What does the township offer commuters and families?

The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township for 5.3 miles and meets the Garden State Parkway at Interchange 7, which is Parkway Interchange 38. The Parkway runs 8.6 miles through, and Routes 40, 322 and 9 plus county routes 559, 563, 575 and 585 carry local traffic. NJ Transit buses 502, 507, 508 and 509 link the township with Atlantic City. Most of Atlantic City International Airport lies in the northern part of the township. The Census puts mean travel to work at 23.3 minutes, the shortest of the four towns.

The township has 297 miles of roads, 207 of them municipal. Harbor Square, the former Shore Mall, is the regional shopping center, and the Atlantic County Bikeway runs 7.5 miles from the mall toward Hamilton Township.

  • Malibu Beach Wildlife Management Area covers 95.7 acres of marsh, dunes and back-bay shoreline and is known locally as Dog Beach, one of the few New Jersey beaches that permits dogs.
  • Storybook Land, a 20 acre children's park, opened in 1955 on the township's mainland side.
  • The township was one of the first five in the state, in 2017, to authorize medical cannabis dispensaries.
  • The township borders Ocean City and has Great Egg Harbor Bay shoreline in its eastern segment.

Name the nearest of these in your listing, since they are what a buyer from outside Atlantic County will recognize.

Which schools serve Egg Harbor Township homes?

Egg Harbor Township Schools run seven schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12. The 2023-24 enrollment was 7,473 students with a 10.9 to 1 student-teacher ratio. Davenport and Swift-Slaybaugh serve the early grades, the Dr. Joyanne D. Miller school takes grades 4 and 5, Alder Avenue and Fernwood Avenue are the middle schools, and Egg Harbor Township High School had 2,299 students. Students can also go to the Atlantic County Institute of Technology in Mays Landing or the Charter-Tech High School for the Performing Arts in Somers Point.

How do I appeal an assessment or record a deed in Atlantic County?

Atlantic County's Board of Taxation sits in Mays Landing at 5909 Main Street and can be reached at (609) 645-5820. Petitions are due by April 1, and hearings are typically held between April and September at the Historic Courthouse. The board mails a hearing notice at least ten days ahead, and any comparable sales you rely on must reach the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk at least seven days before the hearing. Good comparables are real sales in the same town within the year before the prior October 1; most foreclosures, sheriff's sales, estate sales and short sales are treated as not usable. A reduction comes back as a credit through a revised bill from the tax collector, and you have 45 days from the judgment to go to the State Tax Court.

A resident seller signs GIT/REP-3 for the deed. Nonresidents use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a listed assurance applies.

Is Egg Harbor Township the same as Egg Harbor City?

No. The state lists Egg Harbor Township and Egg Harbor City as separate municipalities. This page covers the township, which had 48,435 residents in the 2025 Census estimate.

Yes, a change of ownership calls for a state smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Ask the township's Bureau of Fire Inspections for its form, fee and timing before you pick a closing date.

The Census Bureau reports $312,700 for owner-occupied homes in the 2020 to 2024 period, and 84.4 percent of homes are owner occupied.

When is the Atlantic County tax appeal deadline?

April 1 of the tax year, filed with the Atlantic County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation was done, the deadline is May 1.

How long are Atlantic County hearing notices sent in advance?

At least ten days before the hearing. Comparable sales evidence is due to the board, the assessor and the clerk at least seven days before.

Why does the size of Galloway Township, NJ matter to a house seller?

Galloway Township is the largest municipality in New Jersey by area, so two houses with the same Galloway address can sit miles apart and attract very different buyers. Total area is 114.49 square miles, of which 88.67 are land and 25.82 are water.

The Census Bureau estimates 38,380 residents for July 2025, up from 37,813 at the 2020 census. That is a density of only 426.5 people per square mile, compared with 15,469 in Garfield, Bergen County. Galloway serves as a growing edge city to neighboring Atlantic City.

For 2020-2024 the Census Bureau shows 79.8% owner-occupied housing, a median home value of $298,900 and median gross rent of $1,619. Residents aged 65 and over make up 21.6% of the population.

How did Galloway Township develop, and which communities do buyers search?

Galloway began as a royal grant and was later divided into many smaller towns. A royal patent from King George III created the township on April 4, 1774, when it belonged to Gloucester County, and the legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. After Atlantic County formed in 1837, pieces were cut away to create Mullica Township, Egg Harbor City, Absecon, Brigantine and Port Republic.

The township now has no single downtown. Census-designated places inside it are Absecon Highlands, Cologne, Germania, Leeds Point, Oceanville, Pomona (7,416 residents in 2020), Smithville (7,242) and the Stockton University campus area. Other place names, including Higbeetown, Pinehurst and Somersville, show up in older deeds.

Galloway borders Absecon, Atlantic City, Egg Harbor City, Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton Township, Mullica Township and Port Republic in Atlantic County, plus Bass River and Washington townships in Burlington County and Little Egg Harbor in Ocean County. A buyer shopping for a Galloway address often compares it with houses in those towns.

What inspection does Galloway Township require when a house is resold?

Galloway requires a fire certificate on every residential resale, covering smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers only. Township code Chapter 153 says the inspection must happen before the new owners can occupy the dwelling.

The application, inspection and certificate go through the Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road. The fee depends on how much notice you give, so ask for the inspection as soon as you have a closing date.

Violating the ordinance can bring a fine of up to $2,000, up to 90 days in jail or community service, and each day counts as a separate offense. Unlike Freehold Township, Galloway's resale inspection does not cover the rest of the house, since the ordinance limits it to the three fire safety items.

What does Galloway Township ask of an owner who rents out the house?

Rentals follow a separate and fuller inspection than resales. Under Galloway's rental ordinance, a certificate of occupancy is required on any rental, renewed every year or at each new occupant, whichever comes first, at $50 per inspection.

  • The lease must accompany the application and list every occupant's name and age.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are required in every rental unit.
  • A detached one- or two-family rental needs a fire extinguisher of at least 2A:10B:C and at most 10 pounds, mounted within 10 feet of the kitchen with its top no higher than five feet from the floor.
  • A rental with a fireplace needs a chimney certification and proof that the dryer vent has been cleaned, or a notarized letter from the owner.
  • More than two follow-up inspections trigger another $50 fee.

The Housing Department handles applications at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249. Inspection requests themselves must now be emailed to the Construction office at inspect@gtnj.org with the permit number, address, type of inspection and your phone number.

How do the Pinelands and past storms affect a Galloway Township house?

Much of Galloway lies inside a protected landscape, and some parcels carry extra rules. The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, a 1.1 million acre area Congress established in 1978, and parts of Galloway also fall in the state-designated Pinelands Area. Ask the Community Development office whether your parcel is in that area before you promise a buyer an addition or a new outbuilding.

Weather history is part of the picture too. In spring 2007 gypsy moth caterpillars defoliated a large swath of oak and other hardwoods in the township, and the township did not apply for state spraying that year. Tropical Storm Irene made its second U.S. landfall at Brigantine on August 28, 2011, next to Galloway.

The Community Development Department says the homeowner, not the contractor, is responsible for obtaining a permit. Residential contractors need a state Consumer Affairs 13VH number, so keep contractor names and permit numbers for any work you did before selling.

What do nonresident and out-of-state owners owe on a Galloway Township sale?

A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax at the closing table. The state's formula multiplies the gain by 10.75%, but the payment can never be below 2% of the consideration written in the deed, even if there is no gain.

On a $300,000 deed, the floor works out to $6,000. The payment goes with the deed and the GIT/REP-1 form to the Atlantic County Clerk, who forwards it to the state. A seller who wants to avoid delays can prepay at a Division of Taxation regional office and receive a stamped GIT/REP-2 before closing.

  • A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3 instead and pays nothing up front.
  • A nonresident can still use the GIT/REP-3 if one of its listed assurances fits, such as a deed for $1,000 or less or a settlement with no net proceeds to the seller.
  • Selling a principal residence that qualifies under Internal Revenue Code section 121 is another listed assurance, when the entire gain can be excluded.

The Division of Taxation's GIT/REP Unit answers questions at 609-322-9275, and the Division suggests contacting it at least two weeks before a complicated closing.

How do schools, the Parkway and Stockton University influence Galloway Township buyers?

Buyers care about the Garden State Parkway and the schools. The Parkway runs 5.7 miles through the township, with Interchange 40 for U.S. Route 30, Interchange 41 for Jimmie Leeds Road and Interchange 44 for Pomona. Route 50 and County Routes 561, 563 and 575 also cross the township, and NJ Transit buses 508, 554 and 559 reach Atlantic City. The mean commute is 23.6 minutes.

Galloway Township Public Schools serve pre-K through grade 8 in six schools, with 3,164 students in 2021-22. High school students attend Absegami High School, in the township, as part of the Greater Egg Harbor Regional High School District, and families in the western part may choose Cedar Creek High School in Egg Harbor City.

Stockton University sits in the Pomona section, and Atlantic Cape Community College, with campuses in Mays Landing, Atlantic City and Cape May Court House, serves the county. A house bought as a rental brings the inspection rules above into play.

Frequently asked questions

Does Galloway Township require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes, a fire certificate. Galloway requires an inspection of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers on every residential resale, and it must be done before the new owners occupy the home.

What does the Galloway Township resale fire certificate cost?

It costs $45 when the request arrives more than 10 business days before the change of ownership, $90 for four to 10 business days, and $161 for fewer than four business days.

Where do I apply for the Galloway Township fire certificate?

The application, inspection and certificate are handled by the Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road. The township's Housing Department can be reached at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249.

How much tax does a nonresident owe when selling in Galloway Township?

At least 2% of the deed consideration is prepaid at closing as estimated New Jersey gross income tax. The actual figure can be higher, since the formula uses the gain times 10.75%, and the seller can claim a refund after filing a nonresident return.

Is Galloway Township in the Pinelands?

Yes, in part. Galloway is within the Pinelands National Reserve, and parts of it are in the state-designated Pinelands Area. Ask the township's Community Development office about your specific parcel.

What speeds up a house sale in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County?

Three things set the pace here: a resale inspection arranged through the township, a clear tax payoff and a deed recorded at the courthouse in Mays Landing. This page covers the Atlantic County township around Mays Landing, a different place from the Hamilton near Trenton.

The Census Bureau estimates 28,845 residents for July 1, 2025, up 5.0 percent from its 2020 base. Owners live in 70.7 percent of homes, and the typical owner-occupied value is $246,200. Listings range from suburban streets in the developed east to rural lots in the pine forest of the west, and a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands removes loan approval and repair negotiations from that timeline.

What sets Hamilton Township apart from other Atlantic County towns?

Hamilton Township has the most land of any municipality in New Jersey at 110.90 square miles, and it calls itself the state's largest municipality. Counting water as well, only Galloway Township is bigger. Mays Landing, the Atlantic County seat since the county formed in 1837, sits inside the township with the census-designated places of McKee City and Mizpah.

A great deal of that land is protected. The township belongs to the New Jersey Pinelands National Reserve, and the Pinelands Commission regulates the western three-quarters, which remains pine forest. The eastern quarter is a Regional Growth Area where development is allowed and encouraged, and most residents live there, near the Hamilton Mall and other shopping centers.

  • McKee City: 9,758 residents in 2020, the largest census-designated place in the township.

If the house sits on or near undeveloped land, ask the township planning and zoning office whether the parcel lies inside the Pinelands Area before you describe what a buyer could add or build.

How did Hamilton Township grow into what it is now?

The township was incorporated on February 5, 1813, from parts of Egg Harbor and Weymouth townships. Its early economy followed the Great Egg Harbor River: a shipyard and trading post opened near Babcock Creek at Mays Landing in 1756, and more than 200 vessels were built along the river between 1830 and 1880.

The population stood at 6,017 in 1960, 16,012 in 1990 and 27,484 in 2020. Retail is part of the economy, with more than 3,000,000 square feet of stores including Hamilton Mall, Consumer Square and Hamilton Commons, and a winery on a 57-acre vineyard.

How do assessments and appeals work in Hamilton Township?

Appeals go to the Atlantic County Board of Taxation at 5909 Main Street in Mays Landing. A petition must arrive before the close of business at 4 p.m. on April 1, because a postmark does not count, and petitions about added or omitted assessments follow the same rule on December 1. The 2026 April deadline has passed.

The board accepts filings online through MyNJAppeal.com, where evidence can be uploaded until seven days before the hearing. Assessment cards usually arrive in late January, and the board publishes lists of usable comparable sales. The test is whether your assessment exceeds what the house would sell for.

Request a payoff figure from the township tax collector before closing, and check the parcel in the county's property assessment search before you set a price.

The state's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording. The state's own example for a $325,000 deed is $1,910, and the township's average 2025 sale of about $312,000 sits in the same bracket, with a rate that begins at $2.00 per $500.

The Atlantic County Clerk records deeds at the Historic Court House Complex, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, which lies inside the township. A satellite office serves Atlantic City at 1333 Atlantic Avenue. Make recording and transfer fee checks out to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, and send any nonresident Gross Income Tax prepayment to the State of New Jersey Division of Taxation.

  • GIT/REP-3 residency certification for New Jersey residents.
  • Gross Income Tax prepayment for nonresident sellers, set at 2 percent of the price or more.
  • A deed prepared by the closing attorney or title company.

Which schools, highways and buses serve Hamilton Township buyers?

Hamilton Township Schools teach prekindergarten through eighth grade in three schools: Shaner Memorial, the George Hess Educational Complex and William Davies Middle School. Older students attend Oakcrest High School in the township, part of the Greater Egg Harbor Regional High School District. Atlantic Cape Community College's Mays Landing campus has operated since 1968.

A 14-mile stretch of the Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township with three interchanges, and U.S. Routes 40 and 322 and Route 50 cover other directions. NJ Transit buses 502 and 553 reach Atlantic City, and the 315 runs between Cape May and Philadelphia.

Is an inspection mandatory before selling in Hamilton Township, Atlantic County?

Where does a Hamilton Township deed get recorded?

At the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, inside the township. A satellite office is at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

What is the assessment appeal deadline here?

April 1 at 4 p.m., with December 1 as the date for added or omitted assessments. Filing works online, and a postmark does not satisfy the deadline.

Is this the same Hamilton as the one in Mercer County?

No. They are separate municipalities in different counties, each with its own tax board, clerk and inspection office. This page covers the one around Mays Landing.

How can I sell a house in Teaneck?

Teaneck owners choose between listing with an agent, selling privately, and accepting an as-is offer from a cash buyer. Teaneck is a dense, close-in suburb, so a conventional listing draws plenty of attention, while a direct sale suits an owner facing an inherited property, tenants, deferred repairs or a tight deadline.

Whatever the route, the township has two checks to clear before closing: the Fire Prevention Bureau's resale inspection for smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers, and a clean record with the Building Department. Start both early. A house with an open permit or a missing detector can slow a closing whether the buyer is financing or paying cash.

What kind of township is Teaneck?

Teaneck is a Bergen County township of 6.24 square miles, 6.04 of them land, with 41,246 residents at the 2020 Census and a density of about 6,800 people per square mile. That made it the second most populous of Bergen County's 70 municipalities, behind Hackensack. It borders River Edge and Hackensack across the Hackensack River, New Milford and Bergenfield to the north, Englewood and Leonia to the east, and Ridgefield Park and Bogota to the south.

Route 4 divides the township into northern and southern halves, and the CSX River Subdivision rail line divides it east from west. Shopping and services cluster in four districts:

  • Cedar Lane, which had a $3.9 million streetscape project completed in 2006
  • North Teaneck Road
  • West Englewood Avenue and Queen Anne Road, known as The Plaza
  • Queen Anne Road and DeGraw Avenue

The township also keeps 24 municipal parks, 14 of them developed.

How did Teaneck develop, and which houses are historic?

Teaneck was created on February 19, 1895, from parts of Englewood and Ridgefield townships and Bogota. It chose the township form of government at a time when most new Bergen County communities were becoming boroughs. Early settlement followed Teaneck Road and River Road, where several Dutch stone houses from the 1700s still stand and some are on the National Register of Historic Places.

The big change came when the Phelps Estate opened for development in 1927 and the George Washington Bridge opened in 1931, tying the town to Manhattan by way of Route 4. The population nearly quadrupled between 1920 and 1930, from 4,192 to 16,513. The United States Army named Teaneck a model community in 1949, and in 1965 the township voluntarily integrated its public schools. A second major wave of building followed World War II, so many Teaneck houses are decades old, and older wiring, heating and permit gaps are the items to check before you list.

On the owner's request, the construction official can issue a certificate of continued occupancy for an existing building when no violations or orders are pending and records show the use has lawfully existed. That certificate reflects a general inspection of the visible parts of the building and confirms that no unsafe conditions were found. Teaneck's page for certificates of occupancy cites N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.23 and points owners to the Building Department for the application.

Before listing a house with a deck, pool, shed, driveway or fence, find out whether the work had a zoning permit. Which schools, hospitals and employers shape demand in Teaneck?

Teaneck Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 in eight schools and enrolled 3,487 students in 2023-24. The schools are Bryant, Theodora Smiley Lacey, Hawthorne, Lowell and Whittier for the early grades, Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson middle schools, and Teaneck High School with 1,261 students. Teaneck Community Charter School is a separate public charter school, and Bergen County Technical Schools, including the Bergen County Academies in Hackensack, accept students by application.

Holy Name Medical Center and the Metropolitan Campus of Fairleigh Dickinson University are major institutions. Cognizant keeps its global headquarters at the Glenpointe Centre, which includes a 350-room hotel and 650,000 square feet of office space, and Phibro Animal Health is based at the I-95 and I-80 junction. Local employment gives some buyers a short commute.

What parks and open space does Teaneck offer?

Votee Park is the largest, at 40.51 acres, with ball fields, playgrounds, the township pool and a Sportsplex that opened in 2014. The 3.5-mile Hackensack River Greenway through Teaneck became a National Recreation Trail in June 2009. Overpeck County Park, more than 800 acres along Overpeck Creek, is shared with neighboring municipalities, and the Teaneck Creek Conservancy maintains 1.3 miles of trails near the Interstates. Photograph a park or greenway within walking distance, because buyers often ask how close one is.

Teaneck has 77.5% owner-occupied housing, a median home value of $546,100 and a population that grew 5.0% since 2020, so buyer interest is steady. A fast sale still depends on the house's condition, permit record and price.

Call the Building Department at (201) 837-1600, extension 1100, with your Zoning Control Number to check an application. Incomplete applications are not accepted, and the application must include an accurate survey.

How can a Mahwah homeowner sell on a short timeline?

Selling to a buyer who pays cash takes the loan approval and the lender's appraisal out of the calendar, which is where most delays arise. A standard listing remains realistic here, since the Census Bureau puts the median home value at $606,000, but it leans on buyer financing and on the township's pre-sale inspection.

Whichever way you go, four items decide how fast things move.

  • The township's Inspection Prior to Sale, booked through the Department of Inspections.
  • Health Department clearance if the house has a septic system, cesspool or well.
  • A current tax payoff, with any open permits closed.

What makes Mahwah different from other Bergen County towns?

No Bergen County town is bigger by area. Mahwah holds 25.39 square miles of land, roughly a tenth of the whole county, along the New York line beside the Ramapo Mountains and the Ramapo River. At about 1,004 people per square mile, it is far less crowded than the county's older boroughs.

Voters approved incorporation as Mahwah Township on November 7, 1944, replacing Hohokus Township. Ford's Mahwah Assembly plant operated from 1955 to 1980 and helped build the town's reputation for modest home property taxes. County parks fill much of the west, including Campgaw Mountain Reservation, Darlington County Park and Ramapo Valley County Reservation, and the township falls within the state's Highlands preservation area, which adds environmental rules to some parcels. Campgaw Mountain Reservation alone covers 1,351 acres across Mahwah and part of Oakland, with campgrounds and ski slopes.

Place names on listings include Darlington, Cragmere, Masonicus, Ramapo Farm and West Mahwah. Ramapo College is based here, and the public school district operates six schools that end at Mahwah High School.

How do commuters reach Mahwah, and why does it matter to a seller?

Interstate 287 and Route 17 join inside the township, and U.S. Route 202 and County Route 507 pass through as well. Trains leave the Mahwah station for Secaucus Junction, Hoboken Terminal and Newark Penn Station on the Main and Bergen County lines, while Short Line coaches head to midtown Manhattan. Express trains stop at Ramsey Route 17 and at Suffern, just over the state line.

Access helps a listing, but QuickFacts records a mean commute of 28.2 minutes, so buyers weigh the drive against larger lots and school reputation when they compare Mahwah with towns closer to the city.

Who buys houses in Mahwah?

Demand comes from corporate relocations and commuters as much as from local move-ups. Employers listed in the township include the North American headquarters of Jaguar Land Rover and Volvo Cars, UPS's technology headquarters, Stryker's orthopedic business, a New York Stock Exchange data center and the family-owned Inserra Supermarkets group.

A seller on a short fuse, such as an executor settling an estate or an owner relocating for work, may weigh a quick cash offer against waiting for one of those buyers. Compare net figures, since a cash price usually sits below a retail sale.

Development news also reaches buyers. The former Sheraton Crossroads hotel closed in late 2023 and was brought down by implosion on May 10, 2025, on a site where the planning board approved a shopping mall in January 2014. Ask a local agent how nearby projects might affect your street before you set a price.

What does the Census Bureau say about Mahwah homeowners?

A high-ownership township with an older population.

  • Population stood at 25,678 in the July 2025 estimate, a gain of 0.8 percent over the 2020 base.
  • Owners live in 81.1 percent of occupied homes, and the median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $3,273.
  • Median household income is $131,327.
  • Residents aged 65 and over make up 23.5 percent of the population.

Turnover is low. Nine in ten residents (91.1 percent) lived in the same home a year before the survey, and college graduates account for 60.3 percent of adults.

The township uses a visual Inspection Prior to Sale. Its form lists a $175 fee and warns applicants to check with the Health Department first if the property has a septic system, cesspool or well tank. The Department of Inspections is at 475 Corporate Drive.

State fire code separately calls for a smoke detector certification: detectors on each level, carbon monoxide detectors outside bedrooms and a 2A:10B:C extinguisher. Mahwah adds that it has no certificate of continued occupancy for tenant rentals.

How does the Mahwah revaluation affect a sale?

Mahwah is revaluing all taxable real estate for the 2027 tax year with Appraisal Systems, Inc., under direction from the Bergen County Board of Taxation. The township held a public information session on March 23, 2026. A revaluation resets assessments to current market levels, so a 2027 bill can differ sharply from the 2026 one.

The state says the usual April 1 appeal deadline becomes May 1 where a revaluation has been undertaken. Ask the Mahwah assessor or the Bergen board which date covers your parcel, and keep any notice of the new value because a buyer's attorney will want a copy.

The township's March 2026 newsletter says the municipal budget accounts for about 24 percent of a tax bill, with the 2026 plan projected to add $98.52 a year for the average assessed home. The remaining share goes to other taxing bodies, so request the complete bill when you ask for a payoff.

What will a Mahwah seller pay at closing?

The seller owes the state transfer fee on the deed. With a median value above $600,000, a number of Mahwah sales cross $1,000,000, and those add a graduated percent fee: 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000, climbing in bands to 3.5 percent above $3,500,000. County clerks have flagged the revised fee for deeds received since July 10, 2025.

Property tax bills come due four times a year, starting February 1 and ending November 1. The collector says payment must reach the office by the 10th to avoid interest, which state law sets at up to 8 percent a year on balances to $1,500 and 18 percent above that. A penalty of up to 6 percent can attach to delinquencies over $10,000 left open at year end.

A seller who lives outside New Jersey files the nonresident GIT/REP form and generally prepays at least 2 percent of the price as estimated income tax.

Does Mahwah inspect homes before a sale?

Yes. The township offers an Inspection Prior to Sale, visual only, with a $175 fee on its form. Call the Department of Inspections to schedule it.

What if my Mahwah house runs on a septic system or well?

Speak with the Health Department before you apply for the sale inspection. The township form tells applicants to settle septic, cesspool and well questions first.

When does the Mahwah reassessment take effect?

The township is revaluing for the 2027 tax year. Its public session took place on March 23, 2026, and Appraisal Systems, Inc. is handling the work.

Do Mahwah homes over $1 million pay extra transfer costs?

Yes. The seller pays a graduated percent fee, 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000 and rising to 3.5 percent above $3,500,000.

Is there a grace period on Mahwah tax payments?

Yes, of up to 10 days after each due date. The office must receive the payment by the 10th, and postmarks do not count.

What should an Evesham Township owner know before selling quickly?

Evesham Township is a large South Jersey suburb in Burlington County, and a quick sale there depends mostly on a short list of local steps: a resale certificate through the fire department, permits for past work, and the state paperwork filed with the deed.

The township covers about 29 square miles and counted 46,826 people in 2020. The Census Bureau estimated 49,525 residents in July 2025, which makes Evesham the most populous municipality in Burlington County. People often say Marlton when they mean Evesham, because Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it.

Part of the township sits inside the Pinelands Area, a state-designated zone with its own land use rules. If your lot is near the wooded edge of town, check the zoning map before you describe the property to a buyer, since it affects what a purchaser can add or build later.

How old is Evesham, and why does the history matter to a seller?

Evesham dates to the late 1600s, so many parcels carry old deeds and older houses sit beside postwar subdivisions. Quakers settled the area in 1672, and the township was established in 1688 as Eversham in the Province of West Jersey. It was incorporated again under the 1798 Township Act on February 21, 1798.

The original township was far larger. The population climbed from 4,548 in 1960 to 35,309 in 1990, so a large share of the housing stock went up in a single generation.

Title searches on older parcels can turn up easements or old liens that a closing attorney has to clear before the deed records.

Which roads and transit lines affect an Evesham sale?

Route 70 and Route 73 are the two highways that define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 crosses the northern part of Evesham from east to west, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two.

The old Marlton Circle at Routes 70 and 73 once handled about 90,000 vehicles a day and was the site of as many as 175 crashes a year. A grade-separated interchange replaced it in 2011, and the change made commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.

Which schools serve Evesham homes?

Evesham Township School District covers prekindergarten through eighth grade, and Cherokee High School takes students from ninth through twelfth grade. In the 2021 to 2022 school year the local district ran eight schools and enrolled 4,384 students.

The elementary schools named in the district are Beeler, DeMasi, Jaggard, Marlton, Rice and Van Zant, and the two middle schools are DeMasi and Marlton Middle. Cherokee High School had 2,165 students that year after a 210,000 square foot addition opened in 2001.

Families searching for a house usually sort by elementary school zone, so name the school attached to your address in the listing or in any direct conversation with a buyer.

What does Evesham require before a house changes hands?

Evesham directs residential resale certificate requests to the Evesham Township Fire Department, and the fire department's own site, eveshamfire.org, is where inspection scheduling and fees are posted. Start that request early so the certificate is ready when the closing date arrives.

The Community Development office handles permits from the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton, Room 204, Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The construction office can be reached at 856-983-2914, then option 4. Its published guidance is direct about unpermitted work: a construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • Sheds and fences need a zoning permit, and a fence around a pool also needs a building permit meeting the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • Flood zone questions can be checked on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and the township mapping portal.

If a past owner finished a basement, deck or pool without paperwork, sort that out before you list. A buyer's attorney will ask for permit history, and a gap can stall a sale for weeks.

Can you sell an Evesham rental or short-term rental house?

Yes, but the rental registration and fire inspection records go with the property, so gather them first. Evesham treats short-term rentals such as Airbnb and Vrbo listings like long-term rentals: they must pass a fire department inspection and register with the Township Clerk's Office.

The township requires a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm, and Portable Fire Extinguisher Compliance each time a new tenant occupies the property, under N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3. Failing to comply carries a $500 penalty, and the fire department sets the fees for the inspection.

If tenants live in the house, a buyer will want the lease, the deposit amount and the last inspection certificate. A cash purchaser who wants the house empty should say so in writing before the contract is signed, so that notice periods can be planned. For landlord and tenant disputes, the township points residents to the Burlington County court system and Legal Services of New Jersey.

What does the seller handle at closing in Evesham?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee and signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, and both are filed with the deed at the Burlington County Clerk. The Division of Taxation charges the fee per $500 of the price recited in the deed. For a standard sale over $350,000, the band from $200,000 to $550,000 is $4.80 per $500, which is the band a price near Evesham's median home value reaches.

Homes sold above $1 million add a graduated percent fee that the seller owes, starting at 1 percent of the total price. Most Evesham sales fall well under that line.

The Gross Income Tax form for most New Jersey residents is the GIT/REP-3. Burlington County notified filers that any GIT/REP form signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the current version, and older versions are rejected at recording. Questions go to the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275. Nonresident sellers owe an estimated payment of at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

The Burlington County Clerk also runs a free Property Fraud Alert system that alerts owners when a document is recorded in their name, and it is worth joining before and after a sale.

How does a fast as-is sale in Evesham usually move?

A fast sale follows a short sequence, and each step has a clear owner. The steps below assume you have clear title and no open permits.

  • Gather the deed, the last tax bill, any rental registration and your mortgage payoff figure.
  • Request the fire department resale certificate and fix anything it flags, or agree in the contract who fixes it.
  • Have your closing attorney order the title search and prepare the deed with the RTF and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over keys, and let the attorney record the deed with the Burlington County Clerk.

Cash buyers often agree to take a house in its current condition, which removes repair negotiations but not the certificate or the state filings. Ask any buyer to put the price, the closing date and who pays for each inspection in one written document before you commit.

Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?

Yes, residential resales go through the Evesham Township Fire Department for a certificate. The township construction pages send resale and rental requests there, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Ask for the inspection date as soon as you decide to sell.

What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?

A buyer's attorney will likely require it to be resolved before closing. The township says a construction permit confirms work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. Call the construction office at 856-983-2914, option 4, to learn what a retroactive permit needs.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?

The seller pays it. The state charges it when the deed is recorded with the Burlington County Clerk, based on the price in the deed, and an extra graduated fee applies above $1 million. Your closing attorney or title company will calculate the exact figure.

Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?

Yes. A nonresident seller files a GIT/REP form and pays an estimated Gross Income Tax of at least 2 percent of the price at closing unless an exemption on the form applies. The payment can be claimed back against the final tax owed when you file.

Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?

Yes, a portion of the township lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area, and the township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered. Check your parcel before marketing the property, since Pinelands rules may affect additions or new structures.

The age mix is balanced, with 21.7 percent of residents under 18 and 21.2 percent at 65 or older, and 62.2 percent of adults have a bachelor's degree or higher. Workers spend 33.9 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

What sets Medford's location and history apart?

Medford sits inside the Pinelands National Reserve, the first national reserve Congress established, in 1978, and part of the township falls in the state-designated Pinelands Area. At 38.80 square miles of land it is far more spread out than its population suggests. The independent borough of Medford Lakes sits entirely inside the township, one of New Jersey's 21 "doughnut" pairs.

Samuel Coles bought 900 acres here in 1670, and the Legislature separated Medford from Evesham Township on March 1, 1847. Glassmaking ran from the 1820s until about 1925, and nearly 30 workers' homes survive on Trimble Street and Mill Street. Local landmarks buyers recognize include:

  • Historic Medford Village, home of the Dickens Festival.
  • Kirby's Mill, a grist mill added to the national historic register.
  • Freedom Park, with playgrounds, courts, bike paths and a dog run.
  • Woodford Cedar Run Wildlife Refuge, a 170-acre preserve on the southern border.
  • The Dr. James Still Historic Office Site, preserved by the state in 2006.

Annual precipitation is about 41 inches, and snowfall averages about 23 inches. If a home sits in the Pinelands Area, ask the township zoning office what that designation means for additions, tree removal or new outbuildings before a buyer's attorney raises it.

How does a resale certificate of occupancy work in Medford?

In Medford the Fire Department handles the resale certificate of occupancy, since the construction office inspects existing housing only when someone complains. A house on public water or sewer also needs a visit from the utility billing office for a final meter reading and a sewer inspection, and wells and septic systems fall under the Burlington County Health Department, reached at 609-265-5515 in Westampton.

The fire inspection is checked against these items from the township's published requirements:

  • Working smoke detectors on every level, basements included, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. A system installed with the house and interconnected cannot be swapped for stand-alone battery units.
  • At least one carbon monoxide detector near the bedrooms, with more where bedrooms sit on more than one level.
  • A residential fire extinguisher rated 2A-10BC, no heavier than 10 pounds, mounted no higher than 5 feet and not hidden behind a door or inside a cabinet.

The township asks sellers to leave the detector manuals for the next owner. Contact the Fire Department and the utility office early, since each needs its own visit.

The Burlington County Clerk records the deed. Its recordable-deed checklist calls for the names of seller and buyer, the buyer's address, the price and transfer fee, the seller's residency form (GIT/REP), the municipal block and lot, the seller's notarized signature, the preparer's printed name and a county summary sheet. The recording fee is $45 for the first page, with the summary sheet counting as that page, and $10 for each additional page. A seller claiming a fee exemption also files an Affidavit of Consideration.

How do roads, schools and transit shape Medford sales?

Route 70 is Medford's main road, joined by County Routes 532, 541 and 544, and the township maintained 153 of its 179 miles of roadway as of 2010. The old NJ Transit bus to Philadelphia that ended in Evesham has been discontinued, and Greyhound runs from nearby Mount Laurel, so most buyers plan on driving. Flying W Airport, a public-use field, sits near the Lumberton line.

Medford Township Public Schools covers pre-kindergarten through eighth grade in seven schools, with 2,517 students in 2020 to 2021. Its elementary schools are Milton H. Allen, Chairville, Cranberry Pines, Kirby's Mill and Taunton Forge, followed by the Haines Sixth Grade Center and Medford Memorial Middle School. Older students attend Shawnee High School in the Lenape Regional High School District, and Burlington County Institute of Technology has a campus in Medford. St. Mary of the Lakes School is the local Catholic option.

Medford owners can pick a listing agent, a private sale or a cash buyer for a house that needs work, and every route needs the Fire Department certificate and, where applicable, the utility and county health sign-offs.

The Medford Fire Department handles the residential resale certificate of occupancy. Homes on public water or sewer also need the utility billing office for a final meter reading and sewer inspection.

Smoke detectors are needed on every level, including basements, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. At least one carbon monoxide detector must be near the bedrooms, and the home needs a 2A-10BC extinguisher of 10 pounds or less.

The seller pays it at recording. At Medford's Census median home value of $514,800, the state schedule works out to about $4,317, and larger sales cost more.

Yes. One- and two-family rentals are inspected annually under Ordinance 2018-24 for $200, registered with the Township Clerk, and need a Lead Safe Certificate if built before 1978. Houses on wells need a water test every 5 years.

How did a farming township become a Burlington County suburb?

The township also lent its name to the Mount Laurel Doctrine, the New Jersey Supreme Court's 1975 decision, reaffirmed in 1983, requiring municipalities to zone for housing that low- and moderate-income households can afford. A home with an affordable housing deed restriction follows its own resale rules, so check with the township's affordable housing staff before you pick a price.

The climate is humid subtropical, with monthly averages running from 33.0 degrees in January to 76.9 degrees in July, and the township sits in plant hardiness zone 7a. Heating, cooling and roof condition are routine inspection topics for buyers here.

  • Area: 21.99 square miles, with Parkers Creek and the South Branch Pennsauken Creek draining the east and west.
  • Place names: Ramblewood (6,655 people), Rancocas Woods, Centerton, Hartford, Masonville and Fellowship.
  • Neighbors: Moorestown, Evesham, Medford, Lumberton, Westampton, Willingboro, Hainesport, Maple Shade and Cherry Hill.
  • Green space: Laurel Acres Park and the southwestern corner of Rancocas State Park.

Which highways and schools shape Mount Laurel property values?

This is a highway township. The New Jersey Turnpike runs about 7.5 miles through it, with Exit 4 leading to Route 73, while Interstate 295 has exits 36, 40 and 43. Route 38 and County Route 537 round out the local network, and NJ Transit routes 317, 413 and 457 reach Philadelphia and Camden.

Mount Laurel Schools teach pre-kindergarten through grade 8. Six neighborhood schools serve K-4: Countryside, Fleetwood, Hillside, Larchmont, Parkway and Springville. Everyone then moves to Hartford School for grades 5 and 6 and Harrington Middle School for grades 7 and 8. Lenape High School in Medford, part of the Lenape Regional High School District, takes grades 9 through 12. Since the K-4 school is set by address, an ad that names the zone speaks to families directly.

What does the Mount Laurel CCO involve?

The township posts a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist under its Community Development / Construction pages, and states that emailed applications are not taken. Bring a paper application to the municipal building at 750 Centerton Road.

Phone the office for the current fee and the inspection calendar, then walk through the checklist on your own before the inspector arrives. Buyer attorneys often ask for the certificate, and an unmet item can push the closing date back. Landlords selling a rental should also read the township's rental ordinance and safety inspection checklist, which have a separate Landlord Information page along with rental registration.

  • Download the application and the checklist from the township page.
  • Close any open building permits before you book.
  • Check the checklist items room by room.

How do Mount Laurel's quarterly tax dates work at closing?

The Tax Collector bills in February, May, August and November, due on the first, with ten days of grace under N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. A postmark does not count, and arrears accrue 8% on the first $1,500 and 18% beyond it under N.J.S.A. 54:4-67.

The third installment shifts each year with the state's rate. In 2026, bills went out late and the due date for the third quarter was pushed to September 16 with no grace after it. The township ties the extension to the mailing: 25 days from the day bills are sent. If your sale closes around August, ask the Tax Collector for the exact figure before the closing statement is drawn.

The office at 750 Centerton Road accepts payment at the window, by mail, in a drop box or online. If a lender escrows your taxes, confirm that it received the bill, because a bill that never arrived is no defense against interest.

What does Burlington County charge to record a Mount Laurel deed?

The Burlington County Clerk records the deed. Its checklist for a recordable deed lists $45 for the first page, counting the summary sheet, and $10 per extra page, in addition to the state realty transfer fee set by the sale price.

The deed must name grantor and grantee, give the grantee's address, state the consideration and carry the municipal block and lot, a notarized signature and the seller's residency declaration. Seller tax declarations signed on or after October 1, 2025 must use the latest state form. For deeds over $1 million, the graduated percent fee in P.L. 2025, c. 69 starts at 1% and falls on the seller. Call the clerk at 609-265-5122, and consider the free Property Fraud Alert, which warns you when anything is recorded under your name.

Is a listing or a direct cash sale better for a Mount Laurel house?

A tidy house in a K-4 school zone with a passed CCO does well on the open market. A direct cash sale is better when the checklist looks expensive, an estate is involved, or you want a certain closing day.

  • Listing: the broadest set of buyers, with repairs and the CCO done beforehand.
  • Owner sale: no listing commission, though pricing and paperwork fall to you.
  • Cash purchase: bought in its present state, with fewer showings and a price reflecting condition.

Collect the CCO status, tax figure and payoff letter, then set each offer side by side on net proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Does Mount Laurel Township ask for a CCO at sale?

Yes. The township publishes a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist, and it does not take applications by email. Call Community Development / Construction for fees and scheduling.

What are the installment dates for Mount Laurel taxes?

They fall on the first of February, May, August and November, followed by a ten-day grace period. The township does not honor postmarks.

What recording charges apply for a Mount Laurel deed?

The Burlington County Clerk lists $45 for the first page and $10 for each added page, plus the state realty transfer fee. Sales above $1 million may owe the graduated percent fee.

Where do Mount Laurel students attend high school?

Lenape High School in Medford, within the Lenape Regional High School District. The township's own district ends at grade 8.

Could I sell my Mount Laurel house as-is to a cash buyer?

Yes, an as-is sale is permitted. The CCO items and any open permits still need an owner, so ask the township and your attorney who must finish them and by when.

How can I sell a house in Pemberton Township?

Three routes exist for a Pemberton house: an agent listing, a sale the owner runs alone, or a direct purchase by an investor who accepts the property in its present state. Condition and timing usually decide it, because the township wants its own inspection finished before title passes.

The township spreads over roughly 62 square miles of Burlington County, fourth largest of the county's 40 municipalities by area. Browns Mills, Country Lake Estates, Pemberton Heights, Presidential Lakes Estates and part of Fort Dix all sit within it. Pemberton borough is a separate municipality surrounded by the township, one of New Jersey's doughnut towns, so check which jurisdiction holds your parcel before you request forms.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers, and puts showings, a buyer's home inspection and the township's resale inspection on your calendar.
  • Owner-run sale: keeps the commission, but you handle pricing, advertising and every municipal form yourself.
  • Investor purchase: a shorter path with fewer contingencies, and an offer priced for whatever repairs the buyer inherits.

What do the numbers say about Pemberton homes and owners?

Pemberton skews toward owners who stay put. The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 27,611 people, compared with 26,903 counted in April 2020, spread over 9,785 households of about 2.73 people each.

Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows a typical owner-occupied Pemberton home valued at $234,500, while the national typical value sits at $332,700. Owners live in 73.3 percent of homes. Household income runs $80,843 at the midpoint, and the average trip to work takes 31.7 minutes. Residents 65 and over make up 16.6 percent of the population.

Traffic moves along County Route 530, Route 70 in the south and U.S. Route 206 on the western border. The New Jersey Turnpike and Interstate 295 pass through neighboring Springfield, so the closest interchanges are two towns over. NJ Transit bus 317 connects the area to Asbury Park and Philadelphia. One school district, Pemberton Township, serves most of the township, with nine schools and 4,443 students in 2021 to 2022.

Does Pemberton require an inspection before a house changes hands?

Yes. A Certificate of Occupancy Transfer is required every time a residential unit gets a new occupant, and a sale counts. The seller submits a resale application to Code Enforcement along with the inspection fee.

Under the township's packet, the first inspection costs $150 and each repeat visit costs $50. Staff will not book a visit until the paperwork is complete and the fee is paid, and inspectors in the field cannot accept either. Applications lapse after 60 days, so file when a closing is realistic.

A buyer who wants to take over the certificate must tell the office in writing before it is issued. That option matters when the buyer plans repairs after closing. Code Enforcement answers at 609-894-3376. Items the inspector looks for include:

  • House numbers in reflective material, at least 3.5 inches tall, visible from the road.
  • Battery smoke detectors on every level, in each bedroom and outside sleeping areas, with carbon monoxide detectors near bedrooms where a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage exists.
  • An anti-tilt bracket on the stove, rails on stairs with four or more risers, and a mounted ABC extinguisher of 5 to 10 pounds.
  • Window screens, egress windows that open easily, and GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths, garages and outdoors.
  • Every utility switched on for the visit.

What else gets reviewed on the Pemberton resale application?

The form follows the account history of the property as well as the structure. Each department initials its own box, so clearing balances early keeps the file from stalling.

  • The tax office confirms liens, taxes paid, and the solid waste, water and sewer accounts.
  • Public Works notes the water and sewer units billed.
  • The housing office checks open permits, open code violations, vacant property fees and any board-up or clean-up charges.
  • Houses on private water or septic attach a well report or a septic report.

The attached checklist lists what Pemberton will not do. Inspectors skip air conditioning, pools, hot tubs and termites, decline basements with standing water, and do not remove leftover furniture or appliances. For the roof, wiring, structure or heating, a bonded contractor's certification may be requested.

How does the Pemberton tax bill affect a closing?

Each installment is due on the first of its month, and a ten-day grace period runs to the 10th. After that, interest reaches back to the first. Balances left open on December 31 pick up a 6 percent year-end penalty on top.

One bill covers the township, Burlington County, the county farmland and open space fund, the local school board and the county library. Because the township collects for all five, a tax search before closing shows what is outstanding across the whole bill. Payments are credited on arrival, never by postmark, and a bill that never arrived does not excuse a late installment. The tax office is at 609-894-3370.

A lien can be redeemed only by someone with a legal interest in the parcel. Requests go in writing to TaxOffice@pemberton-twp.com, and the payoff must arrive in full as certified funds. Title companies typically handle this step.

Do Pinelands rules touch a Pemberton sale?

They can. Pemberton is one of 56 southern New Jersey municipalities inside the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of the township lies in the narrower state-designated Pinelands Area. Congress created the reserve in 1978.

A plain change of ownership rarely hits those rules. They matter when a buyer wants an addition, a new outbuilding or a lot division. Ask the township's Community Development office whether your parcel is in the Pinelands Area before you make promises about future building.

What do the state and Burlington County add to a Pemberton deed?

The seller owes the state a realty transfer fee when the deed is recorded, set by bracket on the sale price. Nonresident sellers, including heirs who live elsewhere, also prepay Gross Income Tax at closing. That payment is the greater of a figure based on the gain and 2 percent of the price in the deed.

Burlington County's Clerk records the deed. Seller tax forms signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the newest version, or the office returns them. The same office runs a free alert service that emails, texts or calls an owner when anything is recorded under their name. Call 609-265-5122 to ask about it. The county names seniors and owners of vacant properties as common targets of deed fraud.

When is a cash offer a good fit for a Pemberton house?

It suits a house that needs more work than the township checklist tolerates, a vacant property, or a seller with a firm move date. Ask any buyer who orders the transfer inspection, who pays the $150, and who signs for the repair list.

Judge an offer by what lands in your account after repairs, carrying costs and the state fee. Open permits and unpaid sewer or solid waste balances do not block a sale, though they have to be settled or credited at the table.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my house in Pemberton Township?

Yes. Pemberton requires a Certificate of Occupancy Transfer when a residential unit changes occupant. The resale application lists a $150 first inspection, a $50 reinspection and a 60 day life.

Can a buyer take over the Pemberton certificate?

Yes, once the code office has that request in writing before it issues the certificate. The buyer then owns the repair list, which suits as-is and investor purchases.

When are property taxes due in Pemberton?

They are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a grace period to the 10th. After that, interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 owed and 18 percent beyond it.

Who pays the state transfer fee on a Pemberton sale?

The seller pays it at recording. For a sale at the Census median of $234,500, the state's brackets give about $1,204.

Check before assuming so. The borough is its own municipality inside the township, and the forms and dates quoted here come from the township. Ask the office serving your address which set applies.

What makes a Willingboro sale different from a typical New Jersey sale?

Willingboro makes the seller clear a township certificate of occupancy before ownership changes, and the inspection must be booked a full 15 days ahead of settlement. That clock drives the rest of the sale: heating certification, any repairs, a possible reinspection and then the filing in Mount Holly.

Willingboro is a Burlington County suburb of Philadelphia, home to 32,824 people. The sections below cover local numbers, resale rules, tax steps and the trade-offs between an agent, a sale on your own and a cash buyer.

What do the Willingboro numbers say about homes and households?

Willingboro grew from a single builder's plan, and the figures still reflect it. Owners live in 84.3 percent of homes, households average 3.02 people, and 7.73 square miles of land hold about 4,128 people per square mile. The 2020 count was 31,889, and the mid-2025 estimate reads 32,824.

What is the Levittown story behind Willingboro's neighborhoods?

Willingboro began as the Constabulary of Wellingborrow on November 6, 1688, and the legislature made it a township on February 21, 1798. Its present shape comes from the 1950s and 1960s, when Levitt and Sons built its third and largest Levittown here. The first homes sold in June 1958, and the population climbed from 852 in 1950 to 43,386 in 1970.

Residents voted in 1959 to call it Levittown Township, and a second referendum in November 1963 brought the old name back. The planning left a pattern buyers still use to find a house:

  • Neighborhoods are called parks, such as Pennypacker Park, Millbrook Park, Windsor Park and Hawthorne Park.
  • Streets inside each park start with the same letter as the park's name, so a Pennypacker address starts with P.
  • Country Club Ridge was planned around a golf course in the 1960s.
  • Pennypacker Park and Country Club Park hold the community pools.

Many houses here came from a small set of Levitt floor plans, so a buyer can often compare yours with the same model a few streets away. Mention additions and the age of the roof and furnace when you present the house.
