How do Route 130, the bus lines and the schools figure in?

U.S. Route 130 marks the northwest boundary, while Rancocas Creek drains the southwest side. Willingboro borders Burlington Township, Delanco, Delran, Edgewater Park, Moorestown, Mount Laurel and Westampton. Of its 122.11 miles of roads, 109.02 miles are township-maintained.

Transit is by bus. NJ Transit routes 409, 417 and 418 run between Trenton and Philadelphia, BurLink runs two local routes, and Academy Bus links Willingboro to Midtown and Lower Manhattan.

The district, Willingboro Township Public Schools, ran nine schools with 3,456 students in 2020-21. Hawthorne, W.R. James Sr. and Twin Hills serve grades 1 to 4, Levitt Intermediate covers grades 5 and 6, Memorial Middle School covers 7 and 8, and Willingboro High School covers 9 to 12. Families will ask which school serves your park, so find out before the first showing.

How does the Willingboro certificate of occupancy process work?

Chapter 199 of the township code, the housing standards chapter, bars a change of ownership or occupancy until the Department of Inspections issues a certificate of occupancy. The ordinance sets these steps:

  • The owner or agent applies and pays the fee set in the township fee schedule.
  • The visit must be set no later than 15 calendar days ahead of settlement, and a request made within four days of it adds an $80 expedite charge.
  • Cancel or move the appointment with a day's notice, or the first fee is charged regardless.
  • The inspector makes a visual check of accessible parts of the structure, which is not a guarantee of electrical, plumbing or heating systems.
  • A qualified technician authorized by the township must separately certify the heating equipment, and that certification can be no more than 30 days old when the certificate issues.
  • If the house fails, the department sends a written list of defects, and the owner then has 30 days from the visit to repair them and ask for a recheck.

Ask the Department of Inspections for the current fee and application steps. If the buyer will take on repairs, say so in the contract so both sides know who pays.

Where does the Willingboro deed go, and what fees does the state add?

The Burlington County Clerk's main office, 50 Rancocas Road in Mount Holly, takes deeds on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. The clerk also runs a free Property Fraud Alert service that flags any paper filed under your name.

One paperwork rule changed recently. County staff reject any GIT/REP seller declaration signed on or after October 1, 2025 that is not on the latest state form.

For prices up to $350,000 the state's realty transfer fee runs $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, then $3.35 per $500 through $200,000, then $3.90 per $500 through $350,000. At a $270,300 price, those three tiers total roughly $1,480, a number your closing agent will confirm.

What are Willingboro's tax dates and the October tax sale?

Bills follow the calendar year, with installments due on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace period after each. From the eleventh day, interest is figured back to the first, and a postmark earns no credit.

Payments go to the window in the municipal building, the Police Department drop box, the mail or the township's online portal. The tax office sits in Suite 205 at One Rev. Dr. M. L. King Jr. Drive, with window hours from 9 in the morning to 4:30. The portal rejects prior-year balances, so get an exact payoff figure from the collector before closing.

A balance left open past December 31 enters the township's electronic tax sale, held every October for earlier unpaid taxes and municipal charges. The 2026 auction was set for October 14. Senior, veteran and disabled-person deductions are handled by the assessor's office at 609-877-2200.

Which fits a Willingboro owner best: agent, own sale or cash buyer?

A listing can bring the strongest price for a clean house, a cash buyer removes the repair cycle, and selling alone falls between them. Timing is the real difference, because of the 15-day inspection lead.

  • An agent suits a house in good repair that can pass inspection without a long defect list.
  • A solo sale suits an owner who follows recent prices in the neighborhood and will hire an attorney for the contract.
  • A cash purchase suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate, since the buyer can take over the defect list.

Book the township inspection the moment a closing date exists, and measure each offer by the cash that reaches you after transfer fee, taxes and payoff.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection mandatory before a Willingboro sale?

Yes. A certificate of occupancy is needed before ownership changes, and the visit must be booked 15 calendar days ahead. A qualified technician must also certify the heating equipment.

What if the inspector finds defects?

The department issues a written notice of defects. You have 30 days from the inspection to finish repairs and request a reinspection, and the certificate follows once the house passes.

What are the Willingboro installment dates?

The first of February, May, August and November, each followed by ten grace days. Postmarks are ignored, and balances still open after December 31 enter the October tax sale.

Which office records a Willingboro deed?

The Burlington County Clerk's main office, 50 Rancocas Road in Mount Holly, which serves the public on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Can a Willingboro house with tenants or repair needs be sold?

Yes. The certificate rules still apply, but an as-is buyer can agree to take over the defect list and the occupancy. Spell out who handles the inspection and repairs in the contract.

Cherry Hill sellers face two separate township inspections before closing, one covering the property's exterior and one covering smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and each is booked through a different office. Booking both early keeps the closing date from slipping.

The township is large, mostly owner-occupied and built largely in the decades after World War II, so the typical seller owns a single-family house on a suburban lot with trees, fences, driveways and sidewalks that the township cares about. How big is Cherry Hill and how did it develop?

Cherry Hill covers about 24 square miles of Camden County, which makes it the county's most populous municipality. It began as Delaware Township in 1844, and in 1961 took the Cherry Hill name from a local farm. Quaker settlers arrived in the late 1600s, the first small cluster was Colestown, and 19th-century farms supplied produce to the Campbell's soup plant across the river in Camden. Growth then jumped after World War II, from about 10,400 residents in 1950 to 31,500 in 1960 and 64,400 in 1970.

Its neighborhoods include Ashland, Barclay, Erlton, Greentree, Kingston Estates, Springdale, Woodcrest and the area around Cherry Hill Mall. Private options include Camden Catholic High School and the King's Christian School.

What are the two Cherry Hill inspections before closing?

A seller here needs a Certificate of Continued Occupancy from the township and a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate from the fire department. A single-family sale cannot reach closing without them, and they are separate appointments with separate costs.

The occupancy certificate comes from Community Development, which handles property maintenance, at 820 Mercer Street, Room 202. The property maintenance officer looks at exterior areas only. The township lists these items:

  • Sidewalks, driveways and fences.
  • Trees and natural growth.
  • Sanitation and exhaust vents.
  • Grading and drainage, including where sump pumps discharge.
  • Accessory structures and ground surface hazards.

The inspection costs $100, payable ahead of the visit, and you can apply online, in person or by mail. Online applications need office approval before a payment request is emailed, cancellations after payment are not refunded, and the property maintenance line is 856-834-3364. Some condominiums and townhomes are excluded, and the township posts a list of properties that skip the inspection.

The fire department certificate is a different step. It is required for one- and two-family homes before settlement, and sellers are asked to request the appointment three to four weeks early. If the home passes and payment is made, the certificate is handed over at the visit; temporary certificates are not issued, and fire extinguishers are no longer required. The fire department's inspection line is (856) 429-7441. Because the two appointments run on separate calendars, book both the week the contract is signed.

Does the township help with move-out trash after a Cherry Hill sale?

Yes, Cherry Hill offers a one-time courtesy collection for house clean-outs after a sale, covering furniture, carpets, bedding and similar household items. Proof that you applied for a Continued Certificate of Occupancy is required before Public Works will schedule it, pickups happen on Fridays, and the number to call is 856-424-4422.

The same guidelines say no trash or recycling service goes to dwellings under construction, vacant lots or properties lacking a valid certificate of occupancy, so a vacant house waiting on its paperwork may go without pickup. Plan the clean-out around the certificate date, and keep contractor debris out of the cart, because construction waste generated by a contractor has to be hauled away by that contractor.

When are Cherry Hill property taxes due and who collects them?

The four installments land on the first of August, November, February and May, and a ten-day grace period rolls forward to the next business day if it ends on a weekend or holiday. The township mails two bills a year: July covers the third and fourth installments, and January covers the first and second. Money has to be in the tax office by the last grace day, because postmarks do not count.

Late payments accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any amount beyond that, running from the original due date. The tax collector also bills sewer rent: residential sewer is a flat annual fee due April 1, with a 10 percent discount for owners 60 or older who live in the property. Ask the tax office at 856-488-7880 for a closing figure that includes any sewer balance. The office gathers money for the school district, the fire district and Camden County along with the township, so the bill you pay includes those shares.

Appeals follow state deadlines, April 1 or May 1 after a revaluation, and go to the Camden County Board of Taxation.

How much is the transfer fee and where does the deed get filed?

The Camden County Clerk files the deed, and the seller owes the state realty transfer fee when it is filed. Above $350,000 the state schedule runs $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 for the slice from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000. On a $400,000 price, those slices add up to about $3,215: $870, then $425, then $1,920. Confirm the figure with your closing attorney, since senior, disabled and low-income rates run lower.

The county's recording schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for every added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge, with a $55 floor. Camden County's online land records start in 1978, and the clerk's office answers at 856-225-5300. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification at closing, while a seller who is leaving the state prepays estimated income tax, so tell your attorney early if you are relocating.

Yes, two of them. The township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for single-family resale, and the fire department requires a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before settlement.

What does the Cherry Hill resale inspection cost?

The occupancy inspection is $100, paid before the inspector arrives. The fire department sets its own charges, which are posted on its checklist.

How early should the Cherry Hill fire inspection be scheduled?

Three to four weeks before settlement. The certificate is given at the appointment if the home complies and payment is made, and temporary certificates are not available.

What are the Cherry Hill tax installment dates?

August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day grace period applies, and the money must reach the tax office by then because postmarks do not count.

Who files a Cherry Hill deed?

The Camden County Clerk. The posted schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for each added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge.

Gloucester Township Public Schools teach prekindergarten through eighth grade in eight elementary schools and three middle schools: Glen Landing, Charles W. Lewis and Ann A. Mullen. Ninth through twelfth graders attend Highland Regional in Blackwood, Timber Creek Regional in Erial or Triton Regional in Runnemede, assigned by address within the Black Horse Pike Regional School District.

In 2010 the township listed 239.44 miles of road, 186.25 of them municipal. The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the southwest corner, Routes 42 and 168 run through the west, and County Routes 534 and 544 cover the center and the northern edge. NJ Transit's 400 bus reaches Philadelphia, and the 403 and 459 serve local trips.

The township's downloads page carries a Landlord Identity Registration form, so a rental owner should confirm the registration is current before listing. Search your street address in the township's property tax lookup and read the Special Taxing Districts line. F04 means Fire District No. 4.

The first of February, May, August and November, each with a 10-day grace period. Late balances accrue interest, and taxes still delinquent after November 11 can go to tax sale.

By when must I appeal a Gloucester Township assessment?

By 4:00 p.m. on April 1, or May 1 where the town did a revaluation or reassessment. The Camden County Board of Taxation hears appeals at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood and offers a summary hearing with no appearance.

May I sell a Gloucester Township house with liens or a foreclosure pending?

Yes, if the sale price covers every payoff. Get written figures from each lender and from the tax collector, since tax sale charges add fees beyond the posted tax total.

The township lies in Camden County directly across the Delaware River from Philadelphia, joined to the city by the Betsy Ross Bridge, which opened April 30, 1976. It covers 10.48 square miles of land plus 1.65 of water, was set off from Stockton Township and incorporated on February 18, 1892, and had an estimated 37,742 residents in mid-2025. Petty's Island, a 392-acre island in the river, belongs to Pennsauken, and the Camden Drive-In, the first drive-in theater in America, opened here in 1933.

Industry shapes the local map. A large industrial park holds a beverage bottling plant and a snack food manufacturer, and the old Pennsauken Mart site became a luxury apartment complex completed in 2018 after the market closed in January 2006.

What does the Pennsauken housing resale inspection involve?

Township ordinance calls for an interior and exterior inspection plus a Certificate of Occupancy before settlement. The Building Department's packet lists a combined $175 fee, made up of $100 for the housing resale certificate and $75 for the fire certificate.

Sellers send both forms and payment to the Building Department, then wait about two to three days after the visit for a written report. The housing office takes scheduling calls at 856-665-1000, extension 145, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Certificates cover one change of ownership or six months, whichever ends first. The application also asks whether the buyer plans to flip the house, rent it or live in it, and whether the property is vacant, rented or owner-occupied.

If the report lists repairs, the buyer may sign a notarized affidavit for a temporary certificate, accepting the report and responsibility for the final certificate. When the report forbids occupancy before a final certificate, the temporary version covers work only. Open construction permits must be inspected and closed first, and the packet warns that missed permits can push back a settlement date.

Which fire safety items does Pennsauken check?

The fire certificate looks at alarms and extinguishers, with smoke alarm rules that depend on the year the house was built.

  • Before 1975: sealed 10-year battery alarms only.
  • 1975 to 1977: a hardwired detector on the top level and sealed battery alarms elsewhere.
  • 1977 to 1983: interconnected hardwired alarms on the top level and in the basement, battery alarms on other levels.
  • 1983 to 1991: interconnected hardwired alarms on every level.
  • 1991 on: interconnected hardwired alarms with battery backup on every level and in each bedroom.

A carbon monoxide alarm must sit within ten feet of every sleeping area, and combination units are accepted. At least one extinguisher rated 2A:10-BC, no heavier than ten pounds, must hang within ten feet of the kitchen with its top three to five feet above the floor, and carry a service tag from the last 365 days or a dated receipt if new.

The climate is humid subtropical. Recorded extremes run from 108 degrees Fahrenheit on July 16, 1995 to minus 4 degrees in January 1994, and 13.59 percent of the township's area is water, so expect buyers to ask about drainage and basement history.

The township mails one bill each summer. It combines a final bill for the current year and a preliminary bill for the next, with four stubs due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. The district listed five schools in the 2019-20 school year: Hamilton, Kresson, Osage and Signal Hill elementary schools, and Voorhees Middle School with 1,018 students. High school students attend Eastern Camden County Regional High School, which the township shares with Berlin Borough and Gibbsboro.

Edward T. Hamilton Elementary was named a National Blue Ribbon School in 2003-2004. The Camden County Library's largest branch, the M. Allan Vogelson Regional Branch, is in Voorhees. Voorhees has four elementary schools, so find out which one your street feeds before you list.

What else do Voorhees buyers look at besides the house?

Buyers compare more than square footage. Voorhees has a 368-bed hospital, Virtua Voorhees, on Route 73, and the largest branch of the Camden County Library at the M. Allan Vogelson Regional Branch, open since 1969. Two private schools, Kellman Brown Academy (a Jewish day school for ages 3 through grade 8) and the Naudain Academy Montessori program, add options beyond the public K-8 district.

The Flyers Training Center, expanded in 2018, and a community park with a running track, playground, gazebo and dog areas round out the amenities. Saddlehill Vineyard and Winery opened in 2021 on the former Stafford Farm. Mention the ones near your street in the listing.

What does the township require before a Voorhees house changes hands?

The township construction office handles certificates of occupancy and continued occupancy, so call it first. Ask whether a change of owner needs a resale certificate, what the inspection covers, and how long the certificate lasts before closing.

Unpermitted work is the usual snag. A finished basement, deck or converted garage built without a permit can hold up the certificate until the permit is closed or the work removed, so pull your permit history before you sign a contract.

  • One- and two-family homes need smoke alarms with 10-year sealed batteries before a sale (N.J.A.C. 5:70-4.19).
  • That rule leaves hardwired and low-voltage alarm systems and carbon monoxide alarms alone.
  • Ask the construction office for its current checklist, inspection fee and scheduling window.

What taxes and fees apply when you sell in Voorhees?

The seller pays the state's Realty Transfer Fee, set per $500 of price by bracket. For sales over $350,000 the $200,000 to $550,000 bracket carries $4.80 per $500, and Voorhees's Census median of $429,700 sits inside it. Above $1 million the buyer owes an extra 1% and the seller a graduated fee.

Every owner on the deed signs a GIT/REP form. Staying in New Jersey means GIT/REP-3 and no prepayment. Moving out of state can mean prepaying the state either 2% of the price or 8.97% of the gain. A main home that you owned and lived in for two of the last five years may qualify for the federal gain exclusion.

Have your closing attorney file the transfer fee affidavit with the deed. The county clerk can refuse a deed that arrives incomplete.

How do property tax assessments and appeals work in Voorhees?

Disputes over a Voorhees assessment go to the Camden County Board of Taxation, 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, phone 856-225-5238. Camden County keeps the regular calendar: April 1, or May 1 after a municipal revaluation. A property valued above $1,000,000 can go straight to Tax Court.

The board weighs comparable sales more than your opinion of fair value, and an appeal does little for a seller about to close. A buyer or heir who keeps the house might benefit. Owners of a main home may qualify for the state's Homestead Benefit or Senior Freeze, and the township handles local deductions for seniors, disabled owners and veterans.

How does Voorhees weather affect a house for sale?

Voorhees sits in a transition zone between humid continental and humid subtropical climates. Average July highs reach 87 degrees, record lows have dropped to minus 13, and the year brings about 41 inches of precipitation across roughly 117 wet days and nearly 23 inches of snow.

That mix tests roofs, gutters, sump pumps and heating systems. Buyers and inspectors look at those items first, so a house with a recent roof or serviced boiler needs fewer repair credits. A cash buyer pricing the house as-is will weigh the same items.

  • Roof and gutters: ask for the install year and any warranty paperwork.
  • Basement: note any past water, and what was done about it.
  • Heating and cooling: gather service records for the last few seasons.

Frequently asked questions

How soon could a Voorhees house sale close?

A cash sale often closes within a few weeks. A listed sale runs longer because of showings, the buyer's loan and any township review, so ask the construction office how long its resale inspection takes.

Does Voorhees need an occupancy certificate for a sale?

Call the township construction office, which issues the certificates of occupancy and continued occupancy used when a house changes owners. State law separately calls for 10-year sealed-battery smoke alarms in one- and two-family homes.

Who covers the transfer fee on a Voorhees sale?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. The buyer's extra 1% starts at $1 million, far above the $429,700 Census median for Voorhees homes.

What is the last day to contest a Voorhees assessment?

April 1 in Camden County, or May 1 after a revaluation. Use Form A-1 and call the Camden County Board of Taxation in Blackwood at 856-225-5238.

Will open permits stop a Voorhees sale?

They can slow the township's sign-off. Have the construction office review your permit history, then close the permits or agree in writing with the buyer on who repairs what and by when.

What sets a Winslow sale apart from other Camden County sales?

A Winslow closing depends on two separate approvals: a township resale certificate from the Construction Official and an alarm certificate from the Winslow Township Fire District. The township is also the biggest in Camden County by area, and much of its land lies in the Pinelands.

Below you will find market figures, both inspections with their fees, the Camden County filing and the township's tax rules, ending with a plain comparison of an agent listing, a sale by yourself and an as-is cash buyer.

What do the Winslow figures show about homes and incomes?

The 2020 census put Winslow at 39,907 people, and the mid-2025 estimate is 40,562. Those residents are spread across 57.42 square miles of land, only 695 per square mile, which fits the pine woods and farm parcels between its villages.

What shaped Winslow's neighborhoods and the Pinelands around them?

Winslow was incorporated on March 8, 1845 from part of Gloucester Township, and its early economy ran on glass works that drew on local timber, clay and sand. By the 1970 census it still had only 11,202 residents.

Growth followed the Atlantic City Expressway interchange at Williamstown Road, finished in 1965. Levitt and Sons then built thousands of homes in the Sicklerville section, and the population reached 20,034 in 1980 and 30,087 in 1990. Today the township includes unincorporated communities such as Sicklerville, Cedar Brook, Blue Anchor, Tansboro, Braddock, Albion and Williamstown.

Much of the land is protected: Wikipedia reports that around 80 percent of the township sat inside the Pinelands National Reserve in 2006. The New Jersey Pinelands span 1.1 million acres, and the Pinelands Commission can be reached at (609) 894-7300. For a large lot, or a buyer who plans a new structure, ask the Commission which approvals apply before you promise anything.

How do the Expressway, the buses and the schools affect Winslow buyers?

Roads total 245.16 miles, divided among the township, Camden County, the state and the South Jersey Transportation Authority. The Atlantic City Expressway cuts through the southwest with Exits 31, 33, 38 and 41, and Route 73, Route 143 and U.S. Route 30 also run through town.

Transit means buses. NJ Transit's 400 route links Sicklerville with Philadelphia, and the Avandale park-and-ride has 322 parking spaces. No bus stops within reasonable walking distance of the municipal building, so most households drive.

Winslow Township School District had eight schools and 5,024 students in 2023-24, with four elementary schools through grade 3, two upper elementary schools for grades 4 to 6, one middle school and Winslow Township High School. The district formed in 1998 after voters approved a split from the Lower Camden County Regional district, and it also teaches students from Chesilhurst.

What does the Winslow resale certificate involve?

Under Chapter 205 of the township code, retitled Resale Certificates by a February 2025 ordinance, every existing dwelling needs a certificate of continued occupancy before occupancy changes. Applicants go to the Township Construction Official, who inspects for habitability and compliance with the code.

  • Residential applications cost $100.
  • Payment by check triggers a 10 working-day wait before the inspection.
  • The Construction Official has 10 working days from a complete application and fee to inspect and then issue the certificate or list the violations.
  • The first reinspection is free, and each later one costs $50.
  • No one may occupy the dwelling until life-hazard violations are corrected.
  • Violating the chapter carries a penalty from $250 up to $1,000.

The ordinance has an unusual option. A buyer can assume the seller's duty through a written waiver acknowledging responsibility for the certificate, and the waiver is filed with the Construction Official.

What happens at the Winslow fire inspection?

State law calls for an alarm inspection before a home is sold, and the Winslow Fire Prevention Division performs it. A firefighter sprays test smoke into each smoke alarm, presses the carbon monoxide test button and checks for a secondary power source label. A passing house earns a certificate to carry to settlement.

  • The fee is $65 with eight or more days of notice, $100 with four to seven days and $150 with three days or fewer.
  • A senior aged 62 or older with proof of age pays $30.
  • Reinspections and missed appointments cost $35 each.
  • Alarms past ten years of age must go, and the manufacture date is printed on the underside of each device.
  • Solar panels, a generator or battery storage call for a permanent printed label at the panel and meter warning of multiple sources of power.
  • The fire district will not go in on a lockbox, and its office says it answers online applications within 24 hours.

An all-electric house with no fireplace or attached garage needs only smoke alarms. Questions about your layout go to the Fire Marshal at 609-561-4225.

Which county office records a Winslow deed, and how do local taxes work?

Camden County's Clerk records Winslow deeds from Room 102 at 520 Market Street in Camden, phone (856) 225-5300. The clerk's page advertises electronic recording and appointment booking, so a title company can usually file on your behalf.

Installments come due on the first of February, May, August and November. A ten-day courtesy period follows, but the collector must physically hold the payment by the end of the tenth day, since postmarks do not count. Delinquent amounts up to $1,500 carry 8 percent interest and larger ones carry 18 percent, and a balance above $10,000 at year end adds a 6 percent penalty. Anything left in the township drop box counts as received the next business day.

Added and omitted assessment bills go out in October and fall due November 1. The 2026 tax sale was scheduled for October 8, and the township points out that taxes and utility charges attach to the property itself. Request a payoff figure from the tax office before closing.

Is an agent, a solo sale or a cash buyer right for a Winslow house?

An agent listing usually reaches the widest pool of buyers, a cash buyer sidesteps the repair cycle, and a solo sale saves commission for owners who can manage the paperwork. The house's condition and your deadline settle the question.

  • Use an agent if the house is in good order and you can wait while a mortgage buyer passes the township inspection.
  • Go solo if you will manage showings, the contract and both Winslow inspections.
  • Choose an as-is cash buyer if repairs, tenants or an estate would slow a conventional sale, because that buyer can sign the resale waiver and take over any violations.

Whatever you pick, request a Fire District date as soon as a closing is set, and file the township application early enough to give the inspector the 10 working days the ordinance allows.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Winslow resale certificate?

The township charges $100 for a residential dwelling. The first reinspection is free and later ones cost $50. The separate fire inspection runs $65 to $150 depending on notice, with a $30 senior rate.

Who must obtain the Winslow certificate, seller or buyer?

The seller by default, though a buyer may assume the duty through a written waiver filed with the Construction Official. The waiver must say the buyer knows the responsibility is being taken over.

How fast can a Winslow fire inspection be arranged?

The fire district says it replies within a day of an online application, and fees rise with less than eight days of notice. Bring the certificate to settlement.

What are the Winslow tax installment dates?

The first of February, May, August and November, followed by ten grace days. Postmarks are not honored, and late interest runs back to the original due date.

Where do Winslow house deeds get filed?

With the Camden County Clerk, Room 102 at 520 Market Street, Camden. The phone number is (856) 225-5300.

What is Belleville's history and where does it sit in Essex County?

Belleville grew from a settlement called Second River, renamed Belleville in 1797, and it was incorporated as a township in 1839 from part of Bloomfield. Congress passed a resolution in 1994 recognizing Belleville as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution in the United States.

The township borders Bloomfield, Newark and Nutley in Essex County, Lyndhurst and North Arlington in Bergen County, and Kearny in Hudson County. The Second River forms much of the border with Newark through Branch Brook Park, and Belleville calls itself the Cherry Blossom Capital of America because of the park's spring display. Silver Lake, split between Belleville and Bloomfield, is the best-known unincorporated community, alongside Belwood, Big Tree and Soho.

The local economy is also worth a line in a listing. Census figures show 68.5% of residents aged 16 and over in the civilian labor force for 2020-2024, retail sales of about $381 million in 2022 and a per capita retail figure of $10,163. Belleville Township spans only 3.37 square miles in total, so most blocks are within a short walk of a bus line or a commercial street.

Gather the permit paperwork for any work you finished in the house, including fences, pools and driveways, since the township keeps separate applications for each. Having those approvals ready lets a buyer's attorney confirm the work was permitted without waiting on township offices.

Buyers of tenant-occupied buildings will want copies of leases and the rent roster, so organize them before you list. A clean file shortens attorney review and reduces last-minute price talks.

The township also links the Essex County Board of Taxation and the state's Property Tax Relief Program.

Pull your latest tax bill and any open balance before you list, because buyers and title companies ask for them. If you have a PD-5 deduction or veteran's credit, the buyer will not inherit it automatically, so ask the Tax Collector whether those benefits change after a sale. The township website also lists a Home Improvement Program with an application and a contractor application, which a buyer planning repairs can read.

It has a Rent Leveling Board, with a Vacancy Decontrol Application and a complaint form on the township website. Landlords should confirm their status before selling.

What kind of town is Bloomfield, New Jersey?

Bloomfield packs 56,375 people (Census estimate, July 2025) into 5.34 square miles of land in Essex County, which is 6.2 percent more than in 2020. In 2020 the count was 9,950.3 per square mile. The township borders Belleville, East Orange, Glen Ridge, Montclair, Newark and Nutley in Essex County and Clifton in Passaic County, and it includes the Brookdale and Watsessing neighborhoods plus a slice of Silver Lake.

The land was first patented to colonists from Newark and assigned to Essex County in 1675. The Presbyterian Society of Bloomfield formed in 1794, and the township's population jumped from 9,668 in 1900 to 38,077 in 1930, which points to an older housing stock and a long paper trail of permits.

The form states that the inspection shows only that a general check of the visible parts of the building found no code violations or unsafe conditions at that time. The township's FAQ adds that if a bank insists on a separate certificate, the Fire Prevention Bureau issues one for $35, although state law allows a single certificate.

What does the Bloomfield inspector check?

The Township publishes a checklist, and the inspector may ask for more than it lists. Most items are quick repairs, though a few take weeks, such as closing old permits and replacing a lead service line.

  • All construction permits, past and present, closed with final inspections.
  • Proof that any lead or galvanized water service line on private property has been replaced, documented by a New Jersey plumber.
  • A township-approved water meter in place, even if the building is winterized.
  • Sump pumps and downspouts not tied into the sanitary sewer.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors on each floor and near bedrooms, 10-year sealed battery or hard-wired.
  • A fire-rated, self-closing door between an attached garage and the house.
  • Handrails on stairs with four or more risers, no loose siding or roofing, and numbered units.
  • No unregistered vehicles, debris or trip hazards on the property.

Three-family and larger buildings also need portable fire extinguishers, mounted near an exit within 10 feet of the kitchen. If the new owner will rent the property, the form says the rental must be registered within six months of closing.

Do oil tanks and basement apartments cause problems in Bloomfield?

They can. The township's fire FAQ says an unused oil tank must be removed or abandoned in place within one year, and either path needs a Fire Sub-Code permit from the Building Department. If a tank was removed with a permit, the Fire Department or Building Department may have the paperwork on file, so call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you hunt for records.

Basement apartments are a larger issue. The FAQ states that most are illegal, especially in three-family houses, because they do not meet egress requirements. Check with the Building Inspector before you advertise one as a rental unit, because an unpermitted unit can stall a Transfer of Property Title and spook a lender.

How are Bloomfield property taxes billed and appealed?

Four quarterly installments come due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, with interest running once ten calendar days have passed. Under N.J.S.A. 54:4-64 a bill that never arrives does not cancel the tax. A new owner or a seller with a lost bill should ask the Tax Collector for the amount due and a duplicate.

The Tax Assessor runs assessments, deductions for senior citizens, disabled persons and veterans, and appeals. Filing closes April 1 of the tax year, and May 1 in a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect. State relief programs listed by the township include the Homestead Rebate, NJSAVER, the Property Tax Deduction or Credit and Property Tax Reimbursement, so an owner receiving one should tell the closing attorney.

The Tax Assessor's Office sits at 1 Municipal Plaza, first floor, Room 108. Payments to the Tax Collector can be made online or in person.

What do trains, highways and schools add to Bloomfield listings?

The Garden State Parkway has four interchanges in the township, numbered 148 through 151, with 148 and 151 complete and 149 and 150 partial. The Essex toll plaza sits southbound just south of interchange 150. County Road 506, its spur and County Road 509 also cross the township, and Bloomfield has 95.39 miles of roadway in all.

South Bloomfield is served by two NJ Transit Montclair-Boonton Line stations, one off Bloomfield Avenue downtown and one at Watsessing Avenue and Orange Street. About 55 percent of weekday trains continue to New York Penn Station, and weekend trains end at Hoboken. Mean travel time to work is 32.4 minutes. Bloomfield Public Schools run 11 schools and enrolled 6,191 students in 2021 to 2022, from pre-kindergarten through Bloomfield High School and Bridges Academy. Bloomfield Tech High School is a countywide magnet school.

When should a Bloomfield owner look at a cash bid?

A cash bid deserves a look when the Transfer of Property Title would take longer than you can wait, or when repairs would cost more than the discount. Get in writing from any buyer who orders the inspection, who pays the fee and who replaces a lead service line if one turns up.

For an estate, the state treats an executor's sale to an outside buyer as taxable for the realty transfer fee, while a transfer to a named heir is exempt. Compare what each path nets and let a New Jersey attorney review the contract.

Frequently asked questions

Is a smoke detector certificate separate from the Bloomfield Transfer of Property Title?

Usually not. The township's application form says the Transfer of Property Title inspection also serves as the smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate. A separate certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau costs $35 if your bank refuses the single one.

How long before closing should I apply for a Transfer of Property Title in Bloomfield?

30 days. The township's form says the application must be submitted 30 days prior to the closing date, and the certificate is valid for six months. Reinspection after a failed visit costs $25.

Do I have to replace a lead water line to sell in Bloomfield?

Yes, if the service line on your property is lead or galvanized. The township says the owner must replace it and show proof before a Transfer of Property Title is issued. A plumber from New Jersey must inspect and document the line's material.

By what date must a Bloomfield assessment appeal be filed?

April 1 of the tax year, moving to May 1 in a year when a revaluation or reassessment takes effect. The Tax Assessor's Office has the forms.

Does selling to my own child avoid the New Jersey transfer fee?

Yes, a sale from parent to child is exempt, adopted children included. A stepchild does not qualify, so a parent selling to a stepchild owes the fee unless the child was legally adopted.

Orange covers 2.21 square miles in Essex County and has 35,642 residents by the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, up from 34,447 at the 2020 census. That works out to more than 15,000 people per square mile. It borders East Orange, Glen Ridge, Montclair, South Orange and West Orange.

How did Orange grow, and what does that mean for the housing stock?

Orange began as part of Newark, was known as Newark Mountains, and adopted the name Orange in 1780. It separated as a township in 1806, was incorporated as a city in 1872 and switched back to township status in 1982. East Orange, South Orange and West Orange all split away from it in the 1860s.

The Morris and Essex Railroad reached the city in 1836, and the F. Berg & Co. hat factory building dates from 1907. Orange was a transport crossroads on the Newark and Mount Pleasant Turnpike long before it was a commuter suburb. For a seller, the practical point is that the inspection fee rises with the number of units, so owners of two- to five-unit buildings should read the fee schedule first.

Orange is a renter-majority city. Only 25.5 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied value is $365,500 and the median gross rent is $1,550. With three in four housing units renter-occupied, expect some buyers to be small landlords rather than owner-occupants.

What is a certificate of habitability, and how do I get one in Orange?

Chapter 156, Article VII of the city code requires a certificate of habitability, issued by the Division of Code Enforcement, before any residential property is sold, purchased, conveyed or transferred. The application is filed at 29 North Day Street, Room 305, and it must include a fully executed sales contract. The steps from the city's application are:

  • Complete the transaction information and attach the sales contract or deed.
  • Pay by certified check or money order made out to the City of Orange Township.

Condominiums and townhouses skip this form and apply for a Certificate of Occupancy through the Building Division instead.

How much does the Orange certificate of habitability cost?

Can I sell an Orange house as-is?

The seller's Realty Transfer Fee is separate. The state's example lists $1,910 on a $325,000 deed with no exemption. The buyer's extra 1 percent fee starts above $1,000,000. Every deed needs a Gross Income Tax form too: the GIT/REP-3 for New Jersey residents, and GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 for nonresident sellers who must prepay. If you appeal an assessment, the Essex County board of taxation must receive the petition by April 1, or 45 days after notices are mailed if later.

How do Orange transit, roads and schools affect buyer demand?

Interstate 280 crosses the city from West Orange to East Orange, and Central Avenue is County Route 508. Valley Street, Lincoln Avenue, Scotland Road and Highland Avenue carry local traffic. The Orange and Highland Avenue stations on NJ Transit's Morris and Essex Lines reach Newark Broad Street, Secaucus Junction and New York Penn Station, and ten NJ Transit bus routes serve Newark and local trips.

The Orange Board of Education runs 12 schools and enrolled 5,629 students in 2020-21. It is one of 31 former Abbott districts, where the state pays all costs of school building projects. Schools include Rosa Parks Central Community School for grades 3 to 7, Orange Preparatory Academy for grades 8 and 9, Orange High School for grades 10 to 12 and the STEM Innovation Academy of the Oranges. The Orange Public Library, opened in 1901, holds about 200,000 volumes.

Do I need a certificate of habitability to sell a house in Orange, NJ?

The application lists $200 for a one-unit property, $300 for two units, $400 for three, $500 for four and $600 for five. Pay by certified check or money order payable to the City of Orange Township, and confirm the current schedule with Code Enforcement.

Can a buyer take an Orange house with violations?

Sometimes. For an as-is sale, Code Enforcement may issue a temporary certificate of habitability valid for up to six months, and it cannot be renewed. The contract and a buyer's attorney letter go with the application.

Are any Orange transfers exempt from the certificate?

Yes. The code exempts transfers between immediate family members, properties certified in the previous six months, properties bought for demolition and probate transfers to heirs or beneficiaries under a will.

It affects what buyers will pay. The 2020 equalized rate was 4.679 percent, compared with 2.279 percent statewide. A seller who believes the assessment is too high can petition the Essex County board of taxation by April 1.

How can you sell a house fast in Irvington, New Jersey?

An Irvington owner can hire an agent, sell without one or take a cash offer for the house in its current state. Whichever it is, the township wants a housing inspection before title passes. That requirement drives the timeline, so begin it when you decide to sell.

Fewer than one in three housing units here is owner-occupied, so a good number of sellers are landlords or heirs. The inspection fee scales with the number of dwelling units in the building.

  • Listing: best for a house that will pass inspection with little work and appraise well.
  • Private sale: works if you can manage the inspection, the contract and the buyer's financing without an agent.
  • Cash sale: fits a house with code violations, tenants or probate complications, because the purchase contract can be written around the condition.

Where is Irvington and how did it get its name?

Irvington is a small, dense township of 2.92 square miles in Essex County. Maplewood lies to the west and Newark to the east, with Hillside and Union to the south and southwest. The Elizabeth River runs through it near Civic Square.

Until the middle of the 1800s the place was called Camptown. After a well-known ballad about Camptown races was published in 1850, residents worried about the association and renamed it for the author Washington Irving. It became an incorporated village on March 27, 1874, a town in 1898, and a township after a 1982 referendum.

An amusement park, Olympic Park, straddled the Irvington and Maplewood line from 1887 to 1965. Population rose from 1,677 in 1880 to 56,733 in 1930. It has stayed between about 54,000 and 61,500 since then, reaching 61,176 in the 2020 census and an estimated 62,233 in July 2025.

What do Census figures show about Irvington housing and residents?

Irvington is a rental-heavy township with the lowest home values of the four municipalities in the same Census comparison. Owners in 29.6 percent of units, with a median owned home worth $335,600.

Rent at the median is $1,386 a month. Owners pay $2,489 with a mortgage and $1,026 without. Across 23,542 households of roughly 2.57 people, median income is $61,609, and 19.0 percent of residents fall below the poverty line.

Foreign-born residents account for 35.5 percent of the population, and 32.4 percent of people aged 5 and up speak another language at home. If several relatives share ownership, a short written summary of key dates in their own language keeps everyone on schedule.

Irvington's code makes it unlawful to sell, convey or transfer a building with residential units, or for a buyer to take title or possession, until a Certificate of Housing Compliance has been issued. The Department of Housing issues it after an application and an inspection. The online portal at irvingtonportal.us handles the application and the separate Fire Department inspection.

For an as-is sale, the contract must be attached to the application and signed by both seller and buyer. Ask the Housing Department how those exemptions apply to your sale. A denied certificate can be appealed in writing to the Business Administrator, who must decide within five business days.

Where do you apply, and who inspects?

The Housing and Building office sits in the Municipal Building, Room 201, at 1 Civic Square. Its page lists an evening housing inspector available Monday to Friday from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m. and Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m., which helps working owners schedule around a job.

  • Owners of any building in the township, residential or commercial, must give the Housing Department, Tax Collector and Tax Assessor their true home address and company address.
  • Vacant properties go through the Vacant Property Registration Program, with registration on the township portal.
  • Violation notices become orders if no written petition for a hearing is filed within 10 days, so respond to any notice quickly.
  • Fines under the property maintenance code run from $50 for a first violation to $1,000 for a fourth, which also requires a court appearance.

Of the 69.44 miles of road within the township, Irvington maintains 55.98.

How do roads, buses and schools shape the Irvington housing market?

Irvington sits between Newark and the suburbs, and transit is a selling point. The Garden State Parkway passes through the center of the township with exits 143 and 144. Interstate 78 touches the southeastern edge at Exit 54, and County Road 509 is the main local road.

  • Air: Newark Liberty International Airport is in neighboring Newark and Elizabeth.
  • Schools: Irvington Public Schools run pre-kindergarten through grade 12 and are one of 31 former Abbott districts. The district had 12 schools and 8,020 students in 2019-20.
  • Business incentives: parts of the township lie in an Urban Enterprise Zone established in May 1996, which expires in May 2027 and allows a reduced 3.3125 percent sales tax at eligible merchants. The area around the bus terminal became a state-designated transit village in July 2015.

Deeds for all 22 Essex County municipalities are recorded by the county Register of Deeds and Mortgages, whose files reach back to 1637. Assessment appeals are filed with the Essex County Board of Taxation on Form A-1, normally by April 1, and the Tax Court hears further appeals filed within 45 days of the board's judgment.

State law puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller. Because Irvington's median owned home, $335,600, sits under $350,000, the lower schedule governs, topping out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A landlord living outside New Jersey files GIT/REP-1 and prepays tax of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the net gain, unless the form's exemptions apply.

Yes. The Township Code requires a Certificate of Housing Compliance before any building with residential units is sold, conveyed or transferred. The Housing Department issues it after an application and an inspection, and a Fire Department inspection is also required, with both started on the township's online portal.

How much does the Irvington sale inspection cost?

The code sets $237 per dwelling unit up to three units in a building and $116 for each unit above three. A single-family house therefore costs $237 and a three-family $711. Reinspections carry their own fee, so fix the listed items before the first visit and confirm current amounts with the Housing Department.

Can I sell an Irvington house as-is if it has violations?

Yes, with conditions. The as-is contract must be attached to the application and signed by both parties. If violations remain unrepaired at closing, the director may issue a nonrenewable temporary certificate lasting up to six months, and the buyer acknowledges in writing the duty to bring the property into compliance.

The code's exemption section lists family transfers, a property inspected within six months before the transfer, a purchase for demolition and probate transfers to heirs under a will. The wording is older than the latest amendments, so ask the Housing Department to confirm in writing that an exemption covers your sale.

Where is the deed recorded for an Irvington sale?

At the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which covers the county's 22 municipalities. A title company or attorney typically files the deed together with the transfer fee affidavit and GIT/REP form, so you seldom visit in person.

Cooperman Barnabas Medical Center, a 597-bed hospital established in 1865, sits in the south of town. More than 470 acres of wooded parkland has hiking trails, and roughly a quarter of the township's land stays in a natural state. Riker Hill Complex is a 204-acre park on the township's edge.

Retail is changing. The Livingston Mall at the southwest corner has lost several anchors, and the Route 10 corridor and the Livingston Avenue center, including the Livingston Town Center mixed-use project, carry more everyday shopping. Office parks along Eisenhower Parkway house companies such as CoreWeave and a Verizon customer service center.

How do residents get to New York and Newark from Livingston?

The township is 21.9 miles from New York City, and rail service runs through stations in neighboring communities. Options buyers compare:

  • Highways: Interstate 280 and Route 10 cross the town, and I-80, the Parkway and the Turnpike are reached via I-280.
  • Bus to Manhattan: the Community Coach 77 line runs to Port Authority in Manhattan, and OurBus operates a commuter route serving Livingston and West Orange.
  • Bus to Newark: NJ Transit routes 70, 71 and 73, with local route 873.
  • Rail: Morristown Line stations in Short Hills, Millburn and South Orange sit 5 to 7 miles away, and the fee-based Livingston Express Shuttle makes a 15-minute run between Livingston Mall and South Orange Station.

Is a C.O. needed to sell in Livingston?

No, the township's FAQ says a C.O. is not required for a sale. It does recommend phoning the Building Department (973-992-5000, extension 5200) to see whether any permits are still open on the property, and to call well ahead of closing because open permits can hold up a sale.

A smoke detector certification is required, and the Livingston Fire Department issues it at 973-992-2373. The department's Fire Prevention Bureau also inspects residential properties at resale or when a rental changes hands, and enforces the state fire code for smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. The Building Department sits at 357 S. Livingston Avenue, second floor.

  • Replacing a sink, toilet or tub in the same spot needs no permit, but moving fixtures does.
  • New electrical or plumbing work needs a permit even when you only swap cabinets.
  • Sheds larger than 200 square feet need a building permit plus zoning approval; smaller ones need zoning approval only.
  • Fences enclosing a pool, spa or hot tub need a building permit.

What fees come due at a Livingston closing?

The seller pays the state's transfer fee when the deed is recorded. At $821,100, a typical Livingston sale reaches the $550,000 to $850,000 band of the over-$350,000 schedule, charged at $5.30 per $500 for that slice, with lower bands applying to the dollars beneath it.

Above $1 million, a graduated fee applies to residential deeds, starting at 1% of the whole price and rising to 3.5% for prices over $3.5 million. The seller is responsible for it, and the deed must carry the state's affidavit form (RTF-1EE). Run the number before you accept an offer close to that line.

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages handles recording for all 22 Essex municipalities, Livingston included, and its record room reaches back to 1637. Confirm the office's current address and hours with the Register before sending documents, or leave it to your closing attorney or title company. If you are an executor distributing an inherited house to an heir, the state's exemption list covers a deed from an executor or administrator to a devisee or heir, though a sale to an outside buyer is a normal taxable transfer.

List it or sell it as-is in Livingston?

Where the typical home is worth more than $800,000, a house that is updated and shows well gives a listing room to work. An as-is sale fits better when the house needs a roof, kitchen or systems work, when you have a fixed moving date, or when you inherited the property and want a quick close.

Measure each offer by what you keep. Subtract the transfer fee, repairs a buyer will request, the carrying costs of a listing period and the cost of the smoke certification, and get every offer in writing before you choose.

Frequently asked questions

Does Livingston want a C.O. before a sale?

No, the township says a C.O. is not required. A smoke detector certification from the fire department is, and the Building Department can tell you about open permits, ideally well ahead of closing.

Where do I obtain Livingston's smoke detector certification?

Phone the Livingston Fire Department at 973-992-2373. Its Fire Prevention Bureau covers detector compliance when residential properties are resold.

Is the transfer fee a seller cost in Livingston?

Yes. The state computes it from the price stated in the deed and collects it at recording. Sales above $1 million also carry a graduated percent fee, which the seller owes.

Which office records a Livingston deed?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which serves all 22 county municipalities. A closing attorney or title agent usually files the deed.

What if my Livingston house has unpermitted work?

You can still sell, but expect questions. Call the Building Department at 973-992-5000, extension 5200, to learn what is on file; a buyer's lender or attorney may want the work permitted or reflected in the price.

What does the housing market in Maplewood, NJ look like for a seller?

Maplewood is a dense, high-value Essex County township, and the 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey numbers show it. The middle owner-occupied value is $720,700, the middle gross rent is $2,269 and the middle household income is $173,500. Owners occupy 74.9 percent of homes, which leaves a real rental segment, and 72.7 percent of adults have finished a four-year degree.

The township's estimated population was 26,320 in mid-2025, packed into 3.87 square miles of land at roughly 6,630 people per square mile. Families are a large share, with 28.4 percent of residents under 18, and 22.1 percent of residents were born outside the United States. Residents 65 or older make up 11.8 percent of the population. Owners who would rather not renovate before listing sometimes weigh an as-is sale against the cost of preparing the house.

How is Maplewood laid out, and what is its history?

Maplewood grew from three Colonial-era trails that now carry Springfield Avenue, South Orange Avenue and Ridgewood Road. Settlers followed Ridgewood Road to found Jefferson Village, the downtown "village" or Maplewood Center, which grew up around mills and orchards, while Springfield Avenue led to a hamlet that became the Hilton section. Seth Boyden, who settled in the area in 1855, built the first steam engines to serve the railroad through town.

The township borders West Orange and South Orange to the north, Newark and Irvington to the east, Union to the south and Millburn to the west. Green space sits close to most blocks:

  • Memorial Park, 25 acres beside the train station, laid out in the 1920s with the Olmsted Brothers and a landmark on the national historic register.
  • Maplecrest Park, DeHart Park and Milo S. Borden Park.
  • South Mountain Reservation, a 2,100-acre county reserve along the northwest edge.
  • The East Branch of the Rahway River, which runs through the township.

Hilton and Valley View are the unincorporated place names inside the township. A buyer or seller who knows which pocket a house sits in can price against nearby sales far more accurately.

What certificate does Maplewood require before a house is sold?

Maplewood requires the seller to obtain a certificate of continued use and occupancy from the township's construction official before ownership transfers. The rule sits in Chapter 204 of the township code. An inspector visits the property, and every open building permit has to be closed first.

Maplewood certificate of continued use and occupancy, per dwelling unit. Source: Township of Maplewood Code, Chapter 204.

Filed 10 or more business days before closing$150
Filed 6 to 9 business days before closing$300
Filed 5 or fewer business days before closing$500

How long the certificate lasts180 days, for the buyer named on the application
Penalty for transferring without one$1,000 fine

The application must include the prospective owner's driver's license number or passport. An application filed after 4:00 p.m. counts as filed the next business day, and a change of buyer means a new application. Seller timing matters here, since filing late lifts the fee from $150 to as much as $500.

What does the Maplewood fire department inspect at sale?

The fire department issues a Certificate of Smoke Detector and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Compliance before a detached one- or two-unit dwelling is sold, leased or reoccupied. The department's page defines those dwellings as detached one and two family homes, and says portable fire extinguishers are no longer required for this certificate in Maplewood.

Payment goes to the fire inspector at the inspection itself. The township accepts cash, a check or a money order payable to the Township of Maplewood, and does not take online payments. Plan to have the alarms working before the visit, since a second trip adds time to a closing that may already be tight.

Investors should also know that a lessor cannot collect rent after a change of tenancy until a certificate has been issued for the unit. A new owner of a rental property updates the township rental registration, and the certificate satisfies the first year of initial registration under the township's rental rules.

What does the state take at closing on a Maplewood sale?

The seller owes New Jersey's realty transfer fee, and at Maplewood's median value of $720,700 the state schedule works out to about $6,464. The rate steps up with price: for sales over $350,000 the first $150,000 is charged at $2.90 per $500, with higher rates on each layer above it.

Sales above $1,000,000 also carry a graduated percent fee, which is 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000. Since July 10, 2025, the law places that fee on the seller. In Essex County the Register of Deeds and Mortgages records the deed, and the seller's residency form (GIT/REP) travels with it.

How do trains, buses and schools affect a Maplewood sale?

Maplewood's value comes largely from its commute. NJ Transit's Maplewood station sits on the Morristown Line and Gladstone Branch, with trains to Newark Broad Street, Secaucus Junction and New York Penn Station. Bus routes 25, 31, 37 and 70 reach Newark, route 107 runs to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and the township runs a rush-hour jitney to the station. The average trip to work takes 38.5 minutes.

By road, Springfield Avenue is Route 124, and the Garden State Parkway and Interstate 78 pass nearby. The township counts about 226 streets and 59 miles of roadway, most of it maintained by the township.

Public schools belong to the South Orange-Maplewood School District, which in 2019 to 2020 had 11 schools and 7,353 students. Maplewood hosts Columbia High School, Maplewood Middle School, and the Seth Boyden, Clinton, Jefferson and Tuscan elementary schools. Since 2021 to 2022 the district has been rebalancing its elementary and middle schools by socioeconomic status, so a buyer should confirm the school assignment for a specific address.

How can a Maplewood homeowner sell without a long listing?

Maplewood owners can use an agent, sell directly, or accept a cash offer that skips repairs. All three still require the township certificate and the fire department's alarm certificate.

  • With an agent, the house goes in front of the widest set of buyers, though the commission and any repair requests come out of proceeds.
  • Selling directly keeps the commission, and the owner arranges the attorney review, disclosures and closing.
  • A cash purchase suits houses with deferred repairs, an estate, a tenant in place or a short timeline. The contract should name who files for the certificate and who pays if the inspector cites a problem.

Whichever route is chosen, calculate net proceeds after the payoff, the transfer fee, the certificate fee and any open-permit costs.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a certificate to sell my Maplewood house?

Yes. Chapter 204 of the township code requires a certificate of continued use and occupancy before ownership transfers, and the fire department separately issues the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certificate. Selling without the first one carries a $1,000 fine.

How much does the Maplewood certificate cost?

The fee is $150 per dwelling unit if the application comes in at least 10 business days before closing, $300 at 6 to 9 business days and $500 at 5 or fewer. A failed inspection adds a $100 reinspection fee.

How long does the certificate stay valid?

It lasts 180 days and only for the buyer named on the application. If the buyer changes, the seller files a new application.

Can open permits block a Maplewood sale?

Yes. The township will not issue the certificate until all open permits are closed, so check the permit history for decks, finished basements and electrical or plumbing work well before listing.

Which office records the deed for a Maplewood home?

Maplewood is in Essex County, where deeds go through the Register of Deeds and Mortgages. The seller's residency form (GIT/REP) and the transfer fee payment go in with the deed.

What sets a Montclair sale apart from other Essex County towns?

Montclair does not ask sellers for a fresh certificate of occupancy, but it does insist that every permit and violation on the property be closed out before the deed changes hands. Add a median home value above $900,000 and a tax bill driven mostly by the school district, and the sale has a few features you will not find in neighboring towns.

The sections that follow cover the housing figures, the paperwork at the Building Department, the 2026 tax levy, the appeal path, deed recording at the Register's office, and how a cash purchase compares with a listing.

How expensive and how settled is Montclair housing?

The typical owner-occupied home at $906,400 and shows 56.9% of households owning. The township counted 40,921 people in 2020 and 37,669 in 2010, and the July 2025 estimate is 44,633.

Low turnover means a listing is measured against very few comparable sales, so a well-prepared house can set its own price level while a house with open permits gets marked down quickly.

How did Montclair's railroad origins shape its neighborhoods?

Montclair began as a township in April 1868, carved from Bloomfield so that a second rail line could reach it. It reincorporated as a town after a February 1894 referendum, then went back to township status in 1980 to qualify for a larger share of federal revenue sharing aid.

Today the rail legacy shows up in where people buy. The town climbs the eastern slope of First Mountain in the Watchung range, and higher streets look toward Manhattan about 12 miles away. Named areas include Upper Montclair, Watchung Plaza, Church Street, Frog Hollow and South End, split between ZIP Codes 07042 and 07043.

  • Six business districts: Montclair Center at Six Corners, Upper Montclair, Watchung Plaza, Walnut Street, South End and Valley Road.
  • Toney's, Nishuane, Wigwam, Pearl and Yantacaw brooks all drain east, so a wet basement is a common buyer question.
  • Borders: Bloomfield, Cedar Grove, Glen Ridge, Orange, Verona and West Orange, plus Clifton and Little Falls in Passaic County.

Which stations, bus lines and schools do Montclair buyers ask about?

Seven NJ Transit rail stops on the Montclair-Boonton Line serve the township: Bay Street, Walnut Street, Watchung Avenue, Upper Montclair, Mountain Avenue, Montclair Heights and Montclair State University. Trains go to New York Penn Station and Hoboken. Bus routes 11, 28, 29, 34, 97, 191 and 705 mostly follow Bloomfield Avenue, and about 24% of commuters ride transit.

The public district educates kindergarten through grade 12 in seven elementary schools, three middle schools and Montclair High School. It enrolled 6,216 students in 2022-23, with 1,961 at the high school. Montclair State University and independent schools such as Montclair Kimberley Academy add to the education draw, so listings tend to name the elementary zone alongside the station.

Can I close in Montclair without a new certificate of occupancy?

Yes. A Building Department notice from June 2025 says the township does not require a new certificate of occupancy as a condition of selling, mortgaging or refinancing. Instead, every current construction permit must be closed, and every open violation must be cleared, before closing.

Order the permit history first through an Open Public Records Act request. Then phone the department at 973-509-4951 to schedule the closeouts. The office sits on the second floor of the Municipal Building at 205 Claremont Avenue and keeps Monday to Friday counter hours between 8:30 and 4:30.

  • A finished basement, new deck or swapped boiler without a final inspection is the usual culprit.
  • A second kitchen needs evidence that it was permitted, such as a closed permit.
  • Landlords with tenants should ask the township's Rent Control Office what applies to a rental building.

What goes into a Montclair tax bill?

Montclair bills in four installments, on the first of February, May, August and November, and the township gives a ten-day grace window. Arrears up to $1,500 carry 8% interest and the excess carries 18%.

The July 2026 bill notice breaks the levy into pieces. For a home assessed at $641,700, the municipal portion rose about $160.42, the county portion fell about $25.67, and the school operating budget added about $847.04. A voter-approved school referendum adds $558.27 in 2026 and about the same in 2027. By share of the whole levy, schools take 54.25%, the township 23.72%, Essex County 14.53%, the Type I district 2.90%, the referendum 2.32%, the library 1.57% and open space 0.71%.

Because the school share dominates, a buyer's monthly cost can change by more than the township's own budget would suggest. Have the latest quarterly amount ready, since your closing attorney will prorate the quarter underway.

Where do I contest a Montclair assessment?

Challenge the assessed value with the Essex County Board of Taxation. The township's Q&A says the appeal must be received before May 1, and a dissatisfied owner may then go to the New Jersey Tax Court within 45 days of the Board's notice.

The tax rate itself is not appealable under state law, only the value it is applied to. Montclair also auctions tax sale certificates, generally once each year, and the winning bidder buys a lien, not the house. Clear any unpaid municipal, water or sewer balance before you sign a contract.

What happens to the deed and the state transfer charge on a Montclair sale?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records Montclair deeds. The office holds every deed and mortgage recorded since 1637 and covers all 22 county municipalities, and an attorney or title agent usually files yours.

With values this high, the state's graduated fee matters. For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, a sale over $1 million carries a percentage of the full price: 1% up to $2 million, 2% up to $2.5 million, 2.5% up to $3 million, 3% up to $3.5 million and 3.5% beyond. The law shifted the charge to the seller, so build it into your net proceeds before you accept an offer close to a threshold.

Which route fits a Montclair seller: agent, owner sale or direct cash buyer?

A listing usually earns the top price in a market with this much demand, provided permits are closed and the house is staged. A direct buyer who pays cash and accepts the house as it stands makes sense when permits are unfinished, an estate needs settling, or tenants complicate showings.

  • Agent listing: widest exposure and strongest price, with preparation and showings on your side.
  • Owner sale: you keep the commission but also take on pricing, disclosures and negotiation.
  • Cash buyer: condition is not an obstacle and the date is flexible, at a price set below a polished listing.

Line up the net from each route after payoffs, taxes and permit closeouts, then decide. A cash quote costs nothing to request and carries no obligation.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Will Montclair demand a new certificate of occupancy before my closing?

No. The Building Department's June 2025 notice states that a new certificate is not a condition of a sale, mortgage or refinance. Open permits and violations still have to be closed before closing.

Which date does Montclair use for tax installments?

Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with ten days of grace. Late arrears up to $1,500 accrue 8% and amounts above that accrue 18%.

Which office files a Montclair deed?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages. It records transactions for all 22 municipalities in the county, and closing attorneys or title agents normally submit the paperwork.

Can an unfinished permit hold up a Montclair closing?

Yes. Any current construction permit must be closed first. Request the permit history under the Open Public Records Act, then call the Building Department at 973-509-4951 to arrange inspections or closeout.

By when must a Montclair assessment appeal be filed?

The township says the appeal must reach the Essex County Board of Taxation before May 1. A further appeal to the New Jersey Tax Court must be filed within 45 days of the Board's notice.

How does a house sale work in Nutley, NJ?

Nutley is a compact Essex County township, and a resale there cannot close until the municipality has issued a Certificate of Occupancy. Whether the buyer arrives through an agent, a private deal or a cash purchase, the same inspection step sits in the middle of the timeline.

Only 3.37 square miles of land make up the township, with Belleville and Bloomfield on its Essex County sides, Lyndhurst across the Bergen County line and Clifton in Passaic County. About 30,700 people live here according to the 2025 federal estimate, a rise from 30,143 in 2020. At nearly 8,900 residents per square mile, houses sit shoulder to shoulder on small lots, so buyers pay close attention to roofs, sump pumps and basements.

Nutley has been run under the Walsh Act commission form since 1912, with five elected commissioners who each head a department. A permit question or a zoning answer therefore goes to a department head's office rather than to a manager.

What in Nutley's history shapes its older houses?

The area grew out of the Satterthwaite estate, which gave the place its name, and out of mill and quarry work along the Third River. Brownstone quarrying in the Avondale section employed Italian and Irish immigrants, and the mills left street names behind. Nutley was set off from Belleville as Franklin Township in 1874, became a town in 1902 and became a township in 1981.

The practical result is older housing. A transfer inspection here checks panels, venting and water heater piping, and anyone who finished an attic or basement long ago should dig out the permit and confirm it was closed.

Nutley was also the U.S. base of Hoffmann-La Roche from 1929, and the company's roughly $9 million in local property taxes had made up about 9 percent of township tax revenue. Roche announced in 2012 that the site would close, with the shutdown slated for the end of 2015.

What does Nutley look for when it inspects a house for sale?

  • Work done without permits, and any open building permits, which must be closed through final inspections first.
  • Smoke detection on each floor, with the basement unit placed near the stairs, and units within 10 feet of every bedroom.
  • Carbon monoxide detection outside bedroom areas when the house burns fuel or has an attached garage.
  • Relief valves on the water heater and boiler, with discharge pipes ending near the floor.
  • A sump pump that empties outdoors, with no connection to the sanitary sewer and no flow onto the next lot.
  • Handrails or guardrails past four steps, sound treads and bricks, and plates on every switch and outlet.
  • Address numerals 4 to 8 inches tall and readable from the street.

Illegal conversions and unpermitted living areas get attention too. If you suspect a bedroom or basement apartment was built without approval, raise it with Code Enforcement before listing, since no Zoning Certificate comes out while a permit sits open.

How do I book the Nutley transfer inspection?

Code Enforcement is on the second floor of the municipal building at 1 Kennedy Drive (973-284-4951). Written requests became mandatory on July 1, 2026, through the township portal or a request form, and the department wants them a full day in advance.

  • Building and zoning transfer visits are available every weekday from the morning start until 3:30 in the afternoon.
  • Fire and zoning transfer visits are limited to Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays between 11 and 3.
  • The Fire Department takes its own smoke and carbon monoxide application, which adds a second stop.

Under the state fire code, a dwelling with one or two units also needs a smoke alarm compliance certificate, which the Division of Fire Safety limits to six months. Book the visit late enough that the certificate survives until closing and early enough to fix whatever fails.

What state-level costs follow a Nutley closing?

The seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee at recording, and the Division of Taxation publishes a rate schedule your closing attorney will apply to the deed price. A separate 1 percent charge falls on buyers of homes above $1,000,000, which seldom applies at Nutley's median value.

A GIT/REP form signed by the seller travels with the deed. Residents use the simplest version, while an out-of-state owner may have to prepay estimated tax.

An owner who thinks the assessment is too high files with the Essex County board of taxation, which needs the petition in hand by April 1 unless notices went out late. Only the value is open to challenge, and the state form accepts comparable sales as proof but rejects neighbors' assessments.
