How do Nutley's roads, buses and schools figure in a listing?

The Garden State Parkway grazes the southwest corner, Route 7 skirts the north and Route 21 traces the east side. NJ Transit's 192 bus reaches Midtown Manhattan, and the 13, 27, 72 and 74 go to Newark. Passenger trains stopped in 1966, which leaves the bus as the main commuter link. Of the township's 67.94 miles of road, 57 are township-maintained, and the rest belong to Essex County, the state and the Turnpike Authority.

Seven schools make up Nutley Public Schools, which enrolled 4,034 students in 2021-22: Lincoln, Radcliffe, Spring Garden, Washington and Yantacaw for the early grades, John H. Walker Middle School and Nutley High School. Franklin Avenue's shops and parks such as Memorial, Booth and Kingsland are the neighborhood draws listings tend to mention.

Is a cash buyer a good fit for a Nutley house?

A cash purchase suits a house with defects the inspection will flag, an inherited property that is costing money to hold, or a seller whose schedule matters more than the final bit of price. Any as-is buyer should say in writing who deals with the township's inspection and with open permits.

Set the offer beside what a listing would net after commissions, repairs, fees and carrying costs. A written figure with a closing date is more useful than a spoken one.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Certificate of Occupancy mandatory for a Nutley resale?

Yes. Section 700-116 of the Nutley code ties every sale, conveyance or rental to an issued certificate, and the zoning certificate will not be released while building permits remain open.

What notice does Nutley need for a transfer inspection?

One full day at minimum, and longer if repairs are likely. Written requests have been required since July 1, 2026, and fire and zoning visits happen only on three weekdays.

How long does a New Jersey smoke alarm certificate stay valid?

Six months, counting from issue, per the Division of Fire Safety. The owner of a one- or two-unit dwelling gets it through the municipality before transferring the property.

When must a Nutley assessment appeal be filed?

April 1 is the usual date, with May 1 after a town-wide revaluation. Petitions that arrive late are dismissed, so file with room to spare.

Can a Nutley house sell as-is?

It can, though the inspection still happens. Missing detectors and unpermitted work will be flagged, so the contract should say who pays for any corrections.

West Orange sits on the slopes of the Watchung Mountains in Essex County, and the township asks for a Certificate of Continued Occupancy before any residential property is sold. After that the path is standard: contract, title search, closing, and a deed filed with the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages.

Downtown Newark is about five miles east and Manhattan about 12, so buyers tend to weigh commute times and hillside streets alongside school names.

What do West Orange's population and housing figures look like?

The 2020 census recorded 48,843 residents, up from 46,207 in 2010, and the July 2025 estimate is 49,557. Those residents share 12.00 square miles of land, roughly 4,069 per square mile.

How do West Orange's four neighborhoods and history affect value?

The area began as part of Newark, then Orange Township, and West Orange was incorporated as a township on April 10, 1863. It reorganized as a town in 1900 and became a township again in 1980 to qualify for a bigger share of federal revenue sharing. The local landmarks are Thomas Edison's laboratory, now a national historical park on Main Street, and Llewellyn Park, laid out in the 1850s as one of the first planned residential communities in the country.

  • Downtown West Orange and the Valley lie in the low basin along the border with Orange and Montclair. This is the densest and oldest part, with the municipal building, police headquarters and the library nearby.
  • The First Mountain climbs along Northfield, Mount Pleasant and Eagle Rock Avenues, with Victorian, Tudor and mid-century houses, estates, and views of the Newark and Manhattan skylines. Hutton Park, Gregory and Llewellyn Park sit here.
  • Pleasant Valley and Pleasantdale hold postwar suburban streets and a walkable business district.
  • The Second Mountain borders South Mountain Reservation and resembles neighboring Millburn and Livingston.

South Mountain Reservation and the 400-acre Eagle Rock Reservation frame the township, and the Essex Green Shopping Center, at 350,000 square feet, is the largest outdoor mall in the county.

Private choices include Seton Hall Preparatory School and Golda Och Academy. Parents ask which elementary school covers a street, and the district can answer that for your address.

What is a Certificate of Continued Occupancy in West Orange?

A CCO is the township's written confirmation that a residential building meets health, safety, fire and land use standards when it is sold or rented. Chapter 25 of the township code makes the owner of record apply before selling any existing residential structure of one unit or more, and the Construction Official signs it.

  • The Township Council sets the fee by resolution, so ask for today's amount. The township's form says there are no refunds after an application is processed.
  • Questions go to 973-325-4111 or planning@westorange.org, the contacts printed on the township's residential application, which asks for the seller, buyer, closing date and any minor children who will live in the home.
  • The assessor's office must warn anyone requesting a tax search that a CCO is needed for the sale.
  • Minor violations can earn a temporary CCO of up to 30 days, and the permanent certificate that follows carries no extra fee.
  • Closing without one leaves the owner liable for a separate violation for every day until a CCO issues, and agents or attorneys who take part in the deal can be held responsible too.

If you think no CCO applies, the Construction Official will issue a written determination for a $25 fee.

How do West Orange property taxes and appeals work?

An owner who disputes an assessment petitions the Essex County Board of Taxation. The cutoff is April 1, extended to 45 days after the notice date when that is later, and owners assessed above $1 million may file with the State Tax Court.

Since the assessor flags the CCO during every tax search, expect your title company to contact the township early. Ask the assessor and the tax collector about your balance and any open sewer charge so the settlement statement is accurate.

Where is a West Orange deed recorded and what does the seller pay?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records deeds for all 22 county municipalities and keeps copies of every deed and mortgage recorded since 1637. On a West Orange sale the seller owes the state realty transfer fee, and the portion of a price between $550,000 and $850,000 is charged at $5.30 per $500. A price over $1 million also brings the Graduated Percent Fee.

The township's middle home value of $557,300 sits right at the $550,000 break, so a typical sale lands where that rate begins. Your attorney will total the fee.

Which sale route fits a West Orange house?

Whichever route you pick, the township's residential CCO application asks for the buyer's name, the closing date and any children who will live in the house, so line up a buyer before you file.

  • An agent listing gives a First Mountain house with views or period detail the widest exposure, and it fits a home in good shape.
  • A direct sale skips the commission and still needs a lawyer for the contract and the CCO paperwork.
  • A cash buyer suits a house that needs repairs, a building with several units and tenants, or an estate where heirs want a fast close.

The CCO inspection applies on every route, so settle in writing who pays for any corrections.

Is a CCO needed to sell a West Orange house?

Yes. Under the township land use code, an existing residential structure of one unit or more needs a CCO before a sale or rental. The owner of record applies, and the Construction Official issues it.

What does a West Orange CCO cost?

The Township Council sets it by resolution, so it can change. Call 973-325-4111 to confirm the amount, and know that a processed application is not refunded.

What happens if a West Orange house fails the CCO inspection?

For minor violations the Construction Official may grant a temporary CCO lasting up to 30 days. The permanent one that follows the repairs costs nothing extra.

Where is the deed for a West Orange sale filed?

With the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages. The title agent or closing lawyer usually sends it in with the seller's transfer fee.

Can a West Orange owner appeal an assessment?

Yes. Petition the Essex County Board of Taxation by April 1, or 45 days after the notice date if later. An assessment above $1 million may be taken to the State Tax Court.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Deptford?

Deptford owners have three ways out: an agent listing, a private sale, or a straight purchase by a cash buyer. The choice usually follows the condition of the house and the calendar. A tidy house with months to spare suits the open market, while worn systems, tenants, an estate, or a payoff date on the horizon point toward a direct sale.

Deptford Township had an estimated 32,600 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 31,977 at the 2020 count. Delays tend to come from paperwork and repairs, so the sections below cover the township offices, the Gloucester County Clerk, and the state forms that go with every deed.

  • Agent listing: the most exposure, with showings and a buyer who typically needs a mortgage and an appraisal.
  • Private sale: no commission to pay, though pricing, disclosures and the attorney review fall to you.
  • Cash purchase: no showings and no repair list, and the offer reflects the work the buyer inherits.

What should I know about Deptford before I price a house here?

Deptford is a southeastern suburb of Philadelphia, about 10 miles from the city on the New Jersey side of the Walt Whitman Bridge and roughly 50 miles northwest of Atlantic City. Deptford spreads over 17.33 square miles and touches Woodbury, Woodbury Heights, Wenonah, Westville, West Deptford, Washington Township and Mantua Township, with Bellmawr, Runnemede and Gloucester Township across the Camden County line.

The place is old. It was formed in 1695 as Bethlehem and incorporated as a township in 1798. Its best-known story is the 1793 balloon landing at the Clement Oak, the first hot air balloon landing in North America. Most of the housing, though, came with the post-war boom: the population went from about 7,300 in 1950 to nearly 17,900 in 1960 and passed 24,000 by 1970. A lot of the housing stock dates from that boom, which is why roofs, heating systems and wiring draw attention at inspection.

Neighborhood names matter to buyers. Oak Valley, a Census-designated place with about 3,500 residents, lies inside the township, along with the unincorporated communities of Almonesson, Good Intent, Lake Tract, Jericho, Hammond Heights, Westcottville and Woodbury Gardens.

How do Deptford's roads, transit and shopping affect a sale?

Access to Philadelphia is a selling point for Deptford. Routes 41, 42, 45, 47 and 55 all cross the township, and county routes 534, 544, 551 and 553 fill in the grid. The New Jersey Turnpike is reached at Exit 3 in Bellmawr and Runnemede, and a short 0.07-mile piece of Interstate 295 touches the township. NJ Transit buses on the 400, 401, 402, 408, 410 and 412 lines run to Philadelphia, with local service on the 455 and 463.

Deptford Mall, the largest mall in the South Jersey region at about 1.07 million square feet of leasable space, anchors the retail side, with strip malls, restaurants and a movie theater around it. Tall Pines State Preserve, a 111-acre park that opened in November 2015 as Gloucester County's first state park, sits on the border with Mantua Township.

As of 2010 the township had about 150 miles of road: roughly 99 municipal, 29 county, 19 state, and 3.4 under the Turnpike Authority.

Which schools serve Deptford homes?

One district, Deptford Township Schools, covers the whole township and had 3,942 students in 2020-21. The elementary schools are Good Intent, Lake Tract, Oak Valley and Shady Lane for grades 1 to 5, with Central Early Childhood Center and Pine Acres Early Childhood Center covering the youngest grades. Monongahela Middle School takes grades 6 to 8, and Deptford Township High School takes grades 9 to 12.

County students may also apply to the Gloucester County Institute of Technology, a no-tuition technical high school based in Deptford. Ask the district which of the four elementary schools your street feeds and give that answer to buyers early.

Does the 2021 tornado still matter when I sell?

It can. An EF3 tornado with winds up to 150 miles per hour, produced by the remnants of Hurricane Ida, struck Deptford on September 1, 2021 and damaged more than 100 homes. A repaired house should have closed permits and passed final inspections on file. One that was patched without permits, or left half-fixed, can stall a mortgage buyer at the inspection or appraisal.

If your house had storm repairs, collect the permit numbers, contractor invoices and insurance papers before you list. The township construction office at 1011 Cooper Street answers questions about open permits and final inspections at (856) 845-5300, weekdays from 8:30 until 4:30. A cash buyer can take unfinished work as it stands, and the offer will account for it.

The township construction office takes applications for a Housing Certificate of Occupancy. Before signing a contract, ask that office whether your sale needs one and what the inspection covers, since the buyer's attorney is likely to raise it.

Landlords have one more item. The township clerk's page cites N.J.S.A. 46:8-28, which requires rental owners to register with the clerk, and warns of fines reaching $500 for owners who skip it. Selling a tenant-occupied house means checking that your registration is current; the Clerk's Office number is 856-686-2203.

What will closing cost a Deptford seller?

The seller owes the state a realty transfer fee, charged on a sliding scale per $500 of price. Applying the schedule to a $277,100 sale, the Census median for owned homes here, produces roughly $1,536. A $350,000 sale comes to about $2,105, and anything above $350,000 uses a higher schedule.

  • Transfer fee: paid by the seller, with an affidavit (form RTF-1) filed whenever an exemption is claimed.
  • Recording: the Gloucester County Clerk adds a $20 indexing fee when a paper deed shows up without its cover sheet.
  • Seller's tax form: a GIT/REP form signed at closing. New Jersey residents sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification, and nonresident sellers may owe a prepayment of at least 2 percent of the price.
  • Payoffs: mortgages, liens and unpaid municipal charges are subtracted from your proceeds.

A listing agent's commission is whatever your agreement says, so get the figure in writing before you compare a listing with a cash offer.

Where does the deed go after a Deptford closing?

Deptford deeds are filed with the Gloucester County Clerk. The clerk's land records page requires one of the GIT/REP forms with every deed, and the Record Room answers at 856-853-3230. The county also runs a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies you whenever a document is filed under your name, which is worth setting up after a sale or an inheritance.

For a copy of an older deed, the clerk's page points owners to the online land records search, where one can be printed free, and warns about mailers that charge $75 to $86 for the same document.

A direct purchase fits when speed or condition matters more than the final few thousand dollars. Get offers in writing, ask which closing costs the buyer covers, and set the net figure beside your best listing estimate.

The Gloucester County Clerk. The deed has to carry a GIT/REP form, and a paper filing without a cover sheet adds a $20 indexing fee. The Record Room number is 856-853-3230.

What transfer fee would a Deptford seller owe?

It scales with price. On the state schedule, $277,100 produces about $1,536 and $350,000 about $2,105. The seller is responsible for it.

Is there a township inspection before a Deptford sale?

Call the construction office at (856) 845-5300. It handles Housing Certificate of Occupancy applications and can say whether your sale needs one and what gets checked.

Does a rented Deptford house need landlord registration before I sell?

Rental owners register with the township clerk under N.J.S.A. 46:8-28, and the clerk lists fines reaching $500 for skipping it. Make sure yours is current before the buyer's attorney asks.

What should I know before selling a house in Monroe Township, Gloucester County?

Monroe Township in Gloucester County, the Williamstown ZIP 08094 township, runs a resale certificate of occupancy inspection that the buyer's paperwork must accompany. Do not mix it up with the other Monroe Township in Middlesex County, which has a different office, fee chapter and appeal calendar.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 38,137 residents, and its 2020 to 2024 survey counts 14,116 households of about 2.65 people. Owners live in 85.2 percent of homes, with a median value of $283,100 and a median household income of $96,980. How did Monroe Township in Gloucester County take shape?

The legislature created the township on March 3, 1859, out of Washington Township, when the area still belonged to Camden County. It moved to Gloucester County on February 28, 1871 and was named for President James Monroe. In 1950 a section went to Winslow Township. The 2020 census count of 37,117 is the highest on record, after a 24.7 percent jump between 2000 and 2010.

The township covers 46.93 square miles, nearly all of it land, and is the second largest in the county by both area and population. Williamstown (15,082 people in 2020) and Victory Lakes (1,999) are the census designated places, and Berryland, Broad Lane, Cecil, Cross Keys, Downer, New Brooklyn and Radix are other place names. Neighbors are Clayton, Franklin, Glassboro and Washington Township in Gloucester County, Buena Vista Township and Folsom in Atlantic County, and Winslow Township in Camden County. The Hall Street School, built in 1887, was added to the National Register of Historic Places on September 27, 2006.

What does the Monroe resale inspection cost and how long does it take?

The Monroe Township Housing Office requires a resale certificate of occupancy application, and the township asks for it 3 to 4 weeks before settlement. A completed inspection is valid for only 60 days. The office is at 125 Virginia Avenue in Williamstown, reachable at 856-728-9800 ext. 289 or 296, and applications go in person or by mail.

Payment must be exact cash, a check or a money order payable to Monroe Township Housing. The office does not take credit or debit cards, and every fee is non-refundable. The buyer must also complete a notarized Acknowledgement of Responsibility, and inspections cannot be scheduled without it.

What does the Monroe resale checklist cover?

  • Smoke detectors on every level, either ten-year sealed battery units or hardwired units under ten years old, and carbon monoxide detectors outside sleeping areas unless the house is all electric with a detached garage.
  • A 2A-10B:C fire extinguisher mounted and visible when leaving the kitchen, with a service tag from the last 12 months or a receipt for a new one.

  • Pool barriers with a 4 foot fence and a 4 foot gate that opens outward, closes itself and latches with the release 54 inches off the ground, plus working safety straps on hot tubs.
  • All zoning, construction and Board of Health permits and violations closed, and any abandoned property fees or emergency work charges paid.

What if the Monroe house needs repairs or has unpermitted work?

Section 162-11 of the township code lets a buyer of a dwelling that is unfit at transfer sign an affidavit listing the repairs needed. The affidavit lasts 60 days, work must start right after the sale, and the Housing Official can extend the period only for good cause. The buyer applies for the transfer before the scheduled closing, and the buyer can also assume the seller's duty to obtain the certificate by a written waiver filed with the Housing Department.

The township says a certificate is not a warranty. The buyer signs that acknowledgment and accepts responsibility for fixing violations or unpermitted work found later. The form recommends the buyer get a survey no more than 90 days old and file an OPRA request for permits with the Zoning and Construction Offices, and, where it applies, check for Pinelands Commission approval.

The Black Horse Pike crosses the township from northwest to southeast, carrying Route 42 in the northwest part and U.S. Route 322 in the southeast. Typical drive times run about 30 minutes to Philadelphia and 35 to Atlantic City, and the Atlantic City Expressway runs just outside its border. U.S. 322 on the west side reaches the New Jersey Turnpike in about 30 minutes. NJ Transit buses 315, 400 and 463 serve the area, and Cross Keys Airport is in the Cross Keys section.

Monroe Township Public Schools run six schools: Holly Glen, Oak Knoll, Radix and Whitehall elementary schools for kindergarten through grade 4, Williamstown Middle School for grades 5 to 8 and Williamstown High School. Enrollment was 5,736 in 2019-20. Students countywide can apply to the Gloucester County Institute of Technology in Deptford, which charges no tuition, and St. Mary School serves kindergarten through grade 8 under the Diocese of Camden.

How do Monroe appeals and recording fees work in Gloucester County?

Gloucester County uses an alternative assessment calendar, so the Board of Taxation takes appeals from November 15 through January 15, with a 4:00 pm cutoff on the last day for paper or online filings. Assessment postcards are mailed on or before November 15, and paper appeals need a check made out to the Gloucester County Board of Taxation. Online filing accepts credit cards.

The seller's state Realty Transfer Fee at the Census median value of $283,100 works out to $1,583.18 under the rates for sales up to $350,000: $600 for the first $150,000, $335 for the next $50,000 and $648.18 for the last $83,100.

Deeds are recorded with the Gloucester County Clerk, whose posted fee is $30 for the first page and $10 for each additional page. Since July 1, 2026 the Clerk's Office takes only money orders, checks or credit cards, checks of $10,000 or more must be certified, and out-of-state personal checks are not accepted. The Clerk's recording line is 856-853-3235.

How much is the Monroe Township resale certificate fee?

The Gloucester County township charges $200 for the resale inspection application, or $300 when the request comes less than seven business days before it is needed. A reinspection is $25, and the fees are not refundable.

How early should I apply for a Monroe resale certificate?

Apply 3 to 4 weeks before settlement. The township's inspection stays valid for 60 days, so time the visit to your settlement date, and the notarized buyer acknowledgment must be filed with the application.

Do I need a well test to sell a Monroe house on a private well?

Yes. The resale checklist requires a satisfactory lab report that includes mercury for a private well, and a Gloucester County Department of Health certification for a private septic system.

Can a buyer take on repairs after buying a Monroe house?

A buyer can sign an affidavit listing the repairs needed for legal occupancy. It lasts 60 days, repairs must begin right after the sale, and the buyer applies for the transfer before the closing.

What is the deadline to appeal a Monroe assessment in Gloucester County?

The county's appeal window runs from November 15 to January 15, and filings must be in by 4:00 pm on January 15. Assessment postcards go out on or before November 15.

Where is Washington Township and how did it grow?

The township covers 21.35 square miles of land in northern Gloucester County and borders Deptford, Mantua, Monroe, Glassboro, Pitman and Gloucester Township. The legislature incorporated it in 1836 out of Deptford Township. It belonged to Camden County from 1844 until 1871, when most of it returned to Gloucester County.

The oldest community, Grenloch Terrace, began as a Lenape settlement called Tetamekon. Each owner also signs a GIT/REP form for the deed. A resident who stays in the state files GIT/REP-3 and prepays nothing, but a seller leaving New Jersey may prepay income tax at closing. Your title company can match the form to each owner.

Gloucester County is on the alternative assessment calendar, so the deadline to appeal is January 15. File Form A-1 with the Gloucester County Board of Taxation, 1200 North Delsea Drive, Clayton, or call 856-307-6445. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 can file with the Tax Court.

What is the land like in North Bergen?

The township is shaped like an inverted L. A northern arm runs east to west, and a southern arm runs north to south between Secaucus and the Hudson-side towns of Guttenberg, West New York and Union City. The Hudson River forms the eastern border, facing Manhattan, and the Hackensack River separates the township from Carlstadt. The Palisades rise from the waterfront, and a steep slope on the west side drops toward the Meadowlands.

That slope makes North Bergen the city with the second most hills per square mile in the United States, after San Francisco. Steep driveways, retaining walls and stairs up to the front door are features a buyer will want to inspect, so photograph and describe them honestly.

Retail clusters along Bergenline Avenue, Tonnelle Avenue and near the Transfer Station, and the New York, Susquehanna and Western Railway runs five intermodal freight facilities in the township. Of 64.74 miles of road, the township maintains 50.00, Hudson County 7.85, the state 5.49 and the Turnpike Authority 1.40, so a complaint about a street goes to a different office depending on who owns it.

Low-lying ground on the west side is part of the New Jersey Meadowlands, so ask your insurance agent whether your parcel sits in a flood zone before you quote a closing date.

  • Bergenwood, clinging to the west-facing slope of the Palisades.
  • New Durham, near the Bergen Turnpike and Tonnelle Avenue.
  • Meadowview behind the Municipal Building, and Babbitt out in the Meadowlands.
  • Bulls Ferry and Woodcliff, toward the Hudson and North Hudson Park.

The Hackensack band of the Lenape lived here until the Dutch repurchased the land in 1658, and the township was incorporated on April 10, 1843. Spanish speakers began arriving in the 1960s, giving rise to the nickname Havana on the Hudson. 71.4% of residents as Hispanic or Latino and 74.5% of residents age 5 and up speak another language at home, so Spanish-language listings can reach a large share of local buyers.

The state's realty transfer fee falls on the seller. A deed from an executor or administrator to an heir or devisee under a will or intestacy law is exempt, which matters for inherited houses, and so is a deed recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. Prices above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee, 1% up to $2,000,000 and more above that.

A seller or heir who lives out of state prepays at least 2% of the deed price toward state income tax. The estimate is 10.75% of the gain when that comes out higher.

Is the transfer fee owed on an inherited house?

Not on the executor's deed that moves the house to an heir under the will or intestacy law. If the heir then sells to a buyer, that second deed is a sale and the fee applies to it.

The Census Bureau counted 7,835 residents in 2020 and estimates 8,516 for July 2025, a rise of 8.7 percent from the 2020 base. How did Raritan become the town it is?

Raritan grew around the river and a woolen mill. The Raritan Woolen Mills opened in 1846, became the Somerset Manufacturing Company in 1882, and employed as many as 400 people at its peak, making blankets and uniforms for the Union Army and later the U.S. Army in World War I.

The state legislature first set Raritan off from Bridgewater Township as a subdivision on April 3, 1868. After lawsuits in the 1930s and 1940s, it became a fully independent borough by an act of May 12, 1948, following a referendum held that June. The Nevius Street Bridge, built in 1886 by the Wrought Iron Bridge Company, still carries pedestrians over the river. President Harding signed the Knox-Porter Resolution ending U.S. involvement in World War I at the Frelinghuysen estate here on July 2, 1921, and a plaque marks the site.

  • Fire detection systems must be inspected every year under state rules, so a house with a monitored alarm needs its alarm company or an electrician to put the system on test during the visit.

Raritan states that fire code violations have no statute of limitations, which means a violation noticed late must still be corrected. Contact the borough fire prevention office before you set a closing date, and book the inspection as soon as the contract is signed.

The Property Maintenance office keeps the register of rental properties and inspects each rental unit before it is reoccupied. If you are selling a two-family house or a house with a tenant, expect the buyer's attorney to ask for proof that the unit was registered and inspected.

The same office responds to complaints about upkeep on residential and commercial buildings and enforces the rules for putting out trash, recycling and bulk items. An open complaint on your address can slow a closing, so ask the office whether any is on file.

Which roads, trains and schools define Raritan?

Raritan sits where U.S. Route 202 meets U.S. Route 206 and Route 28 at the Somerville Circle, with the eastern half of the circle inside the borough. The circle was handling an average of 70,000 vehicles a day as the area suburbanized, and the state transportation department has reworked it several times for safety. The Raritan station, whose building dates to the early 1890s, sits on Thompson Street north of the town center and is often the end of the line for NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line trains toward Newark Penn Station. How do Raritan property tax appeals work?

Somerset County lists Raritan among the boroughs where an assessment appeal must reach the county tax board by 4:30 p.m. on April 1. The 2026 listing used that date, and it has passed for that year. Neighbors such as Bridgewater Township, which is in a reassessment district, have until May 1.

Petitions go in by hard copy, by mail or in person, with the fee, and a copy must also reach the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk. You appeal the assessment, not the tax bill. The assessment is presumed correct, so you must bring evidence of market value, such as comparable sales from the year before the October 1 assessment date, and all taxes and charges must be paid through February 1 of the hearing year or the appeal can be dismissed.

The Somerset County Tax Board is at 27 Warren Street, fourth floor, Somerville, and its number is 908-541-5701. An added assessment appeal, for new construction picked up mid-year, has a December 1 deadline.

What are the closing costs and tax forms for a Raritan sale?

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. On a sale at the borough's median home value of $456,900, applying each band of the state schedule to the slice of price inside it comes to about $3,761, before any other closing charges.

An out-of-state owner, such as a landlord who lives elsewhere, completes a GIT/REP-1 at closing unless a seller assurance applies. The estimate is the gain times 10.75 percent, and it can never fall below 2 percent of the price in the deed. A New Jersey resident signs a GIT/REP-3 instead. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so a rejection goes back to the clerk first and then to the state GIT/REP unit at 609-322-9275.

Does Raritan require a certificate of occupancy to sell a house?

Raritan's fire prevention office certifies smoke detectors for the sale of dwellings, and that is the document the borough's page describes. Ask the borough office whether any other resale paperwork applies to your address.

What smoke alarm rules apply to a Raritan sale?

Every occupied level needs a working smoke detector, and hard-wired interconnected units must all sound together. Carbon monoxide detectors go within 10 feet of each sleeping area. The state removed the fire extinguisher item from resale inspections on February 3, 2025.

When is the Raritan appeal deadline?

April 1 at 4:30 p.m. Somerset County lists Raritan Borough among the municipalities with that deadline, and hearings come later in the year. Added assessment appeals are due December 1.

Who inspects rentals in Raritan?

The borough's Property Maintenance office. It keeps the rental register and inspects each unit before it is reoccupied, so a seller with a tenant should confirm the unit is on the register.

How big is the transfer fee on a typical Raritan sale?

About $3,761 on the borough's $456,900 median home value, using the state's rate bands. A higher price raises it, and the seller pays it when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.

Where is East Windsor and what surrounds it?

In Mercer County, East Windsor covers 15.57 square miles where the Delaware Valley meets the Raritan Valley, an outer-ring New York suburb that also touches the Philadelphia metro area. Its neighbors are Robbinsville and West Windsor in Mercer, Cranbury, Monroe and Plainsboro in Middlesex, and Millstone and Upper Freehold in Monmouth. The independent borough of Hightstown sits wholly inside East Windsor, making the pair one of 21 doughnut towns in New Jersey.

Windsor Township divided on February 9, 1797, producing East and West Windsor, and East Windsor was incorporated on February 21, 1798. Growth arrived late: 2,298 residents in 1960, then 11,736 in 1970 and 21,041 in 1980. Twin Rivers, home to 7,878 people in 2020, was described in a state guide as New Jersey's first planned unit development. Yes for a single-family home or condominium. The Bureau of Fire Prevention certifies detectors and an extinguisher before the sale, at $50, with a certificate good for 60 days.

Smoke detectors up to 10 years old and carbon monoxide detectors up to 7, per the manufacturer's label. The kitchen also needs a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current-year tag.

Fix the items and run the process again with a $25 re-inspection fee. The certificate expires after 60 days, so book early enough to leave room for a second visit.

Ewing requires every home sold in the township to pass a housing inspection first, so the main variable in a fast sale is how quickly the property can pass that check. The rest of the process is the usual New Jersey deed, transfer fee and tax filings.

Ewing sits in Mercer County on the Delaware River, directly north and west of Trenton. It covers about 15.6 square miles, and the 2020 Census counted 37,264 residents, the highest count in the township's history. The Census Bureau estimated 39,030 people in July 2025, a rise of 4.5 percent from the 2020 base. The 2020 density was about 2,450 people per square mile of land.

How did Ewing Township grow into the community it is today?

Ewing became a township on February 22, 1834, cut from Trenton Township and named in honor of Charles Ewing, a former chief justice of the New Jersey Supreme Court. It joined the new Mercer County in 1838. Before that the land was mostly farms and small hamlets: Carleton is now Ewing, Cross Keys is Ewingville, and Birmingham is West Trenton.

The township grew as a suburb of Trenton through the 20th century. Its population rose from 6,942 in 1930 to 26,628 by 1960 and has stayed between about 32,800 and 37,300 since 1970. Blocks near the Trenton line are distinctly urban, while most of the township is residential subdivisions.

Neighborhood names show up in listings and appraisals, so use the local one. Examples include Ewingville, West Trenton, Prospect Heights, Fernwood, Hillwood Lakes, Parkway Village, Scudders Falls and Wilburtha. Many were built in separate phases, and house styles change noticeably from one to the next.

Church and Dwight moved its corporate headquarters from Princeton to Ewing in 2013. Interstate 295 crosses the northwest corner, Route 29 follows the Delaware River as the Delaware River Scenic Byway, U.S. Route 206 skirts the southeast, and Route 31 (Pennington Road) runs north to Pennington and Flemington.

West Trenton station is the terminus of SEPTA's West Trenton Line, which mainly carries riders to Philadelphia. NJ Transit buses 601, 607, 608, 609 and 624 connect the township with Trenton. Trenton-Mercer Airport, open since 1929 and served by Frontier Airlines, is also inside Ewing's borders.

The Delaware and Raritan Canal passes near the river, and the strip of land along it is part of the Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park. Homes along River Road and Route 29 sit near the water, so check flood-zone status with the township before quoting a price to a buyer who asks.

Ewing Public Schools run prekindergarten through twelfth grade in one district, with five schools: Antheil, Lore and Parkway elementary schools, Fisher Middle School and Ewing High School. Enrollment was 3,444 students in the 2020 to 2021 school year. The district is also known for the 1946 case Everson v. Board of Education, a U.S. Supreme Court decision on bus transport for parochial school students.

The climate is hot-summer humid continental. Based on 1991 to 2020 normals, the township averages 48.2 inches of precipitation a year and about 8 inches of snow in each of January and February.

That much rain is why the housing inspector looks at grading and drainage, roofs, gutters and foundation walls. Fixing a downspout that empties against the foundation costs little and removes an easy objection before the inspection.

What does Ewing's resale inspection check?

Every dwelling or commercial building offered for resale must be inspected and approved by the Ewing Division of Housing, and the residential fee on the township's 2025 form is $125. The inspector works from the International Property Maintenance Code and township ordinances. Requests can be made through the township's SDL portal, which needs an account, or through the Construction Office at 1666 Pennington Road, 609-883-2900, extension 7676.

The township's printed checklist is not limited to these items, but they come up often:

  • A portable fire extinguisher rated at least 2A-10B:C within 10 feet of the kitchen, mounted no higher than 5 feet, and tagged or receipted within the last 12 months.
  • Ground-fault outlets in kitchens, baths and outdoors, and at least two receptacles per bedroom.

Under township ordinance 10-07, residential rentals must be registered every year regardless of tenant changes, with the registration and rental fire prevention forms due January 31. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection whenever a tenant changes.

If you sell a rental, give the buyer the registration record, the latest fire prevention form and any open violation notices. A buyer who wants to occupy the house will need the unit vacated on a schedule written into the contract.

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee, and the deed is recorded with the Mercer County Clerk in Trenton, whose office has kept property records since 1838. For total consideration of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. Ask the closing attorney for the final figure.

The county charges $43 for the first page of a regular deed and $10 for each additional page. What alarms does a Ewing resale inspection require?

The township asks for smoke alarms on every level, using ten-year sealed lithium battery single-station units, and carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas. It also asks for a labeled fire extinguisher near the kitchen that is tagged or receipted within 12 months.

How much does the Mercer County Clerk charge to record a deed?

A regular deed costs $43 for the first page and $10 for each added page. The state transfer fee is paid separately at recording and is set by the sale price. The county clerk accepts cash, cashier's check, money order, attorney trust account or business escrow account for that fee.

Do I have to register a rental before selling it in Ewing?

Registration is a yearly requirement under ordinance 10-07, with forms due January 31, so it should already be on file. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection on each tenant change. Bring the paperwork to the sale so the buyer sees a clean record.

Can I sell a Ewing house with open permits?

Open permits must be closed out before the resale inspection can be passed, according to the township's inspection list. Call the Construction Office to learn what final inspections are outstanding. Some repairs also need new Uniform Construction Code permits before work begins.

How is Hamilton Township laid out for a seller?

Hamilton covers 39.44 square miles and is the largest suburb of Trenton, the state capital, which lies to its west. It has no true downtown. Separate communities act as commercial centers instead: Mercerville (13,447 residents in 2020), Hamilton Square (12,679), White Horse (9,791), Yardville (6,965) and Groveville (3,106).

Incorporation came on April 11, 1842, and the name comes from Hamilton Square. Open space is a draw: Veterans Park fills 350 acres inside the township, Mercer County Park's 2,500 acres adjoin it to the north, and Grounds For Sculpture occupies 42 acres. Retirement communities and assisted-living facilities have gone up near Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital Hamilton, and new restaurants, banks and stores have opened along Route 33.

What approval does Hamilton Township require before occupancy changes?

Before any change in occupancy of a house or apartment, the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance has to issue a Certificate of Approval stating that the building and premises meet township ordinances. The township names life safety as the first priority of the inspection.

Applications go through the Change of Occupancy Application Portal or on paper to the office. A Change of Occupancy Checklist is published, and reading it before the inspector arrives is the cheapest way to avoid a second visit. How do assessments and appeals work in Hamilton Township?

The Mercer County Board of Taxation, at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton, certifies assessments and hears appeals. Regular appeals are due April 1, appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1, and in-person filing runs from 8:30 a.m. until 4:00 p.m. Postcards with the new assessment go out at the end of January, so read yours before deciding to file.

The county's Property Information Portal shows property record cards, sales, deeds and tax information, which helps you locate comparable sales near your street before you decide whether to file. Request a written tax payoff from the township collector before closing.

The county clerk adds that deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under a new state law.

Real estate transfers are recorded at the Mercer County Clerk's Office, 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, where title searchers and the public can view a property's history in the records room or online. Resident sellers sign the GIT/REP-3 residency certification. Sellers who live elsewhere prepay Gross Income Tax of 2 percent of the price or more.

Hamilton is the only New Jersey municipality hosting Interstate 95 along with both of its auxiliary routes, I-195 and I-295, plus U.S. Routes 130 and 206 and Routes 29, 33 and 156. With the Mercer County Board of Taxation at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton by April 1. Appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1.

No, it does not test houses for lead on request. A seller who wants a test has to hire a private inspector.

The Mercer County Clerk's Office at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. Deeds above $1,000,000 recorded since July 10, 2025 carry a revised fee under the new state law.

The Postal Service officially treats many Hamilton addresses as Trenton even though the house is in Hamilton Township. Name the township in your listing so buyers can find the right tax and school information.

How does a sale work in Lawrence Township, NJ?

Lawrence Township is a Mercer County suburb between Trenton and Princeton. Before a house changes owners, the township's housing office must inspect it, and that step has its own application, fee and waiting period. Start there, since it often takes longer than the rest of the paperwork.

Census estimates for July 2025 show 34,165 residents on 21.73 square miles of land, compared with 33,077 in the 2020 count. Many people say Lawrenceville when they mean the whole township, since most addresses carry a Lawrenceville mailing label, while others have Princeton or Trenton mailing addresses. Write the legal municipality on any contract so the township, not the postal name, controls which rules apply.

How did Lawrence Township get its name and layout?

The area was set up as Maidenhead Township on February 20, 1697, named by Quaker settlers for a village on the Thames. It was renamed Lawrence Township on January 24, 1816, after a naval captain from the War of 1812, and it became part of Mercer County at that county's creation on February 22, 1838.

The township has a historic village center in Lawrenceville (3,751 residents in 2020) and many named neighborhoods around it, including Slackwood, Eldridge Park, Colonial Lakelands, Port Mercer, Lawrence Station and Quaker Bridge. Stony Brook drains the north toward Princeton and Shabakunk Creek runs south toward Trenton. A tornado in September 2003 followed Princeton Pike and damaged homes, a point to mention when buyers ask about roof age.

Owners live in about two thirds of Lawrence homes, and median household income of $130,142 is well above the $80,734 national figure. The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $439,700.

What jobs, schools and shopping affect Lawrence home values?

Lawrence is a work destination, not just a bedroom town. Rider University, founded in 1865, sits just south of Lawrenceville, and the Lawrenceville School dates from 1810.

Those are Eldridge Park, Ben Franklin, Lawrenceville and Slackwood elementary schools, Lawrence Intermediate School for grades 4 to 6, Lawrence Middle School and Lawrence High School. Notre Dame High School and Saint Ann School are the Catholic options, and eighth graders from across the county may apply to Mercer County Technical Schools.

How do commuters reach Lawrence Township?

Buyers check the commute first. Interstate 295 loops through the township and U.S. 1 splits it, while U.S. 206 (Lawrence Road) is the main local artery from Trenton to Princeton. County routes 533, 546 and 569 handle cross-town trips.

The Housing office issues a Certificate of Inspection for sales, and the seller normally pays for and obtains it.   • Scheduling: the office books a visit only after it has the form and fee, and says it usually finds a slot within two weeks, though busy periods run longer.
  • Visit length: roughly 60 to 90 minutes for a house, about 30 for a condo or townhouse.
  • Validity: the certificate expires one year after the inspection. Return visits cost nothing.

A buyer can take on most violations by writing to the township, listing them and giving a repair date. Life safety items are different: they must be corrected and checked again before anyone lives there. A failed septic system or open permits fall to the seller to resolve before closing. In an as-is or bank-owned sale the buyer may be the one to get the certificate, so settle that in the contract. The township's Pre-Inspection Checklist lists the usual items.

Who records the deed in Mercer County, and what does it cost?

The Mercer County Clerk, at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, records Lawrence deeds. A regular deed costs $43 for page one and $10 for every page after that, per the clerk's fee list, and the public records room keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30.

The seller pays the state's transfer fee. A $439,700 median means many Lawrence sales use the schedule for prices over $350,000, and the rate rises in steps with the price. The county clerk notes that deeds over $1 million recorded from July 10, 2025 onward carry a revised fee under a new state law, again paid by the seller.

The clerk accepts transfer fee payments only by cash, cashier's check, money order or an escrow account held by an attorney or business, and anything above $10,000 needs a certified or bank check. Closing attorneys and title agents usually arrange this.

Is listing or a cash sale better for a Lawrence house?

A house in good condition with time for showings does well on the open market, in a township set between Trenton and Princeton. A house needing repairs, occupied by tenants, or facing a tight inspection date may suit an as-is cash purchase better. Whichever buyer you choose, get in writing who orders and pays for the Certificate of Inspection and how a failed item is handled.

Before you decide, call the Housing office at 609-844-7032 to ask for the next open inspection slot. Because the office does not expedite appointments, that date often sets the earliest possible closing.

Yes. A Certificate of Inspection must exist before title passes. It is normally the seller's job, costs $80 with the application, and lapses one year after the visit.

Usually within two weeks, though holidays and busy periods can stretch it. Appointments cannot be expedited, and the office books nothing until it holds the application and fee.

For most items, yes: the buyer writes to the township naming them and a fix date. Life safety violations still have to be corrected and re-inspected before move-in, and the seller must clear a failed septic system or open permits.

The Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. Its list shows $43 for the first deed page and $10 for each extra page.

No, apart from a short list of affordable-housing complexes named by the Housing office. Most single-family rentals and owner-occupied houses are not covered.

April 1, unless the notice went out late, in which case it is 45 days from the mailing. Most petitions go to the Mercer County Board of Taxation, and an assessed value over $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

The last revaluation was in 2006, and the assessor posts an assessed-to-market ratio of 59.42 percent. A tax bill is the assessed value times the tax rate, so it follows the assessed figure.

At the Mercer County Clerk's office, 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. The closing attorney or title agent usually files it and pays the seller's transfer fee.

East Brunswick was incorporated on February 28, 1860, carved from parts of Monroe and North Brunswick. It stayed mostly farmland until suburban building began in the 1930s, and the New Jersey Turnpike extension of 1952 set off the big surge: the population went from 5,699 in 1950 to 19,965 in 1960. Since the 2000 census, New Jersey's population center has fallen inside East Brunswick.

Commuting drives much of the demand. The township sits at Exit 9 of the Turnpike, and Route 18 crosses its eastern half toward New Brunswick, U.S. Route 1 and the Shore. In the introduced text the fee was $50 per unit with more than 10 business days of notice before the change of occupant, $75 at 4 to 10 days, and $125 under 4, plus $20 for a re-inspection after a failure. How did Edison get its name, and why does it matter to a seller?

The township carries the inventor's name because voters changed it in 1954, and it sits on the ground where Thomas Edison ran his Menlo Park laboratory from 1876. The place was earlier called Raritan Township and was carved out of Piscataway and Woodbridge. Colonial-era buildings still stand near Piscatawaytown in South Edison, and three are listed nationally: the Laing House, the Benjamin Shotwell House and the Homestead Farm at Oak Ridge.

The township has many named sections, among them Stelton, Menlo Park, Oak Tree, Raritan Manor, Clara Barton, Lindenau and Washington Park. A house that has changed hands more than once is more likely to carry a finished basement, deck or addition from an earlier owner, and those are the items the township inspector checks for permits.

What does the Edison resale certificate require?

Edison Township Ordinance 14-1.6 says a Certificate for Change of Ownership must be obtained before the property closes, and the township form warns of fines up to $2,000 for skipping it. The application fee is $150, paid by certified check, credit card or money order. The form says no cash, no personal checks and no refunds. Timing is the part that trips people up. One line of the form asks for the inspection at least four weeks before the closing date, and another says three weeks, so plan on four. The township's climate is humid subtropical, and rain and melted snow add up to about 49.6 inches a year, the wettest stretch running through late summer, and snow falls several times each winter. Recorded extremes run from minus 17 degrees in 1934 to 106 degrees in 1936 and 1949.

A buyer's inspector will therefore look closely at the roof, gutters and basement walls, and the township checklist adds the water heater and stair rails. Fixing a damp basement corner or a loose guardrail before you list costs less than negotiating it after the inspection report.

When you list, name the attendance zone for the street you are on. The zone is part of how a listing is described.

Property tax appeals go to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which has said it will not hold virtual hearings. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 where a municipality has done a revaluation.

At closing the seller pays the state realty transfer fee. The state's own example shows $1,910 on a $325,000 deed with no exemption. The Middlesex County Clerk records every deed for Edison at the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Many more followed, and the census designated places include Rossmoor (2,992 people in 2020), Clearbrook (2,909), Concordia (2,455), Whittingham (2,348), Monroe Manor (2,178), Forsgate (2,056), Regency at Monroe (2,036), Stonebridge (1,616), The Ponds (941), Renaissance (637) and Encore (625). Thompson Park is a 675-acre county park on the Monroe and Jamesburg line and the largest in the Middlesex County Park System, with Lake Manalapan, trails, a dog park and a small zoo. Monroe has three cricket fields, and its high school started New Jersey's first high school cricket team in 2023.

April 1, or May 1 in a year the municipality was revalued. Gloucester, Monmouth and Burlington counties use January 15, but Middlesex follows the general state rule.

What is North Brunswick like?

The township touches East Brunswick, Milltown, New Brunswick and South Brunswick in Middlesex County, plus Franklin Township in Somerset County. The Lenape lived here first, and European settlers bought the land in 1772. A state act made it a township on February 21, 1798, and later splits created East Brunswick in 1860 and Milltown in 1889.

Lawrence Brook drains the area, and its watershed covers 48 square miles across five towns. Farrington Lake, a freshwater reservoir, sits along the boundary with East Brunswick and South Brunswick. Local place names include Adams, Berdines Corner, Black Horse, Franklin Park, Livingston Park, Maple Meade, Patricks Corner and Red Lion.

The northern end near New Brunswick is mostly middle class, while the southern and eastern sections tend to be more affluent. Of 101.51 miles of road, the township maintains 77.57, the state 16.71 and Middlesex County 7.23, so a pothole report goes to a different office depending on the street. The township bought the 104.91-acre Otken Farm on Route 130 and opened it as North Brunswick Community Park in April 2007.

How is North Brunswick governed, and who handles a home sale?

The township uses the Faulkner Act's Mayor-Council-Administrator plan, one of only three municipalities in the state's 564 that do. Higher education is nearby as well. The township faces the usual questions of sprawl and open space, and redevelopment of the former Johnson & Johnson pharmaceutical plant site on Route 1 has gone through a public hearing process. Ask the Community Development department what is planned near your block.

A new NJ Transit station on the former Johnson & Johnson site on Route 1 has been proposed for years. Do not promise buyers that it will be built; describe the rail access that exists at Jersey Avenue.

Which state fees and forms apply to a North Brunswick sale?

Expect a transfer fee charged to you at recording. Seniors, blind or disabled sellers and low and moderate income housing use a lighter scale.

Two exemptions are worth knowing: deeds between spouses and deeds from parent to child escape the fee. Residency paperwork still applies to family transfers, since the seller form has no special assurance for them.

An estate selling a house files under its own residency status, signed by the executor or administrator. An LLC, corporation or partnership marks box 5 on the GIT/REP-3. The nonresident formula, found at N.J.S.A. 54A:8-9, takes 10.75% of the gain and never goes below 2% of the price.

The Middlesex County Clerk, based in New Brunswick, takes North Brunswick deeds. Its staff want the tax block, lot and price shown on the deed, an original signature with the signer's name printed below, and a return address. To cancel a mortgage, the original recorded mortgage must be presented with a proper endorsement, which is why you should ask your lender for it when you request the payoff.

Fixing a deed already on file takes a new affidavit, a fresh residency form and a new cover sheet, along with a stated reason. Owners may also join the clerk's free email alert program, which flags any filing against their block and lot. Anyone who suspects fraud can call 732-745-3364 or 732-745-3365.

Is an inspection required to sell in North Brunswick?

Ask the township's Community Development department. It handles building and occupancy certificates, and staff can say whether a Certificate of Continued Occupancy or another inspection applies to your sale and how long it takes.

What is a typical home worth in North Brunswick?

A median owner-occupied value of $431,500 for 2020 to 2024. Actual prices depend on the section, condition and lot, so treat the median as a rough guide.

Where does the deed get filed?

With the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in the County Administration Building at 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Title companies often file electronically through the county's e-recording portal.

Is the transfer fee due if I deed the house to my child?

No, a deed between parent and child is exempt from the realty transfer fee. You still file the seller residency form, because the GIT/REP-3 has no special assurance for family transfers.

What changes if I live in another state?

You complete a GIT/REP form and, unless an assurance on the GIT/REP-3 applies, prepay at least 2% of the deed price toward New Jersey income tax. A refund is possible later if your actual tax is lower.

Where does a seller in Old Bridge, NJ begin?

Old Bridge Township is the largest of the four towns on these pages, with 70,228 people in the 2025 federal estimate, and a sale there should begin with a call to the township's Housing Inspection Division. Whatever route you pick, agent, private buyer or cash, the same municipal and state paperwork stands between you and a recorded deed.

Old Bridge spreads over 38.18 square miles of land in Middlesex County, roughly 25 miles from New York City and across Raritan Bay from Staten Island. Laurence Harbor, Madison Park, Brownville and the Route 9 corridor are all different settings within one municipality, so describe your house by its section of the township, because buyers search that way.

Why was Old Bridge once called Madison Township?

Madison Township was incorporated on March 2, 1869, cut away from South Amboy Township. A referendum on November 5, 1975 renamed it Old Bridge by 7,150 votes to 4,888, a change made to get one postal designation and to end mix-ups with the borough of Madison in Morris County.

Early work here meant farms, snuff mills, clay pits along Cheesequake Creek and an apple orchard with its own distillery. Then came the postwar boom: 7,366 residents in 1950, 22,772 in 1960 and 48,715 in 1970, as subdivisions replaced fields. Much of the housing stock therefore dates from those decades, so roofs, windows and heating systems are common repair topics at sale.

How does Old Bridge compare with the rest of the country on housing?

Owned homes in Old Bridge are valued below those in Nutley or Ocean Township, at $461,000 in the 2020 to 2024 figures. Roughly 70 percent of households own, and 94.4 percent of residents did not move in the past year, the steadiest rate among these four towns.

What should an Old Bridge seller ask the Housing Inspection Division?

The township maintains a Housing Inspection Division with a requirements page of its own. Before listing, ask it whether a resale inspection applies to your address, and get the present checklist, fee and booking steps directly, since the township sets and can change them.

State fire rules add a second layer. A house with one or two units needs a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued through the municipality and good for six months. Ask the township which office issues it for your address.

  • Close open building permits first, since an unfinished permit can hold up a municipal sign-off.
  • For a deck, a finished basement or a new furnace, find the permit and final inspection paperwork.

An owner who cannot afford needed repairs may qualify for the township's Home Improvement Program, which funds health, safety and code fixes for low- and moderate-income households. Ask whether you qualify before choosing between repairing and selling as-is.

Which Old Bridge sections and landmarks come up in listings?

Four Census-designated places sit inside the township: Old Bridge with 27,210 people in 2020, Madison Park with 8,050, Laurence Harbor with 6,635 and Brownville with 2,383. Laurence Harbor has a 70-acre bayfront with a boardwalk, playgrounds and fishing, and Cheesequake State Park spans about 1,600 acres.

Nearness to the bay or a park helps a listing, though homes beside the water also raise flood questions. Streams in the township include the South River, Matchaponix Brook, Deep Run and Cheesequake Creek. Collect your flood insurance history and elevation details before a buyer asks.

Old Bridge Township Raceway Park, off Englishtown Road near the Manalapan and Monroe borders, hosted drag racing from 1965 until a 2018 reorganization ended it, and it has kept kart and motocross racing, car shows and concerts. Houses near it are a different sale from houses near the bay, and buyers will ask about event noise.

Recent temperature records place Old Bridge in a humid subtropical climate, in hardiness zones 7a and 7b. Humid summers make basement moisture and attic ventilation points that buyers and inspectors check, so a dry, clean basement helps a listing.

How do the Parkway, Route 9 and the schools figure in Old Bridge demand?

About 1.9 miles of the Garden State Parkway pass through, with Interchange 120 signed for Laurence Harbor and Matawan. U.S. 9 and Routes 18, 34 and 35 also cross the township, along with county roads 516, 520, 527 and 615. Drivers reach the New Jersey Turnpike at Exit 9 in East Brunswick or Exit 8A in Monroe. Of the township's 222 miles of roadway, about 179 are municipal.

NJ Transit buses on Route 9 serve the Port Authority terminal, Newark and Jersey City, and a park and ride sits on Route 9 northbound near Ernston Road. For trains, riders drive to Aberdeen-Matawan or South Amboy on the North Jersey Coast Line.

The public school district has 14 schools and enrolled 8,096 students in 2022-23. Eleven are elementary schools, two are middle schools named Jonas Salk and Carl Sandburg, and Old Bridge High School held 2,707 students. County magnet schools also admit eighth graders from across Middlesex County.

What state charges and filing dates reach an Old Bridge seller?

A Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording, and the amount comes from the state's rate schedule applied to the deed price. Buyers face an added 1 percent only above $1,000,000. A seller's GIT/REP form is filed with the deed as well.

Assessment appeals go to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation in New Brunswick, where petitions can be filed online and evidence uploaded as late as seven calendar days before the hearing. April 1 is the default deadline, and the appeal covers value only, never the tax amount.

Does a cash offer suit an Old Bridge owner?

Cash can suit a house with deferred maintenance, an estate property or a short timeline. Weigh the offer against a listing's net after commissions, repairs, carrying costs and the charges above. With any buyer, put in writing who obtains the township approval and the smoke alarm certificate and who pays for repairs the inspection demands.

  • Ask what the buyer will do if the township or fire inspector finds a defect that cannot be fixed before the closing date.
  • Ask who is responsible for permits left open by earlier owners.
  • Ask for the closing date and the proof of funds in the same written offer.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an Old Bridge inspection before a resale?

Ask the Housing Inspection Division what applies to your address and get its checklist and fee in writing. The state separately requires a smoke alarm compliance certificate for homes with one or two units.

How long is an Old Bridge smoke alarm certificate valid?

Six months. It is issued through the municipality, and the Division of Fire Safety requires it before such a dwelling is sold, leased or changes occupancy.

What is the Old Bridge assessment appeal date?

April 1 for the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, or May 1 after a town-wide revaluation. The challenge can address assessed value only.

What is a typical Old Bridge home worth?

The Census Bureau lists $461,000 as the typical owned-home value for 2020 to 2024, against $332,700 nationally. Your own house will differ by section, age and condition.

Is the 1 percent state fee the seller's cost?

No. Buyers pay it, and only on prices above $1,000,000. Sellers owe the standard transfer fee, which has partial exemptions for qualifying senior, blind or disabled owners.

What should a seller know about Piscataway before listing?

Piscataway will not let a home change occupants without a Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance. The requirement has applied to sales and rentals since January 1, 2019, and it is the step that most often sets the calendar for a closing.

The township sits on the south side of the Raritan Valley in Middlesex County, covering 18.79 square miles of land. Settlers from New England received land here in 1666, making Piscataway the fifth-oldest municipality in New Jersey, and it was incorporated in 1798. The Census Bureau estimated 62,253 residents on July 1, 2025, up 2.4 percent from the 2020 base.

Rutgers University defines much of the place. The Busch and Livingston campuses lie inside the township, along with SHI Stadium. Neighborhood names residents use include Arbor, Bound Brook Heights, Fellowship Farm, Johnson Park, Lake Nelson, New Market, North Stelton, Randolphville, Riverview Manor and Society Hill. Camp Kilmer, opened in 1941 on land in Piscataway and Edison, processed more than 2.5 million soldiers during World War II before closing in 2009.

How does the Piscataway MCCC inspection work?

The Community Development Department inspects each dwelling for fitness for habitation and issues the certificate if it passes. Inspections take place weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., excluding holidays, and inspectors show a township vehicle and photo identification at the door.

The township asks sellers to apply at least four weeks before closing. Applications and fees go to the MCCC office at the Public Works Center, reachable at (732) 562-2393 or mccc@piscatawaynj.org. Section 14-4 of the municipal code governs the program.

  • Single-family home, condo or townhome: $150 per unit.
  • Two-family: $150 per unit, so $300 in total.
  • Temporary MCCC: $125 per unit, available after an application is filed.
  • Reinspections: $100 per unit starting with the third inspection.

One rule catches many sellers: if work was done without a required permit, the permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Dig out old deck, basement and kitchen permits early.

Why does Piscataway sell differently from nearby towns?

Its buyers are drawn by the university, a corporate base and highway access. The township lists companies such as Colgate-Palmolive's research and development operation, Hapag-Lloyd America, IEEE, GenScript Biotech, Cintas and a Pepsi bottling plant among its corporate residents.

  • Interstate 287 crosses the township with exits 6 through 9, and Route 18 reaches it along Hoes Lane.
  • The New Jersey Turnpike is close at East Brunswick Exit 9 and Edison Exit 10.
  • No train station stands inside Piscataway, but the Raritan Valley Line stops at Dunellen and the Northeast Corridor at Edison.
  • NJ Transit bus 114 serves Port Authority in Manhattan, and routes 65 and 66 go to Newark.

The school district runs eleven schools and enrolled 7,331 students in 2024 to 2025, including Piscataway High School. The district also includes three middle schools named Conackamack, Quibbletown and Schor.

What do Census figures show for Piscataway homes?

Values in Piscataway sit well above the national figure of $332,700. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates give a median owner-occupied value of $449,900, a median gross rent of $2,024 and median household income of $127,832.

Owners live in 63.8 percent of homes, and the township has 17,664 households averaging 2.95 people. About 48.9 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Foreign-born residents make up 33.9 percent of the population, 30.7 percent identify as Asian alone, and 43.4 percent of those five and older speak another language at home.

Preparation starts with paperwork, because the township treats unpermitted work as a hold on the certificate. The partial checklist on the township site is described as a guide to what homes most commonly fail, and it does not cover every possible reason for failure.

  • Submit the application and fee at least four weeks before the closing date.
  • Collect permits for decks, finished basements, additions, water heaters and electrical work, and close any that are still open.
  • Plan the visit for a weekday window, and expect inspectors to show photo identification.
  • Budget for the third inspection onward, which costs $100 per unit.
  • Ask whether a temporary certificate fits your timeline if repairs will run past closing.

Older housing stock is part of the picture. The Road Up Raritan Historic District holds nine historic homes along River Road and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999, and a house dating to 1741 operates as a county museum. Owners in or near historic areas should ask the Planning Division what local review applies before promising a buyer exterior changes.

How do Piscataway taxes work for a seller?

Ask the township Tax Collector for a current statement before you set a closing date, because balances and installments change through the year. The tax office also publishes the township's rates.

In April 2026 the township announced a budget that lowered the municipal tax rate by another 4.72 percent to offset gains in property value. A lower rate does not guarantee a lower bill, since assessed values and county and school levies move too, so compare your own bill line by line.

Taxes and sewer charges can be paid online through the township website, which helps when a title company needs proof that accounts are current.

Who records the deed for a Piscataway sale?

The Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick records deeds for Piscataway properties. The office opens weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:10 p.m. and asks walk-in filers to arrive by 4 p.m.; appointments are optional but get priority.

A deed must say "Prepared by" and name the drafter, show the tax block, lot and consideration, and give a record-and-return address. Signatures must be original with the names printed beneath. A re-recorded deed needs a new affidavit, a new seller's residency form and a new cover sheet. Title companies commonly file electronically through the New Jersey County Recording system instead.

State forms go with the deed. Married sellers who file a joint state return may sign one Gross Income Tax form, while unmarried co-owners each sign their own, matched to their ownership share. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2 percent of the sale price. Heirs selling an inherited house sign according to their own residency.

Is a cash sale worth considering in Piscataway?

It can be, when a house is likely to fail the MCCC inspection, has open permits or has sat vacant. A cash buyer may accept the property without the repairs a seller would otherwise fund, but the certificate still comes before any change of occupancy, and the township also offers a temporary version at $125 per unit once an application is filed.

Ask any buyer who files the MCCC application, who pays the fees, and what happens if reinspections run past the second visit. Weigh the offer against what you would net after repairs, the seller's transfer fee and the months a listing may take.

Does Piscataway require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes. A Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance is required when selling or renting a home, and the township asks for the application four weeks before closing.

How much does a Piscataway MCCC cost?

It costs $150 per unit for a single-family home, condo or townhome, $300 for a two-family, and $125 per unit for a temporary certificate. Reinspections cost $100 per unit starting with the third.

What happens if I did work in Piscataway without a permit?

The permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Start that step early because it can hold up a closing.

Where is the Piscataway MCCC office?

It operates from the Public Works Center. Call (732) 562-2393 or email mccc@piscatawaynj.org for an appointment.

Where are Piscataway deeds recorded?

At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick, or electronically through the county's e-recording service for title companies.

What are the main ways to sell a house in South Brunswick?

South Brunswick owners have three routes: an agent's listing, a private sale, or an as-is offer from a buyer paying cash. All three routes meet the same township step: a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy, which the Planning office issues before the deed changes hands.

Listing reaches the most buyers where the Census Bureau's typical owner-occupied home value is $582,700, but it adds commissions, showings and a township inspection that you schedule around the sale. A direct sale gives up some price for speed and usually skips repair negotiations. Whichever you choose, sort out the permit history first, because the township will not issue the resale certificate while any permit or inspection is still open.

Where is South Brunswick and which villages does it include?

South Brunswick is a Middlesex County township of 41.02 square miles, 40.61 of them land, in the middle of the Raritan Valley. It borders Cranbury, East Brunswick, Monroe, North Brunswick and Plainsboro in Middlesex County, Princeton in Mercer County and Franklin Township in Somerset County. The Lawrence Brook runs through the center of the township, and Pigeon Swamp State Park holds 1,078 acres of undeveloped land off Deans Rhode Hall Road.

There is no single downtown. Instead the township is a set of unincorporated villages, each with its own mail address, and buyers often search by village name. Several ZIP codes share the township, including 08810 for Dayton, 08824 for Kendall Park, 08852 for Monmouth Junction and 08528 for Kingston, so a listing should name the village clearly. The 2020 Census counted these communities:

  • Kendall Park: 9,989 residents
  • Monmouth Junction: 8,895
  • Dayton: 8,138
  • Heathcote: 7,154
  • Deans: 1,615
  • Kingston: 1,581

How did South Brunswick grow, and what does that mean for the houses?

The township was incorporated on February 21, 1798, and farmed for most of its first two centuries. The Straight Turnpike, now Route 1, opened in 1804, a trolley line followed in 1900, and the New Jersey Turnpike arrived in 1951. Suburban building began after World War II, and Kendall Park was started in 1957 off Route 27, an old Native American trail.

The population was close to 18,000 in 1980, reached 25,792 in 1990 and stood at 47,043 in 2020, the highest decennial count on record. Because so much of that growth came after 1980, many homes are old enough that a furnace, water heater or central air unit has been replaced at least once. The township resale form asks about each of those replacements, so keep invoices and permit numbers together before you apply. Warehouses now fill much of the land between Route 130 and the Turnpike on the southeast side.

What do the Census numbers say about South Brunswick homeowners?

47,454 residents for July 2025, up 0.9% from the April 2020 base. Of the 16,770 households counted for 2020 to 2024, 76.9% own their home, and the average household has 2.81 people. Median household income is $150,933, median gross rent is $1,935, and 68.9% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

About 42.2% of residents were born outside the United States and 52.7% of people age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home. Sellers who advertise in more than one language, or who share a floor plan and inspection summary with buyers ahead of a tour, tend to avoid repeat questions. Workers travel 34.4 minutes on average to their jobs, which matches the township's role as an outer-ring New York suburb. Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

What does the South Brunswick resale certificate cover?

The Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy, under section 22-425 of the township code, is a general inspection of the visible parts of the dwelling. The application says it confirms three things: no work was done that needed a construction or zoning permit, no permits or inspections remain outstanding, and no visible violations or unsafe conditions exist. If an inspector finds a problem, you must obtain the missing permits and satisfy the inspections before the certificate is released.
