Which past projects should I check before booking the inspection?

The application asks whether the home has had any of the following, and for the permit number if so. Anything done without a permit has to be permitted and inspected before the certificate can issue, even if a previous owner did the work.

  • Replacement central air conditioning, furnace or water heater
  • Generator or radon system
  • Addition or finished basement
  • Fireplace or wood stove
  • Shed larger than 200 square feet
  • Swimming pool, hot tub, deck or gazebo

The Building Department administers the state Uniform Construction Code and handles permits, but it does not process resale certificates. Direct resale questions to the Zoning office. Any permits and certificates of approval that come out of the process are passed to the Tax Assessor, so the new work will appear on the property record.

Which schools, roads and bus lines do South Brunswick buyers ask about?

South Brunswick Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 with 12 schools and 7,936 students in 2023-24, down from 8,620 in 2018-19. The elementary schools are Brooks Crossing, Brunswick Acres, Cambridge, Constable, Greenbrook, Indian Fields and Monmouth Junction, with Dayton and Deans preschools. Crossroads Middle School North and South serve grades 6 to 8, and South Brunswick High School has 2,728 students.

A 3.5-mile stretch of the New Jersey Turnpike crosses the east side, with the toll gate for Exit 8A just over the line in Monroe. U.S. 1, U.S. 130, Route 27 and Route 32 cross the township, along with county routes 535 and 522. A park and ride near Routes 32 and 130 offers Suburban Transit lines 300 (Port Authority, Grand Central and the East Side) and 600 (Downtown Manhattan). The Middlesex County Area Transit shuttle links to NJ Transit, and the nearest train stations are at Princeton Junction and New Brunswick.

Large employers in the township include Dow Jones, International Flavors and Fragrances, L'Oreal, Canon, UPS, Tris Pharma and the school district itself, which gives many buyers a job base inside the township.

What state paperwork comes with a South Brunswick closing?

New Jersey puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller, collected at recording and scaled to the price stated in the deed. A deed that claims an exemption, such as a transfer between spouses or between parent and child, needs Form RTF-1. For Class 2 residential sales above $1,000,000, a supplemental graduated fee starts at 1% of the total price.

The seller also signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, GIT/REP-3 for New Jersey residents. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2% of the total consideration unless a stated exception applies. Both sets of rules are on the Division of Taxation realty transfer fee page and its GIT/REP FAQ. Your closing attorney or title agent will prepare the forms.

Does the Kingston historic district affect a sale?

The Kingston Mill Historic District covers 49 acres around the village of Kingston, which sits where South Brunswick meets Princeton and Franklin Township. It was added to the federal historic register on April 10, 1986, and includes the 1888 Kingston Mill and the 1798 Kingston Bridge. Owners of older Kingston houses should ask the township Planning office whether an address lies inside the district before they plan exterior changes ahead of a sale.

Is a township inspection required before closing in South Brunswick?

Yes. South Brunswick requires a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy under section 22-425 of the township code. The inspection looks at visible components and checks for unpermitted work, open permits and unsafe conditions.

How long does the South Brunswick resale certificate last?

It is effective for 120 days, and the inspecting officer may grant one extension of up to 30 days. If the house has not sold by then and is still on the market, the owner must apply again and obtain a new certificate.

Which township office handles resale certificates?

The Zoning office does, at 732-329-4000 ext. 7240. The Building Department says it handles construction permits and new construction certificates, and sends resale questions to Zoning.

Can I sell with work that was done without a permit?

The township wants the permits and inspections satisfied before it issues the resale certificate, so unpermitted work has to be brought into compliance first. Ask your attorney how the sale contract should address any cost of doing so.

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in South Brunswick?

The seller does. The state collects it at recording, and the rate rises with the price in the deed. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry the graduated percent fee, starting at 1%.

What does a Woodbridge seller need to clear before closing?

Woodbridge Township skips the certificate of continued occupancy, yet a house still needs an alarm certificate and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection to close. The sewer check is where sellers stumble, because floor drains, sump pumps and downspouts tied into the sewer must be fixed first.

Woodbridge is also large and varied. Roughly 105,000 residents live across ten communities, from waterfront flood zones to older streets in the Rahway Valley and neighborhoods beside the highways, so one inspection list lands very differently from section to section.

What do the Woodbridge figures show about homes and renters?

The 2020 census recorded 103,639 residents, and the mid-2025 estimate is 104,802. On 23.26 square miles of land, owners occupy about 66 percent of homes, which leaves roughly a third of households renting.

Which of the ten Woodbridge communities is my house in?

Woodbridge Township is an umbrella over ten unincorporated communities. The Census Bureau tracks them as separate places, and their 2020 populations show the scale:

  • Iselin, 20,088 residents;
  • Woodbridge Proper, 19,839;
  • Colonia, 18,609;
  • Avenel, 16,290;
  • Fords, 12,941;
  • Port Reading, 3,921, with Keasbey, Sewaren, Hopelawn and Menlo Park Terrace making up the rest.

A mailing address may say Iselin or Colonia, but the municipality that bills the tax and requires the inspections is Woodbridge Township in every case. Woodbridge itself is the oldest original township in the state, granted a royal charter on June 1, 1669.

How do the Turnpike, the Parkway and the rail stations affect value here?

The New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway meet here, and the township houses the headquarters of the authority that operates both. The Parkway covers 7.5 miles of town between Exits 127 and 132, while the Turnpike crosses for about 5.25 miles and has Exit 11. With U.S. 1 and 9 and several state routes, the road network totals 303.32 miles, 244.16 of them municipal.

Three train stations serve the township. Metropark, on the Northeast Corridor, recorded 3,702 average weekday boardings in 2025, seventh highest on NJ Transit, with Amtrak service as well. Avenel and Woodbridge stations sit on the North Jersey Coast Line, and buses 115 and 116 head to Port Authority.

Houses near Metropark or a Parkway ramp suit commuters, while houses beside the highways face road noise, so describe both plainly in a listing.

The school district ran 25 schools for 13,836 students in 2022-23, including Colonia, John F. Kennedy Memorial and Woodbridge high schools and the RISE program.

How much does flood risk matter to a Woodbridge sale?

Per Wikipedia's summary of floodplain studies, about 19 percent of the township sits inside FEMA flood hazard areas. Water wraps three sides: the Arthur Kill to the east, the Raritan River to the south and the Rahway River to the north, and some built-up land lies only five feet above sea level.

Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 struck the Watson-Crampton area beside the Woodbridge River hard, and the township afterward used the state's buyout program to purchase and remove many homes in flood hazard areas. For a house near the Woodbridge River, Heards Brook, the Raritan in Keasbey, or the Arthur Kill in Sewaren and Port Reading, expect questions about flood zone status and insurance history.

Pull together your flood insurance policy, any elevation certificate and past claim records before listing. A cash buyer cares about the same facts but can price the risk straight into an offer.

Which inspections does Woodbridge require for a resale?

The township's certificate of compliance sheet says no Certificate of Continued Occupancy is required, but a smoke detector inspection applies under an ordinance from April 15, 1980, and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection under one from March 3, 1998. There is no online form, so you book by phone and need the buyer's name, address, email and phone number plus a closing date.

  • Smoke detectors must be on every level, mounted with screws, and battery models must be the ten-year sealed type since January 1, 2019.
  • Carbon monoxide detectors go within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • Open permits and violations must be closed before the inspector releases the certificate.
  • The owner or a representative has to be at the house for the visit.
  • The finished certificate stays valid for 60 days.

The sewer rules are where houses fail. The township's sanitary sewer page names the banned connections: roof drains and downspouts, basement floor drains, sump pumps, yard and driveway drains, and missing or cracked trap caps. Floor drains get plugged and covered with concrete, and sump pumps and downspouts must send water to the street rather than the sewer. Fix these before you request the inspection.

Where is a Woodbridge deed recorded, and when are taxes due?

Middlesex County records the deed at the County Clerk's Registry, 4th Floor of the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office stays open until 4:10 p.m. on weekdays, but you must be in line by 4. Appointments are optional, though booked customers go first. A deed must include the words "Prepared by," the tax block and lot and the consideration, and a paper filing with no cover sheet draws a $20 indexing charge.

Bills are mailed every January and July, with payment dates on the first day of every February, May, August and November. The Tax Collection Office, on the first floor of Town Hall at 1 Main Street, opens at 8:30 in the morning and closes at 4:30 on weekdays, staying open until 6:30 on Tuesdays. A drop box stands in front of Town Hall. Sewer has its own bill, with the second half due October 1, and the township counts the date it receives the money, not the postmark.

How should a Woodbridge owner choose between an agent, a solo sale and a cash buyer?

An agent listing suits a well-kept house in a strong section, a cash buyer suits one with flood, sewer or repair problems, and a solo sale fits an owner who can run showings and the contract. Sewer and flood questions often tip the balance here.

  • Use an agent if your sewer connections are clean and the house shows well.
  • Go solo if you will handle the inspections and the Middlesex County recording yourself or through an attorney.
  • Pick an as-is cash buyer if the house has an illegal sewer connection, flood damage in its past, open permits or tenants, since that buyer can absorb the cost.

Whatever you choose, book the township inspection once a closing date is set, and judge written offers by the amount you keep after the transfer fee, taxes and payoff.

Must a Woodbridge house have a certificate of occupancy to sell?

No. The township says a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required. A smoke and carbon monoxide inspection and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection are.

What does the sewer discharge inspection look for?

It checks that no roof drains, floor drains, sump pumps or yard drains feed the sanitary sewer and that trap caps are intact. An ordinance adopted March 3, 1998 requires it before a resale.

How long does a Woodbridge compliance certificate last?

Sixty days from the inspection. Time the visit so the certificate has not lapsed by closing.

When do Woodbridge tax installments fall due?

The first day of February, May, August and November. Bills are mailed in January and July, and payments are taken in Town Hall at 1 Main Street.

Which office records a Woodbridge deed?

The Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, on the fourth floor. Weekday service ends at 4:10 p.m., and you must arrive by 4.

Is selling in Freehold Township, NJ the same as selling in Freehold Borough?

No. Freehold Township and Freehold Borough are separate municipalities with separate offices, and the township completely surrounds the borough. New Jersey counts this as one of 21 pairs of doughnut towns, where one municipality wraps around another, so check which one your deed and tax bill name before you call anyone.

The township covers 38.65 square miles of land in western Monmouth County. The Census Bureau estimates 36,052 residents for July 2025, up 1.9% from the April 2020 base but still below the 36,184 counted in 2010.

Homes here skew toward owners: 83.7% of housing is owner-occupied, and 94.2% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $553,600 for 2020-2024, with median gross rent of $2,194.

How does Freehold Township's history show up in a house sale today?

It shows up in the street names, the farmland and the parks. The township was first formed on October 31, 1693, and the legislature incorporated it on February 21, 1798. The word freehold is an English legal term for fee simple ownership, which is the kind of title you are transferring.

The Battle of Monmouth was fought on June 28, 1778, on ground now preserved as Monmouth Battlefield State Park, partly inside the township. Later, highways such as U.S. Route 9 and Route 33 let residents commute to Newark, Philadelphia and New York, and large neighborhoods of single-family homes followed.

Commercial growth came in layers. Brockway Glass built a plant off Center Street in 1955 and closed it in 1991, 3M opened a tape plant in 1957, CentraState Medical Center opened in 1971 as Freehold Area Hospital, and Freehold Raceway Mall opened in 1990 as the second largest mall in the state. Farms with crops, thoroughbreds, sod and orchards still operate in the township.

What does Freehold Township require before a house can be sold?

Freehold Township requires both a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (CCO) inspection and a fire inspection whenever a residential property is sold or rented. The two applications must go to the Housing Department together, each with its own check or money order, and the township does not take cash or cards.

The inspection appointment can be scheduled only after both applications and payments are in. A CCO issued for a resale is valid for up to 120 calendar days, or until occupancy changes, so do not apply so early that it lapses before closing. For scheduling, call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066.

What does the Freehold Township inspector look for?

The township's own checklist is mainly about safety and open permits, and it states that buyers should still hire a private inspector. Any violation the inspector considers a safety issue must be fixed even if it is not on the list.

  • Permits: work done without permits, such as water heaters, furnaces, AC, decks, sheds, fences and finished basements, must be permitted and closed first.
  • Utilities must be on, and the house number must be six inches high and visible from the street.
  • Doors: entry doors with deadbolts need an inside thumb latch, and double-key deadbolts and slide bolts are not allowed.
  • Electrical: GFCI outlets within six feet of every sink, and covers on all outlets, switches and junction boxes.
  • Garage: entry doors need a solid core wood or steel door with a 20-minute fire rating.
  • Dryer vents must be flexible metal, and a sump pump needs its own outlet and must discharge outdoors.
  • Pools need self-closing, self-latching gates and must be running or closed.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are handled on the separate fire checklist. Alarms are required on every level including the basement and within ten feet of bedrooms, and detectors must be replaced every ten years.

What if the Freehold Township house cannot pass the CCO before closing?

The township offers a document called Transfer of Title, No Occupancy, which lets a closing go forward while the buyer fixes the remaining items. The state still requires every property to pass the fire inspection before the sale, so the smoke and carbon monoxide work cannot be skipped.

The process runs in steps. Both applications and payments go in first, and the inspector lists deficiencies, sometimes marking the house as having too many items to list. The buyer's attorney then writes a letter on the township's sample, agreeing there will be no occupancy until a new inspection and CCO, and agreeing to hold the township harmless. After the fire inspection passes and the letter is filed, the Housing Department emails the document for closing.

After closing the buyer owns the repair list and schedules the final CCO inspection. This path suits a cash buyer who plans to renovate. Rental properties follow stricter rules: they must be registered, vacant at inspection, freshly painted and, if built before 1978, supported by a lead-safe certificate that lasts two years.

How do estates, trusts and co-owners handle state forms at a Freehold Township closing?

Each seller on the deed completes a GIT/REP residency form, and the Monmouth County Clerk will not record the deed without one. Married couples who file a joint New Jersey return can sign one form, but unmarried co-owners each sign their own.

  • Estates: the estate completes the form under its own residency status, signed by the executors or the administrator if there was no will. One form can carry several executors' signatures.
  • Trusts: the trustee signs for the trust, and a trustee who is also a beneficiary signs a second form in a personal capacity.
  • Percent of ownership: if one owner holds 50% and two others hold 25% each, each form shows that share.
  • LLCs and corporations complete the GIT/REP-3 and check the box for sellers that are not individuals.

For a nonresident seller, the state's formula multiplies gain by 10.75% but never lets the estimated payment fall below 2% of the deed consideration. Sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are the only exceptions to the form requirement.

What do roads, schools and employers mean for Freehold Township buyers?

Buyers weigh the commute first. Mean travel time to work is 30.9 minutes (2020-2024). Route 9, Route 33, Route 18 and Route 79 cross the township, with county routes 522, 524, 527 and 537, and Interstate 195 is reachable through Howell on Route 9 or Jackson on County Route 537. Garden State Parkway Exit 100 is about ten miles east.

NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run along Route 9 to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. The nearest rail stops are Aberdeen-Matawan, Asbury Park and Long Branch, and the SeaStreak ferry from Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive from the east side of the township.

High school students attend Freehold Township High School or Freehold High School, both in the Freehold Regional High School District, and assignment depends on the home address. CentraState Medical Center, a 287-bed hospital inside the township, ranks as the county's fourth-largest employer. The township sits on the northern edge of the humid subtropical climate zone, next to the humid continental zone.

Frequently asked questions

Does Freehold Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. Freehold Township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection and a fire inspection for every residential sale or rental. Both applications are submitted together to the Housing Department, each with a check or money order.

How long is a Freehold Township resale CCO good for?

Up to 120 calendar days from the date of issue, or until the occupancy changes, whichever comes first. A rental CCO lasts only up to 60 days.

Can a Freehold Township house close without passing the CCO?

Yes, with a Transfer of Title, No Occupancy document. The buyer's attorney signs a letter agreeing there is no occupancy until the final CCO is issued, and the property must still pass the fire inspection first.

Which phone number do I call to schedule a Freehold Township CCO?

Call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066. The township's FAQ also lists 732-294-5109, and the zoning office line is 732-294-2068.

Do estates in Freehold Township need special state tax forms?

They need the same GIT/REP form as any seller, filled out in the estate's name. If there was a will, the executors or beneficiaries who sign the deed sign the form; with no will, the administrator signs it.

How can you sell a house fast in Howell, New Jersey?

Howell sellers can hire an agent, go it alone or take a cash purchase. All three meet the township's fire inspection, the one local step nobody skips. Howell is a large, mostly single-family township in Monmouth County, so many sellers have a detached house on a sizeable lot, sometimes with older systems.

  • Agent listing: exposure to the most buyers, which suits a house that shows well, though appraisals, mortgage approval and repair requests stretch the calendar.
  • Private sale: you skip the commission and handle the price, the contract and the alarm inspection yourself.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair haggling, which fits an inherited home, a vacant house or a short move deadline.

Under any of them, book the Fire Bureau inspection early. Failing it for a missing detector is the most avoidable delay in a Howell sale.

Where is Howell Township and how did it grow?

At roughly 61.21 square miles, Howell is Monmouth County's biggest municipality by area, and 60.27 of those miles are land. It borders Colts Neck, Freehold Township and Wall in Monmouth County and Brick, Jackson and Lakewood in Ocean County. Named communities inside the township include Ramtown, Adelphia, Ardena, Land of Pines, Southard and Squankum.

The Legislature carved Howell out of Shrewsbury Township on February 23, 1801. Brick split off in 1850 and Wall in 1851, and Farmingdale became its own borough in 1903. Because the township still surrounds Farmingdale completely, it is one of the state's 21 pairs of doughnut towns.

The area was once iron country. Bog iron fed the Howell Works in the 19th century, and the preserved Allaire Village now sits inside Allaire State Park along the Howell and Wall border. The ground is sandy Outer Coastal Plain soil with pine and oak woods, wetlands and the 1,204 acre Manasquan Reservoir nearby.

What do Census figures show about housing in Howell?

Howell is firmly a township of owners: QuickFacts puts owner occupancy at 88.8 percent, the highest of the four places in its comparison table. The median owned home is valued at $507,200. Typical monthly costs are $2,846 for owners with a mortgage and $1,133 for those without.

Households number 19,134, each with 2.81 people on average, and median household income is $134,854. The poverty rate is 6.8 percent. Retail sales came to $23,830 per resident in 2022, far above the other three places in the same table, and shopping centers line Route 9. The 2020 count was 53,537 people, and the estimate for July 2025 is 55,156.

Residents 65 and older make up 17.2 percent of the township, and 89.3 percent of people stayed at one address through the prior year. A house needing work still sells, and a buyer who accepts its condition shortens the path.

How do Howell residents get to work and school?

Most working residents leave the township. The state labor department places Howell in the Monmouth-Ocean labor area, and more than 70 percent of employed residents work outside it, per the township's encyclopedia entry. Health care and social assistance employs 16.3 percent, retail 13.8 percent and education 11.1 percent.

  • Roads: Interstate 195, U.S. 9, Route 33 and Route 34 all cross the township, plus County Routes 524, 547 and 549. The Garden State Parkway is reached from I-195 and Route 33 at exits 98 and 100.
  • Buses: NJ Transit routes 131, 135 and 139 head to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Resident-only park-and-ride lots sit at Aldrich, in Land of Pines, and in Adelphia. Belmar is the nearest train station.
  • Schools: the Howell Township district serves pre-kindergarten through grade 8 in 12 schools with 6,045 students in 2024-25. High schoolers attend Howell, Freehold Township or Colts Neck High School in the Freehold Regional district depending on address.

Horse farms and nurseries remain part of the landscape, which is why rural lots and acreage show up in local listings.

What does the Howell Fire Bureau require before a house changes hands?

Howell uses a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Secondary Power Source Compliance for resales, handled by the Fire Bureau at 4567 Highway 9 North, second floor. Clean and test every alarm before the inspector arrives. The required type depends on when the house was built or renovated.

The sheet adds more details sellers miss.

  • Alarms must be under 10 years old by manufacture date, and replacing electric alarms with battery models is not allowed.
  • One and two family homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage need carbon monoxide alarms on each sleeping level and near every bedroom door.
  • A solar array, generator or battery system calls for a printed label reading CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter.
  • House numbers must be at least 4 inches tall, contrast with the background and be visible from the street.
  • The sheet drops the old extinguisher rule for one and two family homes that change hands.

The Fire Bureau's number is 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

How do Howell property tax appeals and payoffs work?

Monmouth County follows a different calendar from most of New Jersey, so a Howell appeal is due January 15 rather than April 1. The state's appeals page lists Monmouth County alongside Burlington and Gloucester, and gives the Monmouth County Board of Taxation number as 732-431-7404. Appeals are filed on Form A-1 with that board.

If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey must receive your appeal within 45 days of that judgment. Owners of property assessed over $1,000,000 can skip the board and file with the Tax Court.

The township forms page lists Tax Collector requests for lien redemption figures, bank code removal and prepaid taxes. Ask for a redemption figure early if the house has a tax lien, since the payoff has to be in the closing statement.

Who records a Howell deed and what do the state rules add?

Deeds for a Howell sale are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, whose site lists real property recordings, e-recording and a recording fee schedule. Your title company normally files the deed and the tax forms together.

The seller pays the State Realty Transfer Fee. A sale at Howell's median value of $507,200 lands in the over-$350,000 schedule, where $4.80 per $500 applies between $200,000 and $550,000. Sellers who remain in the state sign GIT/REP-3. Someone relocating out of New Jersey becomes a nonresident for tax purposes on this sale, and an estimated payment of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the gain may come due at the table unless an exemption covers it.

Frequently asked questions

What inspection does Howell require before I sell?

A smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source compliance inspection by the Howell Fire Bureau. The alarm type required depends on the year the house was built or renovated. Test and clean the alarms first, then confirm the appointment with the bureau at 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

Do I need fire extinguishers to sell a Howell home?

No, for a one or two family dwelling. According to the Fire Bureau's sheet, extinguishers no longer come into play when ownership or occupancy changes in those homes and in attached single-family units. Alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and any power-source label do still need to pass.

When is the deadline to appeal a Howell tax assessment?

January 15, because Monmouth County follows an alternative assessment calendar. Most other New Jersey counties use April 1. File Form A-1 with the Monmouth County Board of Taxation, and call that office at 732-431-7404 if you are unsure which date applies to your parcel.

Which county office records the deed on a Howell sale?

The Monmouth County Clerk. The office handles real property recordings and e-recording, and its website carries the recording fee schedule. Closing is where the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the GIT/REP form usually get bundled and sent in by the title agent.

Can I sell a Howell house with tenants in it?

Yes. The township keeps rental forms, including a combined rental certificate, a landlord registration for multi-unit property and a single unit rental application. Pull those filings and the current lease before you list, since buyers on either side will want to see the terms.

What speeds up a home sale in Manalapan Township?

Speed here comes from clearing the township's Housing Certification early and choosing a buyer with no long loan process. Cash offers shorten the timeline most, though a well-prepared listing can also move in a township where owners occupy nearly nine in ten homes.

The steps that most often decide the calendar are these.

  • Apply for the Housing Certification, which the township says is the seller's responsibility.
  • Close out every open building permit before the inspection.
  • Get Health Department approval first if the house has a well or septic system.
  • Confirm the quarterly tax payment and get a payoff figure for closing.

Where is Manalapan, and how did it take shape?

Manalapan is a large township of 30.65 square miles in western Monmouth County. It was formed by the Legislature on March 9, 1848, from part of Freehold Township, and it completely surrounds the borough of Englishtown, which makes the two a "doughnut" pair. The Battle of Monmouth was fought in 1778 on land now split between Manalapan and Freehold, and Monmouth Battlefield State Park covers 2,928 acres across the two townships.

Yorketown, a census-designated place of 6,617 people in 2020, lies inside the township along with older hamlets such as Clarks Mills, Gordons Corner, Millhurst, Smithburg and Taylors Mills. The population grew from 14,049 in 1970 to 40,905 in 2020, the highest count the township has recorded.

How do residents get around, and does it affect the sale?

Manalapan is car-oriented. U.S. Route 9 runs through the northeast, Route 33 passes near the south, and County Routes 522 and 527 cross the township. The Garden State Parkway, Interstate 195 and the New Jersey Turnpike are reached through neighboring towns. NJ Transit bus 139 goes to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 64 and 67 reach Newark and Jersey City. The nearest rail stations are Metropark, Metuchen, New Brunswick and Princeton Junction on the Northeast Corridor.

The average trip to work takes 43.2 minutes, so buyers study highway access and school boundaries closely. Newark Airport is about 32 miles away, and Trenton-Mercer is 21 miles west.

Who owns Manalapan homes, according to the Census Bureau?

Because most sellers are owner-occupants rather than landlords, the typical Manalapan sale is an owner-occupied family house, and the permit file matters to the buyer's attorney.

What is the Manalapan Housing Certification?

The township now calls its Certificate of Continued Occupancy a Housing Certification, required when a home is sold or rented. The cost is $225, paid either in exact cash or with two separate checks or money orders: $150 for the certification and $75 for the smoke certificate. Both are payable to Manalapan Township.

Students in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade attend the Manalapan-Englishtown Regional School District, which runs eight schools and enrolled 4,653 students in 2023-24. For grades 9 through 12, Manalapan residents attend Manalapan High School or Freehold Township High School in the Freehold Regional High School District. Manalapan High houses the district's Science and Engineering magnet and a Law Enforcement and Public Safety program.

The township's Recreation Center covers 162 acres with tennis, basketball and sports fields. CentraState Medical Center in neighboring Freehold Township is the local hospital. High schoolers can also apply to one of the five career academies run by the Monmouth County Vocational School District. Buyers often name schools and the recreation complex before they name the house, so list them in your marketing even if you sell for cash.

How did Manalapan grow, and what does it mean for older houses?

The township counted 3,990 people in 1960 and 14,049 in 1970, then added thousands every decade: 18,914 in 1980, 26,716 in 1990, 33,423 in 2000 and 38,872 in 2010. That pace suggests a large share of the housing dates from the 1970s onward, so buyers will check the age of roofs, windows and mechanical systems.

Shopping is mostly across the line: Freehold Raceway Mall in Freehold Township is the major destination for residents, and the township sits inside the New York metropolitan area. The Monmouth Battlefield Historic District covers 1,819 acres along County Route 522 on the Manalapan and Freehold border, and it keeps part of the township open.

What should you do about open permits before a Manalapan inspection?

The Construction Office says all existing open permits must be closed out before the Housing Certification inspection, and closed permits are what become part of the block and lot file. Walk through the house and list every deck, finished basement, addition, water heater, furnace or fence that was permitted or should have been.

If a permit is open, the contractor who pulled it or you as owner must schedule the final inspection. That step can take longer than the certification itself, so start with permits and only then pay for the Housing Certification inspection.

What will a Manalapan seller pay at closing?

The seller pays New Jersey's transfer fee as the deed is filed. Above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee joins it, starting at 1 percent of the total price, and with a midpoint value of $655,500 a good number of larger Manalapan homes can reach that range.

At the Monmouth County Clerk, a deed costs $40 for its first page and $10 for each added page, with transfer tax due at filing. A seller living outside New Jersey submits the nonresident GIT/REP form and prepays income tax estimated at no less than two percent of the price.

Property tax bills arrive in four installments, the first on February 1 and the last on November 1, and state law lets a town allow up to 10 days of grace, so ask the collector how Manalapan applies it. Because Monmouth County runs an alternate calendar, assessment appeals are due January 15; the county board of taxation answers at 732-431-7404.

Yes. The township requires it on a sale or a rental, and the seller is responsible. The cost is $225 in all.

How long does the Manalapan certification last?

The Housing Certification is good for 90 days from issuance, and the smoke detector certificate lasts six months. If your closing slips past those dates, you will need to reapply and pay again, so time the inspection close to the closing day.

Do I need Health Department approval for a well or septic system?

Yes. The township says homes with well and septic systems must have Health Department approval before the Housing Certification is issued.

What is the Manalapan assessment appeal date?

January 15, since Monmouth County follows an alternate assessment calendar. The county board of taxation can confirm the date for your filing year.

Can a cash buyer take my Manalapan house as-is?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it in its present condition, though the Housing Certification inspection still has to be passed or its items handled in the contract.

What is the Marlboro, NJ housing market like for a seller?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey puts median home value at $701,200, median household income at $186,292 and median gross rent at $2,699. The township's estimated population was 42,254 in mid-2025.

Households average 2.89 people, 23.4 percent of residents are under 18 and 17.9 percent are 65 or older. About 24.8 percent were born abroad and 31.8 percent speak a language other than English at home. Retirement communities in town include Greenbriar North, with more than 750 homes, and Marlboro Greens, with 341 homes built from 1986 to 1988.

How is Marlboro Township laid out?

Marlboro covers 30.34 square miles of land in the Raritan Valley region, and its neighborhoods read as scattered villages rather than a single downtown. The legislature formed it on February 17, 1848, from part of Freehold Township and named it for the marl beds in its soil. Morganville (6,203 residents in 2020) and Robertsville (11,399) are the two census-designated places, and Wickatunk, Pleasant Valley, Spring Valley and Montrose are among the other names on local maps.

A few details shape how houses present:

  • The Monmouth County Agricultural Railroad once ran through town with stops at Bradevelt, Marlboro, Morganville and Wickatunk, and its right of way is now a county rail trail.
  • In 1958 the township set aside 1,500 acres off Vanderburg Road for the Marlboro Industrial Park.
  • Average rainfall is about 47 inches a year, with about 23 inches of snow and some 179 freezing days.

Neighbors include Aberdeen, Colts Neck, Freehold Township, Holmdel, Manalapan and Matawan in Monmouth County, and Old Bridge in Middlesex County.

What does Marlboro require before a house is sold?

Marlboro Township requires a Continued Certificate of Occupancy for every home sale or rental. The Zoning/Code Enforcement Division issues it, and the paperwork is available on the township website or at the zoning office. Reach the zoning officer at 732-536-0200, extension 1809, on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30.

They can, because Marlboro's history includes contaminated sites that buyers and their lenders sometimes ask about. It also describes the Burnt Fly Bog Superfund cleanup site, about 1,700 acres off Tyler Lane and Spring Valley Road on the Old Bridge border, where waste oil was stored in lagoons in the 1950s and early 1960s.

For an owner, the practical step is to know what is buried or stored on the lot. The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee at recording, and a sale at Marlboro's median value of $701,200 comes to about $6,258 on the state schedule. Deeds are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, whose record room is at the Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street in Freehold, open weekdays until 4:00 in the afternoon. The clerk's fee page lists $40 for the first page of a deed and $10 for each additional page. The seller's residency form (GIT/REP) is filed with the deed, and a signer who lives out of state may owe estimated income tax on the gain, which the form is designed to determine.

How do roads, trains and schools affect buyers in Marlboro?

Marlboro is a driving town: U.S. Route 9, Route 18, Route 79 and County Road 520 are the main thoroughfares, with Route 34 in the northeast corner. The township has 229.71 miles of road, most of it township-maintained. NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan. The nearest commuter rail stop is Aberdeen-Matawan on the North Jersey Coast Line. Workers average 41.2 minutes to get to their jobs.

Public schools through eighth grade belong to the Marlboro Township Public School District, which ran eight schools and enrolled 4,537 students in 2022 to 2023. Marlboro High School, part of the Freehold Regional High School District, had 1,816 students that year, and some Marlboro students attend Colts Neck High School instead. Private options in or near town include High Point Schools, Shalom Torah Academy and Christian Brothers Academy in Lincroft.

Marlboro owners choose among a listing agent, a do-it-yourself sale and a cash buyer who accepts the house with its flaws. All three require the Continued Certificate of Occupancy, so the real differences are speed, cost and how much repair work the owner takes on.

  • An agent listing exposes the house to the most buyers and works well for a move-in ready property, although commissions and requested repairs reduce what the owner nets.
  • A sale without an agent keeps the commission while shifting pricing, showings and negotiation to the owner.
  • A cash purchase can fit an inherited house, a vacant property, or a house with an old oil tank or unpermitted work that would complicate a mortgage-financed buyer.

Put in writing who orders the HVAC form, the chimney inspection and the well or septic certification, and who pays for any fix the inspector requires.

It depends on price and falls on the seller. At the Census median home value of $701,200 the state schedule comes to roughly $6,258, and sales above $1,000,000 also pay a graduated percent fee.

The Monmouth County Clerk records it, at the Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street, Freehold. The clerk's fee page lists $40 for the first page of a deed and $10 per added page, with the transfer fee due at recording.

Yes, check it before listing. The state environmental department lists 39 underground storage tank contamination locations in Marlboro, so a buyer's attorney is likely to ask whether a tank was removed and whether closure records exist.

What should I know before selling a house in Middletown, NJ?

Middletown Township sells like a large shore suburb with one gate every seller passes through: a Residential Certificate of Occupancy that the township says must be issued before title transfers. Start that inspection early, then fit the rest of the sale around it.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 67,135 residents, and its 2020 to 2024 survey counts 25,211 households. About 85.7 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, the median owner value is $608,300, and median household income is $141,810. Workers spend an average of 34.9 minutes getting to their jobs, which fits a township built around commuter rail, ferries and the Garden State Parkway.

How big is Middletown Township, and where do its sections sit?

Middletown is the largest municipality in Monmouth County, with 67,106 people at the 2020 census. Its 58.72 square miles include 40.95 of land, and roughly 30 percent of the total area is water along Raritan Bay and Sandy Hook Bay. The Sandy Hook peninsula belongs to the township even though it is not joined to the rest of Middletown by land.

Addresses read "Middletown," but local descriptions use section names. The township's own forms list Belford, Chapel Hill, Fairview, Harmony, Leonardo, Lincroft, Locust, Middletown Village, Monmouth Hills, Navesink, New Monmouth, North Middletown, Nut Swamp, Oak Hill, Port Monmouth and River Plaza. Lincroft is the largest of the census designated places, at 7,060 people in 2020.

The township was formed on October 31, 1693, alongside Shrewsbury and Freehold, and incorporated under the 1798 Township Act. A railroad junction in 1875 turned fishing and farming villages into a commuter suburb, and the Seabrook-Wilson House of 1663 and Marlpit Hall of 1686 still stand. Houses from different eras carry different electrical, plumbing and addition histories, so pull the permit record before the inspector arrives.

What does Middletown require before a house changes hands?

Middletown requires a Certificate of Occupancy before transfer of title, and the township's application form warns that violators may face fines or a summons. The same form covers a sale or a rental, goes to the Housing Department at 1 Kings Highway, and asks for the block, lot, number of bedrooms and the prospective transfer date. If the house is occupied, an adult must be home for the inspection, and the form says the visit time depends on the inspector's daily workload.

What does the Middletown inspector look for?

The township's checklist follows the International Property Maintenance Code and says it is not all inclusive, so other items can be noted on the day. Open permits need a final inspection, and recent construction needs approvals before a certificate can issue.

  • Address numbers at least 4 inches high, readable from the street.
  • A water heater relief valve discharge pipe ending no more than 6 inches above the floor, in copper, galvanized, black or CPVC pipe. PVC is not permitted.
  • Ground fault outlets in the garage, outdoors, on kitchen counters, in unfinished basements and in bathrooms, plus no extension cords in place of wiring.
  • Handrails where stairs have more than four risers, and guards on any open side more than 30 inches above grade.
  • A metal flex hose on the dryer, working burners on the range and no leaks or missing shingles on the roof.
  • A debris-free yard, no peeling exterior paint, a septic system that is not visibly failing, and a self-latching 48 inch barrier around any pool deeper than 24 inches.

Smoke detector and carbon monoxide compliance is now inspected by the Fire Prevention Office at 732-615-2270, and the township's Building & Inspection Department issues the certificate once every requirement is met.

How do buyers see Middletown's location?

Buyers rank Middletown by how it gets them to New York, and the township offers more than one route.

  • Rail: NJ Transit's Middletown station sits on the North Jersey Coast Line between New York Penn Station and Bay Head.
  • Ferry: NY Waterway runs from a slip in Belford, a trip of roughly 50 minutes to West Midtown, and SeaStreak sails from neighboring Highlands to Pier 11 and East 35th Street.
  • Roads: Garden State Parkway exits 109 and 114, Routes 35 and 36, and County Routes 516 and 520, across 350 miles of local, county and state roadway.
  • Bus: NJ Transit local routes 817, 833 and 834.

Health care is close at hand. Memorial Sloan Kettering has a regional center in Middletown, and Bayshore Medical Center in Holmdel and Riverview Medical Center in Red Bank serve the area.

How do schools and shoreline weather affect a Middletown listing?

The Middletown Township Public School District serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 with 16 schools and 8,895 students in 2023-24. Its three middle schools are Bayshore, Thompson and Thorne, and the two four-year high schools are Middletown High School North and South. Students can also apply to High Technology High School on the Brookdale campus in Lincroft and the Marine Academy of Science and Technology on Sandy Hook, and Christian Brothers Academy is a private option in Lincroft.

The township averages about 46.75 inches of precipitation a year, with July highs near 83 degrees and January lows near 27. A buyer's inspector will look hard at roofs, gutters and grading as a result. The township's certificate page mentions elevation certificates for new construction in mapped flood zones, so ask the township floodplain manager whether your lot sits in one.

How do Middletown property tax appeals and the transfer fee work for a seller?

Monmouth County follows an alternative assessment calendar, so an assessment appeal must be received, not just postmarked, by the County Tax Board on or before January 15. A separate petition goes in for each parcel, the owner needs three to five comparable sales, and hearings run from January through April. The county guide adds that taxes themselves cannot be appealed, only the assessment, and a change-of-assessment postcard gives 45 days to file.

The state charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. Under the state's rate table for sales over $350,000, a sale at the Census median value of $608,300 comes to about $5,273. Deeds above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee of 1 percent to 3.5 percent of the full price, and deeds between spouses, parent and child, or from an estate to an heir are among the listed exemptions.

Where does a Middletown deed get recorded?

Deeds for Middletown are recorded with the Monmouth County Clerk in Freehold. The clerk's fee list shows $40 for the first page of a deed, $10 for each additional page and $10 for a marginal notation, and it states that transfer tax must be paid when the deed is recorded. Mortgage discharges are $30 for the first page and $10 for each added page, so ask your closing agent which pieces are being filed.

The clerk also posted a notice that deeds over $1,000,000 received after July 10, 2025 may be subject to a revised transfer fee under P.L. 2025, c. 69. Anyone selling a higher priced home should confirm the amount with the Division of Taxation before closing.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a Middletown certificate of occupancy cost?

The township application lists $150 for each house sold, plus a $15 filing fee on a separate check. A reinspection at the third inspection costs $75. Fire Prevention handles the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate as part of the same process.

Who issues the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate in Middletown?

The Middletown Fire Prevention Office issues it. The township says the certificate is now a component of the Residential Certificate of Occupancy and is sent to Building & Inspection, which issues the CO once everything is met.

What is the Middletown deadline to appeal an assessment?

The deadline is January 15. Monmouth County uses an alternative calendar, and the petition must be received by the County Tax Board, not just mailed, with separate paper copies to the assessor and municipal clerk.

Can a Middletown house with open permits still sell?

It can go under contract, but the township's checklist says open permits must have a final inspection before a certificate of occupancy can issue. Ask Building & Inspection for the permit history before you list so no surprises delay the closing.

Which office records a Middletown deed?

The Monmouth County Clerk records it. The posted fee is $40 for the first page and $10 for each additional page, and the seller's Realty Transfer Fee is paid at the time of recording.

What does a seller face first in Neptune Township?

Neptune's gatekeeper is Code Enforcement. A Certificate of Inspection has to be in hand before a buyer can move in, and the township's checklist backs that rule with fines up to $2,000. The township covers 8.13 square miles of land in Monmouth County, running from the ocean at Ocean Grove to the Garden State Parkway.

This page sets out the township's numbers and neighborhoods, the inspection checklist, rental rules, tax dates and county recording, and ends with how an as-is cash sale compares with a listing.

How does Neptune compare on income, age and home values?

The July 2025 population estimate is 28,273, only 0.4% above the 2020 base. Neptune had 27,935 residents in 2010 and 28,061 in 2020, so the township has been about the same size for years.

Which Neptune neighborhoods draw different buyers?

Neptune became a township on February 26, 1879, cut from Ocean Township. It later gave up land to Neptune City and Bradley Beach, and a short-lived 1920 split of Ocean Grove was reversed in 1921.

Today buyers shop by neighborhood. Ocean Grove is a 220-acre Victorian seaside district on the National Register, bounded by Fletcher Lake, Route 71, Lake Wesley and the Atlantic, and its Camp Meeting Association dates to 1869. Shark River Hills sits along the estuary on the south border. Mid-Town is in a township-led revitalization, and West Neptune holds the Route 66 commercial strip. The Gables, Green Grove, Summerfield, Bradley Park and Seaview Island complete the list.

What roads, rail and school information do Neptune buyers weigh?

Five state routes (18, 33, 35, 66 and 71) pass through, and Garden State Parkway access comes at Exits 100 and 102. Bradley Beach station on the North Jersey Coast Line takes riders to Newark Penn, Secaucus Junction, New York Penn and Hoboken. NJ Transit buses 317, 830, 832 and 836 serve the township.

Neptune Township Schools enrolled 3,411 students in 2022-23 across seven schools: Gables, Green Grove, Midtown Community, Shark River Hills and Summerfield for PreK-5, then Neptune Middle School and Neptune High School. It is a former Abbott district, now an SDA district, where the state funds school construction.

What must a Neptune house pass to get its Certificate of Inspection?

Selling, buying or renting without the certificate risks a fine up to $2,000 and as many as 90 days in jail, according to the township checklist. The Transfer of Title application costs $65, is non-refundable, and has the buyer swear not to occupy the home until the certificate is clear, with a fine up to $1,250 otherwise.

Before an inspection is booked, every construction permit and violation must be closed and municipal charges, meaning property taxes and sewer, must be current. An estate needs the surrogate's certificate naming the executor. The application expires after 30 days, and the home must be empty on inspection day.

  • Outside: house numbers at least 3 inches tall, no flaking paint, gutters and downspouts attached, safe railings and walks, and a trash and recycling cart left behind.
  • Inside: smoke detectors on every level, carbon monoxide alarms near bedrooms where required, GFCI outlets in kitchens and baths, and a marked furnace shut-off.
  • Unused oil tanks come out or get filled, which requires a demolition permit.
  • Wood stoves and fireplaces need a certified chimney sweep's letter.

Code Enforcement works from 25 Neptune Boulevard, phone 732-988-5200, extension 260, and the township's forms page takes online applications.

How do Neptune's rental and short-term rental rules affect a sale?

Neptune separates rentals into categories. A standard rental application is for leases of a year (365 days) or longer, and a pre-1978 building needs a lead certificate or lead inspection. Short-term rentals are filed per season: winter runs October 1 to May 22 and summer runs May 23 to September 30.

Tenants complicate a sale because the unit must be vacant when the inspector visits. Match move-out dates to your closing date, and ask Code Enforcement whether the buyer needs an owner-occupancy certificate or a rental certificate once the deed is recorded.

When are Neptune taxes billed, and who handles an assessment error?

Installments are the first of February, May, August and November, each with ten days of grace. Arrears up to $1,500 carry 8% a year and larger balances carry 18%, and a penalty of up to 6% may be added to unpaid balances above $10,000 at year end. Sewer bills come separately, on March 1 and September 1.

In 2026 the township mailed its third-quarter bills on July 29 and moved that quarter's grace deadline from August 10 to August 24. A municipal charge still open on November 11 can be sold at tax sale. The Tax Collector cannot adjust an assessment, so errors go to the assessor, whose Q&A describes the 2014 revaluation that took effect in 2015 and the annual reassessments since.

Seniors and Social Security disability recipients can apply for property tax relief on the PAS-1 form, and veterans' deduction forms are on the Tax Office page. Call 732-988-5200, extension 251, for the exact payoff.

Where does Neptune's deed get recorded, and at what cost?

Recording happens at the Monmouth County Clerk's main office, Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street, Freehold, where recording runs 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. The clerk's phone is 732-431-7324.

The fee page lists $40 for a deed's first page and $10 for extra pages, and says transfer tax is due when the deed is recorded. It also flags the revised fee for sales over $1 million that took effect on July 10, 2025 under P.L. 2025, c. 69. Confirm current numbers with your closing attorney.

Is a listing or a direct cash purchase better for a Neptune house?

The inspection step makes a conventional sale slower when a house needs work. As-is buyers suit estate properties, houses with tenants and homes with unfinished permits.

  • Listing: broadest exposure, especially for Ocean Grove and Shark River Hills.
  • Owner sale: you keep the commission and do the paperwork.
  • Cash purchase: no repairs asked, a closing date that fits you, and the inspection still due before anyone moves in.

Subtract inspection costs, the tax payoff and closing costs from each offer, then pick the timeline you prefer.

Must a Neptune house have a Certificate of Inspection to be sold?

Yes. The township checklist lists fines up to $2,000 and up to 90 days in jail for buying, selling or renting without one, and the Transfer of Title application costs $65.

Can buyers move into a Neptune house before the inspection clears?

No. The Transfer of Title affidavit commits the buyer not to occupy the home until a clear certificate exists, and the form lists a fine up to $1,250 for doing so.

What dates does Neptune use for property tax installments?

The first of February, May, August and November, each followed by ten days of grace. Sewer charges fall due on March 1 and September 1.

Which items does Neptune Code Enforcement look at?

Permits and violations, current taxes and sewer, house numbers, detectors, GFCI outlets, the furnace, stairs, gutters and trash carts, among others. The township's Certificate of Inspection checklist has the full list.

Which county office records a Neptune deed?

The Monmouth County Clerk at 33 Mechanic Street in Freehold, open for recording on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.

What does selling in Ocean Township, NJ involve?

Ocean Township occupies east central Monmouth County, and no buyer may move into a house there until the Housing Division has issued a Code Compliance Inspection Certificate. The requirement follows the property, so it applies to an agent listing, a private sale and a cash purchase alike.

Federal estimates put the population at 28,088 spread across 10.87 square miles of land, up from 27,672 in the 2020 count. This page covers the Monmouth County township, which is a different place from Ocean Township in Ocean County. There is no central downtown. Homes cluster in three communities, Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside, so people usually describe a house by its neighborhood.

The township has used the council-manager form under New Jersey's Faulkner Act since July 1, 1963. A five-member council sets policy, and an appointed manager runs daily administration, so permit and inspection questions go to staff offices rather than to elected officials.

Where do Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside sit within Ocean Township?

State lawmakers formed the township on February 21, 1849 out of Shrewsbury Township, and over the following decades Long Branch, Asbury Park, Deal, Allenhurst and other shore towns were cut away. The remainder touches Eatontown and West Long Branch on the north, Long Branch, Deal, Allenhurst and Interlaken on the east, Neptune and Asbury Park on the south and Tinton Falls on the west.

ZIP code 07755 covers Oakhurst, and 07712 covers Wanamassa and Wayside. Deal Lake, 158 acres shared among seven municipalities along roughly 27 miles of shoreline, touches the township and has been under the Deal Lake Commission since 1974. A house near the water should be ready for questions about basement moisture, which is also something the inspector checks.

What are Ocean Township homes worth, and who lives in them?

A typical owned home carries a $678,300 value in the 2020 to 2024 figures, and 62.7 percent of households own their place. More than one in five residents is 65 or older, and over 90 percent stayed put last year, so many houses change hands rarely and may be due for updates.

What does the Ocean Township Housing Division inspect?

The Housing Division covers every sale and every rental that changes hands. Its forms page says sale permits must be closed before you call for the visit, post-dated checks are sent back and the office keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30. The checklist is a visual look at:

  • The outside: flaking paint, gutters and leaders, doors, windows, screens, siding, sheds, fences, trash and weeds.
  • A street number at least 3 inches tall that can be read from the road.
  • A handrail once stairs pass four risers, and a guardrail on any open porch or landing above 30 inches.
  • The inside: kitchen and bath plumbing, walls and ceilings, leaks or cellar water, outlets with covers, locks and ventilation.
  • A water heater fitted with a pressure and temperature valve and extension pipe.
  • An anti-tip bracket for stoves manufactured after 1991.

Before the visit, line up three things:

  • Close every open permit.
  • Keep gas, electric and water running on inspection day.
  • Gather a lab report if the house has its own well.

A private well needs a certified lab report that meets state environmental standards. The forms page also offers a lead paint information sheet.

Which fire district handles the smoke and carbon monoxide forms?

Those forms are separate from the Housing Division visit. Ocean Township has Fire District No. 1 and No. 2, and the township's forms page links an online smoke detector, carbon monoxide and extinguisher application for both. Ask the district covering your street which one applies.

State rules also demand a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued through the municipality, for a house with one or two units. It stays valid for six months, so schedule the fire visit so it still covers your closing date.

Which state fees and deadlines touch an Ocean Township sale?

Recording the deed triggers the seller's Realty Transfer Fee, and the Division of Taxation's schedule shows lower rates for qualifying senior, blind or disabled sellers. The buyer's extra 1 percent starts above $1,000,000, a level that most local sales will not reach with a median near $678,300.

The seller also signs a GIT/REP form that goes to the county with the deed.

Monmouth County runs a calendar of its own for assessment appeals. According to the state's Form A-1, the Monmouth County Tax Board must receive a petition by January 15, or 45 days after notices are mailed if that is later, and a petition that arrives after the close of business that day is dismissed.

How do Route 18, the shore trains and the schools affect Ocean Township buyers?

Route 18 runs through the western side and Route 35 through the east. Route 66 marks the southern edge with Neptune, and Route 71 follows the eastern boundary beside Deal, West Long Branch and Long Branch. The Garden State Parkway lies just west, in Tinton Falls. Of its roughly 132 miles of road, about 120 belong to the township. Retail gathers along the main routes, with Ocean Commons on Route 35 and Seaview Shopping Center off Route 66.

A brief piece of the North Jersey Coast Line crosses the east side, though the nearest stops are Allenhurst and Elberon. NJ Transit buses 832 and 837 serve the township, and the SeaStreak ferry terminal in Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive.

The Ocean Township School District ran five schools and enrolled 3,263 students in 2023-24: elementary schools in Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside, an intermediate school for grades 5 to 8 and the high school in Oakhurst. Expect buyers to ask which elementary school serves a given address. Joe Palaia Park, the township's largest, hosts the July 4 event and has a disc golf course, and the township also runs a membership pool and tennis club that is open from Memorial Day to Labor Day.

When should an Ocean Township owner consider a cash offer?

A cash price deserves a look when the house would struggle with the checklist and repairs are unwelcome, when it came to you through an estate, or when a firm closing date matters. Have the buyer put in writing who orders the Housing Division visit and who covers corrections.

Landlords should note that the township requires rental registration and payment before March 1. If a tenant-occupied house is being sold, agree with the tenant and buyer how the change of occupancy will be handled.

Frequently asked questions

Must an Ocean Township house be inspected before it changes hands?

Yes. The Housing Division performs the code compliance inspection on sales and on rentals with a new occupant. Open sale permits have to be closed first, and nobody may move in before the certificate exists.

What is on the Ocean Township checklist?

A visual review inside and out: paint, gutters, a 3-inch street number, handrails beyond four risers, plumbing, leaks, outlet covers, the water heater valve and extension pipe, and an anti-tip bracket on newer stoves.

What is the Monmouth County assessment appeal date?

January 15, unless notices were mailed late enough to extend it. The state form names Monmouth, Burlington and Gloucester as the counties with this earlier date, while other counties keep April 1.

How long does an Ocean Township smoke alarm certificate last?

Six months. The certificate comes through the municipality, and in Ocean Township the fire districts supply the application forms.

Does the seller pay the extra 1 percent state fee?

No, the buyer does, and only above $1,000,000. A seller pays the regular Realty Transfer Fee, which follows the price in the deed and any exemption claimed.

What should a Wall Township homeowner know before selling quickly?

Wall Township sits close to the Jersey Shore with highway and rail access, yet a quick sale still depends on the township's occupancy rules, the state's closing fees and the condition of the house. With a Census median home value above $700,000, the percentage-based charges at closing deserve a close look.

Owners choose between hiring an agent, handling the sale alone, and signing with a buyer who pays cash. The sections below cover local facts behind each choice.

Where is Wall Township and what shapes its housing market?

Wall covers 30.66 square miles of land plus 1.03 square miles of water in eastern Monmouth County. The legislature formed it as a township in 1851, and later pieces of its territory became Spring Lake, Sea Girt, Manasquan, Brielle, Belmar and other shore boroughs. What remains is a large, mostly suburban township with the census-designated places of Allenwood and West Belmar, plus neighborhoods such as Glendola, Old Mill, Allaire and Remsen Mills.

Wreck Pond, a tidal pond on the Atlantic coast, lies on the township's edge with Spring Lake, Spring Lake Heights and Sea Girt, and its watershed covers about 12 square miles. Allaire State Park and the Edgar Felix Bikeway run through the township, and the Brick Township Reservoir, shared with Brick, has a 1.7-mile trail. If your lot is near a pond or tidal stream, ask your surveyor or insurer whether it falls in a mapped flood zone, since buyers will ask.

Allaire Village began as an iron-making community in 1822 and later became part of Allaire State Park. The township grew from 7,386 residents in 1950 to 16,498 in 1970 and 25,261 in 2000. The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,753, only slightly above the 2020 count of 26,525, which points to a settled housing stock.

Ask both offices whether your sale needs a resale or transfer approval, what it costs, and what permits the property has on file. Fire inspections for the whole township come from the Fire Prevention Bureau, which also has an office at 2700 Allaire Road.

Monmouth County follows the alternative calendar, so an assessment appeal is due January 15. The county board sits at the Hall of Records in Freehold (1 East Main Street, 732-431-7404). Assessments above $1,000,000 can skip the county board. Wall's township site offers an online page for tax account lookup and payment.

The board expects evidence such as comparable sales. A leaving seller gains little from a win, while a buyer or an heir keeping the house might.

What local landmarks and history do Wall buyers notice?

Wall's character comes from its shore-adjacent geography and a few well-known sites. Allaire Village, founded as an iron works in 1822, is a living-history museum inside Allaire State Park, and the Old Wall Historical Society keeps the Allgor-Barkalow Homestead of 1840 as a museum. Camp Evans began as a Marconi wireless receiving site around 1900, and Wall Stadium, open since 1950, still hosts racing.

Wall is also a landing point for several transatlantic subsea cables, and about 68 sworn officers staff the township police department from headquarters on Allaire Road. By January 15, since Monmouth County uses the alternative assessment calendar. File with the Monmouth County Board of Taxation in Freehold, or call 732-431-7404.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 show median owner costs of $3,162 with a mortgage and $1,378 without. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $720,400, and 83.4% of homes are owner-occupied.

Which highways and train lines serve Wall?

The Garden State Parkway has an interchange here and Interstate 195 ends at Route 34. NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line stops at Belmar, Manasquan and Spring Lake.

Wall has three fire districts: West Belmar (District 1), Glendola (District 2) and South Wall (District 3). Fire inspections for sales come from the township's Fire Prevention Bureau at 2700 Allaire Road.

The Registry Department in the Morris County Clerk's Office records property documents for Mount Olive. Every land document needs a cover sheet and a cover letter with the submitter's name and address, and the document itself must say "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return".

Recording hours at the Registry run between 8 and 4 on weekdays, and the line is 973-285-6130. Your attorney or title agent usually files the deed after closing. Ask the Tax Collector for a written balance through closing so the title company can pay it from your proceeds.

When does a cash sale beat a listing in Mount Olive?

A house with working detectors, clear permits and fresh paint is a natural candidate for an agent listing in a township where families rarely move. A cash purchase wins when repairs are unfinished, an estate needs closing out, or the date matters more than the last few thousand dollars.

The Morris County Clerk's Registry Department, at 973-285-6130. It asks for a cover sheet, a cover letter and record-and-return wording on the document.

How are Budd Lake and Flanders related to Mount Olive?

Both are communities inside the township rather than separate towns. Budd Lake uses ZIP 07828 and Flanders uses 07836, with 9,784 and 9,832 people respectively in 2020.

Parsippany-Troy Hills is a township in Morris County in northern New Jersey. What does a seller need to know about Parsippany-Troy Hills as a place?

The township was settled by English farmers around 1700, drawn by flat land, fertile soil and fresh water, and it later grew into a suburb. About one third of the township is open space, and the Census Bureau counts 56,633 residents as of July 1, 2025. The township also contains Lake Hiawatha, Lake Parsippany, Mount Tabor, Intervale, Rainbow Lakes, Powder Mill and Greystone Park, and Lake Hiawatha and Mount Tabor have ZIP codes of their own. Parsippany residents could live in one of 12 ZIP codes as of 2011.

Parsippany borders Boonton, Denville, East Hanover, Hanover, Montville, Morris Plains, Morris Township, Mountain Lakes and Randolph. With 208.45 miles of road it has the most of any municipality in the county. Interstates 80, 280 (which ends here) and 287 cross the township along with U.S. Routes 46 and 202 and State Routes 10 and 53. Commuters can ride NJ Transit trains from Mount Tabor station in neighboring Denville, and a township-funded weekday bus, Parsippany Transit, runs two routes.

Corporate offices are a large part of the local economy, with Avis Budget Group, Zoetis, B&G Foods and PNY Technologies named among the employers. The Parsippany-Troy Hills School District runs 14 schools, with 7,082 students in the 2021-22 school year: ten elementary schools, Brooklawn and Central middle schools, and Parsippany High School and Parsippany Hills High School. Long before the suburbs, glacial Lake Passaic covered about half the area, and Native Americans fished along the Rockaway and Whippany Rivers. Winters are cold and summers hot, and the weather station near Boonton records an all-time low of minus 21 degrees and a high of 104.

  • $60 when the request arrives ten or more business days ahead.
  • $90 when it arrives four to nine business days ahead.

Payment by check or money order is due before the inspector arrives, and an adult has to be at the house. New owners who move in before the inspection face a $500 penalty. The township says requests made inside ten days are not always accommodated, so file when the contract is signed.

The standard follows the year the house was built or last altered. Homes built before 1977 need at least one ten-year sealed battery smoke alarm on each level, while houses built from 1984 on need hard-wired, interconnected alarms, with battery backup added to the rule from 1993. Smoke alarms need to be under ten years old and carbon monoxide alarms under seven. A house with solar panels, a generator or battery storage must carry a permanent label near the panel and meter reading "Caution: Multiple Sources of Power." Rental properties also need a separate certification from the Housing Department.

What state forms and fees apply when a Parsippany-Troy Hills house sells?

At the Morris County recording step, the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee. On sales above $350,000 the Division of Taxation's bracket rate runs from $2.90 to $6.05 per $500, depending on the slice of the price, and seniors or blind and disabled sellers can claim lower rates on Form RTF-1. A sale above $1,000,000 adds a Graduated Percent Fee.

The deed also carries a GIT/REP form signed by the seller or a representative with a power of attorney. It lets the State check whether a seller from out of state must prepay income tax. Transfers from an executor to an heir, between spouses and from parent to child avoid the transfer fee.

Flood answers are mandatory as well. The disclosure statement must say whether the house sits in a FEMA flood hazard area and what the seller knows about past flooding, before the buyer is bound. With the Rockaway and Whippany Rivers and several lakes inside the township, run your address through the DEP Flood Risk Notification Tool.

How do I appeal property taxes in Parsippany-Troy Hills?

Parsippany-Troy Hills assessments reflect market value on the prior October 1, and disputes are heard by the Morris County Board of Taxation. Any owner may file, whatever the assessment.

  • Form A-1 has to be on the board's desk by April 1, or May 1 once a revaluation has happened.
  • An assessment over a million dollars may bypass the board and go to the State Tax Court.
  • An unhappy owner has 45 days from a board judgment to go on to Tax Court.

To win, show that the figure misses market value or falls outside the common level range, set at 15 percent either side of the district's average ratio. Ask the township tax collector for your balance ahead of closing.

The $60 fee becomes $90 at four to nine business days out and $150 inside three business days. A failed or missed appointment adds $60 for reinspection.

Randolph is a 21-square-mile Morris County township with a high owner-occupancy rate, so owner-occupied houses make up most of the market. Whether you list, sell privately or accept an as-is cash purchase, the inspection and the deed recorded in Morristown apply to the house.

How did Randolph begin and which communities make up the township?

The Lenni Lenape were the first inhabitants, and Quakers followed. New Jersey's first iron mine opened here in 1713, and the area supplied the Continental Army during the winter encampment at nearby Jockey Hollow. Hartshorne Fitz-Randolph bought 1,000 acres around Mine Hill in 1753, and the township took his name. The legislature incorporated it on January 1, 1806, out of Mendham Township.

In the early 20th century it became a vacation area known for woods, ponds and lakes, with farms, large hotels and bungalow colonies through the 1950s. The township includes named communities that appear in addresses and listings:

The township sits upstream of the Black River, the South Branch of the Raritan, the Whippany River and the Rockaway River.

Recorded temperatures range from a high of 102 degrees in 1953 to a low of minus 24 in 1943. July is the warmest month and September has the heaviest average precipitation. If your lot is on a slope or beside a stream, collect any drainage or retaining wall records before listing. The standards differ by the age of the house:

  • Homes built before 1977 may use battery detectors, but changeable-battery units are no longer accepted, so choose sealed 10-year batteries.
  • Homes built in 1977 or later, or with a substantial addition, must keep their hard-wired detectors working and interconnected, and may not replace them with battery types.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm goes outside the bedrooms on each level that has them.
  • A central station alarm system must work fully, including battery backup, with sounders loud enough to reach each bedroom at 70 decibels with the door closed.

What is the secondary power label and what else might Randolph ask for?

A house with generators, solar panels or battery storage must carry a label within 18 inches of the main electrical panel and meter. It reads similar to "CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER" and cannot be handwritten. A label that meets ANSI Z535.4 satisfies the rule. Put one up before the inspector arrives.

The township fee schedule also lists a letter stating that a certificate of occupancy is not required for a change of title. Ask the Building Department whether your sale qualifies for that letter and what it costs now.

What state fee brackets and recording steps apply to a Randolph sale?

The seller pays the state realty transfer fee. For consideration above $350,000, the Division of Taxation lists $5.30 per $500 for the portion from $550,000 to $850,000, which covers the area around Randolph's $670,700 median value.

Deeds go to the Morris County Clerk's Registry department, which is open from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm. Every land document needs a cover sheet and a cover letter with the submitter's name and address. Each document must also carry "Record and Return" or "Cancel and Return" instructions, and a return envelope should be large enough for the deed. The Registry's phone is 973-285-6130.

Which sale route fits a Randolph owner?

A listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you have a few months. Plan for a clean inspection report and a closing date that allows for the Monday morning slot.

An as-is cash sale shifts repair risk to the buyer. You still need the inspection certificate, so compare which party orders it and who pays a failed visit's reinspection. If tenants live in the house, remember that the same certificate applies to rentals and changes of occupancy.
