Does Randolph require an inspection when I sell my house?

Yes. A smoke detector, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source certificate is needed for the sale of a one- or two-family dwelling. The Randolph Fire Prevention Bureau performs it.

How much does the Randolph fire inspection cost?

The first inspection is $100 and each reinspection is $100. An inspection requested on another day costs $150. Appointments run Monday mornings from 9:30 to 11:30 and fill up quickly.

Can I use battery smoke detectors in my Randolph house?

Only in some cases. Homes built before 1977 may use battery units, and they must have sealed 10-year batteries. Homes built in 1977 or later, or with a substantial addition, must keep hard-wired interconnected detectors working.

Where is a Randolph deed recorded?

The Morris County Clerk's Registry department records it, with a cover sheet attached to the document. Registry recording hours are 8:00 am to 4:00 pm.

What transfer fee applies to a Randolph sale near the median home value?

The seller pays the state realty transfer fee. A $670,700 sale falls between $550,000 and $850,000, where the Division of Taxation schedule lists $5.30 per $500 for that portion of the price.

What must a Rockaway homeowner finish before closing?

Rockaway Borough's sheet on selling a home lists three items due before closing: a Certificate of Compliance for Fire Prevention, a final water reading, and property taxes paid in full. Each has its own office and its own fee, so start all three as soon as you have a contract.

This page covers Rockaway Borough in Morris County, a 2.07 square mile municipality of 6,598 residents at the 2020 census. The Census Bureau estimates 6,631 for July 2025, up 0.8 percent from its 2020 base. Rockaway Township borders the borough and is a separate municipality with its own offices, so confirm which one holds your address before you call anyone.

The borough has a mayor and six council members, with council seats staggered so that two are elected each year. Zoning questions go to the borough zoning officer by email at Zoning@rockawayborough.org, and the zoning office takes appointments through 973-627-2000, extension 229.

How does the Rockaway fire prevention certificate work?

The Bureau of Fire Prevention issues the certificate, and you schedule by calling 973-625-3473 (973-625-FIRE) and leaving your name, address and phone number. Staff answer on weekdays, with a 4:30 p.m. close. The borough's sheet is dated October 1, 2022, and it sets the fee by how early you ask.

  • 10 or more business days before closing: $55 for the first inspection.
  • 4 to 10 business days before closing: $90.

The sheet asks for a working smoke detector on each level including the basement, a carbon monoxide detector on each level that has bedrooms, no open building permits, and a house number at least 4 inches tall. It also lists a portable extinguisher, but state law removed that item from resale inspections in February 2025, so ask the bureau what it checks now. A house with a monitored fire alarm needs a test report dated within 12 months and someone present who can reset the panel.

What are the final water reading and trash rules for a Rockaway sale?

Call the Water Clerk at 973-627-2000, extension 223, for the final reading. The fee in the borough sheet is $60 with 72 hours or more of notice and $95 with less.

For clean-out, a single-family house may set out three 32-gallon cans plus three bulk items each week. Condominiums and townhouses arrange their own collection of large items. For anything beyond that, hire a hauler, because a vacant inherited house can hold more than curbside service will take.

The Construction Office, reached at 973-627-8035 on weekdays, handles the open permit check. Rockaway's property maintenance article requires a certificate of continued occupancy to sell or lease, but that article says it applies to nonresidential and mixed-occupancy buildings and not to residential structures, so a house is not swept into it.

Where did Rockaway come from?

Rockaway became a borough on June 19, 1894, carved from Rockaway Township after a referendum held the day before, and took in more township land in 1908. The name matches the Rockaway River and has been said to mean place of sands, creek between two hills, or bushy.

The First Presbyterian Church of Rockaway was founded in 1758, its cemetery holds many Revolutionary War veterans, and the current brick church dates to 1832. The borough's population reached 6,852 in 1980, dipped to 6,243 in 1990, and has hovered near 6,500 since 2000, which fits the low turnover in the table above.. Main Street and the Mill Lane Tavern appear in the 2003 film The Station Agent, which was shot in the borough.

The climate is a hot-summer humid continental type, so a house here faces hot humid summers and moderately cold winters.

Which roads, buses and schools serve Rockaway?

The borough has 25.88 miles of roads, 20.16 of them municipal. Interstate 80 clips the northeast corner, reached from Exit 37 on County Route 513, and U.S. Route 46 crosses the south end. NJ Transit trains do not stop in Rockaway, but the Denville and Dover stations are close, on the Morris and Essex and Montclair-Boonton lines. NJ Transit local bus 880 serves the borough, and Lakeland Bus Lines runs Route 46 and Route 80 service along Main Street to Port Authority.

  • Rockaway Borough Public Schools teach prekindergarten through grade 8: Lincoln Elementary (PreK-3) and Thomas Jefferson Middle School (4-8), with 574 students in 2024 to 2025.
  • High school students go to Morris Hills High School, which sits in the borough and belongs to the Morris Hills Regional High School District.

How do Morris County tax appeals and estate sales work for a Rockaway house?

The Morris County Board of Taxation, at P.O. Box 900, Morristown, holds appeal hearings in person only. Its guidance says an assessment is excessive only if it fails one of two standards: full market value as of the prior October 1 in a revaluation year, or the municipality's common level range in other years. Ask the board for the Rockaway filing date for the tax year you care about.

If you inherited the house, an executor signs the deed and the New Jersey GIT/REP form. A New Jersey estate uses the GIT/REP-3, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. The Bureau of Fire Prevention. Call 973-625-3473 to schedule, and expect fees from $55 to $200 depending on how close to closing you book, according to the borough's October 2022 sheet.

Does Rockaway require a certificate of continued occupancy for a house sale?

The borough's property maintenance article requires one for nonresidential and mixed buildings and says it does not apply to residential structures. Ask the Construction Office at 973-627-8035 whether anything else applies to your address.

How do I get a final water reading in Rockaway?

Contact the Water Clerk at 973-627-2000, extension 223. The borough sheet lists $60 with at least 72 hours of notice and $95 on shorter notice.

Is Rockaway Borough the same as Rockaway Township?

No. They are separate Morris County municipalities with separate offices, and the borough was split off from the township in 1894. Check your tax bill to see which one you are in.

What does the state transfer fee cost on a typical Rockaway sale?

About $3,677 at the borough's $448,100 median home value. The seller owes it at recording, and the amount rises with the price.

What is it like to sell a house in Barnegat Township?

Barnegat Township in Ocean County is a fast-growing, mostly owner-occupied community where sellers deal with a township resale letter, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate and, in many cases, environmental approvals tied to the location of the lot. It covers about 34 square miles of land between the Garden State Parkway corridor and Barnegat Bay.

Because nearly nine in ten homes are owner-occupied, most sales here are between households rather than investors. The sections below cover the local numbers, the township paperwork and the county steps that follow a signed contract.

How has Barnegat grown, and what do the housing numbers show?

The township reached 24,296 residents in the 2020 census, up from 20,936 in 2010, and the Census Bureau estimates 26,151 by mid-2025. That is a 7.6% rise over the estimate base for April 2020. The 2020 count was the highest in the township's history.

Where is Barnegat, and what shapes its history and layout?

Barnegat is a township in Ocean County, incorporated in 1846 as Union Township from parts of Dover and Stafford, and renamed Barnegat Township effective January 1, 1977. The name traces to Dutch explorers who mapped Barnegat Inlet in 1614, and the early spelling is usually translated as "inlet of the breakers."

The township includes the Barnegat census-designated place, part of Ocean Acres, which it shares with Stafford Township, and smaller localities such as Cedar Bridge, Howardsville, Lower Dock and Upper Dock. Barnegat borders Lacey, Little Egg Harbor, Long Beach, Ocean and Stafford townships in Ocean County, plus Bass River and Woodland townships in Burlington County. The Battle of Cedar Bridge, a skirmish near the Cedar Bridge Tavern in 1782, is one of the township's best-known historical events.

Public school students attend the Barnegat Township School District, which Wikipedia lists with six schools and 3,583 students in 2021-22. Include the district name and your bus or school-zone details in your listing, since buyers with children ask first.

The township's construction office also handles permit history, which matters if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shed. Unpermitted work can slow a sale, so ask the office whether your permits were closed. The township routes calls by extension on the same main line: construction permits at 135, 150 and 153, the planning and zoning board at 155, and the fire, electrical and plumbing subcodes at 157, 158 and 115. Having the right extension saves a round of transfers when a buyer's inspector asks for sign-offs.

  • Vacant properties must be registered with the township, and the forms page carries both registration and de-registration forms.

The same page lists county health department approval for septic systems, wells and food handling, and county soil conservation district review for soil disturbance of 5,000 square feet or more. If your house is on septic, ask a buyer's inspector which records they will want. If part of your lot lies west of the Parkway, tell your agent early so buyers understand what Pinelands rules may mean for later projects.

What if I rent the house or my buyer is a senior?

Rental properties in Barnegat need a certificate of occupancy before every new tenant and must be registered with the municipal clerk. Units rented for fewer than 30 days need a yearly certificate, and failure to file can bring a summons to the owner.

On the state side, New Jersey publishes a reduced realty transfer fee schedule for senior citizens, blind or disabled persons, and for low and moderate income housing. The standard sale above $350,000 starts at $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, while the reduced schedule starts at $1.40. Ask your closing agent whether the transaction qualifies. The township's forms page also lists affordable housing applications for purchase and rental, which matters if your house sits in a program.

Where is the deed recorded and who pays the transfer fees?

Deeds for Barnegat sales are recorded with the Ocean County Clerk, whose office handles land records and property search for the county. The seller pays the state realty transfer fee when the deed goes on record, and a seller who lives out of state also files a GIT/REP form and prepays at least 2% of the deed consideration.

Is Barnegat mostly owner-occupied?

Yes. The Census Bureau reports an 88.0% owner-occupied rate for 2020-2024, with a median home value of $399,000, so most sales are between homeowners.

Do Pinelands rules apply to every Barnegat property?

No. The township lists Pinelands approval for land west of the Garden State Parkway only. Lots east of the Parkway may still need state environmental approval if they are on the water or near wetlands.

Which roads serve Barnegat Township?

The Garden State Parkway crosses the middle of the township, and U.S. Route 9 runs through the east. Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the west, and County Route 554 crosses west to east.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Barnegat sale?

The seller does. The state sets the fee by sale price in steps per $500, the county clerk collects it with the deed, and seniors may qualify for a reduced schedule.

What are the realistic ways to close a sale in Berkeley Township?

Owners here generally pick among a broker listing, a do-it-yourself sale and an as-is cash purchase. Whatever you pick, the township wants a Certificate of Occupancy for the resale, and a house inside an age-restricted community also needs an approval letter from its homeowners association.

Berkeley's population skews old: people 65 and over are 42.6 percent of the total. That makes many sales a downsizing move, a transfer to assisted living or heirs clearing out a parent's place. A listing rewards a tidy house and a seller who can sit through showings and a buyer's loan approval. A cash buyer is the more practical match for an estate, a place that needs work or an owner who has already relocated.

  • Broker listing: most buyers see it, you pay a commission and negotiate repairs.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you arrange the inspection, the certificate and the attorney.
  • Cash purchase: condition is the buyer's problem, and the price reflects the repair bill.

What is the land like in Berkeley Township?

Berkeley covers 54.25 square miles, and 11.53 of those are water, about 21 percent of the total. The township stretches from the Atlantic shore and Barnegat Bay west into the Pine Barrens. About 72 percent of its land lies inside the Pinelands National Reserve, and the barrier island section holds Island Beach State Park and South Seaside Park.

The township was incorporated on March 31, 1875, out of Dover Township, which is now Toms River Township. It surrounds the borough of Ocean Gate and touches Toms River, Lacey, Manchester, Beachwood, Pine Beach, Island Heights and the Seaside communities. The Pinewald area began as a 1920s resort plan that sold about 8,000 lots in 1928 and 1929, and the Holiday City, Holiday Heights and Silver Ridge developments added the age-restricted housing that shapes much of the township.

That geography matters for a sale. Bay and river frontage, flood maps and Pinelands rules can shape what a buyer's lender, insurer or surveyor asks for. If your lot touches the water or the preserved woodland, gather survey and flood paperwork before you list.

Who lives in Berkeley Township, and what do homes cost?

Berkeley counted 45,550 residents as of July 2025, a 4.1 percent gain on the 2020 base. The typical household has only 2.01 people, a pattern that fits a retirement community. Nearly nine in ten homes (88.9 percent) are owner-occupied, and homes in that group have a median value of $310,000 in the latest five-year survey.

On money: a household brings in $66,008 at the median, per person the figure is $48,539, and renters pay $1,683 at the median. Owners with a mortgage spend $1,925 a month at the median, and those without one spend $661. The average commute takes 33.9 minutes.

Which township approvals does a Berkeley Township resale need?

According to the Township's Rental and Resale Inspections page, a Certificate of Occupancy is needed every time a Berkeley home is sold or rented. For a transfer, rental or resale in an age-restricted community, the page adds that an original approval letter from the homeowners association must accompany the application, bearing a live signature and not a duplicate.

Inspectors apply the township's written rules for battery-powered smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Separately, state rules call for a compliance certificate before a one- or two-unit house is sold, available only from the municipality. Town Hall sits at 627 Pinewald-Keswick Road in Bayville; call 732-244-7400 for the current forms.

  • File the resale application the week a contract is signed.
  • Find out from the association how long its letter takes to issue.
  • Confirm that decks, additions and finished basements each have a final inspection on file.
  • Test every alarm against the township's written requirements before the inspector arrives.

How does Berkeley Township collect property tax?

Bills go out once a year, normally in July. Two quarters are billed as estimates, and the other two are adjusted so the year adds up to the real tax. The Ocean County Board of Taxation sets the rate once the township, the school districts and the county file certified budgets.

Berkeley Township installment and penalty rules, as published by its Tax Collector
RuleWhat the Tax Collector's page says
InstallmentsQuarterly, beginning each February 1 and continuing through November 1
GraceA 10-day window after every installment date
Interest8 percent applies to the first $1,500 of a late payment, and 18 percent to the remainder
Added penalty6 percent once a delinquency passes $10,000

How to payOnline, by ACH debit, at the Town Hall counter or in the lock box outside the building

In a mid-year sale the closing statement divides that quarter's tax by days of ownership. Before closing, have the Tax Collector's office confirm what is owed so no installment remains open under your name.

What is happening with South Seaside Park?

Residents of this barrier island neighborhood petitioned in 2014 to leave Berkeley Township for the borough of Seaside Park, pointing out that they live 16 miles from the township's municipal offices. The New Jersey Supreme Court sided with them in 2025.

Following guidance from the Attorney General's Office, the Tax Collector says taxes on South Seaside Park properties remain payable to Berkeley Township through the end of 2026, and that any change in collection starts January 1, 2027. An owner there should confirm with both municipalities which office issues the resale approval and the tax bill for the year of the closing.

How do roads and schools affect a Berkeley Township sale?

Garden State Parkway exits 77 and 80 serve the township. Route 9 crosses the east-central area, Route 35 clips it and ends at the Island Beach State Park road, and a short stretch of Route 37 touches the township. Of about 266 miles of roadway, the township maintains 220.88. NJ Transit bus 559 links to Atlantic City, and Ocean Ride operates routes OC1, OC2, OC7 and OC8.

Four schools in the Berkeley Township School District teach pre-kindergarten through sixth grade to 2,385 students (2024 to 2025). Seventh through twelfth graders go to Central Regional Middle School and Central Regional High School. Just 11.6 percent of residents are under 18, so age-restriction rules and single-level layouts tend to drive buyer questions more than school ratings.

Is a cash buyer worth considering in Berkeley Township?

A cash buyer is worth a call when certainty matters more than the top price: deferred maintenance, an association whose approval drags, or an estate with several heirs. The buyer may still have to secure the township certificate and the association letter, so decide in writing who files and who pays.

Judge any offer against a realistic listing net. Subtract commission, repair credits and the months of tax, association dues and utilities you would carry while waiting. A New Jersey attorney should read the contract and the deed language before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Is a resale inspection mandatory in Berkeley Township?

Yes. Every sale needs a township Certificate of Occupancy, and landlords need one each time a tenant changes. Have working alarms for smoke and carbon monoxide in place before the inspector visits.

What does an age-restricted community add to a Berkeley sale?

An original letter of approval from the homeowners association. The township does not take copies, and the letter must carry an original signature, so request it once a buyer is lined up.

What are the Berkeley Township tax installment dates?

Quarterly: February 1, then May 1, August 1 and finally November 1, each followed by 10 grace days. Late interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent beyond it, with a 6 percent penalty once a delinquency tops $10,000.

Where do South Seaside Park owners send their property tax?

To Berkeley Township through the end of 2026. The township states that any change in collection takes effect January 1, 2027, so confirm the arrangement with the Tax Collector before a closing.

Can a senior seller pay less in New Jersey realty transfer fee?

Possibly. Senior citizens, blind persons and disabled persons can claim a partial exemption, which is personal and not available to a trust or an estate. The Division of Taxation's example shows a $475 fee on a $280,000 sale by a qualifying senior, and your attorney files the seller affidavit.

What are the quickest ways to sell in Brick Township?

A seller in Brick has three realistic paths: hire an agent, handle the sale alone, or sign with a cash buyer who purchases the property untouched. Cash moves fastest and generally pays least. Listing adds commission and fix-up costs and takes longer. The right choice turns on the roof, the flood history, your deadline, and what the house would net after each route.

Ocean County's Brick Township was estimated at 77,402 people in mid-2025, up 5.1% from the 2020 base, per the Census Bureau. That growth, in a place that lost population between 2000 and 2020, means buyers are active, but the housing stock is mostly decades old. Many sellers meet the same questions: flood zones, inspection paperwork, and quarterly tax bills.

What kind of housing market is Brick Township?

Brick is a mature shore suburb where owners dominate. The 2020-2024 survey counts 30,289 households, 82.2% of them owning, with a $410,600 median home value and $106,130 median income. Rent runs $1,756 a month at the median, so a rental is a realistic fallback for some owners but not a cheap one to maintain under the township's inspection rules.

The township covers 25.59 square miles of land plus a lot of water. The mainland sits along the Metedeconk River and Barnegat Bay, and a separate set of ocean beaches (Brick Ocean Beaches I, II and III) lies on the barrier peninsula. Because the two parts do not touch, a street address can mean very different insurance and elevation questions. Older neighborhoods such as Laurelton, Lake Riviera and Baywood grew after the Garden State Parkway opened in 1954 and a building boom ran through the 1980s.

  • Many homes date from the 1950s through the 1980s, so roofs, septic or sewer connections, and electrical panels are common negotiation points.
  • Waterfront and bayfront lots near Cherry Quay, Havens Cove and Shore Acres carry their own flood and elevation questions.
  • Herbertsville and Parkway Pines sit near Parkway exit 91, away from the rest of the township, and attract commuters.

How does flood risk change a Brick home sale?

Flood history is the single biggest local variable. Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 devastated parts of Brick, and barrier island and waterfront properties took the worst of it; some buildings had to be torn down. A February 2026 blizzard also dropped roughly two feet of snow and knocked out power in several areas, which is a reminder that roofs and heating systems matter even away from the water.

The township's floodplain information page says it provides flood zone data to realtors, lenders, insurers and owners, including base flood elevation, whether a lot is in a coastal barrier area, and whether flood insurance is mandatory. Elevation certificates on file can be searched through the township's mapping tool, or requested from the engineering office by address or block and lot. Pull the certificate before you list, because a buyer's lender will ask for it.

Brick takes part in the federal Community Rating System, which can lower flood premiums. Its floodplain plan lists 140 mitigation initiatives, 81 of them completed by the latest annual report. A seller who can show an elevation certificate, a recent flood policy, and any raised-utility work usually faces fewer price cuts.

Which schools and roads do Brick buyers ask about?

Brick Public Schools serves pre-kindergarten through grade 12 inside the township. The district ran 12 schools and about 8,414 students in 2020-21, with elementary schools such as Drum Point, Lanes Mill, Midstreams, Osbornville, Veterans Memorial and Emma Havens Young, two middle schools (Lake Riviera and Veterans Memorial), and two high schools: Brick Memorial and Brick Township High School. Buyers often check which elementary zone a street falls in, so mention it in the listing.

The Garden State Parkway crosses the western side with exits 89, 90 and 91. Routes 70, 88 and 35 and county routes 528 and 549 handle local traffic. The old Laurelton Circle at Routes 70 and 88 once carried about 95,000 vehicles a day before it became a signal-controlled intersection in 1986. NJ Transit runs the 137 bus to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan and the 67 to Newark, and a Park and Ride at exit 91 serves express commuters. Average commute time for workers is 28.2 minutes.

What township paperwork applies when a Brick house is sold or rented?

Brick's Division of Inspections, which is the Building Department, issues construction permits and handles requests for certificates under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code. Open or unclosed permits are the usual cause of delay at closing, so have the division confirm the status of past work before you sign. The building office answers permit and certificate questions by voicemail and email, listed in the table below.

Brick also treats rental homes strictly. Owners must register the landlord with the clerk, apply for a Rental Certificate of Occupancy, and file a mercantile license with proof of at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Code Enforcement then inspects every rental each year, at $100 per inspection and $50 per failed re-inspection. The annual checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ground-fault outlets near water, a mounted fire extinguisher, and lead-safe status for structures built before 1978. Since September 27, 2022, creditors must also register foreclosed or vacant residential and commercial properties with the township within 10 days of filing a foreclosure action.

How are Brick property taxes billed, and what happens at closing?

Brick's tax year follows the calendar, with installments falling on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace window after each. Each bill covers a calendar quarter (the February bill pays for January through March), which matters at closing because the seller owes tax only through the closing date. A missing bill is no defense against interest, the tax collector warns, so make sure the closing agent has the current quarter's figure.

Work done on the house can add a second layer. After construction is finished, the township places an assessment on the improvement and mails an Added Assessment Bill in October, due November 1 and again on February 1 and May 1 of the following year. A seller who finished a deck or addition should ask the assessor whether that bill is still coming.

  • Assessment notices go out each year, usually by February 1, and an owner who thinks the value is wrong may appeal on or before April 1 to the Ocean County Board of Taxation.
  • Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • The assessor processes veteran and senior or disabled deductions, each currently $250.

What does New Jersey charge a seller on a house sale?

The state's Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost, collected as the deed goes on record. On a standard sale of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 on the next $50,000, and $3.90 on the remainder. Above $350,000 the schedule starts at $2.90 and climbs to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. At Brick's median value of roughly $410,600, most sales land in that second schedule. For the exact figure on your price, use the Division of Taxation rate tables.

Closing costs also include deed recording, any payoff of liens, and whatever the buyer negotiates for repairs. A cash buyer typically absorbs repairs, so the realistic comparison is your net after repairs, carrying costs through the winter, and agent fees against a single offer with a closing date you choose.

Is a cash sale the right call for a Brick homeowner?

A cash sale fits best when the home has defects an inspector would flag, when flood or storm damage is unrepaired, when the owner has inherited a house in another town, or when quarterly tax bills and a mortgage are piling up. It also helps landlords who do not want to carry the annual rental inspection cycle. It makes less sense for a move-in-ready home on a good street where a listing will draw several offers.

Whatever the buyer, get the offer on paper, set it beside the proceeds of a listing after commission, and confirm who pays for the certificate and recording steps. If you are close to a foreclosure filing, speak to a housing counselor or attorney in addition to any buyer, because the township's vacant property registration and the lender's timeline both affect your options.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Brick house if it was damaged in a storm?

Yes. Houses with storm damage change hands regularly, mostly to investors and cash buyers who subtract the repair bill. Collect your elevation certificate, flood claim paperwork and permit history first. The engineering office can look up certificates by address or by block and lot.

Which Brick office handles permits and certificates?

Start with the Division of Inspections voicemail line, 732-262-4604, or the permit status email on the township's building page. Rental certificate matters belong to Code Enforcement, 732-262-1033, weekdays.

What is the cutoff for contesting a Brick assessment?

April 1 each year, filed with the Ocean County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

Does a landlord need a certificate before selling a rented house in Brick?

A landlord needs the Rental Certificate of Occupancy to keep tenants in place, and the township inspects each rental every year. Ask the Division of Inspections what is required for your property when the sale closes and whether tenants move out first.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Brick sale?

The seller pays it. Recording the deed triggers the charge, which follows the price written in the deed and the Division of Taxation's published rates. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee.

A listing may fetch more, though the mortgage, tax and utility bills keep running while it sits.

Jackson is a big residential township in Ocean County. Census Bureau estimates for July 1, 2025 show 61,281 residents, 4.6% above the 2020 estimates base of 58,603. The hold-ups in a Jackson sale tend to be local: a fire-code certificate, permits still open on the file, and tax balances.

What is Jackson Township like for sellers?

Jackson covers 99.17 square miles of land, more than any other municipality in Ocean County, which keeps density near 590 people per square mile. Streets run long between pockets of homes and wooded tracts. Interstate 195 carries most traffic through town, and Jackson lands about halfway between Manhattan and Philadelphia.

The legislature incorporated the township on March 6, 1844, and it joined newly formed Ocean County on February 15, 1850. The big housing wave came late. Builders averaged about 100 new homes a year in the late 1950s, roughly 750 a year in the 1960s, and over 1,000 a year through the 1970s and 1980s. A house built in that stretch will draw a buyer's inspector to the roof, heating system, septic or sewer link and electrical panel. Weather adds wear: the township averages about 45 inches of rain and 23 inches of snow a year, with July highs near 86 degrees and January lows near 23.

  • Six Flags Great Adventure, Hurricane Harbor and Wild Safari fill the north side, and Adventure Crossing, a mixed-use entertainment complex, opened in 2023.
  • Jackson Premium Outlets opened in 1997 off Interstate 195, with more than 70 stores.
  • Colliers Mills Wildlife Management Area, about 12,900 acres shared with Plumsted Township, borders some neighborhoods with public forest.

What do Jackson buyers ask about schools and commutes?

Check the district's current attendance map before you promise a buyer a particular school.

Commuters care about access. Jackson is the one Ocean County municipality with an interstate, and I-195 links directly to the Parkway, the Turnpike and I-295. Which Jackson ordinances reach a seller?

Signs, inspections and rentals are where Jackson's own code touches a sale. A lawn sign needs a $25 zoning permit: one per lot, at most six square feet and four feet high, 15 feet back from the curb, and removed within three days of closing or when the listing agreement ends. Up to five open house directional signs are allowed without their own permit. A sign violation costs $500 to $1,000.

  • Inspections: since September 16, 2024, requests go through the township's SDL online portal, and inspections run from 7 AM to 3 PM.
  • Rentals: owners register each rental ($125) and apply for a rental continued certificate of occupancy ($100); code officers inspect before the tenant arrives.

Clear any open building permits before listing. The township makes sign permits wait until open ones are closed, and the buyer's title search will flag them regardless.

Does the Pinelands limit what a Jackson buyer can build?

It can, because part of Jackson lies inside the Pinelands National Reserve, where state Pinelands rules layer on top of township zoning. The Forest Area averages one home per 28 acres, and Regional Growth Areas allow two to six homes per acre where sewers exist.

Which category a lot falls into decides whether a buyer can add a second dwelling or split the parcel. Ask the Pinelands Commission for the lot's classification and mention it when you market the house or talk to a cash buyer. Late land-use surprises often reopen price talks.

How do Jackson's tax bills and deed recording work at closing?

Jackson bills by calendar year, in installments that come due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Interest backdates to the due date once the 10th day has passed. The annual bill is mailed in late June or early July, and the township will not accept a postmark in place of receipt. Keep your latest bill on hand, since the closing agent must know the next installment due.

State law puts the realty transfer fee on the seller, collected as the deed is filed. Working the state's band schedule at Jackson's median value of $485,700 gives a fee near $4,000. File the deed at the Ocean County Clerk, 118 Washington Street in Toms River (Monday to Friday, in-person service until 4 PM). A balance from an earlier year can be sold at a tax lien sale, which is one more reason to pay it off first.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can Jackson owners close?

Listings run longer because buyers need tours, a loan and an appraisal. Order the alarm certificate and look for open permits first, since those stall more closings than price does.

Does a Jackson house need a certificate before it sells?

A one- or two-family house needs the state smoke alarm compliance certificate, which the township issues and which lasts six months. A rental has its own rental continued certificate of occupancy, required before a tenant takes the unit. The construction office can tell you which forms fit your house.

Do I need a permit for a For Sale sign in Jackson?

Yes, a $25 permit from the zoning office. The sign can be six square feet and four feet tall at most, and must sit 15 feet from the curb. Open house signs follow a separate rule and need no permit.

Who covers the state transfer fee on a Jackson sale?

The seller does. The fee climbs with price in bands, and a sale over $1 million adds a graduated percent fee. The closing agent works out the exact amount from the deed.

What if my Jackson house sits vacant or has back taxes?

A vacant house has to be registered with the township each year, $500 at first and $1,000 on renewals. Back taxes can be sold off as a lien, and the payoff comes from your proceeds. Ask the township tax collector for a current balance before setting a date.

How do you sell a house in Lacey Township without a long wait?

The quickest sale in Lacey is a direct cash purchase, since it removes the buyer's loan, the appraisal and most repair negotiations. Listing with an agent usually earns a higher price and takes more weeks. Selling on your own sits between the two, and you handle the paperwork, the showings and the negotiation yourself.

Lacey is a shore-side township in Ocean County with 30,297 residents on the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate, up 5.7% from the 2020 base of 28,661. Owners occupy 88.1% of housing units, and 23.1% of residents are 65 or over. Population jumped from 1,940 in 1960 to 22,141 in 1990, so much of the housing dates from that rush.

What makes Lacey Township different from other Ocean County towns?

Lacey is split by the Garden State Parkway, and the split decides what a house is worth and what can be built next to it. East of the Parkway sit more than 95% of the township's homes, mostly in Lanoka Harbor and the Forked River area. West of it, roughly two-thirds of the township's area is mostly pine and cedar forest governed by the Pinelands Commission under the 1979 Pinelands Act.

The township covers 83.25 square miles of land and another 16.55 of water, with about 344 people per square mile, so the shoreline and the creeks matter. The Forked River area alone had 5,274 residents in 2020, and some in Ocean County use that name for the whole township. Population grew from 4,616 in 1970 to 14,161 in 1980 and 22,141 in 1990, a pace that tells you how much of the stock went up in those two decades.

  • Forked River, Lanoka Harbor and Cedar Creek are among the named communities east of the Parkway.
  • Bamber Lakes and a handful of farms sit west of it, in the Pinelands.
  • Popcorn Park Zoo, a 7-acre animal refuge, and the Old Schoolhouse Museum, a former mid-19th-century schoolhouse, are local landmarks.
  • Big-box shopping arrived in the 2000s, including a Home Depot in October 2007 and a 142,000-square-foot Walmart in October 2009, so residents no longer drive to Manahawkin or Toms River for most errands.

How did Oyster Creek's closing change the local market?

The Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station, which came online on December 1, 1969, closed in September 2018. It had employed about 700 people in 2010 and had contributed roughly a third of the township's budget through taxes. The decommissioning that followed was expected to take about eight years and cost an estimated $1.4 billion.

For a seller, the effect shows up indirectly, through the municipal tax rate rather than anything in your house. Keep your most recent tax bill available when you price, because buyers will want to see what a year of ownership costs.

How do Lacey's schools, roads and transit affect buyers?

The elementary schools are Mill Pond, Cedar Creek, Forked River and Lanoka Harbor, followed by Lacey Township Middle School and Lacey Township High School. Grade ranges have shifted over time, so check them with the district. St. Mary Academy, a Catholic K to 8 school in Manahawkin, also serves the area.

The Parkway runs through town, with Interchange 74 serving Forked River and Waretown and a service area at milepost 76. U.S. Route 9 runs on the east side. There is no rail service, and the nearest train station is in Bay Head. The Census Bureau puts the average trip to work at 31.8 minutes, and the old Central Railroad roadbed along Route 9 is now the Barnegat Branch Trail.

What does a Lacey seller need from the township?

Start with the building department at 124 South Main Street in Forked River, which handles inspections and certificates. It requires inspection requests in writing at least 24 hours ahead, by form, email, hand delivery or the township's online portal. The office is open 8:30 to 4:30 and closes for lunch from 12:30 to 1:30, though a drop box stays out front.

  • Smoke alarm certificate: state fire code requires one before a one- or two-family house is sold, and the municipality issues it. It stays valid for six months.
  • Open permits: finish and close any construction permit before a buyer's attorney asks about it.
  • Pinelands lots: if the property is west of the Parkway, tell buyers early, since the Pinelands Commission limits building and land use there.

The same smoke alarm rule applies if you lease the house instead of selling it.

How are Lacey property taxes billed, and what happens at closing?

Lacey bills property tax once a year and collects it in four installments on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with a 10-day grace period. The township collects for Ocean County and the Lacey Township Board of Education as well as itself, so the bill covers all three. A new bill is mailed when ownership changes, and a buyer should confirm the amount due with the tax collector at 818 West Lacey Road in Forked River.

New Jersey's realty transfer fee falls on the seller and is collected at filing. At Lacey's median value of $409,400 the state's bands add up to about $3,300. The county's Manahawkin office, 179 South Main Street, Room 106, phone (609) 597-1500, accepts deeds and stays open until 8 PM Tuesday through Thursday.

  • Credit cards are taken online or at the office for current-year taxes until November 10, with a 2.95% fee charged by the card company; an e-check costs a flat $1.95.
  • After November 28, payment must be cash, certified check or money order.
  • Any open tax, water or sewer balance on November 11 is subject to the tax sale list.

Does the Pinelands hurt a Lacey sale?

Mostly no, because more than 95% of Lacey's homes sit east of the Garden State Parkway. West of the Parkway the Pinelands Commission limits building, so buyers of those parcels need to ask what uses are permitted.

How soon can a Lacey sale close?

With a clear title, a cash sale can finish in one to two weeks. A listing drags longer through tours, buyer financing and inspection scheduling, and Lacey's building department wants each inspection request in writing a day ahead.

Whose taxes appear on a Lacey bill?

Three: the township, Ocean County and the Lacey Township Board of Education, since New Jersey law makes the municipality the billing and collection agent for all of them. Installments come due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1.

Is a smoke alarm certificate required for a Lacey sale?

Yes, for a one- or two-family home. The municipality issues the state fire code certificate, which stays good for six months, so schedule the inspection early.

Where does a Lacey deed get recorded?

At the Ocean County Clerk's office. The main location is 118 Washington Street in Toms River, and a Manahawkin branch at 179 South Main Street sits closer to Lacey.

What does a house sale in Lakewood, NJ involve?

Lakewood is a flat, fast-growing township in Ocean County, and a house here moves through township code enforcement, an Ocean County recording office and a state fee schedule before the deed changes hands. Whether an agent lists it, you sell it yourself or a buyer pays cash for it as-is, each route ends at the same three desks.

Lakewood has more residents than any other township in Ocean County, spread across 24.68 square miles of land. The 2025 Census estimate is 143,765 residents, up from 135,158 in the 2020 count. Households here average 4.36 people, so floor plan and bedroom count weigh heavily when a buyer looks at a house.

Where did Lakewood come from, and what is the terrain?

Lakewood began as a sawmill and bog-iron area in the 1700s. It was called Bricksburg in 1865, renamed Lakewood in 1880 as a winter resort, and chartered as a township by the state legislature on March 23, 1892, with land from Brick. Cranberry bogs and pine woods made way for large developments in the 1960s, and Leisure Village went on sale in 1963.

Lakewood lies on the flat coastal plain, with about three quarters of the land between 20 and 80 feet above sea level. The Metedeconk River's North Branch marks the northern line and part of the eastern line, and four man-made lakes (Carasaljo, Manetta, Shenandoah and Waddill) anchor several neighborhoods. Greenville, Seven Stars, South Lakewood and Lake Carasaljo are place names you will see on listings. The township touches Brick, Jackson, Toms River and Howell.

The Census counts the Lakewood area as a CDP of 69,398 people in 2020, with the age-restricted Leisure Village and Leisure Village East communities counted separately at 4,966 and 4,189. If your house is in one of those communities, request its own resale rules in writing before you sign a contract.

How big are Lakewood households and home values?

The Census counts 4.36 people in the average Lakewood household. Just over half of homes (51.5%) have their owner living in them, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $466,700.

What drives Lakewood's local economy?

Education and health care lead. For 2022 the Census lists about $1.54 billion in health care and social assistance revenue and about $3.25 billion in retail sales. Beth Medrash Govoha, founded in 1943, is the largest yeshiva outside Israel, and Georgian Court University has sat on Lake Carasaljo since 1924.

Part of the township was a state Urban Enterprise Zone from 1994, and that status expired in October 2025. The zone helped fund ShoreTown Ballpark, the 6,588-seat home of the Jersey Shore BlueClaws. If a buyer asks about sales-tax treatment of nearby stores, point them to the township instead of guessing.

What schools and commuting routes affect resale value?

The Lakewood School District runs eight schools with 5,433 students in the 2021-22 school year, and the district also buses students to private schools, which reached about 25,000 students at yeshivas and other schools by 2016. Many families choose a home by walking distance to a yeshiva or school rather than by the public school zone, so ask your agent which side of a street a buyer would prefer.

Buyers usually ask about these links:

  • Garden State Parkway exit 89, which also feeds Route 70 after exit 88 closed permanently in November 2014.
  • Route 70, Route 88 and Route 9, plus county roads 526, 528, 547 and 549.
  • The Lakewood Bus Terminal, where NJ Transit routes 137 and 139 run toward New York's Port Authority, 317 toward Philadelphia, 67 toward Newark and 559 toward Atlantic City.
  • The in-town Lakewood Shuttle and Ocean Ride routes OC3 and OC4.

What does Lakewood's code enforcement office require before a sale?

Start with the Township of Lakewood's Code Enforcement office at 212 4th Street, phone 732-364-3760. Its rental and housing window runs 8:30 AM to 4 PM, and its page carries a legal notice to residential property owners about smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. Ask the staff what resale paperwork and inspection your closing date needs, and request the form list in writing.

One question in the township's FAQ asks whether a certificate of occupancy is required when selling a home, so get the current answer by phone. Ask about open permits too. The office warns that the penalty for unpermitted work can reach $2,000, with another $2,000 added for every week the violation continues.

  • Permit review under the state construction code can take up to 20 business days.
  • The engineering section of the township FAQ covers flood zone lookups and elevation certificates, property surveys and wetlands questions.
  • A rented house also needs a rental certificate of occupancy application on file ahead of a tenant change.

Who records a Lakewood deed, and what does the seller owe?

Lakewood deeds are recorded by the Ocean County Clerk, whose main office (118 Washington Street, Toms River) answers at (732) 929-2018. Posted hours are weekdays 8 to 4:30, with counter service ending at 4. The clerk's contact page also lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, phone (732) 370-8850.

Since Lakewood's median home value is $466,700, a typical sale falls under the state schedule for prices above $350,000. The seller owes that fee, and the rate climbs in steps as the price rises. Sales above $1 million add a graduated percentage fee of 1% to 3.5%, also charged to the seller.

For back taxes, request a payoff figure from the township's tax collector. The township advertised an online sale of 2025 and prior-year delinquent taxes and water or sewer charges with a sale date of October 28, 2026, so accounts that were not redeemed may carry a certificate now.

Which sale route suits a Lakewood house?

Choose by timeline and condition. A listing reaches the widest set of buyers, but it comes with showings, an appraisal and a township inspection step. Selling alone saves the commission and leaves the paperwork with you. A buyer paying cash for the house as-is removes repairs and loan approval from the picture; compare written terms, including who pays the transfer fee and who orders any township certificate.

Pull together the survey, permit records, current leases and the latest tax bill before anyone makes an offer. Clean paperwork keeps Lakewood deals moving, while a late permit or occupancy question tends to stall them.

Is a township inspection part of selling in Lakewood?

Ask the township. Code Enforcement at 732-364-3760 handles smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules and resale paperwork, and its FAQ lists a certificate of occupancy question for home sellers. Get the requirement for your address from them before fixing a closing date.

Is the transfer fee my cost as a Lakewood seller?

Yes. The state bases it on the price in the deed and collects it when the Ocean County Clerk records the deed. Sales above $1 million also trigger a graduated percentage fee, again on the seller.

Which office records a Lakewood deed?

The Ocean County Clerk. The main office is in Toms River at (732) 929-2018, and the clerk's contact page lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, (732) 370-8850.

What if my Lakewood house has open permits?

You can still sell, but deal with them first. Code Enforcement can tell you which permits are open, and unpermitted work can draw fines that grow weekly. A buyer or lender may require the permit closed before the sale.

Is cash faster than listing in Lakewood?

Often, because a cash sale skips mortgage approval and an appraisal. A listing may reach more buyers. Deed recording, the transfer fee and any township certificate apply either way, so compare the written terms.

Who is selling a house in Manchester Township, NJ?

Manchester Township sellers skew older: nearly half the population, 48.1 percent, is past 65, and the average household has only 1.92 people. That mix points to retirees moving closer to family, heirs settling an estate, and owners who no longer want to maintain a house.

Ocean County's Manchester Township had a Census estimate of 46,556 people in mid-2025. Owners occupy 86.7 percent of the housing, the middle home value is $219,100, and tenants pay $1,477 at the median (2020 to 2024 survey). Median household income was $56,885.

Those numbers make a quick, as-is sale a practical option for some Manchester Township owners, especially when a house needs work that a retiree or an estate does not want to fund.

What is Manchester Township's geography, and why does it matter to a seller?

Manchester Township is a wide, mostly wooded township of 81.42 square miles of land, so a sale here depends heavily on which neighborhood the house sits in. The township was created by the New Jersey Legislature on April 6, 1865, from part of Dover Township, which is now Toms River Township. Lakehurst Naval Air Station, where the Hindenburg burned in May 1937, lies within its borders, and the borough of Lakehurst is completely surrounded by the township.

The Census Bureau counts several unincorporated communities inside the township as their own places. Their 2020 populations, as listed on Wikipedia:

  • Pine Lake Park: 8,913, built around a man-made lake from the 1970s.
  • Crestwood Village: 8,426.
  • Leisure Village West: 3,692.
  • Pine Ridge at Crestwood: 2,537, plus Leisure Knoll at 2,562.
  • Cedar Glen Lakes at 1,517 and Cedar Glen West at 1,379.

Whiting is the largest section by area and population, with 33,180 of the township's 45,115 residents in 2020. When the house belongs to a planned community, ask the association for its resale package and any rules on who may buy before listing, since those can add weeks.

What does Manchester Township check before a house can change hands?

Manchester Township requires a Certificate of Re-occupancy for a resale, applied for through the Building Department's online citizen portal. The owner creates a login, chooses the non-rental application, notes whether the house is vacant or occupied (a lockbox or combination can be left for the inspector), submits, and pays the fee online by check or card. The township then emails or calls to schedule the inspection.

The township's printed inspection list covers a good deal of the house. Items it names include:

  • Water, electric and gas on, with heating and plumbing in working order.
  • Smoke detectors on every level and within 10 feet of sleeping areas, less than 10 years old, at least 3 feet from vents.
  • Carbon monoxide detectors within 10 feet of bedrooms but not inside them.
  • GFCI outlets that trip on the test button, and covers on every electrical box.
  • House numbers at least 4 inches high, visible from the street.
  • A warning label within 18 inches of the electric panel and meter if solar, a generator or battery storage supplies a second source of power.
  • Open permits closed out, and any unpermitted work cited as a violation.

Houses on well water need a water analysis certification from the Ocean County Health Department. Since April 15, 2025, the state fire code also calls for 18 inches between mulch and combustible parts of a building such as decks and porches.

Because the inspection runs through the township's portal, starting it early keeps the closing date from slipping. If the inspector cites a problem, the repair and a second visit have to happen before the certificate issues.

How much is the state transfer fee on a Manchester Township home?

New Jersey puts the realty transfer fee on the seller, collected at recording. Using the state's rate schedule, a sale at the Census median value of $219,100 comes to roughly $1,084, and the Division of Taxation's own example puts a $325,000 sale with no exemption at $1,910.

The same schedule gives partial relief to sellers who are qualifying senior citizens aged 62 or older, blind persons, or disabled persons. The Division's example is a $280,000 sale by a qualifying senior, which comes to $475. That matters in Manchester Township, where so many owners are over 65. A seller claiming the reduction files an Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, which must be notarized and recorded with the deed. Sales above $350,000 use a higher rate table, and a graduated percent fee applies only above $1,000,000.

How do roads, schools and transit shape a Manchester Township sale?

Buyers weigh the drive more than anything else in Manchester Township, since no limited-access highway crosses it. Route 70 runs through the heart of the township and Route 37 through the east, with County Routes 530, 539, 547 and 571 also in use. The nearest Garden State Parkway entrances are in Toms River, Berkeley and Lacey, and Interstate 195 is reached through Jackson Township. Ocean Ride local bus service runs the OC1 Whiting, OC1A Whiting Express and OC2 Manchester routes. Workers spend 33.3 minutes getting to their jobs on average, per the Census Bureau.

The Manchester Township School District serves pre-kindergarten through twelfth grade in six schools and had 2,916 students in 2024 to 2025. It operates Manchester Township Elementary, Ridgeway Elementary, Whiting Elementary, a middle school and a high school, and students from neighboring Lakehurst attend its high school. Only 11.1 percent of residents are under 18.

What choices does a Manchester Township owner have for selling?

An owner can hire an agent, go it alone, or take an offer from a cash buyer that takes it without repairs. Each route still needs the same township certificate and the same state forms, so the difference comes down to timing and cost.

  • Hiring an agent usually reaches the widest pool of buyers, at the cost of a commission, and the house often needs repairs to pass inspection and satisfy a buyer's lender.
  • Going without an agent saves the commission, though the owner handles pricing, showings, the contract and the paperwork alone.
  • Selling for cash without repairs removes the lender from the picture, which suits inherited, vacant or tenant-occupied houses. Settle in the contract who obtains the re-occupancy certificate and who pays for any repairs it requires.

Whichever route fits, ask from more than one buyer or agent and compare the net proceeds after the transfer fee, any mortgage payoff and unpaid township charges.

Does Manchester Township require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The township issues a Certificate of Re-occupancy for resales after an inspection, and the application goes through its online citizen portal. Open permits must be closed first, and wells need an Ocean County Health Department water analysis.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Manchester Township sale?

The seller does, at the recording counter. At the survey's middle home value of $219,100 the state schedule works out to about $1,084, and qualifying seniors aged 62 and older can claim a reduced rate by filing an Affidavit of Consideration.

Where is the deed recorded for a Manchester Township house?

The Ocean County Clerk records deeds, whose main office is at 118 Washington Street in Toms River. The seller's residency form (GIT/REP) goes in with the deed, and the clerk can reject paperwork that is incomplete.

Can I sell a Manchester Township house that needs major repairs?

Yes, though the re-occupancy inspection still applies. A cash buyer will often accept the condition, but the contract should say who fixes anything the inspector cites and who pays for it before the certificate is issued.

Do mulch and secondary power labels really matter at inspection?

They can. The township's checklist lists a label near the electric panel for solar, generators or battery storage, and the state fire code has required 18 inches between mulch and combustible building parts since April 15, 2025. Fixing both ahead of time avoids a failed visit.

What are the ways to sell a house in Stafford Township?

A Stafford owner can list through an agent, handle the sale without one, or take an as-is offer from a buyer who pays cash. Every path ends at the same municipal checkpoint, a resale Certificate of Occupancy for an existing structure from the township's Office of Inspection.

With 90.3% of homes owner-occupied, a $426,200 median home value and 22.0% of residents aged 65 or older, many Stafford sellers have owned for a long time. A listing gives the widest market and the most time pressure around inspections. A direct sale shortens the calendar and usually leaves repairs to the buyer. Decide which fits before you spend money on touch-ups that the township's visual inspection may not even require.

Where is Stafford Township and what communities does it contain?

Stafford sits on the Jersey Shore in southern Ocean County and stretches from Barnegat Bay west to the Burlington County line. It covers 54.71 square miles, of which 46.12 are land and 8.59 are water, or 15.71% of the total. The ZIP code is 08050 for Manahawkin, and the township borders Barnegat, Eagleswood, Little Egg Harbor, Long Beach Township, Ship Bottom, Surf City and Harvey Cedars.

Stafford is the mainland gateway to Long Beach Island. Route 72 is the only road onto the island and crosses Barnegat Bay on the Manahawkin Bay Bridge into Ship Bottom. The township has these main areas:

  • Manahawkin, the commercial hub around Route 9 and Route 72
  • Beach Haven West, a bayside residential community with 4,143 residents in 2010
  • Ocean Acres, a large residential area shared with Barnegat Township
  • Warren Grove, a rural pocket in the Pine Barrens
  • Bonnet Island, Cedar Bonnet and Mayetta, smaller named places

How did Stafford change from a rural township to a year-round community?

The township was chartered by the Crown on March 3, 1750, carved out of Shrewsbury Township when the area still belonged to Monmouth County. It became one of New Jersey's original townships on February 21, 1798, and joined the newly created Ocean County on February 15, 1850. Over the years it lost land to form what is now Barnegat Township, Eagleswood, Surf City and Long Beach Township.

Growth began in the 1950s with Beach Haven West and Ocean Acres, helped by the Garden State Parkway and a widened Route 72. The 1980s pushed many seasonal cottages into year-round use and brought Stafford Square, the first big shopping center. Population went from 3,684 in 1970 to 10,385 in 1980 and 28,617 in 2020. The practical result for a seller is a stock of 1950s to 1980s houses, some of them converted summer homes, where heating systems and electrical panels draw the township inspector's attention.

What do the Census figures show for Stafford?

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts. Retail sales per capita reached $44,384 in 2022, well above the figures for South Brunswick ($17,998) and Toms River ($34,368).

What does Stafford inspect before a resale closing?

Under Chapter 81 of the Stafford code, a house that changes occupancy needs an inspection by the Code Official, after which a continuing certificate of occupancy is issued. You submit the Application for Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy to the Office of Inspection and can reach the office at 609-597-1000, extension 8532. The township describes the review as visual only. It is not a structural investigation, so a buyer will still want a private home inspection.

Three supporting items come with the application:

  • A notarized Heat Certification from the seller or agent confirming a professional inspected the heating system and any solid-fuel burners, which clerical staff will notarize at the counter
  • A letter from the Stafford Municipal Utility Authority confirming water and sewer service, if the house is connected
  • For a private well, a water test by a licensed well driller or tester, approved by the Ocean County Health Department

The township's list of common violations is a useful pre-listing checklist. It includes missing outlet plates and uncovered junction boxes, open spaces in an electrical panel, unsecured fixtures, leaking pipes, relief valves not piped to within 6 inches of the floor, metal dryer vents, house numbers at least 3 inches high, chimney caps, handrails on stairs with more than 3 risers, and guardrails where a deck or stair is 30 inches or more above grade. Smoke detectors are required within 10 feet of sleeping areas and on every floor including the basement, and carbon monoxide detectors are required in one- and two-family homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage. See the township's rentals and resales page.

How do flood rules affect a Stafford house sale?

Stafford's house raising page refers to the Base Flood Elevation regulations and to the storm of October 27, 2012, and it describes two permit routes. In the first, the owner raises the home under a construction permit and does not reoccupy it until a Certificate of Occupancy is issued. In the second, the owner repairs the home to safe living conditions first, receives a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy, and raises it later.

Either route needs a zoning permit with a survey showing setbacks and structure height, engineered plans for the new foundation, and releases from every utility serving the building. Insurance Increased Cost of Compliance payments are tied to the permit and the final certificate. A seller with a raised house should keep the permit, engineering sign-off and final certificate in one folder for the buyer's lender. A seller near the bay should ask the Zoning office which flood zone and base flood elevation apply to the address.

Stafford Township School District covers pre-kindergarten through grade 6 in five schools: Oxycocus, Ronald L. Meinders Primary Learning Center, Ocean Acres Elementary, McKinley Avenue Elementary and Stafford Intermediate. Grades 7 to 12 attend Southern Regional Middle School and Southern Regional High School in Manahawkin. The Marine Academy of Technology and Environmental Science, part of the Ocean County Vocational Technical School, is also in Manahawkin, and St. Mary Academy is a K to 8 Catholic school near the Manahawkin area.

The Garden State Parkway enters from Eagleswood and meets Route 72 at Exit 63, U.S. 9 runs north to south through the center, and County Route 539 crosses the west. NJ Transit's 559 bus runs to Atlantic City, and Ocean Ride routes OC6 and OC10 serve Stafford and Long Beach Island. The Census puts average travel to work at 31.4 minutes.

The Division of Taxation lists the rates and exemptions on its realty transfer fee page. Shore properties often belong to owners who live elsewhere, so note that a seller who is not a New Jersey resident must prepay estimated Gross Income Tax at closing, never less than 2% of the sale price, unless a listed exception applies. Does Stafford require an inspection when a house is sold?

Yes. Chapter 81 of the Stafford code calls for an inspection by the Code Official on every change of occupancy, followed by a continuing certificate of occupancy. Apply with the Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy form.

What is the Heat Certification?

It is a notarized statement from the seller or the seller's agent that a professional inspected the heating system and any fireplace, wood stove or other solid-fuel burner. The township needs it before it can issue the certificate, and clerical staff can notarize it at the counter.

How is a private well handled in a Stafford sale?

The well water must be tested by a licensed well driller or tester and approved by the Ocean County Health Department. The township asks for that approval in place of the utility letter that houses on public water and sewer provide.

Is the Stafford inspection a full home inspection?

No. The township calls its review visual only and says a complete overview of the property comes from a registered home inspection agency. Buyers usually order their own inspection as well.

What does a Stafford seasonal rental license cost?

The township's seasonal rental page lists a $100 fee, plus $50 for a reinspection. The applicant also supplies proof of paid property taxes, proof of water and sewer payment, and a floor-by-floor drawing. Long-term rentals built before 1978 need lead-based paint inspections.

What are the options for selling a house in Toms River?

Toms River owners can list with an agent, sell privately, or take an as-is offer from a buyer who pays cash. Which one fits depends on the house, the calendar and how much repair work you are willing to finance before closing.

The township is large and varied, with mainland neighborhoods, bayfront streets and barrier-island blocks, so a house in Silverton does not sell the same way as one in West Dover or Ortley Beach. A listing exposes the property to the most buyers and sets the price by comparison with nearby sales. A direct sale is quicker and generally leaves repairs and the township paperwork to the buyer's side of the table.

Where is Toms River and how big is it?

Toms River is the seat of Ocean County, 70 miles south of New York City and 55 miles east of Philadelphia. The township covers 52.89 square miles, of which 40.55 are land and 12.34 are water, or 23.32%. Its 95,438 residents in 2020 made it the eighth most populous municipality in New Jersey. It borders Berkeley Township, Brick, Island Heights, Jackson, Lakewood, Lavallette, Manchester, Seaside Heights and South Toms River.

Most of the township is on the mainland, where the census-designated place of Toms River held 92,830 people in 2020. Two more areas, Dover Beaches North (1,277 residents) and Dover Beaches South (1,331), sit on the Barnegat Peninsula, the narrow barrier strip between Barnegat Bay and the Atlantic. Ortley Beach, in Dover Beaches South, shares the 08751 ZIP code with Seaside Heights. Mainland addresses use ZIP codes 08753, 08754, 08755, 08756, 08757 and 08739.

How did Dover Township become Toms River?

A royal charter created Dover Township on March 1, 1768, and the 1798 Township Act made it one of New Jersey's original townships. Ocean County was formed in 1850 and made the village of Toms River its county seat. Over time, land was carved off to create Jackson, Brick, Manchester, Berkeley, Island Heights, Lavallette and Seaside Heights.

Because the Postal Service used Toms River addresses for the whole mainland, residents and outsiders increasingly called all of Dover Township by that name. Voters approved a name change in the November 7, 2006 referendum, with more than 60% in favor, and the township officially became Toms River on November 14, 2006. Older deeds, title records and tax documents may still say Dover Township, so ask your title company to confirm that the legal description matches the property.

How did Superstorm Sandy and flooding affect Toms River homes?

The October 2012 storm caused the township's worst flooding on record in low-lying areas, including Silverton and the downtown area, as the surge pushed Barnegat Bay up and down the shore. The barrier-island neighborhoods suffered even more severe damage. A mainland or barrier house that was flooded, raised or rebuilt after that storm carries paperwork that buyers and their lenders will want to see.

  • Elevation certificate and flood insurance history, if the address is in a mapped flood zone
  • Construction permits and the final Certificate of Occupancy for any raising or rebuilding
  • Records of repairs to utilities and heating equipment

The climate is humid subtropical, with about 49.8 inches of rain a year and roughly 24 inches of snow. Roof age, gutters and basement or crawlspace moisture are the items a buyer's inspector checks first. Buyers sometimes ask about the former chemical plant site, which the EPA designated a Superfund site in 1983; the plant stopped operating in 1996, and the township water system has been subject to the most stringent testing in the state since then and is considered safe to drink. Keep a current water test on hand if you have a private well.

What do the Census numbers show for Toms River?

The Census Bureau estimates 100,899 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 5.7% from the April 2020 base. There are 38,047 households, 82.1% of them owner-occupied, and the median home is valued at $416,700. Median gross rent is $1,726 and median household income is $99,547, lower than the incomes in South Brunswick or Teaneck. About 21.0% of residents are 65 or older and 21.7% are under 18. Workers commute an average of 30.2 minutes. Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

Retail sales per capita were $34,368 in 2022, and the township is home to the Ocean County Mall, the only enclosed mall in the county.

What documents does a Toms River rental inspection need?

The packet lists the following, and the same paperwork is useful to hand a buyer who plans to keep the tenants.

  • A certificate of insurance, registered each year under state law
  • A heat certificate from a licensed professional for fuel-burning heat sources, except for seasonal barrier-island rentals
  • Proof of ownership if the property was bought within the last 6 months or the owner does not match the tax record
  • A lead-safe certificate for any one-, two- or multi-family rental built before 1978, except seasonal rentals under six months
  • An Ocean County Health Department water analysis certificate, if the house has a well

Smoke alarm rules depend on the age of the house. Homes built before 1984 need 10-year sealed battery alarms on each level, homes from 1984 to 1990 need interconnected hard-wired alarms with battery backup, and homes from 1991 on need them in every bedroom, outside the sleeping rooms and on every level including the basement. Carbon monoxide alarms go within 10 feet of sleeping areas where a home has fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage. The township's property maintenance office can be reached at 732-341-1000, extension 8440.

Does Toms River require an inspection when an owner-occupied house is sold?

Ask the township's construction and property maintenance offices whether a resale certificate or inspection applies to your address before you sign a contract. The township's building page walks through permits and final certificates of occupancy for new homes and raised homes, and any open permit should be closed out before listing. The clerk's forms page also lists an Application for No Knock and an Affirmative Statement to Receive Real Estate Solicitations, so ask the Municipal Clerk how those forms work if you have been contacted by buyers you did not invite.

Which schools, roads and bus lines serve Toms River?

Toms River Regional Schools is the largest suburban district in New Jersey, with 18 schools and 14,654 students in 2023-24. It also serves Beachwood, Pine Beach and South Toms River. Students attend Toms River High School East, North or South, and the district has three intermediate schools for grades 6 to 8. Ocean County College is on Hooper Avenue, and Donovan Catholic High School is the county's only Catholic high school. Community Medical Center has 587 beds and became a teaching hospital in 2021.

The Garden State Parkway and U.S. 9 pass through, along with Routes 35, 37, 70 and 166. Route 37 is the main road from Parkway Exit 82 to the shore, and Hooper Avenue (County Route 549) is among the most congested roads. NJ Transit buses 67, 137, 319 and 559 serve the downtown station off Exit 81, where a Park and Ride has express service toward New York City at rush hour. The nearest train station is at Bay Head.

New Jersey charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded, based on the price in the deed, with exemptions listed by the Division of Taxation on its realty transfer fee page. A price over $1,000,000 adds a graduated percent fee. A seller who has moved out of state prepays estimated Gross Income Tax at closing, never less than 2% of the sale price, under the GIT/REP rules. Ask your closing attorney to run the numbers early.

Is Toms River the same place as Dover Township?

Yes. Dover Township became Toms River Township by a voter-approved name change that took effect November 14, 2006. Old deeds and tax records may still use the Dover name.

How much does a Toms River rental inspection cost?

The township packet lists $150 for each unit, $50 for a failed re-inspection and $50 to amend a registration. The fees are non-refundable.

Are seasonal rentals allowed all year in Toms River?

No. Barrier-island seasonal and short-term rental certificates run from April 1 through November 30, and such rentals are not permitted outside that period.

Do I need a lead-safe certificate to sell?

The packet requires it for rentals built before 1978, with an exception for seasonal rentals under six months. Ask the township and your attorney whether anything applies to an owner-occupied sale.

What is the median home value in Toms River?

The Census Bureau lists $416,700 as the median value of owner-occupied housing units for 2020 to 2024. Your own house may sit well above or below that depending on its location, condition and flood exposure.

What should a Wayne homeowner know before selling quickly?

Selling a house in Wayne, New Jersey is shaped by one township rule that many sellers do not expect: a Continued Certificate of Occupancy, or CCO, that must be issued before most sales close. Add the state's closing fees and Passaic County's assessment calendar, and you have the three items that decide how fast a Wayne sale can move.

Whether you hire an agent, go it alone or sign with a cash buyer, the CCO applies, so start there.

Where is Wayne and what shapes its housing market?

Wayne spreads over 23.72 square miles of land in Passaic County, and water adds another 1.42 square miles. It touches eleven municipalities: Haledon, Little Falls, North Haledon, Pompton Lakes and Totowa in Passaic County, Franklin Lakes and Oakland in Bergen County, Fairfield and North Caldwell in Essex County, and Lincoln Park and Pequannock in Morris County. The legislature formed the township in 1847 out of Manchester Township, and its namesake is General Anthony Wayne. George Washington used the Dey Mansion as his headquarters in 1780.

Water defines many neighborhoods. Lake communities surround Packanack Lake, Pines Lake, Lions Head Lake and Tom's Lake, and half of Pompton Lake lies in Wayne. The Passaic River also crosses the township and often floods near Willowbrook Mall and the riverside neighborhoods, so ask your insurer and surveyor about flood-zone status before you list a house in those areas. Other named areas include Preakness, Mountain View, Pompton Falls, Two Bridges and Barbours Mills.

The township is a bedroom suburb of New York City, less than 20 miles from Midtown Manhattan. William Paterson University, founded in 1855, has more than 11,500 students in undergraduate and graduate programs. Willowbrook Mall holds about 200 retailers, and Valley Bank keeps its headquarters here.

How do highways and trains affect Wayne home values?

Interstate 80, U.S. Routes 46 and 202, Route 23 and county routes 502 and 504 cross the township, and the 229.48 miles of public road include 180.59 miles kept up by the municipality, 41.05 miles by Passaic County and 7.84 miles by the state. NJ Transit's Mountain View and Wayne Route 23 stations on the Montclair-Boonton Line run to Hoboken, with Midtown Direct connections to New York Penn Station. Buses reach the Port Authority Terminal on several routes.

Newark Liberty International Airport is 25.9 miles away and LaGuardia is 30 miles away. If your street is close to a station, say so in the listing.
